News.title: Woman found buried on Spanish holiday beach by horrified couple after being ‘beaten to death’ as murder cops investigate
News.content:
GRUESOME 'MURDER' Woman found buried on Spanish holiday beach by horrified couple after being ‘beaten to death’ as murder cops investigate







Next

A WOMAN feared to have been beaten to death was found partially buried in the sand on a popular Spanish holiday beach by a horrified couple.

The pair stumbled across the grim discovery while walking their dog along Sancti Petri beach, near Cadiz.

Believed to be around 50, the woman had suffered several blows to the head, with her body already in an advanced state of decomposition.

Her remains were discovered at around 11am on Sunday, with investigators estimating she had been lying undiscovered for between six and ten days.





Detectives suspect the woman was initially buried beneath the sand before her remains gradually became exposed over time.

The chilling discovery was made near the entrance to a designated dog beach in an area known as Lavaculos, close to the Sancti Petri breakwater.

Around 500 runners were taking part in a seven-mile race nearby when the body was found.

Police, paramedics and Civil Guard officers rushed to the scene before launching a homicide investigation.



Despite a post-mortem examination, the victim has yet to be identified, with forensic experts only confirming she was a woman following the autopsy.

One unconfirmed local report suggested detectives were investigating whether she had been killed by her current or former partner.

A Civil Guard spokesman in Cadiz said: “This is being investigated as a homicide.

“The woman has not yet been identified so further tests are now taking place following the autopsy.



“We believe the body had laid undiscovered for several days before it was found.”

The horror comes after a former Civil Guard officer was accused of dismembering his wife, boiling parts of her body and dumping her remains along a beach in Gran Canaria.

Investigators discovered plastic bags containing body parts belonging to the 59-year-old woman, including cooked skin from her head.

The gruesome remains were scattered along the seafront at Playa del Ingles, a bustling holiday resort popular with British tourists.

Some were found near the Dunamar Hotel, a shopping centre and a Lidl supermarket.



Prosecutors claim the woman’s husband, who was 70 at the time, killed her inside their apartment at the Aida complex during Spain’s Covid lockdown in 2020.

He is accused of using a saw, knife and hammer in the horrific killing before spending more than two days dismembering her body.

RECOMMENDED STORIES

Forensic experts confirmed some of the remains had been cooked but were unable to establish how the woman died because of the extensive damage to her body.

The former officer faces trial for homicide and desecration of a corpse, with prosecutors demanding a 17-year prison sentence and €250,000 in compensation for the couple’s two children.

News.title: Moment car is boxed in on residential street before six men armed with machetes drag driver out and bundle him into boot
News.content:
Next

THIS is the horrifying moment six machete-wielding thugs swarm a car before dragging its driver out and bundling him into a boot.

The shocking footage shows a red Mercedes being boxed in by two other cars on a residential street.



Six men armed with machetes then close in on the vehicle in a terrifying kidnapping and ransom swoop.

The thugs are seen battering their way into the vehicle.



The attackers can be heard repeatedly shouting “get out of the car”.

Two passengers narrowly escape with slash wounds.



But the driver is dragged out, beaten while on the floor and bundled into the boot of a black Volkswagen Passat.

The brutal attack took place in Alum Rock, Birmingham.



The video plays audio of a horrified witness reporting the chaos as it unfolds to cops.

The onlooker can be heard saying to a police responder, “quick, quick they are trying to steal some cars”.

As the drama unfolds the witness says “send someone asap” and “they’ve put someone in the boot, they kidnapped him, they kidnapped him”.

The vehicles then make their escape from the residential street.

The documentary tells how the area is central to the West Midlands drugs trade and explores how officers tracked down the offenders.



Ghazanfor Mohammed, Adil Ahmed, Eduard Garboan, Umar Khan, and Haashim Hussain were all eventually charged in connection with the terrifying kidnapping.

Mohammed, Ahmed, Hussain, and Khan all faced trial together.

Mohammed was sentenced to 12 years in prison, Ahmed was sentenced to 11 years, Hussain was sentenced to seven years, and Khan was sentenced to nine years.



The convictions they were sentenced for included kidnap, wounding with intent, possession of an offensive weapon, burglary, and conspiracy to supply class A drugs.

Garboan never attended the trial and was eventually arrested in the Netherlands.

He was then extradited back to the UK where he was caged for 12 years behind bars.

Baga was sentenced a year later as he changed his lawyer and didn’t go on trial with the others.

He was later caged for 11 years and two months.



The terrifying encounter featured in the latest episode of Channel 5‘s Major Crime Unit which first aired last night.

The series follows West Midlands Police’s Major Crime Unit as officers investigate some of the region’s most serious offences.

The crimes they tackle include firearms offences, drugs, murder, and attempted murder.

With the injured passengers revealing little, Major Crime Team 1, led by Detective Inspector Francis Nock, are tasked to piece together what happened using the evidence left behind.

RECOMMENDED STORIES

Based at Perry Barr, the Major Crime Unit brings together specialists from across the force – including homicide teams, forensics, the County Lines Taskforce and the Economic Crime Unit.



The unit tackles serious crime across the region, with its work recently helping Birmingham shed its title as the gun crime capital of England and Wales.

News.title: Secret escort agency, steamy affair & £54k debt… how ‘grieving’ husband’s web of lies over murdered cop wife unravelled
News.content:
Next

ALONE late at night, Nisha Patel-Nasri was startled by a noise she heard downstairs in her home in Wembley, North London.

She had already been rattled by an attempted burglary just a week earlier.



But 29-year-old Nisha, who owned a hair salon, was known to be a feisty character amongst her fellow special constables and they were not surprised to hear that she had chased off the three young males.

But had they returned?

As she came downstairs and entered the kitchen, she saw a man brandishing one of her own kitchen knives who began approaching her.



Nisha ran out of the door but he chased after her and stabbed her once in the thigh, severing the artery in her femur.

Neighbours who heard the commotion, just before midnight on 11 May 2006, rushed out and called the emergency services.

One of them rang Nisha’s husband, Fadi – who had just left the house to

play snooker with a friend – to tell him she had been stabbed.



He had yet to reach the snooker hall but turned back as an ambulance rushed her to hospital.

Tragically, they were unable to save her life.

For Detective Chief Inspector Nick Scola and his team, the slaying of a special constable, who works for the police in their spare time, took on special significance.

“Nisha was part of the police family and whilst you investigate every homicide with the same vigour, you do become aware that you’re investigating not just for family itself but also for police officers across the country who have seen one of their own harmed,” he says.

But with no evidence, witnesses to the attack or motive, police had little to go on.



Was it a burglary gone wrong or a targeted attack?

Determined to nail the killer, the police unraveled a complex picture of greed, lust and the criminal underworld, as detailed in the TV documentary, Murder Scene: The Incident Room.

“After we learned that there had previously been an attempted break-in at the house, our first line of enquiry was to try to establish whether there was a link to that and her murder,” says DC Paul Webb who was assigned to the case.



With no sign of forced entry, the investigation team believed a door key that had gone missing, was used by the intruder to gain entry.

Police began knocking on doors to see if anyone had any information about how and why the incident might have happened.

A witness said they had seen a thick set male fleeing the scene, who was possibly Afro-Caribbean.



On the sofa in the house was a substantial amount of cash that had come from Nisha’s hairdressing business – but this had not been touched, which suggested it was not a burglary.

But just as one line of enquiry closed, her husband Fadi, dropped a bombshell.

He handed police his mobile phone with a recording of someone

threatening both his and Nisha’s lives.

Fadi, 34, ran a limousine hire business and had sold one of his cars to the owner of a minicab company in Glasgow.

He told the police it was on the proviso that he could borrow the limo back for one more job but when he tried to, the lady who had

bought it, said that she wasn’t prepared to let him take it.



So he went to Glasgow and took it back, using his spare keys.

“The lady who owned the company was clearly very upset with him and threatened to harm and kill him and Nisha,” says Nick.

Her recorded rant included such threats as “If you value your life and your wife’s you’ll return my f* car now.”

She also warned: “I’m telling you, if you don’t return that car I’m going to come down to your house and your legs are going to be broken, and this is no idle threat,” and “I want my car back or you’re f* dead!”

But when officers went to Glasgow to speak to her, they returned, entirely satisfied that the threats didn’t form a part of their investigation.



“Fadi Nashir told us that on the day of the attack he had been to Nisha’s salon,” says Nick.

“After having a hair-cut, they went home where he cooked Nisha a meal before he left to go and play snooker with his friend at about twenty to midnight.

“As they pulled up outside the snooker club, he received a phone call from a neighbour telling him to come home quickly because his wife had been stabbed.”

With no CCTV cameras in the immediate vicinity of the murder scene, Paul Webb studied some footage from a camera above a shop nearby.

He was intrigued to see a car pull up there at night, the door open slightly, and then drive off after just a five to eight second stop.



It led to them examining the drain there where they found the

missing knife from Nisha’s kitchen.

“We weren’t able to identity the registration of the vehicle but it was a silver Audi A4 that had a small aerial on the back of the roof – what we call a bee sting aerial – which is very unusual for that model,” says Paul.

“Also, one of the two number plate lights wasn’t working. Our intention was to visit every single Audi owner in London, which were about 1,800.

“And if we couldn’t find it in London, we would then have to go to the rest of the country where there were about 3,500 silver A4 Audis.”



Meanwhile, Fadi and Nisha’s brother, Katen, appeared on a Crimewatch TV appeal and while Katen was visibly emotional and traumatised by what had happened to his sister, Fadi was quite measured, which raised concerns.

“Following the appeal, some of my staff came to me and said they weren’t happy with the way Fadi Nasri had come across and thought perhaps he was hiding something,” says Nick.

Their focus was now on Fadi, but his alibi seemed watertight.

“We did find it unusual that he would go out and play snooker at twenty to midnight and leave his wife at home,” he added.



“But everyone lives their life differently. And Nasri’s phone records indicated he was away from the family address the moment

Nisha was attacked.

“Fadi had given us his phone so that we could listen to the minicab owner’s threats but as part of the examination to download the recordings, we also saw some photos.

“One of them was of a lady’s leg.

“When questioned about this, Nasri said he couldn’t recall who it was but later he admitted it was someone he was having an affair with.



“When we looked into Nasri’s background, we found he had a previous conviction for dangerous driving for which he received nine months in prison.

“He’d also run an escort agency and that was where he met the Lithuanian girl in the picture.

“He gave full disclosure of his affair but obviously he realised it was going to cause problems in his relationship with Nisha’s family, which pretty much ended, there and then.”

“I was devastated,” says Nisha’s older brother, Pilesh. “I couldn’t believe that my sister could be with somebody that was involved in that kind of trade.



“I could only take on board that her love was so much for Fadi that she basically put up with it.”

A look into Nasri’s finances showed that his business was failing.

He had a £54,000 debt in loans and had taken out an insurance policy on Nisha a few months before her murder for £350,000.

While looking at texts on Nisha’s phone, the investigation team found another number for Fadi.

It belonged to a phone that he had not told police about.



This was seized and what was found, proved to be vital in solving the case.

In the lead-up to the murder, his phone records showed there was an increase in communication with another number.

This phone belonged to a man called Roger Leslie, who was known to police.



“Roger Leslie was a large guy, an intimidating looking gangster with studs on his face,” says Nick.

“He had contacted Nasri shortly before Nisha was attacked and

immediately after.”

Leslie was brought in for questioning but denied all knowledge of being involved in the killing of Nisha.

However, an examination of his phone in the days before and after the attack showed he was in contact with Fadi Nasri.

He had also been in contact with someone called Tony Emmanuel – another name known to police.



He was a nightclub bouncer who had a foot in the underworld.

And, it transpired, drove a silver Audi A4.

“We went round during the night to have a look at the car parked at Emmanuel’s address and saw the small aerial on the back of it,” says Nick.

“What’s more, the number plate light was faulty, like the one on the CCTV footage.”

On 6 December 2006 Tony Emmanuel was taken in for questioning.



He too, initially denied any involvement in the murder.

But he eventually admitted that he had been the driver of the silver Audi A4 and was told to drive a man called Jason Jones to the location but he didn’t fully understand why.

He said that Jason was out of the car for a few moments and then came running back and told him to drive off.

Jones, who was another well-built nightclub bouncer, matched the description of the eye-witness.

Not only was Tony Emmanuel’s story plausible, crucially, it was backed up by the phone data.



Emmanuel’s phone showed there had been direct contact between him

and Jason Jones.

The confession proved crucial and the pieces started slotting together.

The three men could all be linked back via phone data, to one man at the heart of the conspiracy – Fadi Nasri.

“We formally interviewed Fadi Nasri again and explained to him that we were making arrests that morning which had come directly as a result of analysing his telephone, so there must be some link between them and we asked him to explain what that link was,” says Nick.

But Nasri had now given up the role of grieving husband and was refusing to answer any questions.



Jason Jones also refused to talk.

Despite the silence from the suspects, police developed a theory of how the conspiracy unfolded.

“I believe that Nasri gave the missing keys to Leslie to give to Jones so that he could let himself into the house,” says Nick.

“Nisha heard a noise downstairs. As she came down, she saw Jones in the kitchen.

“He approached her with the knife, she fled out the front the door and ran down the road shouting ‘He’s following me!’



“He went after her and stabbed her once and made good his escape.

“In the event of Nisha’s death, Fadi Nasri would benefit from her insurance policy.

“There were two potential motives. Firstly, his love affair with his mistress.

“And secondly, the amount he would financially gain from his wife’s death.”

All four men were charged with the murder but Tony Emmanuel was acquitted of any wrong doing.



Jason Jones, Roger Leslie and Fadi Nasri were all found guilty and sentenced to life.

“Having to sit through the trial and hear these details about Nisha was an emotional roller-coaster,” says Pilesh.

“I don’t think the family will ever have closure in terms of what happened to Nisha.

“That’s always going to be there in our minds.”

Watch Murder Scene: The Incident Room, airing Wednesday 21st October, 8pm on 5

News.title: Woman, 47, found dead in car after ‘driving with severe injuries before smashing into wall’ – as man held for ‘murder’
News.content:
Add us as a preferred source

CRASH RIDDLE Woman, 47, found dead in car after ‘driving with severe injuries before smashing into wall’ – as man held for ‘murder’







Next

A WOMAN who died after a car crashed into a wall suffered injuries “unrelated to the collision”, as cops arrest a man on suspicion of murder.

The 47-year-old was found in the car after it smashed into a wall in Bridgend, South Wales, on Monday around lunchtime.



Paramedics rushed to the scene but the woman, from North Cornelly, later died in hospital.

Cops said the victim had suffered injuries “unrelated to the collision” as they launched their murder probe.



A 61-year-old man from Bridgend has been arrested following a major police operation.

He remains in custody as detectives investigate the woman’s death.



Officers say the woman’s family have been informed, though a formal identification has yet to take place.

Chief Superintendent Jason Rees said: “A man is now in custody following a significant policing operation in Ger-y-nant overnight.



“This is a deeply distressing incident, and our thoughts are with the victim’s family, and everyone affected.

“We thank the local community for their support, which has resulted in an arrest with no further injuries sustained.

“We thank those displaced from their homes overnight for their co-operation at a worrying time as we support them in returning home

“We thank the local community for their co-operation as our investigation continues.”

A South Wales Police spokesperson said: “Officers were called to Coity Road, Bridgend at around 12:43pm yesterday following a report of a road traffic collision, wherein a car had collided with a wall.



“Upon attendance, officers identified that the driver had sustained injuries unrelated to the collision.

“Despite medical attention, the driver, a 47-year-old woman from North Cornelly, has died at hospital.

“Her family has been informed, though formal identification has yet to take place.

“Following a significant policing operation in the area of nearby Ger-y-Nant, a 61-year-old man from Bridgend has been arrested on suspicion of murder.

“He is currently in police custody.”



Police are calling for anyone with information or footage on the incident to contact the force.

News.title: Woman, 65, mauled to death by shark ‘while swimming with group’ as popular beach closed in South Africa
News.content:
BEACH BLOODSHED Woman, 65, mauled to death by shark ‘while swimming with group’ as popular beach closed in South Africa







Next

A WOMAN was mauled to death by a shark while swimming off a popular beach on South Africa’s southeastern coast.

The attack happened at Orient Beach in KuGompo City, where the public has been urged to stay out of the water.

The woman was swimming with a ⁠group at around 8am local time when she indicated she was in trouble, a witness ⁠told the public broadcaster SABC.



“We all realised she’d ​been ⁠bitten by a ‌shark, and she was in a very bad way,” the witness said.



“The bites ‌were very severe, but there ‌were only two, one on her thigh and one on her upper arm.”

He said ⁠the victim was brought back to shore, where she was declared dead on the beach.

Police confirmed they were called to the scene, where they found the body of the 65-year-old with “open wounds”.



She is understood to have been a regular swimmer and was in the water with a group when the shark ravaged her, local media reported.

A local community group said other swimmers had spotted a shark’s tail and fin.

“The victim sustained severe injuries to the right side of her arm and leg,” the group said in a Facebook post.

Local authorities have since closed off nearby beaches until further notice to prevent more bloodshed.



Fatal shark attacks are uncommon across the world but South Africa has a history of deadly encounters along its long coastline.

There were 65 unprovoked shark bites worldwide in 2025, up from 47 the previous year, including nine fatalities of which one was in South Africa, according to the University of Florida’s International Shark Attack File.

The attack in South Africa comes a month after a great white shark killed a swimmer at Sorrento, in Perth’s north.

This resulted in a rare catch-and-kill order.

Fisheries Minister Jackie Jarvis announced the extraordinary measures, but stopped short of ordering a widespread cull.



“Given the shark had been positively identified, remained in the vicinity following a fatal attack, and was considered to pose an ongoing threat, I authorised Fisheries officers to destroy the shark if it could be captured,” she said.

Researchers say shark encounters can be influenced by a range of factors, including growing coastal populations, increased use of marine waters, environmental changes and shifts in the distribution of sharks and their prey.

News.title: Teacher, 28, ‘groomed girl, 15, and lured teen out of view of CCTV cameras’ even after mum tried to intervene
News.content:
TWISTED MISS Teacher, 28, ‘groomed girl, 15, and lured teen out of view of CCTV cameras’ even after mum tried to intervene







Next

A TEACHER has been accused of grooming a teenage girl even after the student’s mum tried to intervene and stop the alleged abuse.

Softball coach Katie Elizabeth McDevitt, 28, allegedly lured the 15-year-old out of view of security cameras so they could be alone, according to a warrant.



She allegedly groomed the girl while training her on the Georgia Strike softball team.

The teacher has also been accused of sending the youngster romantic messages which made her uncomfortable, according to an affidavit.



McDevitt, who also taught at a Christian academy, repeatedly carried out inappropriate behaviour towards the teen between February 1 and September 22, investigators allege.

The educator would allegedly come up with situations where she and the girl would be alone before and after practice sessions.



These would allegedly take place in a hitting facility but outside the view of CCTV, court documents say.

The alleged inappropriate messages are said to have continued despite warnings from the student’s parent, according to the affidavit.



It says: “The accused had private communication channels with the victim even after intervention from the mother of the victim.”

The student also accused the teacher of being behind other discomforting physical interactions which have not been detailed in the police report.

McDevitt was arrested and booked into jail last Thursday by the Walton County Sheriff’s Office.

She faces felony charges of grooming a minor.

The teacher posted her £5,000 bond the next day, according to 11 Alive.



McDevitt was put on administrative leave from her role at Loganville Christian Academy straight after officials were notified a probe was being launched into her.

The school said the alleged victim was not one of their students.

Georgia Strike Softball said McDevitt was let go from her coaching position shortly after they were made aware of the allegations.

They said: “Georgia Strike is committed to the safety and well-being of our players, and our focus is on them and their families at this time.”

News.title: Met Office storm names: Full list of storms for the 2026/27 UK season with Austen set to hit this week
News.content:
Next

STORM Austen is heading for Britain after forecasters officially named the first major weather system of the season.

The Met Office confirmed the name on Tuesday, October 20, with gusts exceeding 70mph possible on Friday.



When will Storm Austen hit the UK?

Storm Austen is forecast to cross the UK overnight on Thursday, October 22, and through Friday, October 23.

The Met Office‘s yellow wind warning covers 38 local authority areas and runs from midnight to midday on Friday.



Gusts of 50-60mph are possible across affected areas, potentially topping 70mph on exposed coasts.

Met Office deputy chief forecaster Tom Crabtree said: “While the exact track and position of Storm Austen is still being determined, what’s clear is that we have an impactful period of weather on the way and the potential for disruption in places, which has resulted in the system being named.

“Peak gusts in excess of 70mph are possible on the most exposed coastal areas, while 50-60mph are likely more widely within the warning area.

“Weather warnings are under constant review and could be updated as confidence increases, so it’s important to stay up-to-date with the forecast in the coming days.”

Travel disruption, power cuts and dangerous waves are possible, and residents are advised to secure garden furniture, bins and trampolines.

People visiting coastal areas should avoid exposed seafronts when winds are strong, and the Met Office advises checking its latest warnings before travelling, particularly on Friday morning.



Thankfully, winds are expected to ease as the system moves east later on Friday.

What are the Met Office storm names for 2026/27?

On September 1, the list was unveiled by the Met Office, Ireland’s Met Eireann and the Netherlands’ KNMI.

Each organisation contributed seven names, which are used in alphabetical order.

The full list is:

Austen (Ireland)

Boelo (Boo-loh, Netherlands)

Chloe (UK)

Dano (Dah-noh, Netherlands)

Evelyn (Ireland)

Finn (UK)

Gwendolyn (Gwen-duh-lin, Netherlands)

Heather (Ireland)

Ivy (UK)

Jade (Netherlands)

Kilian (Ireland)

Laoise (Lee-sha, Ireland)

Miriam (Ireland)

Nicola (UK)

Olaf (Netherlands)

Phelim (Fay-lim, Ireland)

Ruban (UK)

Shaun (UK)

Theo (UK)

Vesna (Vehs-nuh, Netherlands)

Wende (Vhen-duh, Netherlands)

The letters Q, U, X, Y and Z are excluded in line with international naming conventions.



Who are the 2026/27 storms named after?

Austen honours Austen Nagle, the first director of the Irish Meteorological Service, appointed in 1936.

Shaun is named after Aardman’s much-loved Shaun the Sheep, chosen in a public vote.

Ivy was inspired by a nine-month-old Labrador puppy nicknamed “the absolute destructor”, while Finn was named after a two-year-old boy his family described as “wild and a force to be reckoned with”.

Chloe was nominated by the mother of a young weather enthusiast, and

Theo takes its name from a cat whose habit of hiding before thunderstorms led his owner to joke that he could predict the weather.

Boelo is a nearly extinct name from eastern Groningen in the Netherlands, while Evelyn honours Evelyn Murphy, who became the first female meteorologist to present the weather forecast on Irish TV in 1983.



More than 40,000 name suggestions were submitted to the Met Office last year.

Why does the Met Office name storms?

Giving severe weather a recognisable name helps people follow warnings and prepare for dangerous conditions.

The scheme began in 2015, with names usually assigned when forecasters expect medium or high impacts, typically associated with amber or red warnings.

Strong winds are the main consideration, but heavy rain and snow can also qualify.

RECOMMENDED STORIES

Other European weather agencies use separate lists, which is why Storm Adam in Spain is not among the UK’s names.



And not every name will necessarily be used – last season’s list only reached Storm Dave, the fourth name.

News.title: Terrifying moment passenger plane catches on fire as flames burst from wing just moments before take off
News.content:
Next

THIS is the moment a passenger jet packed with travellers burst into flames moments before takeoff, as a blowtorch-like blast of fire erupted from its engine.

Dramatic footage shows a fierce jet of red-hot flames shooting backwards from the left engine of a LATAM Airlines as thick black smoke billows into the sky.



Passengers were sitting just metres from the inferno as flames engulfed parts of the aircraft’s wing and landing gear.

Shocking footage filmed inside the cabin shows the blaze raging just outside the windows as the plane remains stranded on the tarmac.



The terrifying ordeal unfolded at Jorge Chavez International Airport in Callao, near Lima, Peru, on Monday, October 19.

Flight LA2302 was preparing to depart for Piura in northern Peru, near the Ecuadorian border, when the engine suddenly caught fire.



The ferocious blast continued for some time before abruptly stopping, leaving flames still burning around the engine, left wing and landing gear.

Airport firefighters raced to tackle the blaze as passengers remained trapped on board, according to local media reports.

Emergency crews eventually extinguished the flames before travellers were helped off the stricken aircraft.

Miraculously, nobody was injured.



It remains unclear exactly how passengers left the plane, with footage showing no emergency evacuation slides being deployed.

The near-disaster comes just days after another LATAM passenger jet plunged a staggering 23,000ft in minutes following a technical failure.

Terrified travellers watched oxygen masks tumble from the ceiling as pilots declared a general emergency while cruising at 33,000ft.



The Boeing 767 made a rapid descent near Peru’s Ica region before levelling off at 10,000ft and turning back towards Lima.

Passenger Alejandra Baigorria recalled fearing she was about to die when the pilot announced an emergency landing.

She admitted thinking: “These are the last minutes of my life.”

Baigorria said she was forced to breathe through an oxygen mask for nearly an hour before the aircraft landed safely at Jorge Chavez International Airport at 11.31am on Friday.

Specialist aviation reports suggest a loss of cabin pressure triggered the terrifying descent.



LATAM confirmed the crew followed emergency procedures and arranged another aircraft to take passengers to Sao Paulo, Brazil.

Meanwhile, the cause of Monday’s engine inferno remains a mystery, with the airline confirming an unexpected technical problem had forced passengers to disembark.

LATAM Airlines Peru said: “An unexpected technical event occurred before takeoff, and for this reason the precautionary disembarkation of all passengers was ordered, always prioritising their safety.”



All passengers were immediately transferred to another flight, which the airline confirmed had already landed in Piura, around 900km from Lima.

The company added: “The passengers were immediately rebooked onto a new flight, which has already landed in the city of Piura.

“The causes of this incident are being investigated in accordance with the relevant procedures. LATAM Airlines Peru reiterates that the safety of passengers and crew is its highest priority in all its operations.”

The airline has not revealed the exact technical fault responsible for the blaze.

Peru’s consumer protection authority, Indecopi, said it was monitoring the assistance provided to affected passengers.



RECOMMENDED STORIES

Officials were also checking whether travellers had received clear information about their replacement flights and consumer rights.

Airport authorities confirmed both runways remained operational throughout the emergency, with other arriving and departing flights unaffected.

News.title: Revolut and Lloyds down live: Google Cloud outage hits banks as cards 'declined'
News.content:
Major apps and websites, including banks Revolut and Lloyds, were hit by disruption today amid a Google Cloud outage in western Europe

A Google Cloud outage has disrupted a host of online services across the UK, leaving Revolut customers unable to make payments for hours.

Reports of issues with Revolut, Lloyds Bank, HSBC, Rightmove, Royal Mail, Bank of Scotland and Halifax surged on outage-tracking website Downdetector on Tuesday morning.

Revolut appeared to be down for thousands of customers, with many taking to social media to complain about their cards being declined and difficulties accessing their accounts through the app and website.

Google Cloud said the outage in the western Europe region was caused by a "power event", which was "mitigated" by lunchtime on Tuesday. The companies listed have yet to confirm that their service disruptions were linked to the outage.

News.title: Dementia patient's £9,000 wedding rings disappear and are 'replaced by plastic' in care home
News.content:
Dementia patient's £9,000 wedding rings disappear and are 'replaced by plastic' in care home

Two wedding rings belonging to dementia patient Jacqueline Stockbridge, 69, went missing at Holywell Park Care Home in Sevenoaks, Kent and were replaced with plastic, her daughter Jocelyn said

View 3 Images Jocelyn, 37, with her mum Jacqueline Stockbridge, 69, who has dementia (Image: Jocelyn Stockbridge / SWNS)

Police have launched an investigation after a dementia patient's £9,000 wedding rings went missing - and were replaced with plastic copies.

‌



‌



Jacqueline Stockbridge, 69, was staying in Holywell Park Care Home in Sevenoaks, Kent, after she suffered a stroke last month. Since entering care 15 years ago, Jacqueline has worn her £7,500 opal and gold engagement ring, encrusted with 14 diamonds, and her £1,500 baguette wedding band, which has rectangular diamonds.

‌



However, when her daughter Jocelyn, 37, came to visit her on September 21, she discovered a plastic ring on her finger in place of the tailor-made jewellery.

‌



View 3 Images Jacqueline's original opal and gold engagement ring (Image: Jocelyn Stockbridge / SWNS)

Jocelyn mentioned the missing rings to care home staff - but claims they were "dismissive", and did not do much to help.

She said: “I thought ‘it’s been stolen’, she wouldn’t take it off, she’s never taken it off. My first thought was to panic, but I was actually there to see my mum and see her social worker to discuss her health, so I was due in a meeting.

‌



“I was distressed and panicked, wanting to prioritise my mum’s wellbeing but also wanting to figure out what happened to her rings.” Her mum didn’t realise her rings were gone until Jocelyn told her.

View 3 Images Daughter Jocelyn discovered the ring had been replaced with a poor plastic copy (Image: Jocelyn Stockbridge / SWNS)

‌



She said: “When I said to my mum she said ‘oh my God, it’s not there’. When I pointed it out to her, she was really upset, but 10 minutes later she’ll have forgotten. Then you point it out to her again, and she’s upset again.

“In the moment, she’ll have known what was happening if someone took it off her, but then she will have forgotten, especially if they’ve replaced it with something, she’s going to be thinking about it less.”

‌



Police have since taken the fake ring in for forensic testing.

A Kent Police spokesperson said: “Kent Police is investigating the alleged theft of two rings from the resident of a care home in Hodsoll Street, New Ash Green, between Tuesday 1 September and Tuesday 29 September. Officers have spoken to a relative of the victim and enquiries are ongoing to establish the circumstances surrounding the incident.

Article continues below

“Anyone with information that may assist is urged to call the west Kent appeals line on 01622 604100, quoting reference 46/158636/26.”

The Mirror has approached Holywell Park Care Home for comment.

News.title: Energy debt hits £2,725 for 'squeezed middle' households ahead of Budget
News.content:
Energy debt hits £2,725 for 'squeezed middle' households ahead of Budget

Chancellor John Healey is thought to be considering targeted energy support in his Budget next week, with reports suggesting the Warm Home Discount could be increased

View 2 Images Middle income households reportedly may end up being excluded from help at the Budget (Image: Getty/Natasha Lebedinskaya)

"Squeezed middle" households with average incomes owe an average of £2,725 in energy debt, experts have warned.

‌



‌



Free money advice service Money Wellness looked at households with incomes of between £2,300 to £3,300 a month, around the UK median.

‌



Of those that are behind on their energy bills, the average debt has risen every year. The typical amount of money owed has increased from £2,420 in 2023 to £2,725 so far in 2026. This marks a rise of £305 compared to three years ago.

‌



To see more of the stories you love from The Mirror and to find them easily in Google then make us your preferred source. Free and easy-to-do, just click on the link here to find more from The Mirror at the top of your feed.

View 2 Images Energy bills are forecast to rise again in January (Image: Getty Images)

Families to save money on energy bills under new 'vampire' appliances rule READ MORE :

One in five customers in this income band who receive no benefits at all (21%) are behind on their energy bills. Chancellor John Healey is thought to be considering targeted energy support in his Budget next week, with reports suggesting the Warm Home Discount could be increased by £100.

‌



The Warm Home Discount is currently worth £150 and is awarded to households on certain means-tested benefits. Money Wellness says expanding this scheme only means households that do not claim benefits could be left without help just as bills are forecast to rise again in January.

The Ofgem price cap for the typical household that pays by direct debit is currently set at £1,723 a year - but energy analysts at Cornwall Insight predict this could rise to £1,999 in January.

‌



The government introduced a VAT cut on electricity bills this month - but the Ofgem price cap still went up anyway due to higher wholesale costs from the war in the Middle East, wiping out any saving for households.

The Treasury does not comment on any Budget speculation ahead of the speech.

‌



Sebrina McCullough, external relations director at Money Wellness, said: "These households are the squeezed middle. They're considered too well off for help, but too stretched to pay, and they're carrying an energy debt that's now worth more than a month's income.

"Many of them are working parents doing everything they can to keep up, and they're watching their debt grow every winter. If Budget support is linked only to benefits, these households will face January's price rise on their own.

Article continues below

"We'd urge the Chancellor to make sure any support reaches people based on need, including households who are already behind on their energy bills, rather than drawing a line at benefit receipt."

News.title: New MOT rule as drivers warned about mistake that could cause failure
News.content:
New MOT rule as drivers warned about mistake that could cause failure

UK motorists are being warned about a headlight mistake that could cause a failure

View 2 Images Drivers warned about headlight mistake that could cause a failure (Image: Getty)

Drivers upgrading their car's headlights ahead of winter are being warned about an important MOT rule change. As part of the change, which came into force on October 14, 2026, certain bulbs are now permitted under specific conditions.

‌



‌



Previously, converting halogen headlamp units to use LED bulbs was generally grounds for an MOT failure. However, updated Driver and Vehicle Standards Agency (DVSA) guidance now allows approved LED replacement bulbs in compatible halogen headlamp units for vehicle classes 3, 4, 5 and 7.

‌



The change could benefit motorists looking to replace older halogen bulbs. However, fitting an unapproved or incompatible product can still result in an MOT failure.

‌



Lee Caroline, motoring specialist at car scrap company LJC Autospares , has explained what drivers need to know before changing their headlights. He also details why choosing the wrong replacement bulb could cause an MOT failure.

View 2 Images Guidance now allows approved LED replacement bulbs in compatible halogen headlamp units for vehicle classes 3, 4, 5 and 7 (stock image) (Image: Getty)

Why choosing the wrong replacement bulb could cause an MOT failure

"The new rules don't mean drivers can fit any LED bulb into an existing halogen headlight," Lee said. "The replacement needs to have the correct approval and be suitable for the specific headlamp. Buying a bulb just because it fits the socket could leave you with a setup that doesn't meet MOT requirements.

‌



"Drivers should check compatibility carefully before purchasing replacement bulbs, particularly when buying parts online." Under the updated guidance, approved LED replacement bulbs must be supported by a manufacturer-issued approval sticker permanently attached to the vehicle.

MOT testers are instructed to fail the headlamp if the sticker is missing, illegible, appears to have been tampered with or clearly doesn't match the bulb fitted.

‌



The small detail motorists shouldn't overlook

"The approval sticker is particularly important because it's one of the things an MOT tester will look for," Lee added. "Even if the headlights appear to be working properly, a missing or incorrect sticker can result in a major defect being recorded.

‌



"Keep the manufacturer's fitting instructions and make sure the required approval sticker is properly attached where it can be seen during the test." The new guidance does not apply to all types of headlight conversion. Existing halogen units converted to HID bulbs remain outside the exemption, whereas complete replacement LED headlamp units are subject to different requirements.

Why headlights deserve attention before winter

As the evenings grow darker, drivers are also encouraged to inspect their headlights for signs of damage or deterioration. Lee said: "Headlights that are cloudy, damaged or incorrectly aligned can make it harder to see the road clearly at night.

Article continues below

"If the lights seem noticeably dimmer or the beam isn't illuminating the road properly, have them checked before the problem gets worse."

News.title: Man shot dead at Enfield pub as police release CCTV of person 'possibly in disguise'
News.content:
Man shot dead at Enfield pub as police release CCTV of person 'possibly in disguise'

The fatal shooting took place at the Sun & Woolpack on Hertford Road, in the Freezy Water area of Enfield, and the male victim was pronounced dead at the scene

View 3 Images Police have released a CCTV image following a fatal shooting in north London (Image: Metropolitan Police)

A man has been shot dead at a pub in north London.

‌



‌



The fatal shooting took place last night at the Sun & Woolpack on Hertford Road, in the Freezy Water area of Enfield. Officers and paramedics were called to the scene at around 9.30pm, with the 35-year-old victim treated for gunshot wounds.

‌



However, despite the efforts of emergency services, the man was pronounced dead at the scene. His family have been informed.

‌



No arrests have been made and a crime scene is still in place on Hertford Road between the junctions of Turkey Street and Ordnance Road while evidence is collected. Forensic officers have been spotted at the scene.

So far, CCTV enquiries have identified a person detectives would like to speak to in connection with the shooting. The Metropolitan Police said it is unclear whether the individual is a man or a woman "or if the person is wearing a disguise".

View 3 Images Police are looking to identify this person (Image: Metropolitan Police)

‌



Barber refuses to be called hero after rushing to help Australia MP Helen Haines who was mowed down by car READ MORE :

Woman found dead in Manchester home as police flood street and make 'murder' arrest READ MORE :

Anyone who recognises them is asked to contact the police.

Detective Chief Inspector Allam Bhangoo, who is leading the investigation, said: "Our thoughts are with the victim's family and friends at this unimaginably difficult time as they begin to come to terms with this senseless act. We are releasing CCTV images of a person we would like to identify and speak to in connection with the investigation as our enquiries progress swiftly.

‌



"We are also particularly keen to hear from anyone who was in the area at the time, or who may have CCTV, doorbell, dashcam or mobile phone footage that could assist our enquiries. Even information that may seem insignificant could prove crucial. No piece of information is too small, and I would urge anyone who believes they can help to contact police."

View 3 Images Emergency services at the scene last night (Image: Katie Pickin/MyLonodn)

Article continues below

Chief Superintendent Anna Mccartney, who leads policing in the area, said: "We recognise the concern local people will have and can reassure them that our officers are working urgently to identify and trace those responsible. Serious violence has no place in our community, and the Met remains fully committed to tackling gun crime.

"We are determined to establish exactly what happened and provide much needed answers for those affected by this tragic incident."

News.title: Princess Kate and Queen Camilla deliver masterclass in diplomatic dressing as Oman state visit kicks off
News.content:
Princess Kate and Queen Camilla deliver masterclass in diplomatic dressing as Oman state visit kicks off

The Prince and Princess of Wales have welcomed the Sultan of Oman to Windsor for a three-day state visit to the UK, with both Kate and Camilla dressing in the colours of the Oman flag

View 6 Images The Princess of Wales in Windsor today (Image: Andrew Matthews/Press Association)

Prince William and Princess Kate have joined the King and Queen to welcome the Sultan of Oman to Windsor for a three-day UK state visit. The Prince of Wales kicked off the official welcome this morning as he greeted the Oxford-educated and former businessman Sultan Haitham bin Tarik Al Said at the Omani ruler’s residence in London, as they travelled together to Windsor.

‌



‌



Charles, Camilla and the Princess of Wales were waiting for the Sultan on the special dais in the town centre of Windsor for an official greeting. The King was dressed in top hat and tails, while Camilla wore a red wool crepe dress and coat by Fiona Clare, hat by Philip Treacy and ruby and diamond flower brooch – with the colour seemingly a nod to the Omani flag, as was Kate’s dark green coat dress.

‌



Netflix hits back at Meghan Markle’s claims she served as publicity for The Gentlemen READ MORE :

View 6 Images Kate and Camilla wore the colours of the flag of Oman for the state visit welcome (Image: Getty Images)

‌



The King, Queen, William and Kate braced the drizzly autumn weather on the dais, as Charles took off his top hat to greet the Sultan, giving him a wide smile as he shook his hand following the Omani ruler’s arrival. Kate smiled and gave a deep curtsey as she also shook Sultan Haitham bin Tarik Al Said’s hand in the royal line-up.

The royals then joined the Sultan for a carriage procession through Windsor to the castle. Charles was seen to pat down his hair as he sat in the carriage alongside Oman leader as the Household Cavalry readied their horses for the start of the short journey.

The Queen followed in the second carriage – the Scottish State Coach – accompanied by Oman’s deputy prime minister for defence affairs Sayyid Shihab bin Tariq Al Said. The Prince and Princess of Wales were in the third carriage – the Australian State Coach – with the deputy prime minister for economic affairs Sayyid Theyazin bin Haitham Al Said and secretary general of the diwan of the royal court Sayyid Loay bin Ghalib Al Said.

‌



View 6 Images Kate greeted the Sultan with a curtsey on the dais (Image: James Veysey/Shutterstock)

Arriving at Windsor Castle, a ceremonial welcome and inspection of the Guard of Honour in the quadrangle took place. It is believed the Sultan then joined the royals for lunch inside the castle, before viewing exhibits from the Royal Collection.

‌



Later tonight, William and Kate will join the King and Queen once more as they don their most glamorous formal wear for a state banquet inside St George’s Hall, as is tradition with incoming state visits.

Tomorrow, the Sultan will be farewelled by the King and Queen before heading back to London, where he will hold talks with prime minister Andy Burnham in Downing Street, against the backdrop of the ongoing conflict in the Middle East.

‌



6 View 6 Images The Prince and Princess of Wales on the royal dais (Image: Getty Images) 6 View 6 Images Camilla wore a red wool crepe dress and coat by Fiona Clare (Image: Andrew Matthews/Press Association)

‌



The King met the Oxford-educated Omani Sultan last July for tea at Windsor Castle during the foreign head of state’s private visit to the UK. During their meeting, the two men reviewed the deep-rooted historical relations between their two nations.

Their discussions focused on how to enhance cooperation across various fields to serve mutual interests and future visions, while fulfilling the aspirations of both countries.

‌



The last state visit by a Sultan of Oman to the UK was in March 1982 when Queen Elizabeth Il hosted Oman’s previous leader Sultan Qaboos bin Said.

View 6 Images William escorts the Sultan out of his London residence (Image: Kin Cheung/Pool AP via AP)

‌



Content cannot be displayed without consent

Charles has made four official visits to Oman, the last in January 2020 when he travelled to Muscat to offer condolences after the death of Sultan Qaboos. The Prince and Princess of Wales have also visited the Middle Eastern country, as they made the trip in 2016 for a two-day visit.

Article continues below

The last State Visit took place in March this year, when the King and Queen welcomed the President and First Lady of Nigeria to the UK. Bola Ahmed Tinubu and his wife, Oluremi Tinubu, undertook a three-day visit to Britain, where they were met by the Prince and Princess of Wales for an official welcome.

News.title: Daughter travels 10,000 miles to confront carer who stole £100,000 in jewellery from paralysed elderly mum
News.content:
Daughter travels 10,000 miles to confront carer who stole £100,000 in jewellery from paralysed elderly mum

A daughter made a final promise to her mother and travelled from Australia to the UK to confront the man who stole 62 pieces of jewellery from the OAP while caring for her

View 6 Images Elaine Macgregor with her daughter Tracy Mellor (Image: Tracy Mellor / SWNS)

A daughter flew 10,000 miles to confront a carer who stole £100,000 worth of jewellery from her elderly mum, fulfilling a pledge she made at her deathbed.

‌



‌



Tracy Mellor, 62, travelled from Sydney, Australia, to the UK to face David White, 35, who "betrayed" her paralysed mother Elaine Macgregor. The live-in carer swiped the 82-year-old's engagement ring and heirlooms which had been handed down over generations - despite being treated like a son.

‌



The daughter faced White, from Peckham, London, at Bolton Crown Court where he was jailed for four years after admitting theft by employee.

‌



To see more of the stories you love from The Mirror and to find them easily in Google then make us your preferred source. Free and easy-to-do, just click on the link here to find more from The Mirror at the top of your feed.

View 6 Images White accompanied Elaine on a trip to Sydney, before his crimes were uncovered (Image: Tracy Mellor / SWNS)

Elaine, a former headteacher at Tyldesley Central School, lived in Leigh, Greater Manchester, and died in December 2025 before the case was resolved.

‌



The elderly woman suffered from corticobasal degeneration - a rare disease that damages brain cells and can severely affect movement and speech. The condition left her quadriplegic and dependent on carers, which allowed White to exploit her disability and family's trust to steal 62 pieces of jewellery.

View 6 Images The thefts were uncovered after Elaine asked where her solitaire engagement ring had gone (Image: Tracy Mellor / SWNS)

‌



Facing White in court, Tracy said: "I can stand here, look you in the face and tell you what your betrayal did to my mum. And Mum, I kept my promise."

Tracy, who moved to Sydney, Australia, in 2008, described her mum as fiercely independent, with a love of biking and dinner parties. She said: "Mum was a force to be reckoned with, she was someone who grasped life with both hands."

‌



View 6 Images White was jailed for four years (Image: Greater Manchester Police / SWNS)

White had arrived through a care agency as a live-in carer, initially restoring Elaine's social life with outings and holidays. He was later dismissed by the agency for what Tracy said was "not following rules", however the family employed him privately.

‌



She said: "It's a weird feeling when you have a live-in carer, it's like they're a part of your family. I live in Australia, so he was my eyes and ears. I'd speak to him every day."

White and Elaine drew up a bucket list of destinations, and the pair even visited Scotland and a Titanic exhibition. The carer once even invited her friends round, hung fairy lights and served snacks in black tie. Tracy said: "She was ecstatic because he made her feel like a real person again. He used his personality and character to get us to trust him."

‌



View 6 Images Tracy made a promise to her mum that she would confront the thief (Image: Tracy Mellor / SWNS)

The thefts started to unravel while White accompanied Elaine to Sydney, in March 2023. The mother repeatedly asked about her solitaire engagement ring, which she could no longer wear. He assured both women it was safely locked away in England.

‌



Tracy said: "He kept saying it's in the safe. My mum was physically very disabled but, mentally, she was all there. He tried to make it look like mum was losing her mind. She could only whisper, but she kept saying 'ring, ring'. She absolutely loved that ring."

In her victim impact statement, Tracy said: "Mum could not go home, open the safe and check for herself. She had no choice but to take his word for it." When they returned to England, Tracy asked another carer to check the safe, beginning the discovery of the thefts, which Tracy said left her mum "absolutely distraught".

‌



View 6 Images Elaine suffered from a rare disease called corticobasal degeneration (Image: Tracy Mellor / SWNS)

Elaine also told her daughter that White had started shouting at her and she was frightened of him. In May 2023, despite being able to speak only in a whisper, the elderly woman told at police officer what had happened.

‌



In her statement, later read to the court by Tracy, Elaine said: "I feel distraught that someone I trusted has stolen from me. I am especially upset about the stolen jewellery as this was gifted to me by my late husband.

"I trusted David White; he saw me at my most vulnerable as I relied on him in every aspect of my life. We treated David as family, he has betrayed me and ruined my ability to trust others."

‌



Tracy promised her dying mum she would confront White and did so in court, saying: "He looked at me while I read the statement. I was glad to do it."

The non-executive director and management consultant is writing a book called 'David White Cares' and hopes her experience will help other families.

Article continues below

She said: "It's very difficult to know if a carer is being honest. Sometimes, there's nothing you can do. The guilt and shame is terrible. In the end, we found a lovely carer who stayed until mum died, so there are some brilliant people out there."

News.title: BBC Three, BBC Scotland and Radio 4 Extra broadcast channels to close
News.content:
BBC Three, which is aimed at young audiences and launched hits such as Fleabag and Gavin & Stacey, previously moved online in 2016, but was reinstated as a TV channel in 2022.

BBC Scotland launched as a channel in 2019, broadcasting a variety of Scottish programming including news, sport, documentaries and entertainment.

However, some of the shows that air on the two networks, such as Two Doors Down on BBC Scotland and Sort Your Life Out on BBC Three, are repeats of episodes originally broadcast on other more mainstream BBC channels.

Both networks currently only broadcast TV programming in the evenings, although BBC Scotland simulcasts BBC Radio Scotland during the rest of the day.

The BBC said that the network's nightly programme Reporting Scotland: News at Seven will not move to BBC iPlayer and will cease when the linear channel closes.

Audiences will continue to be served by BBC Scotland's wider news offering, including Reporting Scotland, The Sunday Show, Radio Scotland Breakfast, Debate Night and Scotscast, the corporation said.

While Radio 4 Extra does air some original programming, its schedule is predominantly made up of archive content, much of which is available on BBC Sounds.

Affected staff were told about the changes on Tuesday, although the proposed closure of BBC Scotland and BBC Three had been reported by some media outlets in recent weeks.

The BBC is aiming to cut between 1,800 and 2,000 jobs - almost one in 10 - in an attempt to save Â£500m over two years as it faces "significant financial pressures".

On Tuesday, the corporation also confirmed more job closures in the news division, with more details from the department's newly appointed director Rachel Jupp expected to follow later.

Around 550 job closures have already been announced in news, while more than 30 job cuts have so far been announced for BBC Sport.

Meanwhile, several high-profile BBC TV series have been cancelled altogether in recent weeks.

RuPaul's Drag Race UK, Blankety Blank, Celebrity Mastermind, Live at the Apollo, Football Focus and Ski Sunday are among the programmes the BBC has dropped so far, while other formats such as DIY SOS have been temporarily rested.

News.title: UK to deploy jets to defend Saudi Arabia from Houthi attacks
News.content:
The UK will deploy RAF Typhoon jets to defend Saudi Arabia in response to escalating Houthi missile and drone attacks, the government has said.

The defensive mission will help defend Saudi cities and infrastructure - a move authorised by Prime Minister Andy Burnham - against aerial attacks by the Iran-backed group.

It follows Houthi attacks on the Saudi capital Riyadh, as well as on energy sites on the country's coast.

"These aircraft will operate in a defensive role and will not conduct offensive strikes against the Houthis," Defence Secretary Wes Streeting said in a written statement on Tuesday.

News.title: Chancellor rejects calls to raise Capital Gains Tax in Budget
News.content:
Chancellor John Healey has dismissed calls from some Labour MPs to increase Capital Gains Tax (CGT).

Cabinet ministers Wes Streeting and Louise Haigh both previously voiced support for raising CGT before Andy Burnham became prime minister in July.

Ahead of next week's Budget, as first reported by the Times, external, Healey is minded not to increase CGT - which is imposed on the profit people make when they sell an asset that has increased in value, such as shares in a company or properties which are not primary residences.

The move followed warnings that it could end up costing the government money if wealthy people leave the country or defer selling off assets.

If you pay income tax at the basic rate then CGT is charged at 18%. For higher and additional rate income tax payers, the CGT rate is 24%.

Last year, HMRC estimated, external that lifting the lower rate of CGT by 1% could raise Â£5m by 2028-9 but increasing the higher rate of CGT by 10% would reduce the Treasury's receipts by Â£3.6bn in 2028-9.

The amount raised could be reduced if people adapt their behaviour to the tax rise, for example by moving abroad or deciding not to sell a property.

The chancellor gave an indication of his approach last month in a speech when he spoke about the importance of businesses and self-employed people making profits.

"I want to see this country as a country of wealth creation. I want our government decisions and policies to raise the levels of confidence, and investment, and profit in British business," Healey said.

Burnham has faced warnings against lifting CGT. His former adviser and Goldman Sachs Chief Economist Lord Jim O'Neill suggested it would send "the wrong message to business".

But influential Labour figures had pushed for equalising CGT and income tax, with the former generally attracting a lower tax rate.

News.title: Storm Austen to bring severe gales to UK as weather warning issued
News.content:
The first named storm of the autumn - Storm Austen - is set to batter parts of the UK with severe gales and heavy rain beginning from Thursday night.

Ahead of the storm, the Met Office has issued a yellow severe weather warning for wind, which will come into force at midnight Friday.

Damage to buildings and transport disruption is likely, with the possibility for power cuts.

News.title: Woman describes alleged assault by Russell Brand as 'frenzied' and 'violent'
News.content:
Warning - this report contains graphic content

A woman who claims Russell Brand sexually assaulted her has described the alleged attack as "frenzied" and "violent".

Brand, 51, faces seven charges in the trial - three counts of rape, three charges of sexual assault and one of indecent assault.

The allegations, made by six female complainants, span a 10-year period between 1999 and 2009. He denies the charges.

On Tuesday, the jury heard from the fourth complainant in the trial, who alleges Brand sexually assaulted her at the Choice FM radio studios in central London in the mid-2000s.

She said she came out of a small room in the building to find Brand outside.

"He said 'aye aye'," she told the jury, "he grabbed me by my face, started to kiss me, and when he was kissing me he started pushing me - his body against me."

The woman continued: "He was kissing me, it was very frenzied. There was no time for me to even understand what was going on.

"He was running his hands over my body and I had my back against the wall at that point."

From behind a blue screen, the woman described the kiss as "sloppy" and "very, very rough", when asked by the prosecution barrister about the alleged attack.

"His hands at the same time were all over me," she said. "He touched my bum, my breasts, his body was pressed up against me."

The woman said she pushed him off and swore at him.

She said there were several people with him who she claims didn't say anything about what happened after the alleged assault.

The woman - now in her 50s - said she had never met Brand before and that she believed he'd been in the building because he was on Channel 4 show Big Brother's Big Mouth.

She told the jury: "His whole body was pressed against me - the kisses were hard and sloppy and going down my neck.

"His hands were moving so much - the reason I used the word frenzied was because it was violent. He just wasn't stopping."

She said she felt "dirty" after the encounter and "never told anybody", adding: "I felt shocked and stunned, shaken."

News.title: We asked teens what schools should teach them about work. This is what they said
News.content:
More than four in 10 UK teenagers want more work experience opportunities at school, with a similar proportion calling for more guidance on how to apply for jobs, a survey for the BBC suggests.

The online survey, by Survation,, external asked 2,000 young people aged 13 to 18 about the world of work and the help they need to secure employment once they leave full-time education.

Some called for more support with their communications skills and raised concerns about stress management and personal finances.

Skills Minister Jacqui Smith said it was the government's "mission" to ensure teenagers leave school "confident about their next step and equipped with the skills and experience they need to succeed".

When teenagers were asked in the survey what skills or guidance they would like more of at school, the most common responses were more work experience opportunities (44%) and help managing finances (43%).

Respondents said they also wanted guidance on how to apply for jobs (42%) as well as how to manage stress and mental health (39%) and develop their communication skills (38%).

The survey was conducted as part of the Teen Summit, hosted by Radio 5 Live and BBC Bitesize, where teenagers have been discussing different aspects of their lives.

Speaking to Nicky Campbell at the Newcastle event, some said how difficult they found the cost of living.

"I passed my driving test at the start of the year - I've got a car, but insurance prices, fuel prices, are all going up," audience member Haider said.

"I'm paying like Â£177 a month for a small one-litre [Toyota] Aygo, just because I'm young and we're classed as higher risk."

News.title: Paddy Power cuts 1,400 jobs and blames betting tax rises
News.content:
Paddy Power-owner Flutter has announced plans to cut up to 1,400 jobs as its boss claimed the company "cannot fully absorb" tax rises imposed on the gambling industry.

Staff based in the UK and Ireland, as well as British and Irish workers at Flutter's sites in Portugal and Romania will be affected, but what roles are at risk has not been disclosed.

The government announced increased taxes on online casino and sports betting, with an exemption for horse racing, in the Budget last November.

Flutter boss Kevin Harrington said the tax hikes had "fundamentally changed" the economic model of the UK betting and gaming industry, arguing it had helped "fuel the unlicensed, unregulated market".

"We continue to expect these tax increases to have a very significant impact on the overall market," Flutter said on Tuesday.

Flutter, which also owns Sky Bet and Betfair, employs 28,500 people across the world, including 9,000 in the UK and Ireland.

Harrington, who is chief executive of the betting giant's UK and Ireland business, said: "As we warned a year ago, we cannot fully absorb a rise of this magnitude without reducing our fixed cost base and therefore must restructure our business so that we can best position ourselves for the future."

The company delisted from the London Stock Exchange in August in a blow to the UK, with its shares now solely traded in New York.

In its most recent results, Flutter reported a $299m (Â£224m) pre-tax loss for the three months to June. compared to a $205m profit in the same period last year. Sales rose 3% to $4.3bn.

Revenue in the UK and Ireland rose by 4%, due to strong growth in online gambling games.

Some online gambling tax rises announced in last year's Budget took effect in April. This included remote gaming duty, which is paid on online casino betting, rising from 21% to 40%.

General betting duty, paid on other forms of sports betting, was kept at 15% in betting shops, but is set to rise from 15% to 25% online in April next year.

Betting firms had warned that cost increases would lead to job losses and betting shop closures, but MPs dismissed the warnings as "scaremongering".

Punters' winnings from gambling are not taxed in the UK, nor is VAT charged on bets.

Flutter said its restructuring plan would cost between $80m and $90m.

The company has claimed in previous financial results that the impact of UK tax rises would hit its underlying profit by $320m this year and $540m in 2027, before any savings or restructure to mitigate the impact.

News.title: Burnham vows end to 'rip-off parking charges' under new rules
News.content:
Drivers will be given the right to challenge "rip-off" private parking charges and more grace when using private providers under new rules set out by Andy Burnham.

The prime minister announced the changes after concerns were raised that penalties issued by private providers were too harsh and left motorists unfairly punished.

The new rules include a cancellation of charges for honest mistakes such as stopping to check directions and for non-payment due to broken ticket machines. Drivers will also get a 10-minute window to leave a car park without facing a penalty.

Motoring groups welcomed the changes, but said more needed to be done to stop charges when the driver had done nothing wrong.

Private car parks are different to council-owned car parks and streets, but more tickets at private sites are now being issued than ever recorded.

According to RAC analysis of government data, some 17 million private parking tickets were issued in 2025-26, a 17% increase from a year earlier.

With each charge worth up to Â£100, the data suggests drivers could collectively face private parking charges worth more than Â£4.6m each day.

In one case, a woman was taken to court in a Â£1,906 claim after taking longer than five minutes to pay at a car park in Derby. The charge was eventually dropped.

"Being a few minutes late back to your car or typing one digit of your number plate wrong shouldn't end with a hefty fine landing on your doormat," said Burnham.

He added that such charges left "people feeling ripped off and out of pocket".

The new rules will give drivers:

A guaranteed five-minute period to decide whether to park

A 10-minute window to leave without facing a penalty

Cancellation of charges for issues drivers can't control, such as vehicle breakdowns in car parks

Cancellation of charges for honest mistakes such as stopping to check directions, as well as for medical emergencies or broken ticket machines

Maximum charges of Â£20 on appeal for slip-ups such as forgetting a parking permit, entering the wrong vehicle registration, or forgetting to confirm the registration in the machine when parking

A freeze on the maximum parking charge at Â£100, which is the same limit as the current private parking Code of Practice

The new code will apply in England, Scotland and Wales.

Operators who do not comply risk losing access to DVLA data, making it more difficult to pursue the car's owner even if they do issue a charge.

News.title: Three children injured after school bus roof ripped off in crash
News.content:
Three children have been injured when a school bus crashed into a railway bridge, police have said.

Gwent Police said it received a report of a crash in Tregare Street, Newport, at about 07:45 BST on Tuesday.

The bus was travelling with pupils from St Julian's School, Heather Road, and Ysgol Gyfun Gwent Is Coed, a Welshâmedium secondary school on Duffryn Way.

Worried mum Jo Townsend's 13-year-old son, Gruff, was one of the pupils taken to hospital. She said: "I was worried, frantic. I went under the tape, I was getting to my son."

Newport Transport said it takes matters of safety "extremely seriously" and that it was establishing the full circumstances of the incident.

News.title: Armed police swoop as man, 61, arrested for murder and woman in car crash dies
News.content:
A 61-year-old man has been arrested on suspicion of murder after a woman who crashed her car died.

South Wales Police said the woman, 47, from North Cornelly, Bridgend, crashed into a wall on Coity Road at about 12:43 BST on Monday.

But the force said she had suffered injuries "unrelated" to the crash.

It followed armed police swooping on a nearby sheltered housing retirement complex, Ger-y-Nant, where the man was arrested.

There remains a heavy police presence in the area, including six officers, police cars and vans. A cordon is in place around Ger-y-Nant, which is accommodation for over-60s and consists of 13 flats.

News.title: Criminals detained in hospital set to lose benefits
News.content:
The government said the move followed engagement with victims' families and experts as part of its plan to "put fairness back of the heart of the welfare system".

McFadden said: "We said we'd act to tackle this gross unfairness and we're delivering on that promise.

"For too long these violent criminals have had their living costs paid by the taxpayer twice over, while their victims and families paid the price.

"That ends today, because victims and taxpayers deserve a system that is fair and supports only those who genuinely need it."

Secretary of State for Housing, Communities and Local Government Angela Rayner paid tribute to the families who had campaigned on the matter.

She added: "I'm aware the secretary of state has met with the families regarding this and was quite frankly astonished that the situation was as it was, and that these people were receiving benefits.

"That's why the secretary of state has taken this action and I welcome it."

She added the reallocation of funds was "something for the chancellor and secretary of state".

Shadow work and pensions secretary Helen Whately said: "Killers and rapists should not pocket benefits from a hospital bed.

"Labour has taken all year to stop a loophole it promised to close. And tens of millions saved barely makes a dent in the benefits bill Labour has let spiral out of control.

"The Conservatives would make universal credit a conditional, time-limited benefit, so taxpayers' money goes only to those who genuinely need it."

The proposed regulations apply to individuals subject to a Section 37 order under the Mental Health Act 1983, and a Section 57A order under the Criminal Procedure (Scotland) Act 1995.

The offences covered include manslaughter, attempted murder, wounding with intent to cause grievous bodily harm, rape, assault by penetration and rape of a child under 13.

Murder is not included, because a hospital order is not an available sentence for the offence.

The change in regulation is expected to affect about 2,500 offenders already in hospital and approximately 200 a year in future, the government said, with the full financial impact of the move due to be published as part of the 2026 Budget on 28 October.

News.title: Rantzen felt 'deprived of choice' over her own death
News.content:
A posthumous note written by Dame Esther Rantzen said she was "deprived of any choice over my own death".

The farewell message was released as the 86-year-old broadcaster and campaigner's family confirmed she had been laid to rest in an "incredibly beautiful" private funeral last week.

The Childline founder, who was diagnosed with stage four lung cancer in 2023, died at her Bramshaw home in the New Forest, Hampshire, on 30 September.

A larger memorial service is expected to take place at a later date.

Rantzen's daughter Rebecca Wilcox said the family had been inundated with messages since her death.

"It's been hugely comforting to know that people around the world felt the same way about her as we did," she said.

Dame Esther became a prominent campaigner for assisted dying in her later years, something MPs voted against legalising in September.

In her note, she wrote: "It would have transformed the way I died if the law had allowed me to ask for assistance to die when my life had become unbearable.

"I was extremely lucky because I had the talent, skill and support of my local Oakhaven Hospice.

"But I was still deprived of any choice over my own death by the current messy criminal law."

She said she had become "too physically frail to take the flight" to an assisted dying clinic in Switzerland.

News.title: Isle of Man Assisted Dying Bill given Royal Assent
News.content:
The Isle of Man's Assisted Dying Bill has been granted Royal Assent.

The law will allow adults who have lived on the island for at least five years, who have a terminal illness with a life expectancy of 12 months or less, to request an assisted death.

In a statement, campaign group Dignity in Dying said: "The milestone is a tribute to the Manx families who campaigned for years for a change in the law."

But opponents to the bill have said they are "deeply disappointed" at the news.

The island became the first place in the British Isles to pass laws on assisted dying in March 2025, but they needed amendments before Royal Assent could be given.

A similar bill in Jersey was given Royal Assent in July this year.

The chief executive of Dignity in Dying, Sarah Wootten, said: "Today is a historic and deeply emotional day for the Isle of Man, and above all for the families who made it happen."

News.title: Watch: Pigs on the loose bring A-road to a standstill
News.content:
Motorists filmed the moment 20 pigs brought cars to a halt on an A-road.

The animals caused mayhem on the A127 at Dunton, near Basildon, as they darted in between cars on Sunday afternoon, leading to the road's closure.

Firearms officers from Essex Police decided to fatally shoot five of the pigs due to the perceived danger to road users, while the rest were safely captured.

A spokesman for the force said the decision "was not taken lightly" and that it was unknown where the animals came from.
