News.title: The key moments that have shaped Trump and Zelensky’s rocky relationship
News.content:
Become an Independent member to bookmark this article Want to bookmark your favourite articles and stories to read or reference later? Start your Independent Membership today. Already a member? Log in

Relations between Donald Trump and Volodymyr Zelensky have reached a new low after the US president tore up sanctions on Russia and struck a highly controversial deal to purchase Russian diesel.

The latest fracture followed months of careful positioning by the Ukrainian president and his allies in Europe to avoid upsetting Trump and the US abandoning the country altogether.

But with Ukraine facing another brutal winter of Russian strikes, Washington’s commitment to sharing vital intelligence and interceptor missiles is again in question.

And where Zelensky would once have tried to court the American president with open displays of praise and gratitude, this time he has stood his ground.

As US special envoy Steve Witkoff meets the Ukrainian president in Oslo in a bid to repair ties, The Independent looks back on the key moments that have shaped the rocky relationship between the two leaders.

open image in gallery Donald Trump and Volodymyr Zelensky during the Oval Office showdown last February ( AFP/Getty )

2019: Phone call ‘favour’ threatens to bring Trump down

Shortly after Zelensky was elected in 2019, and during Trump’s first term in office, the US president called his Ukrainian counterpart to discuss a ceasefire proposal over the illegal Russian annexation of Crimea.

In the now-infamous phone call, Trump asked Zelensky to “do us a favour” and investigate then-former vice president Joe Biden, his son Hunter Biden, and the discredited theory that Kyiv colluded with the Democrats in the 2016 election to harm Trump.

That call later ultimately triggered the first impeachment case against Trump by the Democratic-controlled House in December 2019 on abuse of power and obstruction of justice charges. Zelensky later said Trump did not try to blackmail him, while Trump denied wrongdoing and described their interaction as a “perfect call”.

open image in gallery Trump and Zelensky meet for the first time, in New York on September 25, 2019 ( AFP/Getty )

The timing of the July call, shortly after the United States froze nearly $400 million in aid to Ukraine, prompted concern that Trump used taxpayer money approved by Congress as leverage for his personal political gain.

Trump was ultimately acquitted by the Senate in 2020.

2022: Trump acknowledges ‘brave’ Zelensky after praising ‘genius’ Putin

In February 2022 Russia launched a full-scale invasion of Ukraine. It was Moscow's biggest attack on a European state since World War Two.

Trump, having by then been ousted from the White House, condemned the invasion and said he was praying for Ukrainians, after earlier in the week getting flak from Republicans for saying Putin’s attacks were “genius” and “pretty savvy”.

“The Russian attack on Ukraine is appalling. We are praying for the proud people of Ukraine. God bless them all,” Trump said, adding that he thought Zelensky was “brave” for staying in the capital.

open image in gallery Trump and Putin, pictured in Alaska in 2025 ( Getty )

Trump also began insisting that the “horrific disaster would never have happened if our election was not rigged and if I was the president”.

During his 2024 election campaign, Trump would vow to end the war within 24 hours, adding pressure on the administration and a desire to show progress after he missed his deadline.

2025: Trump and Vance ambush Zelensky in White House showdown

Trump won the 2024 election and returned to office in January 2025 with a new mandate and promises to end the war in Ukraine and avoid dragging the US into war.

Zelensky had been among the first world leaders to congratulate Trump and his “decisive leadership” when he won the election. But the two clashed dramatically at their first face-to-face meeting at the White House in February.

open image in gallery Trump and Zelensky clashed in front of the world’s cameras in February 2025, shortly after the American president’s reelection ( AFP/Getty )

The Ukrainian president had seen the meeting as an opportunity to convince Trump not to side with Putin. But Trump and his vice president JD Vance laid into Zelensky, saying he showed disrespect and had not thanked America for its support.

Zelensky was told to leave, a US official said, and a deal to jointly develop Ukraine’s rich natural resources was left in limbo. European allies rushed to Zelensky’s aid, but Washington within days had cut military aid and vital intelligence sharing to Ukraine, blocking billions in shipments.

2026: Trump signs diesel deal with Putin

The relationship between Zelensky and Trump steadily recovered after the White House showdown, with the pair meeting quietly on the sidelines of Pope Francis’ funeral in April last year to discuss peace plans.

Trump later restored intelligence sharing and the US resumed negotiations with both sides, including trilateral talks in Geneva in February 2026, though Russia kept close to its original demands for land and concessions.

open image in gallery Trump and Zelensky met at the Vatican in April 2025 after the disastrous February meeting to get peace talks back on track ( Ukraine Foreign Affair Ministry )

Trump had told Zelensky in the Oval Office that he “didn’t have the cards” in the war with Russia. But by August last year, Ukraine had developed the capability to start hitting oil refineries far across the border, dealing damage to the Russian economy and taking the fight closer to Moscow.

Trump in February 2026 began a costly war with Iran that contributed to rising energy prices in the run up to this year’s November midterm elections. But he directed much of the blame towards Ukraine and its strikes on Russian energy infrastructure, despite Russia’s attacks the other way.

It was against this backdrop that in October the US president announced a deal with Putin to allow Russia to sell diesel, undermining years of mounting pressure for little material difference to prices. When Russia ignored Trump’s ‘energy ceasefire’, Ukraine restarted its attacks across the border, and Trump hit out at Zelensky.

open image in gallery Donald Trump meets with Zelensky during the 81st United Nations General Assembly (UNGA) in New York City, US, September 22, 2026 ( Reuters )

Ukraine subsequently reported difficulty with its Starlink communications service. Elon Musk deflected criticism, saying it was the US government that owned and controlled the military variant in use on Ukraine’s frontlines.

Ukrainian officials also said they were no longer receiving reliable US warnings of incoming Russian attacks, while the White House said there had been no changes to intelligence sharing with Ukraine.

Asked last week whether Trump could be using Zelensky as a scapegoat for his own domestic problems ahead of the November midterms, the Ukrainian president could only smirk and say: “This is my answer.”

News.title: Piers Morgan left stunned after Indiana Democrat admits how much she drank before viral ‘we have guns, too’ interview
News.content:
Become an Independent member to bookmark this article Want to bookmark your favourite articles and stories to read or reference later? Start your Independent Membership today. Already a member? Log in

Piers Morgan was left stunned after Indiana Democratic candidate Jaime West revealed she guzzled “three beers” before her viral interview where she pledged to fire all Republicans and stated: “We have guns, too.”

West, who is running for a seat on the Fayette County Council this Election Day, argued on Piers Morgan Uncensored Monday that she “wasn’t that intoxicated” during her slurring and stuttering interview on a local TV forum earlier this month.

“A lot of people assumed you might have had a drink before you did that interview. Did you?” Morgan asked the Democratic hopeful, to which she replied: “I had a Coors Light. I had a beer.”

Morgan pressed her further, prompting her to admit that she had “a couple” of beers.

“I was nervous! I was going into a room full of Republicans!” West exclaimed.

open image in gallery Jaime West, who is running for a seat on the Fayette County Council in Indiana, went viral after saying she would fire all Republicans if elected ( Local TV3 )

Morgan then gave West a “chance to be completely honest and transparent” and tell the truth about how many drinks she consumed before the seemingly drunken conversation.

“Alright, three. Three beers. What do you want me to say, man? I had three beers,” West revealed to a stunned Morgan.

However, the candidate insisted that she “wasn’t that intoxicated” and still knows “what I’m talking about.” She also insisted to Morgan that she was sober while speaking to him.

Morgan noted that West said “some very inflammatory things about Republicans,” including that she wants to fire them all and calling them “racist and dumb.” When asked whether she wished to retract anything, West declined.

“I say it all the time: I’m not friends with [Republicans]. I don’t like them. They voted for all of this that’s happening in our country,” West told Morgan.

West came to national attention earlier this month after clips of her blunt, bizarre interview responses went viral online. The local TV forum featured candidates for Fayette County Commission, Fayette County School Corp. and the county council.

open image in gallery West (left) spoke with Piers Morgan (center) and conservative commentator Ben Ferguson (right) on Monday’s Piers Morgan Uncensored, admitting she had three beers before the viral interview earlier this month ( Piers Morgan Uncensored )

During the forum, she made bold declarations, including that her most unpopular policy she’d pursue if elected would be to fire all Republicans. West clarified that “there’s Republicans who actually get it, you know? There are good Republicans out there,” she said, but added, “then there’s MAGA.”

“What do you want me to say. I don’t like being around them,” she said. “[They’re] just racist and aren’t very intelligent at all. They call you names.”

When asked for her final words to voters, West simply stated: “We have guns, too,” referring to Democrats.

West does not have an official campaign website or contact information listed online. She acknowledged the amount of attention she has received when asked to comment by IndyStar.

“My recent appearance on TV3 has unexpectedly brought a lot of attention, which has been a bit overwhelming,” West said.“I am deeply concerned about the current political climate in Indiana.”

News.title: Prince Harry ‘wants to work it out’ with his family – but claims others ‘don’t want to’ reconcile
News.content:
Become an Independent member to bookmark this article Want to bookmark your favourite articles and stories to read or reference later? Start your Independent Membership today. Already a member? Log in

Prince Harry has said he “wants it to work out” with his family – but he claimed that others “don’t want to”.

The Duke of Sussex and his older brother Prince William have had a strained relationship since the Sussexes decided to step down from the Royal Family in 2020 and relocate to California.

Harry and Meghan Markle set up home back in England in August and last week visited Nottingham in their first joint engagement since returning.

In an interview with GQ, Harry said that his move back to the UK was partly driven by a desire to be “closer” to his family.

He explained that he wished to reconcile with them, before doubting whether that feeling would be reciprocated.

He said: “People maybe look at us and go, ‘How are you going to work it out?’

“And then, maybe, how I see you’re going to work it out, maybe that will help me work my stuff out.

“And some people don’t want it to work out. I want it to work out.”

“With everything else that’s going on in the world, the most important thing is to reconcile”, he added. “That’s the key point.”

It is believed that Princes William and Harry have not spoken in several years, and have not been seen publicly together since the King’s coronation in 2023.

File picture: Prince William, Kate Middleton, Meghan Markle and Prince Harry in December 2018 ( AFP/Getty )

Harry told GQ that “scars stick around forever” but added that he would encourage everybody to let go of the past.

“If there’s certain things from the past that are still affecting your every day, that’s harder to let go of”, he said.

“But yeah, for me, there’s enough drama in the world and enough drama in people’s lives than to continue with issues with family.”

Asked if he was “grieving” the relationships he had with his father and his brother, Harry said: “Yes, of course. I think from a family perspective, again: another massively relatable issue for so many people.

“There’s sibling disagreements, there’s broken relationships between kids and their parents, kids and one parent.

“That continues to come up with me the whole time by people that I speak to. So I know how relatable it is.”

News.title: 13 best supermarket butters to slather on your toast, taste-tested by a food writer
News.content:
An easy way to make even the simplest dishes taste delicious, butter can be enjoyed slathered on bread like its own topping, melted over a jacket potato, or used for a delicious homemade baked treat. As versatile as it is tasty, the best slabs of butter belong everywhere from lunchbox sandwiches to the more sophisticated butter boards.

Like other food items, the cost of butter has risen around 19 per cent in the past year alone, so it's worth knowing which brands are worth their salt. These days, it’s rare to find a block of butter (not counting the spreadable tub varieties) for under £2, with most hovering just a few pence shy of £3.

Butter is no longer criticised as it once was, leading to far more choice. Margarine used to be seen as the healthier choice because of butter’s saturated fat and its association with higher cholesterol, but today, butter is recognised as something that can be enjoyed in moderation within a balanced, healthy diet.

In fact, butter is reprising its role as kitchen stalwart, with Waitroses’ sales of its Essentials salted butter up 16 per cent compared with last year, while flavoured butter has also grown in popularity, with Worldpanel trend data showing a 24 per cent increase in UK sales over the past 12 months.

And, as the queen of cooking, Nigella Lawson shows, it’s at its best on toast. I usually go for salted butter, but Nigella prefers unsalted, spreading it in two layers so the second leaves little un-melted blobs, and finishing it with a sprinkle of sea salt flakes. If her slightly more elaborate method works, plain salted butter works perfectly too (for simplicity, this guide focuses on salted butter).

If all this butter talk has piqued your appetite, read on for the top supermarket picks right now. After plenty of tasting and countless slices of toast, I’ve rounded up the most delicious options to add to your basket.



I got busy slathering the dairy spread on multiseed bread ( Emma Henderson/The Independent )

The best supermarket butters for 2026 are:

Best overall – Sainsbury's Taste the Difference farmhouse butter: £2.80, Sainsburys.co.uk

Best budget buy – M&S British salted butter: £1.85, Ocado.com

Best luxury buy – No.1 French butter: £3.50, Waitrose.com

News.title: BBC to axe key TV channels in cost-cutting drive
News.content:
Become an Independent member to bookmark this article Want to bookmark your favourite articles and stories to read or reference later? Start your Independent Membership today. Already a member? Log in

The BBC will close BBC Three, BBC Scotland and BBC Radio 4 Extra linear broadcast services in spring 2027 as part of cost-cutting measures, the corporation has announced.

In addition, around 100 jobs will be cut at BBC News, as the corporation faces pressure to make savings of £500 million by 2028.

A number of roles will also be cut as a result of the broadcast closures, including ten in Scotland.

BBC Scotland will remain a channel on iPlayer, but will no longer be a broadcast channel on television. Content will also be available on BBC One and BBC Two in Scotland.

BBC Three content, which is aimed at 16 to 34-year-olds, will be available on BBC iPlayer and on other platforms, including YouTube.

open image in gallery Phoebe Waller-Bridge’s hit show Fleabag first aired on BBC Three ( BBC/Two Brothers )

It is not the first time BBC Three has been cut from linear TV. It returned as a fully-fledged TV channel in January 2022, six years after it moved online.

The channel has since been responsible for major hits including Fleabag, Normal People and Killing Eve.

Programmes from Radio 4 Extra will still be available on BBC Sounds – and The Daily Service will be on BBC Sounds and local radio.

In a note to staff setting out the changes, BBC director general Matt Brittin said: “We need to make every pound work harder for audiences as we respond to the immediate cost pressures and reinvent the BBC for a changing world. We all know that means tough choices.”

He added: “Much of the great content they currently carry will still be found where audiences already enjoy them on iPlayer and Sounds. While this follows media speculation, I recognise the confirmation of this news will be hard for audiences and colleagues.”

New director of BBC News Rachel Jupp will also lay out plans for further savings early next year, while other divisions will confirm savings plans in the coming months.

This follows earlier savings announced in BBC Scotland, Wales, Northern Ireland, Local and Speech and Sounds.

At the weekend the BBC confirmed its long-running home renovation TV series DIY SOS will be “rested” next year amid the corporation’s ongoing “savings challenges”.

The BBC also cancelled plans to build a new bespoke studio for The Archers at its Tea Factory in Digbeth amid its cost-cutting measures.

News.title: The Farmers’ Almanac forecast for this Thanksgiving. Here’s what to know
News.content:
Become an Independent member to bookmark this article Want to bookmark your favourite articles and stories to read or reference later? Start your Independent Membership today. Already a member? Log in

Americans traveling for Thanksgiving could face snow showers in the Midwest, rain in the Pacific Northwest and cooler temperatures across parts of the West, while the Southeast is expected to see milder weather, according to The Farmers’ Almanac.

Its November 23-26 outlook suggests typical late-fall conditions, with no major nationwide storm expected to dominate the holiday week.

“Taken together, it does not look like a major nationwide storm will dominate the week,” the Farmers’ Almanac said in its October 19 forecast.

Thanksgiving falls on November 26 this year, when millions of Americans are expected to travel to celebrate with family and friends. Rain, snow and chilly temperatures could still make travel tricky in some areas, even if a major storm isn’t in the forecast.

First published in 1818, the Farmers’ Almanac issues forecasts up to 16 months in advance, using a proprietary formula that considers planetary positions, tides and sunspots. The publication also offers seasonal advice, gardening and fishing calendars, home remedies and lifestyle tips.

Here’s what the Farmers’ Almanac predicts for each region for Thanksgiving:

open image in gallery Thanksgiving travelers could face Midwest snow, Pacific Northwest rain and cooler weather in the West, while the Southeast is expected to stay milder, according to the Farmers’ Almanac ( AFP/Getty )

open image in gallery The Farmers’ Almanac issues forecasts up to 16 months in advance, using a proprietary formula that considers planetary positions, tides and sunspots ( The Farmers’ Almanac )

Northeast and New England

The Northeast is expected to see cool, mostly fair weather over Thanksgiving, with a chance of light snow flurries in northern areas and higher elevations. Overall, conditions look favorable for holiday travel.

The region includes New York, Vermont, New Hampshire, Maine, Massachusetts, Rhode Island, Connecticut, Pennsylvania, New Jersey, Delaware, Maryland and Washington, D.C.

Great Lakes, Ohio Valley and Midwest

The Great Lakes and Ohio Valley region could see colder, more winter-like weather over Thanksgiving, with scattered snow showers or flurries possible across Ohio, Michigan, Indiana, Kentucky, Illinois and Wisconsin.

Although no major winter storm is currently expected, localized snowfall could slow holiday travel and create slippery road conditions in affected areas.

More follows

News.title: The European cities facing more protests as continent gripped by cost of living crisis
News.content:
Become an Independent member to bookmark this article Want to bookmark your favourite articles and stories to read or reference later? Start your Independent Membership today. Already a member? Log in

Violent protests have broken out across Europe amid growing frustration over the cost of living crisis, a lack of affordable housing and deteriorating school conditions.

As many as 550,000 people turned out across France on Saturday, according to authorities, to demonstrate against declining public services. Protests turned violent in Paris as shops were looted and cars set on fire in some of the city’s worst violence in years.

Young people waved Italian flags and let off flares in Milan as they rallied against the rising cost of living in scenes that were condemned by prime minister Giorgia Meloni.

Police used water cannon and teargas to break up the crowds after some masked rioters clashed with authorities and set off fires.

Tens of thousands of people meanwhile marched through central Lisbon in protest of the soaring cost of living and a deepening housing crisis, echoing weeks of demonstrations in Spain that prompted prime minister Pedro Sanchez to call a snap general election.

Pressure was also on Albania’s prime minister Edi Rama after a week of protests over poor university conditions, high tuition fees and corruption, which saw hours-long violent clashes with police on Sunday.

open image in gallery A protester feeds a fire with a material along the Canal Saint-Martin during ongoing protest action against the ‘high cost of living’, in Paris on 17 October ( AFP/Getty )

Here we look at the factors behind the protests sweeping the continent and the latest developments.

France

Marseille is set to impose a curfew on minors each night until Friday in response to the violent protests that have rocked France.

On Monday night, the French government imposed partial curfews across the country, including in Paris and Nice, after riots and looting amid nationwide protests over the weekend.

It came after thousands of rioters were arrested during the weekend’s widespread protests, with justice minister Gérald Darmanin promising an “unrelenting” response to violence. The unrest gathered momentum from student-led demonstrations that began last month in response to overcrowded classrooms and teacher shortages.

Authorities said more than half a million people turned out to march on Saturday, including 110,000 in Paris alone. Organisers put the figure closer to 800,000.

While hundreds of thousands protested peacefully across France on Saturday, violent fringe groups targeted public buildings, looted luxury boutiques and supermarkets, and attacked police vehicles and officers.

open image in gallery A protester throws a bicycle onto a burning car amid clashes during a day of demonstrations against the cost of living and rising fuel prices in Paris. ( Reuters )

French president Emmanuel Macron appealed for calm on Sunday as some of the protests boiled over into violent clashes with police. The government has blamed the violence on what it said were ultra-left groups, as well as criminals it said had instigated the looting.

More than 2,400 people were arrested across France, while nearly 1,000 officers were injured, according to the government. Police fired teargas in Paris on Sunday afternoon and protesters set fire to piles of bicycles.

One protester died on Saturday after suffering a cardiac arrest during demonstrations in the capital.

open image in gallery Police officers push a demonstrator at the Place de la Comedie in Lyon ( AFP/Getty )

Spain

Tens of thousands of people have turned out across Spain in recent weeks following the eviction of 87-year-old Maria del Carmen Abascal, known as Maricarmen, from her Madrid home.

The pensioner was forcibly removed from her flat of 70 years after the property was bought by the investment firm Urbagestion, which tried to increase her rent by 230 per cent. She died suddenly in early October, two weeks after she was evicted.

Maricarmen’s death reinvigorated a movement long frustrated by home shortages and surging rents across the country.

open image in gallery Demonstrators gather to pay tribute to Maricarmen Abascal, the 87-year-old pensioner whose eviction triggered nationwide protests over Spain's chronic housing crisis. ( AFP/Getty )

Socialist prime minister Pedro Sanchez last month called a snap general election for 29 November after parliament rejected his government’s proposals to address a mounting housing crisis.

Several people who received ⁠eviction orders have died by suicide in Spain in recent months.

Spain's minimum wage is €1,221 (£1,025), while the average monthly rent for an 80-square-meter apartment is around €1,130 (about £949), according to an analysis by the business newspaper Expansión.

Italy

“Italia in Piazza,” or Italy in the Streets, has galvanized thousands of demonstrators against crumbling public services and the rising cost of living.

Milan police clashed on Sunday with protesters throwing stones and looting shops. Meanwhile, police in riot gear fired teargas and used water cannons after several hundred hooded protesters broke shop windows and set bins on fire in the area near central Piazza Duomo, sources told Reuters, adding that more than 60 protesters had been detained for checks.

open image in gallery Protesters run along a street strewn with debris during a protest over the state of public services and the rising cost of living in Milan, on Sunday ( Reuters )

A total of 28 protesters were arrested after similar clashes erupted on Saturday in northern cities including Milan, Bologna, Brescia, Bergamo and Turin, according to a police report on Sunday.

Ms Meloni, facing an election next year, condemned the violence and announced a government meeting on Monday to discuss how to address the situation.

Now a newly formed group calling itself the “17 October Movement” has announced what it describes as a “permanent mobilization” to demonstrate every Saturday at 3 p.m. in cities across Italy.

open image in gallery Italian police detain a protester during a protest over the state of public services and the rising cost of living in Milan ( Reuters )

Portugal

Fifty-five people were arrested as Portuguese police dismantled housing crisis protest camps in the central squares of Lisbon and Porto before dawn on Tuesday.

Activists pitched roughly 200 tents in Lisbon’s Rossio square on Saturday, while Porto’s Dom Joao I square had been occupied for 10 days. Protesters say low wages are failing to keep pace with housing costs and the rising cost of living, leaving many people struggling to make ends meet.

Portugal faces an acute housing affordability crisis, where buying costs have more than doubled since 2017 and new lease rents have almost doubled.

open image in gallery Dozens of tents are pictured during a encampment set up in protest against housing shortage, soaring rents and low wages, at Rossio square in central Lisbon. ( AFP/Getty )

Urban areas feel the greatest strain, compounded by backlash against excessive tourism and digital nomads. Activists want the centre-right government to drop a bill easing evictions and removing rent caps on new leases, which passed its first reading after the far-right Chega party abstained.

Tens of thousands of people also marched through central Lisbon on Saturday. Portugal's biggest union, CGTP, which called the rally, said “many tens of thousands” packed one of the capital's main avenues.

Portugal’s inflation hit 3.6 per cent in September, driven by rising food and fuel prices, the latter up 15 per cent year-on-year following an increase in tensions in the Middle East.

Albania

Anti-government protests have stretched over a week in Albania's capital of Tirana, with clashes escalating after high school and university students joined the broad anti-government “Flamingo” movement calling for Socialist Prime Minister Edi Rama to resign.

Rama has condemned the protesters as “ideologized and radicalized” by antifa, an umbrella term for loosely organized far-left militants in the United States, where President Donald Trump has designated the movement a terrorist organization.

open image in gallery Protesters take part in an anti-government protest by students in Tirana, Albania. ( Reuters )

Ending corruption is a major demand of the movement, which was named for the natural habitat of flamingos in an area where Rama's government agreed to allow a major luxury tourism development linked to Jared Kushner, Trump's son-in-law. They also want protections for healthcare, education, and public pensions, according to its website.

Serbia

Tens of thousands of people are expected to march in Serbia’s capital Belgrade on Thursday as part of an election rally led by student activists.

For nearly two years, Serbian university students have driven mass anti-corruption protests. Now they share a broader aim: defeating the nation's powerful populist leader Aleksandar Vucic in this weekend's early parliamentary election.

Following the 25 October vote, the former authoritarian president is seeking a return as prime minister to extend his right-wing party's 14-year rule. Having previously rattled the populists during their demonstrations, Serbia's youth movement is the sole barrier in his way.

open image in gallery Students walk the streets carrying boxes bearing the certified signatures of their supporters, an initial step toward being included on the voting list, with the submission of the “Students Win” list to the Republic Election Commission in Belgrade. ( Reuters )

Unlike high school students in France who are rallying for better education, Serbia's student movement started out as a struggle for justice after a train station tragedy in the country's north killed 16 people in November 2024. The students' call for accountability for the deaths, which they blamed on rampant corruption, found widespread support. Protests spread, forcing a government collapse and rattling Vucic.

Much is uncertain ahead of Sunday's vote. Tensions remain high alongside the stakes. Vucic's Serbian Progressive Party, or SNS, and the student-supported Students' List are thought to be running close, leaving the outcome uncertain and raising fears of potential violence.

News.content:
Thanks for joining me. Wages have grown at the slowest pace in six years in a sign of the cost of living challenges facing the Chancellor ahead of the Budget.

Total pay excluding bonuses grew by 3.7pc in the three months to August, according to the Office for National Statistics (ONS).

It was the weakest growth since November 2020, when Britain was grappling with the second Covid lockdown.

It raises pressure on John Healey as he seeks to give household finances “breathing room” in his first Budget speech next week. Here is what you need to know.

News.title: French bond sell-off spreads across Europe
News.content:
Thanks for joining me. The cost of French government borrowing has risen at the fastest pace among G7 nations after a second night of riots.

The yield on 10-year French bonds, known as OATs, climbed from 4.80pc to 4.85pc on Monday, the steepest increase among major world economies.

Bond yields are effectively the interest rate paid by governments when they borrow money by issuing bonds to financial markets.

Emmanuel Macron is facing a crisis after shops were looted and vandalised across the country.

More than 2,300 people were arrested on Saturday after protests against the cost of living and poor school conditions.

Jim Reid, an analyst at Deutsche Bank, said: “This won’t make it easy for the international community to be totally comfortable buying OATs, so the modest recovery in French spreads over the last week or so will be tested today.

“With France already facing a difficult fiscal backdrop and the 2027 election approaching, the weekend adds another layer of political risk for markets.” Here is what you need to know.

5 things to start your day

1) Burnham seeks EU embrace over AI | UK presses for access to a scheme that will prioritise investment in sovereign technology

2) Larry Ellison’s TikTok bans ad account for Musk documentary | Social media company blocks promotion for the film because of its political content

3) Profit warnings rise ahead of Budget | Most companies blame government policy and geopolitical uncertainty for worsening outlook

4) Istanbul airport stockpiles jet fuel over shortage fears | Turkish hub can sustain flights for three weeks without topping up tanks

5) GB News to launch ‘all-British’ radio station | New broadcast venture will attempt to win market share from BBC

What happened overnight

Oil prices fell more than 1pc after Donald Trump’s decision to waive sweeping sanctions on Russia.

On Friday, the President signed an executive order that delayed a wave of fresh sanctions and tariffs as they were set to take effect.

Brent crude edged down by nearly 1pc to just under $109 a barrel, with West Texas Intermediate hovered at around $101 a barrel.

Asian shares were mixed as volatility in technology stocks persisted.

South Korea’s benchmark Kospi index was up 1.1pc to 5,729.58 on Monday, after falling sharply last week. The Kospi is down more than 18pc over the past month, and still well below the 9,000 mark it crossed in June at its peak on the global AI frenzy.

Japan’s Nikkei 225 lost 0.8pc to 64,799.03. Japanese chip equipment maker Tokyo Electron lost 2.1pc, and OpenAI investor SoftBank Group dropped 3.6pc.

Hong Kong’s stock market was closed because of a holiday. The Shanghai Composite index edged 0.2pc higher to 3,722.20, after China reported better-than-expected growth of 4.5pc for its economy in the third quarter.

CXMT, China’s leading memory chipmaker, fell more than 7pc despite the company forecasting a strong profit for the first nine months.

China’s official growth data is set to be issued on Monday, giving the markets a glimpse into how the world’s second-biggest economy is faring.

The data is expected to show that China’s economy expanded by 4.4pc in the third quarter, improving on a multi-year low in Q2 but still falling just short of its annual target.

Beijing is aiming for growth of around 4.5pc to 5pc this year, which is its lowest goal in decades.

However, experts think China is on course to miss its annual economic target, weighed down by the Iran war energy shock.

China’s economy has been under pressure from mounting energy costs and faltering domestic demand. Researchers polled by AFP suggested exports were its sole outperformer.

Taiwan’s Taiex fell 1pc. Shares of Taiwan Semiconductor Manufacturing Co., or TSMC, the world’s biggest contract chipmaker, were down 0.6pc. Australia’s S&P/ASX 200 was 0.3pc higher at 8,832.20. India’s Sensex edged down 0.1pc.

Indonesia’s benchmark stock index fell another 5pc to its lowest level since 2020, after it plunged over 11pc on Friday following a warning from index provider MSCI that it would downgrade the country from its “emerging market” status.

News.title: Europe records highest ever number of West Nile Virus cases
News.content:
Mainland Europe has seen the largest number of cases of a debilitating mosquito-borne illness, with Italy hardest hit by the disease.

According to the European Centre for Disease Prevention and Control there have been 1,715 locally acquired cases of West Nile Virus so far this year, compared to 989 cases at the same point last year. Italy has been hardest hit, with 748 cases, followed by Greece with 445 cases, France with 144 and Spain with 139.

There have been 130 deaths, with the greatest number occurring in Italy, which saw 56 deaths.

The number of cases is likely to tail off over the next few weeks as the weather across Europe becomes cooler and less favourable for the Culex mosquito which spreads the disease.

West Nile Virus is in the same family of viruses as dengue, yellow fever and Japanese encephalitis. It causes flu-like symptoms and sometimes vomiting and diarrhoea but in around one in 150 cases it can develop into a disease that affects the brain and nervous system and can be fatal. There is no vaccine or treatment.

The disease is widespread in birds, but humans can only acquire it if they are bitten by an infected mosquito. The disease does not spread from human to human. Most cases of severe disease occur in older people and those with weakened immune systems.

News.title: Arsenal late show keeps heat on Man City
News.content:
In the ordinary course of a Premier League season, you would say Manchester City have applied pressure on Arsenal by opening up a six-point lead before the champions play at Nottingham Forest this afternoon.

This is not a normal Premier League season though, and we await to discover if the top of the league table is simply a mirage.

Regardless, Mikel Arteta and his Arsenal players have their own motivations to accumulate as many points as possible before January as they seek to retain the title for the first time since the 1930s.

Arsenal have struggled at the City Ground, drawing 0-0 on their last two Premier League visits. They also lost at Forest in May 2023, a result which confirmed Manchester City as champions at Arsenal’s expense, and were knocked out of the FA Cup by Forest in January 2022.

Forest are yet to score a home league goal under Oliver Glasner, another data point suggesting this will be a low-scoring game.

That might not be the full story though, with Forest creating a hatful of chances in their defeat at Crystal Palace last week and Arsenal also playing a more inventive, technical game with the ball so far this season.

Arsenal have yet to score from a non-penalty set-piece, and their percentage of goals from open play is now the highest in the Premier League.

Morgan Gibbs-White is a doubt after sustaining what Glasner described as a “minor muscle injury” at Palace and his involvement in the game will be a last-minute call. With the exception of Christos Tzolis, Piero Hincapie and long-term absentee William Saliba, Arsenal’s squad is in pretty good health. Bukayo Saka, Martin Odegaard, Kai Havertz, Riccardo Calafiori and Ben White could be recalled to Arteta’s starting XI after starting the Champions League win over Lille on the bench.

Full team news on the way shortly.

News.title: Slow and dull Man Utd are just not good enough
News.content:
Manchester United are like John Toshack’s duvet. You fix one problem – being far too vulnerable to conceding goals – only to create another – lacking the threat to score. It is all very Meh United not Man United. The indisputable fact is they are just not very entertaining to watch. They are slow and dull.

In the end it also points to another thing. The thing highlighted in midweek by Lisandro Martínez after the Champions League defeat at Atlético Madrid: they do not have the strength in depth to compete.

What they do have appears to not be fit for purpose. Certainly Michael Carrick, the under-pressure manager, is struggling to get the best out of the resources he has.

“It’s like a duvet,” Toshack, the former Real Madrid and Wales manager, famously said of football. “If you pull it up, your feet get cold. If you pull it down, your shoulders get cold.”

There will have been times in the last few days, with the intense criticism and scrutiny over his future, when Carrick will have simply felt like dragging that duvet up over his head and keeping it there.

Defeat by Leeds United would have been unthinkable. It would have put Carrick under potentially intolerable pressure in what appears to be a pivotal week, with Como away in the Champions League and a home Premier League fixture against Bournemouth in the coming days.

Was this a lifeline or the tightening of the noose for Carrick? Time will soon tell. The relief of avoiding defeat was tempered by the reality of it now being just one win in their opening seven league games – at home to newly promoted Ipswich Town – and they are down in 13th place. It is six games without a win in all competitions.

News.title: Pierre Sage fears for his Crystal Palace future after Brighton humiliation
News.content:
Pierre Sage has admitted that he fears for his future at Crystal Palace, adding that he felt “shame” after his side slumped to their joint-heaviest defeat by rivals Brighton and Hove Albion.

Sage replaced Oliver Glasner as manager in June but since then Palace have won just two league matches with him in at the helm. The south London club have taken seven points from seven Premier League games and have already conceded 17 goals, the most of any team in the league.

“I don’t know,” Sage said when asked if he will get enough time to rectify Palace’s slump. He admitted that his shame was about how Palace were overwhelmed, leaking three goals within the first nine minutes of the game before eventually losing 5-0.

“We are not at the level we expected, and I’m really sorry for that,” the 47-year-old said. “I just want to apologise to the fans because it’s not normal to show this face.”

The Frenchman said that he took full responsibility for the 5-0 defeat, and understood why hundreds of Palace fans left well before the final whistle.

News.title: Ruthless Daniel Dubois dispatches Fabio Wardley in just two rounds
News.content:
Welcome to Telegraph Sport’s live coverage of Daniel Dubois vs Fabio Wardley.

When Wardley dragged himself out of the ring at Manchester’s Co-Op LIVE Arena, the physical damage was obvious, but the psychological sting was far deeper. Wardley had Dubois severely hurt early on, flooring the Londoner twice and teetering on the verge of a career-defining stoppage. Instead, he let the knockout slip away, allowed Dubois to find his rhythm, and was ultimately broken down and halted in the 11th round - surrendering his WBO heavyweight belt in a dramatic comeback victory.

Now, just five months after that gruelling night, the two heavyweights meet again at London’s O2 Arena in an immediate rematch that carries potentially massive implications for the entire division.

For Wardley (20-1-1, 19 KOs), the decision to trigger his rematch clause was instant. Dismissing concerns over the severe punishment he absorbed down the stretch, the Ipswich man is motivated entirely by redemption and the belief that his early success proved Dubois is beatable.

Dubois (23-3, 22 KOs), however, views things very differently. Entering as The Ring’s No. 1 heavyweight contender and a proven two-time world champion, Dubois has brushed off Wardley’s power, claiming his rival “punches like a baby” and insists Wardley threw away his one and only chance at glory in Manchester.

With Oleksandr Usyk approaching the final chapter of his career and the Anthony Joshua vs. Tyson Fury blockbuster looming just eight weeks away, this London clash is far more than a personal grudge match. The winner won’t just walk away with the WBO strap; they will stake an undeniable claim as the torch-bearer for the heavyweight division’s next era if they can land another title fight in short order.

Sports.title: Warner slams 'pathetic' Test crowds in South Africa
Sports.content:
Former batter David Warner has hit out at the "pathetic" attendances in the ongoing Test series between South Africa and Australia.

South Africa lost the first Test match by 214 runs in Durban, with large sections of the Kingsmead ground empty, and the crowds haven't really picked up through the first two rain-affected days of the second Test in Gqeberha.

"We keep hearing how important Test cricket is, but where are the fans in South Africa?" former opener Warner said in a social media post on Tuesday.

"Empty stands, no atmosphere, and we're supposed to believe the format is thriving?

"You can't keep calling Test cricket the pinnacle of the game if no one turns up to watch it.

"Harsh reality, but someone has to say it. Pathetic."

Warner was a central figure in the infamous 'sandpapergate' scandal that dominated Australia's last tour of South Africa in 2018.

Vice captain at the time, Warner was found to have led the plot to alter the condition of the ball, including guiding fellow opener Cameron Bancroft on how to use the sandpaper.

Warner was given a one-year ban and told he would never be considered for a leadership position within the team again.

'Thorough internal review' launched into crowd size

Following the poorly-attended first Test in Durban, the Kwa-Zulu Natal Cricket Union (KZNCU) said that they would launch a "thorough internal review" into the reasons for such sparse crowds.

A total of just under 20,000 fans attended the game across the five days, amounting to less than a fifth of Kingsmead's capacity.

The Test was South Africa's first at home since January 2025, and also their first at home since becoming World Test champions.

"A Test match of this quality, featuring the Proteas and Australia, deserved greater support in the stands," Heinrich Strydom, KZNCU CEO, said in a statement. "While we recognise that supporters face competing demands on their time and finances, we must also understand better what influences their decisions to attend and what more we can do to make live cricket an attractive and worthwhile experience.

"This is something we will reflect on as a Union, through a thorough internal review, and as a cricket community. We need to listen to our supporters, reconnect with our communities, and continue to find ways to make Test cricket more accessible, engaging and appealing to families and cricket lovers of all ages."

Athers: South Africa crowds 'a worrying sign'

Sky Sports' Michael Atherton was also critical of the first Test's crowds, or lack thereof.

"It started on a Friday, was played over the weekend. It's the number one and number two ranked teams in the world, the first Test match at home for South Africa since becoming world champions," Atherton said on the Sky Sports Cricket Podcast.

"Plus there was all the context of it being the first Test between these two in South Africa since the infamous [ball-tampering] 2018 series.

"If you can't drag a crowd in given that context, it's a worrying sign."

Fellow former England captain Nasser Hussain added: "It plays into the narrative that Test match cricket is dying when you watch that and see no one there. But I don't think that it is dying.

"Even sometimes out in India the crowds aren't full. Pakistan, we went out there after however many years [of them not hosting Tests], England were back and they weren't sold out. But people there care deeply about their Test side.

"The lights issue, and going off [for bad light] at half past three [on day one], I think that's more the discussion.

"What can we do to make sure that sitting in a stand on a hot day is very much a good experience for the people that have paid their money? That they're sitting there at 5.30pm and not been sent home at 3.30pm due to bad light?"

This is the first time in a summer that South Africa is hosting Tests as early as October, as increasing demands on the cricket calendar squeeze premier fixtures into the shoulder windows.

South Africa's prime Test period is between November and March but with the SA20 occupying most of January and February and the IPL beginning in March, Tests have been cut to the margins.

Sports.title: Lowry moves to McIlroy's Boston Common Golf team in TGL's first-ever trade
Sports.content:
The first trade in TMRW Golf League (TGL) history has seen Ireland's Shane Lowry depart The Bay Golf Club to join close friend Rory McIlroy at Boston Common Golf.

TGL confirmed the move, saying: "Boston Common Golf acquired Lowry from The Bay Golf Club. The familiarity in team competition between Lowry and Rory McIlroy gives Boston Common Golf one of the most recognisable partnerships entering the new season."

In exchange and as part of the move, The Bay received Boston Common Golf's fourth-round selection in the roster formation process for the 2027 season, the right to swap one selection position with Boston Common Golf during one of the next three TGL offseasons, and commercial considerations.

"I'm delighted to be joining Boston Common Golf. Having Rory alongside me and being part of this group makes it particularly exciting, and I'm looking forward to helping the team bring a championship to Boston," said Lowry.

"Shane is a great friend and someone I love having alongside me in team competition," said McIlroy, co-founder of TGL and Boston Common Golf Founding Member.

Please use Chrome browser for a more accessible video player Watch as McIlroy smashes his first drive 392 yards to hit the longest drive in TGL history

"We've had some special wins together, including at the Zurich Classic, and I know the quality of his game and how much he cares about winning for his teammates.

"I'm delighted to welcome him to Boston Common Golf and excited about what we can achieve together this season."

Also for the first time, the league is expanding with Motor City Golf Club joining as a seventh team. Team rosters are expanding to five players per team, up from four players last season.

Motor City joins Atlanta Drive GC, Boston Common Golf, Jupiter Links Golf Club, Los Angeles Golf Club, New York Golf Club and The Bay Golf Club to give the league seven teams for the upcoming season.

Please use Chrome browser for a more accessible video player Take a look at how team golf works in the TGL

The TGL roster process began with the league's six returning teams.

Each team had the option to keep up to four players from its 2026 roster. Alternates like Akshay Bhatia (Jupiter Links GC) and Chris Gotterup (Atlanta Drive) who appeared for a team during the 2026 season were also eligible to be retained by that team.

After this retention period, teams had to fill their rosters up to five players.

Teams will still choose three players to compete in each match at SoFi Center, but the additional roster spot creates more depth and flexibility for strategic lineup decisions across the season.

Sports.title: Boulter puts rain delays behind her to progress at Japan Open
Sports.content:
A day after heavy rainfall caused play to be suspended, Britain's Katie Boulter returned to clinch a 6-3 6-1 victory at the Japan Open over wildcard Himeno Sakatsume.

The world No 58 concluded a dominant victory in one hour and 32 minutes in Osaka, and she will next face Swiss player Viktorija Golubic for a place in the quarter-finals.

The victory gives Boulter a 20-20 record across her last 40 matches, and a confidence boost following a period in which she has only played three matches since September 30, owing to early exits at the China Open (second round) and Wuhan Open (first round).

On Monday, the match between Boulter and Sakatsume had barely started when the players were forced off court after torrential rain arrived in Osaka. Given the venue didn't have a roof, the court was open to all of the elements.

Please use Chrome browser for a more accessible video player Boulter showed the umpire the weather app on her phone on court, ahead of play being suspended for the day shortly after.

By that point, only three games had been played in the first set, with Sakatsume leading 2-1 at the time of the suspension.

Play was resumed, but another rain delay followed with the score 6-3 3-1 (40-30) to Boulter, meaning both players had to leave court and return on Tuesday to finish the contest.

When play restarted again, 30-year-old Boulter continued to dominate, winning seven of her eight service games overall and claiming five of nine break point chances.

Swiatek withdraws from Ningbo Open with left thigh injury

Elsewhere, Iga Swiatek has withdrawn from the Ningbo Open in China because of an injured left thigh, diminishing her chances of contesting the season-ending WTA Finals at Indian Wells next month.

The six-time major winner lost to eventual champion Maja Chwalinska in the semi-finals at the Wuhan Open last week and struggled at times in that match.

"After careful consideration, I've decided to withdraw from the tournament," Swiatek said in a statement posted on social media Tuesday by the Ningbo tournament. "I've been experiencing an ongoing problem with my left thigh over the past weeks and I feel that giving myself the time to rest and recover is the right decision."

Swiatek was one of three players in contention for the last spot in the eight-player field for the WTA Finals with Karolina Muchova and Marta Kostyuk ahead of tournaments this week.

The WTA, in a preview of the Ningbo tournament, said if Swiatek didn't reach the quarter-finals and Kostyuk doesn't reach the final here, Muchova will secure the remaining spot for the season-ending tournament at Indian Wells starting November 8.

Sports.title: Animal rights group urges Crystal Palace to retire bald eagle mascot
Sports.content:
A leading animal rights group has urged Crystal Palace to retire their American bald eagle mascot because, it says, the matchday experience can leave the bird “frightened, disoriented and panicked” and put spectators at risk.

In a letter to Palace’s chief executive, Sharon Lacey, People for the Ethical Treatment of Animals (Peta) called on the club to end Phoenix’s appearances at Selhurst Park and commit never to use a live animal mascot again.

Palace, known as the Eagles since 1973 after the then manager Malcolm Allison changed their nickname from the Glaziers, introduced a pre-match display from Kayla the Eagle in 2010. She died in 2020 after a decade’s service but Kayla’s replacement, Phoenix, made her debut before the game against West Ham in August 2024 at four months old, meeting supporters in the fanzone and being introduced at half-time with her handler.

Phoenix is based at the Eagle Heights Wildlife Foundation in Kent, and its website said at the time that she “had been carefully prepared for her prestigious role as Crystal Palace’s official live mascot since hatching”. Phoenix has yet to appear again at Selhurst Park. It is understood plans for her to make a maiden flight across the pitch before kick-off – a ritual Kayla for which was renowned – were abandoned at a match this season.

In the letter seen by the Guardian, Peta said bright lights, loud noises and boisterous crowds mean stadiums are “no place for animals” and potentially put animals and spectators at risk. It detailed incidents of eagles that have collided with walls or glass windows and a falcon that landed on a spectator’s head, embedding its talons in the man’s scalp. Peta also referred to an incident involving Kayla in 2015 when a Charlton fan was found guilty of trying to punch her during a League Cup tie marred by crowd trouble.

View image in fullscreen Kayla the eagle, who died in 2020, in flight before a Crystal Palace game in 2014. Photograph: Tom Jenkins/The Guardian

Dr Carys Bennett, Peta’s senior corporate projects manager, said: “Bald eagles are revered as symbols of freedom, yet Phoenix is being used as little more than a prop to entertain football fans. Crystal Palace already has a human mascot to energise supporters, so there’s no reason to drag a wild animal into a noisy, crowded stadium. Peta is urging the club to let Phoenix spread [her] wings and retire [her] from matchday duties for good.”

Palace did not respond to Peta’s letter or to a follow-up request last week. They have been contacted for comment. The Guardian sent a number of questions to Eagles Heights to ask about Phoenix’s welfare and did not receive a reply.

Peta’s letter argued that eagles’ natural behaviours make the stadium environment unsuitable for them. In the wild, the birds can travel across vast territories and typically avoid close contact with humans. The organisation said even birds raised in captivity retain their natural instincts and may experience frustration and stress when unable to engage in natural behaviours.

Benfica’s home matches feature appearances from a bald eagle called Águia Vitória – a custom that the Portuguese club started in 2003 when their new Estádio da Luz opened.

Sports.title: Erik ten Hag accuses Cristiano Ronaldo of ‘letting down’ Manchester United
Sports.content:
Erik ten Hag has claimed Cristiano Ronaldo “let the team down” during their time together at Manchester United. Ten Hag has also alleged that promises made by United’s owners went unfulfilled, leading to his sacking by the club in October 2024.

Ronaldo returned for a second spell at United in August 2021 and was already at the club when Ten Hag was appointed in April 2022 as Ole Gunnar Solskjær’s successor. The relationship between the pair quickly broke down, however, with Ronaldo refusing to come on as a substitute in a win against Tottenham in October 2022 before he then publicly criticised the club in a TV interview. The forward’s contract was mutually terminated the following month.

“He let the team down, and he let me down, because we planned with him,” Ten Hag said in an interview with the Athletic. “He’s one of the best in football history. I respected him a lot. But at that time, as a manager, I had to make a rational decision and keep the players I admire in.”

Ten Hag claims Ronaldo did not complete the full run that players were set after they were beaten 4-0 by Brentford early in his reign. “I confronted him with this,” Ten Hag said. “Many times I say: ‘Ronnie, everyone wants to work for you to bring you in the right position, but if you can’t bring yourself in the box, you can’t score.’”

Ten Hag was sacked only five months after he won the FA Cup and then signed a contract extension. The Dutchman claimed in the discussions with the club’s owners about his new deal that he was made promises which were not kept, and he was left “embarrassed” when Scott McTominay was sold to Napoli without his consent. He said: “They promised me loyalty, they promised me backing, they promised communication, that we get aligned. We spoke about the issues. But the promises, they didn’t keep.

“I said: ‘No selling Scott McTominay.’ And in the end they sold him. I got, of course, very embarrassed and disappointed.”

Sports.title: ‘Like a family’: De Zerbi credits players’ talk and bonding trip for improving Tottenham
Sports.content:
Roberto De Zerbi said that Tottenham are playing with more togetherness after holding a clear-the-air meeting before their recent game with Manchester United.

Spurs went on to draw 1-1 with 10 men against United and are out of the bottom three after beating Coventry 3-1 at home on Monday night. De Zerbi felt the performance against Coventry could have been better but was happy with his side’s attitude as they claimed their first Premier League win of the season.

“It’s important,” the Spurs manager said. “The result is important but most important, two things. First one, we are able to realise we can win a game like other teams in the Premier League. The second thing, if we put [in] something from ourselves like we have done in the last two weeks. The day before Old Trafford we had a big meeting and spoke about the situation. We can’t accept and can’t move on if we don’t accept responsibility.”

De Zerbi took his squad to Marbella for a bonding trip and warm weather training last week. “This week has been important because we spend time together and want to be like a family,” he said. “During the game if you have a problem and there is a tough situation you have to play for your friend and your brother, not like 11 robot players on the pitch.”

Spurs took the lead when James Maddison marked his first start in 536 days with a brilliant goal. Coventry equalised through Jack Rudoni but Omar Marmoush responded with his first goal since leaving Manchester City and Ben Davies sealed the result.

Spurs are up to 16th and De Zerbi was happy that Maddison’s first goal since May 2025 was joined by Dejan Kulusevski coming off the bench to make his first appearance since suffering a serious knee injury in the same month.

“They are different players,” De Zerbi said. “Different talent, different experience, different personality. With them in the dressing room there is another atmosphere.”

Frank Lampard was happy with Coventry’s fight but was surprised that Marmoush’s goal was not ruled out after the Egyptian elbowed Milan van Ewijk. “I did think that,” Coventry’s manager said. “If you roll and your elbow is that high and it connects with Milan, I thought VAR would cancel it.”
