Lampard was optimistic about his side. “It was a really big display,” he said. “3-1 changes the view at the end of the game. At 2-1 we were pushing.”

Sports.title: Dwight Yorke: ‘I’m not a kid trying to get into management – I’m a manager’
Sports.content:
Dwight Yorke wants you to stop calling him a former player. “I’m not a kid trying to get into management for the first time,” he says from his home in Dubai. “I’ve done that and I want that message to come across clearly.”

The message has a deadline. Carlos Queiroz left his job as Ghana head coach on 1 October and the Ghana Football Association is searching for his successor. Yorke is among the names under consideration, along with Pape Thiaw, Aliou Cissé and Walid Regragui, the former Morocco head coach, according to Ghanaian media.

He is tired of the shorthand way he is described during these high‑profile job hunts. People focus on his playing accolades, including calling him the treble winner, a label he says belongs to one season in a run of three Premier League titles at Manchester United from 1999-2001. “I’m a manager,” he says.

Over the past four years, Yorke has quietly built a coaching résumé far removed from Old Trafford. His first taste of management came in May 2022, taking charge of Australia’s A-League All Stars against Barcelona in front of more than 70,000 people in Sydney. They lost 3-2. “I realised then that I enjoyed it,” he says.

Macarthur, based in Sydney, followed that July. “We went to a relatively unknown team in the A‑League and managed to win the cup.” The Australia Cup success, three months into his spell, was the club’s first trophy.

It did not last. Macarthur sacked him in January 2023, with the club sixth, after a post-match address when he reportedly called the club a “pub team” run by “muppets”.

A Fifa chamber found Macarthur had dismissed him without just cause. The court of arbitration for sport upheld that in 2024 and ordered the club to pay AU$212,500 (£111,300 at current exchange rates).

“I wish I’d had the opportunity to finish what I started,” Yorke says. The job taught him communication and the importance of being transparent. “There was a disagreement. It was resolved amicably and I’ve moved on.”

Between Macarthur and his next role, he kept his hand in. He worked as a pundit for beIN Sports and on the Saudi Pro League and travelled the world watching coaches at work.

In November 2024, Trinidad and Tobago came calling. The Soca Warriors finished third in their World Cup qualifying group behind Curaçao and Jamaica, missing out on the finals tournament, and Yorke’s tenure ended soon after. The Trinidad and Tobago Football Association said talks over revised terms had not produced an agreement and the contract was ended by mutual consent, announced in March. “The decision to end things was out of my control,” Yorke says.

View image in fullscreen Dwight Yorke smiles on the sidelines as he leads the A-League All Stars to a narrow friendly defeat by Barcelona in May 2022, his first taste of management. Photograph: Rick Rycroft/AP

He does not accept that missing the World Cup defines his time in charge. “People can be blind to success because they focus on whether you qualified.”

He lost once in six qualifiers, 2-0 in Jamaica in September 2025. He had been handed a brief: make people care about Trinidad and Tobago again, boost recruitment and qualify. “I was given three tasks and completed two,” he says.

With Yorke as the head coach, crowds came back and a number of US-born players with Trinidadian and Tobagonian heritage, such as the CF Montréal winger Dante Sealy and Real Salt Lake’s Kobi Henry, opted in and made their debuts. Yorke gave a new generation a fighting chance to emulate the team he captained to the finals in 2006. “I left Trinidadian football in a far better place than I found it,” he says.

The TTFA president at the time described Yorke’s mandate as qualification alone. The team were ranked 102nd by Fifa when Yorke was hired, behind Curaçao (91st) and Jamaica (62nd). “I miss management,” Yorke says. “I miss what we were creating.”

View image in fullscreen Dwight Yorke says he tends to fast for nearly 20 hours a day and eats one meal: ‘I’m a fitness fanatic who trains every day.’ Photograph: Christopher Pike/The Guardian

The players are understood to want him back because his successor, Derek King, is struggling with two draws and eight defeats from his 10 games. Ghana, though, is the live opportunity. “It’s a job I’d be interested in, given Ghana’s history and the players available.”

The Ghanaian FA has not confirmed any approach. The team are bottom of their 2027 Africa Cup of Nations qualifying group with no points, after a 2-0 defeat in Côte d’Ivoire and a 4-2 home loss against the Gambia in which they led by two goals. It is a sharp decline for a side that reached the last 32 of the World Cup this summer, losing 1-0 against Colombia.

skip past newsletter promotion Free newsletter | Every weekday Sign up to Football Daily Kick off your evenings with the Guardian's take on the world of football Enter your email Sign up after newsletter promotion

“You look at the squad and your eyes open even wider,” Yorke says. He says an agent called to tell him Ghana were interested. “The conversation started there and then reached the media before I really knew it.”

From the outside, he says, Ghana “sometimes looks disjointed”. The GFA has said its women’s head coach, Kim Björkegren, will take temporary charge of the men’s qualifying double-header against Somalia next month. In Yorke’s view, outside noise unbalances things, from the administration to the players. So how would he fix it? Organisation, transparency and everyone speaking the same language. “The talent is there. Build the culture and get the players to buy in and the football will follow.”

double quotation mark Pep said that I can’t be him or any other manager – I have to be myself Dwight Yorke

He has considered the effect that diaspora players could have in the role, pointing to Ghana’s Antoine Semenyo and Brandon Thomas-Asante as proof that countries can benefit immensely from UK-born talent. It reflects a broader trend: at the World Cup, 23.6% of the 1,248 squad players represented countries outside their place of birth. For Yorke, the approach is simple: identify the players, establish their heritage and quality and sell them a vision. “I’d make sure that what I say is what I do.”

Older managers might have screamed and shouted to get messages across, but he says: “I’m not sure that approach can last in the current environment.” He would not berate a player in public. “That can be done behind closed doors, while still being assertive.” Respect and punctuality are non‑negotiable. He has sat in dressing rooms with big egos and says nobody gets special treatment. “Everyone starts equally.”

He borrows, but he does not copy. Sir Alex Ferguson, who managed him at United, is the shadow over any such comparison. Among contemporary managers, Pep Guardiola offered him the best advice. “He said, in effect, that I can’t be him or any other manager. I have to be myself.”

View image in fullscreen Dwight Yorke fends off Dominic Matteo in Manchester United’s FA Cup fourth-round win against Liverpool in January 1999. Photograph: Richard Sellers/Sportsphoto Ltd

Other labels have stuck anyway. “People still call me a ‘party boy’. That stigma has been overused and has followed me since I retired from football. I’m not saying I didn’t enjoy myself as a player.” But he says: “You never hear that I didn’t turn up for training or wasn’t fit.”

In Dubai, he tends to fast for nearly 20 hours a day and eats one meal. “I’m a fitness fanatic who trains every day.”

Ask Yorke how he wants to be remembered as a coach and he sits up and answers with a list. Committed. Transparent with players. Decisions made for the team, never for an individual. “I’m straightforward. I don’t mess around, take shortcuts or do the job halfway.”

Yorke has the interest and, by his own account, the answers. “If anyone doubts me, I can prove them wrong.”

Sports.title: Brighton are the apex B club – their next target should be a Champions League place | Jonathan Wilson
Sports.content:
For two or three years now, it’s been standard to nod approvingly at how well-run Brighton, Brentford and Bournemouth are, and to move on. What else is there to say? It’s true, of course – these are sides who have made the most of relatively limited resources. But there’s also an underlying assumption in the designation: that these are clubs who have no higher aspiration, that their limit is earning praise for upper mid-table finishes.

This season, perhaps, offers an opportunity to change that. Other than Arsenal, every major club is undergoing significant transition. Manchester City may have started the season with seven straight wins, but there’s every chance the punishment for their multiple breaches of Premier League regulations takes them out of the race for the top five. In that context, why shouldn’t one of those efficient smaller sides qualify for the Champions League?

Brentford began the weekend in third and with, perhaps, a slight sense of frustration that they had drawn four games. Again, they will feel they might have done rather better on Saturday; they were leading Liverpool 1-0 when Yehor Yarmolyuk foolishly flicked his head towards Jérémy Jacquet and was sent off just before half-time. The result was a 2-1 defeat and a sense of an opportunity missed. Bournemouth have not had the easiest start under Marco Rose, but Sunday’s 2-0 win over Sunderland perhaps hints at a brighter future.

Which left Brighton to carry the charge of the B clubs, which they did in emphatic style, ending a run of four derbies without success with a crushing 5-0 win. Crystal Palace had been extremely fortunate to survive a first-half battering from Nottingham Forest last week. They were thoroughly outplayed in the early stages again, and this time found themselves 3-0 down inside 10 minutes. Perhaps the opening goal, a cross headed into his own net by Jaydee Canvot, was fortunate, but it was an error induced by the intensity of Brighton’s start. The second goal, a perfectly weighted drive from just inside the Palace half from Diego Gómez, spoke of a side playing with immense confidence. Already this season, 11 different players have scored for Brighton in the league. They have become the image of a side without stars, the whole far greater than the individuals who comprise it.

The difference from February, when Brighton last played Palace, is stark. They lost that game 1-0, meaning they had won just one of their previous 12 Premier League games. Generalised grumbling had begun to curdle into calls for Fabian Hürzeler to be sacked. When they lost Carlos Baleba, Jan Paul van Hecke, Danny Welbeck and James Milner over the summer, there were reasons to wonder whether they could keep going with the process of continuous renewal.

There were the usual assorted signings, the usual mix of Premier League experience and exotic unknowns. The 19-year-old centre-back Luka Vušković, who spent last season on loan at Hamburg from Tottenham, already looks at home (and who really thought, when Spurs and Brighton effectively swapped centre-backs, with Van Hecke moving to London, that Brighton would not end up with the better of the deal?). The 21-year-old Spanish midfielder Chema Andrés, who arrived from Stuttgart, sparkled from the bench against Arsenal and has excelled in the two games since.

But the stand-out performer this season has been a far more familiar name: Pascal Gross, who returned in January after a season and a half at Borussia Dortmund. No player in the Premier League has registered more than his four assists this season. Nobody has run further. He has three goals. He averages a league-high 3.0 key passes a game. To bring back a player who is now 35 has been a masterstroke.

The victory over Arsenal before the international break suggested a team capable not merely of accumulating points against the league’s lesser lights, or even of challenging the elite, but of overwhelming them. Arsenal were suffocated by the Brighton press and, while a couple of low-xG long-range finishes in the first half helped, the fact is that Brighton dominated the match to a remarkable extent.

The question is whether they can keep it going. Just as their transfer policy is now an accepted feature of the Premier League, so too is Brighton’s mid-season slump. They haven’t won a game in December since 2023. Is this squad strong enough to sustain the challenge? Europe seems not to be unsettling Brighton as it did on their first foray, or as it appears to be draining Bournemouth, Crystal Palace and Sunderland – which may be a reflection on the relative quality of the Conference League.

skip past newsletter promotion Free newsletter | Twice weekly Sign up to Soccer Desk Jonathan Wilson and Guardian journalists bring expert analysis and reporting on the biggest stories in soccer. Enter your email Sign up after newsletter promotion

They are doing this without Kaoru Mitoma, Yankuba Minteh and Mats Wieffer, all of whom should be back at some point over the next month. That suggests the depth of this Brighton squad. It’s always a major step for a club unfamiliar with the Champions League to haul themselves into the top five. At times it often feels a mental barrier as much as anything.

But if any of those B clubs are ever going to break into the Champions League, they may never have a better opportunity than Brighton do this season.

Sports.title: Villarreal’s Iñigo Pérez ready to meet Iraola again in test of old bond
Sports.content:
On Iñigo Pérez’s first day as a head coach he took a call from Andoni Iraola, just as he had every day for months. They had known each other for 22 years, lived in the same residency, come through the same academy and played in the same team; they had worked side by side, manager and assistant, and embarked on an adventure together. Now, though, Pérez was having to go it alone. At 36, he had become what his friend thought he would be from the moment they met, just not so soon. “He wished me luck and said he was there for me,” Pérez said, “said that if I ever needed anything …”

Well, maybe not anything.

“Sometimes life brings what you never imagined,” Pérez said after his coaching debut. Now he is off to Anfield. It’s funny the way it goes. Had he not been denied a work permit by the Home Office, had a Football Association panel not declared him incapable of contributing to English football, a partnership broken and a family turned back, a career seemingly derailed from the start, Villarreal’s manager wouldn’t be sitting on the bench to the left of the halfway line at Anfield tonight. He would be sitting on the bench to the right.

This time, the man who should have been Iraola’s assistant is instead his opponent, nothing given for 90 minutes. “I’m looking forward to seeing him; we speak continuously, always there,” Pérez says. “To encounter each other pitchside is emotional. When the referee blows, it all ends, but it’s a very nice story.”

The story starts in 2002, when Pérez arrived at Athletic Club Bilbao’s academy, aged 14. Iraola was 19, six months from his first‑team debut. They first played together in the first team in October 2009 but, teenagers and tenants, something had already drawn them together and would do again. If Pérez was more open, Iraola more private, timid even, there was much they shared: an inquisitive mind, an ability to observe and listen, a humility befitting a club where presumptuousness is prohibited.

“Intellectually they’re brilliant,” says a teammate from that time, Carlos Gurpegui, intelligent a word that keeps coming back and with warmth too. “Andoni had a privileged mind and Iñigo was so intuitive. We played [Fantasy Football] and Andoni always won,” the goalkeeper Raúl Fernández recalls.

View image in fullscreen Iñigo Pérez celebrates a goal with Athletic Bilbao teammates, including Andoni Iraola (second left) in the Europa League in March 2012. Photograph: Dennis Grombkowski/Bongarts/Getty Images

If that gave them natural leadership, it was worn lightly, not imposed. As one coach notes: “If everyone was going left and Andoni said: ‘Go right,’ they’d all be like: ‘Yeah, yeah, go right!’ They are two unusually intelligent guys, always rationalising, able to reach others.”

Iraola saw it in the kid coming through, ideas explored together. “Iñigo was always aware of tactical [shifts],” he said later. “At 14 or 15, the way he thought about the game was mature. Ever since I knew Iñigo, I thought he had the personality to be a coach. In fact, he had a clearer idea about being a coach than I did.”

David López, who played alongside them, says: “It’s no surprise they became coaches.” Eneko Bóveda, who came through the academy with Pérez, says: “They might have become coaches individually; together, they were bound to. Iñigo was extremely impressive in personal relationships, inside every dressing‑room circle: emotionally intelligent, empathetic.”

The age difference was no barrier, a product of their place, the communal culture that made them. “When we reached the first team, that generation [above] was established, but it was very easy to talk to them, even take life advice,” recalls Fernández, born in 1988, like Pérez. “I remember asking Andoni what to do about my contract. Under Marcelo Bielsa, the players would come together before games with a hot chocolate, a croissant and talk. Bielsa was super‑demanding, always at your throat; we took refuge in each other.”

Pérez might not have been there at all, unwanted by Bielsa until the training session when he crashed into the goalkeeper Gorka Iraizoz. “There was blood everywhere, his lip split open, but Iñigo carries on and Marcelo thinks: ‘I can follow this guy to the end of the world,’” Gurpegui recalls. Picturing the scene, Fernández starts laughing: “Iñigo didn’t know what would happen to him. I seem to remember him even sleeping at Lezama [the training ground] on a mattress, which showed how committed he was. And that day Bielsa was shouting at the physios: ‘Leave him! Leave him! He wants to carry on!’ He’s going to Iñigo: ‘Bravo! Bravo! That’s it, lad!’”

An opportunity opened at full‑back and Pérez did what he always did: adapted. Above all, they observed, took it all in. “Iñigo and I would speak a lot about the way Bielsa coached,” Iraola recalled. They would ask endless questions of assistants Claudio Vivas, Pablo Quiroga and Diego Reyes, always wanting to know why. “But then they’re football nutcases who learned from everything,” Boveda says.

View image in fullscreen Andoni Iraola, then at Bournemouth, invited Iñigo Pérez and his Rayo Vallecano side to England for a pre-season friendly in August 2024. Photograph: Robin Jones/AFC Bournemouth/Getty Images

Their last game together was in October 2013. Iraola retired in 2016 and started coaching two years later. Unseen, Pérez was drifting in the same direction. Common friends and a shared agent meant they were never far away and in February 2022 they crossed paths again. Pérez didn’t play when Osasuna won 3-0 at Rayo but their conversation that night stuck in Iraola’s mind, a mental note made.

Aged 34, Pérez had told Iraola his role now was really about helping the coaches. Indeed, Osasuna’s manager Jagoba Arrasate was already referring to him as a “player-assistant coach” and soon invited him to join the staff. Bielsa approached him too, furious when Pérez turned down Uruguay. When Iraola heard Pérez was retiring, he called immediately, convincing him to come to Rayo. The assistant coach Unai Mendia was leaving and his old teammate was perfect. The impression made was immediate: “Iñigo’s top,” a member of Rayo’s coaching staff says. “He was special, a phenomenon. Super‑elite, like Andoni.”

skip past newsletter promotion Free newsletter | Every weekday Sign up to Football Daily Kick off your evenings with the Guardian's take on the world of football Enter your email Sign up after newsletter promotion

Together with the fitness coach Pablo de la Torre, who constructed a physical model around which the whole, wild ride was built, they were a revelation, practitioners of organised chaos. Nowhere was football more fun, a shared vision soon enticed to the Premier League.

“When we found out that Andoni was leaving for Bournemouth, I told Iñigo he should be our head coach,” the Rayo striker Sergio Camello recalls, and the club hierarchy agreed. Pérez, though, thought it would be morally wrong: this was Iraola’s construction, not his to take. Besides, he wanted to continue with his friend. Iraola wanted that as well, taking only two staff to England: Pérez and De la Torre. It was a new start, a new life, and he needed his partners there.

But then Pérez was denied a work permit. Bournemouth took it to an FA exceptions panel. Supporting letters were sent, a case made. Iraola wrote, too, explaining their history and describing Pérez as “fundamental”. The panel, though, remained unsatisfied that he was “of the highest calibre and able to contribute significantly to the development of the game at the top level in England”.

“We did everything we could,” Pérez said, which was true: they even requested a permit as youth‑team coach, earning a telling off for trying it on. As he awaited a final resolution, Pérez kept working: he couldn’t wear a club tracksuit, appear publicly or sit on the bench, but he was at the training ground daily. Until, in the late autumn, they had to admit defeat. That hurt, personally as much as professionally. “It was very difficult, an uncomfortable situation for all of us,” Iraola says. “You can’t [work], you can’t put your kids in school.”

Between them, Shaun Cooper, Tommy Elphick and De la Torre had to assimilate Pérez’s duties, Iraola impressed and grateful at the staff he inherited. His tourist visa expiring, Pérez returned to Spain. Calls from Bournemouth continued, some consultation and a lot of conversation, not always about football. Then when Rayo sacked Francisco Rodríguez in early 2024, the club offered him the manager’s job again. Iraola encouraged Pérez to go for it. “In the summer, I didn’t feel ethically comfortable and I wanted to continue with Andoni,” Pérez said. “The circumstances changed.”

View image in fullscreen Iñigo Pérez shows the way during Villarreal’s Champions League 3-2 defeat against Borussia Dortmund in September 2026. Photograph: Jürgen Fromme/firo sportphoto/Getty Images

Camello admits: “I think the transition from assistant to head coach here was hard. He had been so close to us. Iñigo loved us too much: he felt so responsible for us that the inevitable frictions as No 1 were taken to heart. But he opened up to us, reached us. The relationship is still so good: he messaged me yesterday with some bands to listen to. And I doubt I’ll ever come across someone so capable in football terms. It’s amazing how many solutions he gives you on the pitch. Seeing him and Andoni in the Champions League doesn’t surprise. They have no limits; we’re just grateful that two monsters coached us.”

Their paths had separated, but the courses set were similar, the styles too. “My football belongs to Andoni,” Pérez said. Chaos still reigned many miles away and only a phone call apart. Iraola took Bournemouth to Europe for the first time; Pérez achieved Rayo’s first European qualification, and led them to the only final in their history. This summer greater challenges awaited, so here they are at Anfield, where there is relief that a friend’s career was not ruined but rather launched. “I am so, so happy for Iñigo,” one staffer says, “because you want good things to happen to good people and he’s very, very good people.”

They will watch in Bilbao, where it all began. “It’s special: I’m so proud of them,” says López. Gurpegui says: “Iñigo suffered in England but that situation opened another opportunity and now look: Andoni at Anfield. Bloody hell, I’m so pleased, because they’re two incredible people: humble, always there when you need them. Football needs more people like that.” Fernández adds: “And knowing them, it will be fun too: bold, brave football, a great game.”

Iraola says: “These games aren’t good for your relationship. We usually talk a lot but when you’re facing each other you talk less. It’s a special game because he’s my friend. He knows me very well. We’ve been through a lot together.”

Sports.title: Konsa bullish about Arsenal’s Champions League hopes as Bayern clash looms
Sports.content:
For Ezri Konsa, it was just a wonderfully satisfying challenge. The Nottingham Forest striker Liam Delap had stolen in behind him up the inside left channel on Sunday. There were 93 minutes gone, Arsenal were 1-0 up and it was now or never for Forest. Konsa decreed that it would be never, curving his covering run back, matching Delap for pace and stretching into the perfect block tackle.

So, another win for Arsenal: their 10th in 11 matches this season. Another clean sheet. And for Konsa, a continuation of what has been a dreamlike couple of months. Do points-saving last-minute challenges mean more when the defender is actually a fan of the club, too? Basically, yes.

“I’ve been asked this a lot,” Konsa says with a smile, when the subject of his boyhood allegiance is raised. “And, yes, I was [an Arsenal supporter]. I had a lot of Arsenal kits when I was younger. You dream of playing for big clubs like this. When you’re a kid, you see the likes of Arsenal, growing up, and the amount of quality players they’ve had throughout the years and to be here – and not only to be here but to be here with close friends – makes it even more special.”

Konsa is talking about Eberechi Eze, in particular; another boyhood Arsenal fan, with whom he is especially tight. Many supporters have seen the clip of Eze greeting Konsa at the training ground after the latter had completed his £51m move from Aston Villa and how they crack up with laughter before embracing. It is infectious. But Konsa knows a clutch of other Arsenal players from England duty – Declan Rice, Bukayo Saka, Noni Madueke, Myles Lewis-Skelly, Ben White – and he credits them with helping him to settle in.

The 28-year-old’s adaptation has been quick and it has needed to be with William Saliba injured. After making his Arsenal debut as a substitute at Villa – Konsa’s scriptwriters have been hard at work – he has played in every minute of the club’s Premier League and Champions League matches. The victory at Forest, where Arsenal had drawn 0-0 in each of the previous two seasons, was significant. It was not a performance of any attacking pace or spark. Perhaps it made the points feel more precious.

“We hadn’t won here in two seasons, the boss was going on about it,” Konsa says. “It’s something we wanted to change as players and these are the games you have to win. If you want to win titles, you have to come away to tough places like this and get three points.”

View image in fullscreen Ezri Konsa does battle with Liam Delap during Arsenal’s 1-0 win at Nottingham Forest. Photograph: Tom Jenkins/The Guardian

Things are about to get even more interesting for Konsa and Arsenal because on Wednesday they face Bayern Munich at the Allianz Arena in the Champions League. “It’s against my international teammate as well,” Konsa says, and he is straight into an appreciation of Harry Kane, the England captain, who has been on fire since joining Bayern from Tottenham in 2023. Kane’s scoring record for the club bears repeating: 155 goals in 157 appearances.

Konsa has a good record against Kane, having faced him seven times, six of them for Villa against Spurs. The seventh and most recent came in October 2024 when Konsa was in the Villa team that beat Kane’s Bayern 1-0 at Villa Park in the Champions League. It was Villa’s first home match in the competition for 41 years. The defender has four wins against Kane’s teams and three losses. Kane has only scored twice against him, both from penalties.

“The Villa-Bayern game … to beat them at home and keep a clean sheet … it was very special for the players and the fans,” Konsa says. “I don’t really look much at those kind of stats [against individual players] but I am relishing the challenge.”

skip past newsletter promotion Free newsletter | Every weekday Sign up to Football Daily Kick off your evenings with the Guardian's take on the world of football Enter your email Sign up after newsletter promotion

The dynamics against Bayern appear different for Konsa this time. It was a famous victory for Villa that night, in part because of the tie’s history; the club beat Bayern 1-0 in the 1982 European Cup final. Villa were underdogs as they felt their way back into Europe’s elite competition. Arsenal will kick off as Bayern’s equals and among the favourites to win the tournament, having lost on penalties to Paris Saint-Germain in last season’s final.

Konsa won the first trophy of his career a week before that when he was in the Villa team that defeated Freiburg in the Europa League final. He says he has felt the determination of the Arsenal squad to go one step further in Europe.

“One hundred per cent,” Konsa says. “As players, the standards we have, the goals we have … we want to win everything – the Champions League, the Prem. Whatever trophies are in front of us. When I came to Arsenal, I wanted to win. I was hungry to win. Last season I got my hands on the Europa League and this season I want more.”

Sports.title: Football Australia chair Anter Isaac dismisses recent Fifa ructions as ‘growing pains’
Sports.content:
Football Australia chair Anter Isaac has played down concerns around the controversial World Cup privatisation push engineered by Gianni Infantino ahead of a meeting of Asian confederation officials in Tokyo this week.

Isaac’s sentiments come amid a global rebound in support for the embattled Fifa president, who at one stage appeared unlikely to be able to continue in his role following criticism led by officials in Europe and North America.

The Swiss lawyer now enjoys backing from South America, Africa and growing chunks of Asia, which would represent a bloc large enough for him to win March’s Fifa presidential election.

Continental powerbrokers are converging on Tokyo this week for the Asian Football Confederation congress. Fifa’s leadership and governance do not form part of the formal meeting agenda, but will be discussed by those present alongside the likelihood of January’s Asian Cup in Saudi Arabia going ahead.

Isaac, the most senior football official in Australia, was asked about the situation at Fifa in an episode of a little-known sports business You Tube channel earlier this month that has been viewed fewer than 200 times.

“We can look at it and be unsophisticated and say, what a mess,” he told Beyond the Game with Dillon and Rafael. “Or we can take a more responsible, mature view and say, you know what, these are growing pains.”

Isaac pointed out that Fifa’s revenues have exploded in recent World Cup cycles, and “systems and processes” at the organisation may not have kept pace. He was adamant that the intentions and motivations of people in football are “always in the best interests” of the sport.

“Maybe it’s not always aligned, but everyone involved in football really does want that, right? Everyone, at least in my experience and my interactions with them, that’s not even a question. So where has it become misaligned? Maybe it is in approach, maybe in communications and so forth.”

View image in fullscreen FA chair Anter Isaac spoke to a little-known podcast about the situation at Fifa. Photograph: Mark Metcalfe/Getty Images for Football Australia

FA’s previous statement on the controversial proposal dubbed Fifa Forward Enterprise (FFE), issued in August, called for “clear and credible action” but stopped short of calling for Infantino’s resignation.

It was broadly in line with a letter co-signed by Asian Football Confederation president Sheikh Salman bin Ibrahim Al Khalifa which demanded from Fifa “leadership that serves football, not seeks to command it”.

Since then Salman appears to have softened his stance against Infantino, instead calling for strengthened Fifa governance, as a growing bloc of Asian nations including Qatar and the UAE indicate support for the Fifa president.

Isaac said people will criticise bodies like Fifa, AFC and Uefa but will not have the same knowledge of those within the system.

skip past newsletter promotion Free newsletter | Weekly Sign up to Football Desk Australia 

“If I had the same information that most critics or the general public have, I would probably draw the same conclusions as them. But I don’t. I have a lot more information. I see a lot more that happens,” he said.

“So when I reflect on Fifa and major institutions in football, I see a lot of the incredible work that they do, that confederations do, even our association [does], that goes unnoticed in supporting and serving and servicing different stakeholders, especially the ones that need the greatest help.”

Uefa sent a letter to Fifa this week asking it to explain the proposed sale of 20% of its commercial rights under the now-abandoned FFE, the Folarin Balogun affair and relations with Donald Trump.

The missive follows last week’s meeting of the Fifa council in Zurich, the first since FFE came to light. Infantino listened to questions there, but declined to provide comprehensive answers, and called for questions in writing to be submitted before the next meeting in Doha on 16 December.

Isaac said it was “premature” to talk about whether he would support Infantino at next year’s election. While he noted he has his “own views” – and he wanted to avoid being openly critical himself – he sees criticism of Fifa’s president as largely about “process”.

“I’ve been encouraged that, right across the board, everyone is now focusing on that [process] with a view to, OK, let’s try and diagnose, what maybe could have been done differently or better, so that in future – and we codify it – so that in future we avoid it and what’s happened in this particular situation.”

Sports.title: Where to watch Liverpool vs Villarreal? TV channel and how to follow Champions League clash for FREE
Sports.content:

Where to watch Liverpool vs Villarreal? TV channel and how to follow Champions League clash for FREE

Liverpool take on Villarreal in the Champions League this evening, and you can watch it for FREE.

3 Liverpool have scored eight goals across their opening two Champions League games Credit: Getty

Andoni Iraola couldn't have wished for a better start to his first season in the Champions League with an impressive 2-1 win over Atletico Madrid followed by a 6-3 victory against LASK.

Listen talkSPORT through the website or find us on DAB digital radio through your smart speaker and on 1089 or 1053 AM.

Download and listen to all our live commentaries via the talkSPORT app, whilst talkSPORT is also available to watch on Samsung TV Plus.

Subscribe to the talkSPORT YouTube channel for news, views and analysis plus our regular goals show and for more, 



For the latest odds and bet boosts for every big event, visit talkSPORT BET.

Liverpool vs Villarreal: Team news

The Reds were boosted by the return to fitness of Alexander Isak at the weekend, who scored in the 2-1 win over Brentford.

Cody Gakpo is also fit as well, so the Reds are starting to look better in attack.

However, just as two return, they lose another two.

Dominik Szoboszlai limped off at the weekend with his hamstring problem flaring up again.



And he is joined on the sidelines by Jeremie Frimpong, who has suffered a muscle issue as well.

Ryan Gravenberch was suspended for the win at the Gtech, so he'll probably start due to being fully rested.

3 Szoboszlai is facing a spell out of action Credit: AFP

Liverpool vs Villarreal: What has been said?

Despite missing a few opportunities, Iraola was impressed by Barcola's performance and was happy his side beat ten-man Brentford.



Speaking after the game, he said: “I think we played really well the minute until we scored for 2-1 against 10 players.

“I think we were being patient, we were finding good positions and we were controlling the game really well. I’m probably more disappointed after we scored, because you score for 2-1 and then you feel like you have something to lose.

“We were playing freely, finding good spots, sending a lot of players forward. And then at 2-1 we missed clear counters to finish the game.

“Bradley, I think he has missed clear chances. On another day he scores three.



“But I love that he’s having so many chances and being in those situations.”

Sports.title: Transfer Notebook: Man United striker target keen on January move from rival Premier League club
Sports.content:
Jean-Philippe Mateta would be keen on a move to Manchester United in January, sources have told talkSPORT.

Crystal Palace could be forced to cash in on Mateta mid-season with the Frenchman showing no inclination to extend his contract, which expires in the summer.



3 Mateta is keen to leave Crystal Palace and could finally get his exit in January - 12 months after his collapsed transfer to AC Milan Credit: Getty

Man United have considered Mateta in the past and the 29-year-old is one of the more viable options if they decide to bring in another striker.

Benjamin Sesko’s ongoing injury absence means Michael Carrick has been having to play without a recognised No.9.

There is said to be an acceptance among the United hierarchy they could have done more to address that lack of squad depth in the summer transfer window.



Mateta has played just 92 Premier League minutes this season due to a hamstring injury.

Chelsea star admired by rivals to get new deal

Chelsea are set to hand defender Josh Acheampong a bumper new contract.



Acheampong, 20, has featured in six of Chelsea’s seven Premier League games this season.

The Blues rejected offers from clubs in England and Europe in the summer after declaring the England Under-21 star ‘untouchable’.



Sources have told talkSPORT Manchester United were among the clubs who made enquiries for Acheampong.

His current deal expires in 2029, but he is expected to be the next player to be offered the chance to commit his long-term future to Stamford Bridge.

If a deal is agreed, Acheampong would follow in the footsteps of Cole Palmer and Moises Caicedo who recently penned new deals with the Blues.

3 Acheampong is highly-rated at Chelsea, who are keen to tie down the England U21 star's future Credit: Getty



Big clubs on alert over in-form Brighton star

Brighton may have started the season in tremendous form, but doubts remain over the future of one of their star players.

Yasin Ayari produced another stellar performance as the Seagulls thrashed arch-rivals Crystal Palace 5-0 on Sunday.

Only Barcelona have scored more goals than Fabian Hurzeler’s men in the top five major European leagues.

However, Ayari is out of contract at the end of the season and there are fears he will not sign a new deal.



That has put the likes of Manchester United and Arsenal on alert while Italian giants AC Milan are also said to be fans of the 23-year-old playmaker.

Brighton do have the option of an extra year on Ayari’s deal, which would at least increase his value in the transfer market.

3 Ayari's bright start to the season with Brighton has attracted plenty of interested glances from rival teams Credit: Getty

New Toon Massiah cometh?

Newcastle are monitoring Ghanaian teenager Dyeidu Massiah, talkSPORT understands.



Massiah is on the radar of a number of top European sides after starring for UAE side Forte Virtus.

The 19-year-old forward has scored four goals in his first five games after joining the Middle Eastern side in July.

Massiah fits Newcastle's business model of investing in up-and-coming young players.

Sports.title: Man City’s appeal process facing complications as new concerns emerge
Sports.content:
Manchester City's appeal against their Financial Fair Play ruling could become a drawn out process, a financial expert has warned.

The Premier League giants have challenged an Independent Commission's guilty verdict.

4 City's appeal hearing could significantly delay any potential sanctions Credit: Getty

It was announced last month that City had been found guilty of all charges related to alleged breaches between 2009 and 2018.

Reports emerged this week that the club were facing a huge points deduction which would see them spend multiple seasons in the Championship.

The rumoured punishment comes amid suggestions the sanction hearing will run simultaneously to City's appeal process.

Football finance expert Stefan Borson has warned this will slow down the outcome, with complications arising from the two hearings happening at the same time.

How soon could City's sanctions be decided?

Speaking to White & Jordan on Tuesday, he explained: "I think it's quite hard to know exactly where we are in the whole order of process because the appeal may or may not go before a sanction hearing.

"It seems to me it would be sensible for the parties to agree that the appeal to the liability part i.e. how many of the 115 (charges) City have breached, that appeal would take place before we have a sanction hearing.

"Now, there's also just the practical aspect of actually getting the same people to go through two separate processes.

"So, the sanction hearing will have both sides' legal teams presenting, based on the independent commission's findings, their position on sanction. That will be the starting point and also the mitigating and aggravating factors.

"That in itself is a process that needs preparation and time for the lawyers. What I don't think can happen is a situation where they try and run both processes simultaneously.

"The preparation time required for the full appeal of the liability phase, i.e. whether they have done it or not, that to me can't be run while they're also being distracted on a sanction hearing.

4 Reports claim City are set for a huge points deduction following their FFP breaches Credit: Getty

"There's a lot of talk about how this is going to go quick. It just seems to me that it's very unlikely that that's the case."

Will City accept sanctions before appeal verdict?

Borson's explanation prompted Simon Jordan to question whether it would be better for the procedure to focus on liability before moving on to any sanctions.

His argument pinpointed that City would not accept any sanctions as they would be an admission of guilt.

In response, Borson added: "The problem everyone has got is that there's a lot of pressure for this to be done and dusted now, which is understandable of course.

"But what it misses is, the Premier League are pushing the briefing that the latest rulebook applies in that the hearing can happen in 12 weeks and there's a decision very quickly and the hearing itself is only five days.

"I think that is very unlikely to be the case. Certainly, the parties do not agree at this point, so there's going to have to be a hearing even to decide that part."

4 The Premier League giants have appealed against the Independent Commission's ruling Credit: Getty

He continued: "Generally in terms of process, it would make sense for them to deal with liability, then for it to be passed back for sanction, City will then inevitably, if found to have breached any of the 115, appeal the commission's sanction hearing.

"So there's still a process and that's why I think the idea that it can all be squashed into the remaining part of the season, although in a logical sense there's loads of time left, the reality is we're on October 20, and there are probably 1,000 pages in that decision.

"And City have already said that their approach on appeal is going to be forensic and not only look at law, principle, but also on the facts of the case."

Timeframe for potential City sanctions

His comments come after the Daily Mail reported City were set for a points deduction which would guarantee they were relegated from the top-flight.

The Premier League is pushing for the club to receive a significant points deduction, talkSPORT understands.

However, Borson admitted: "They're saying they're going to get on with things as much as possible, but what I'm saying is, my information is things are not all rosy and agreed between the parties about rule books, about processes, about staging.

4 City fans could be set for a lengthy wait to discover their fate Credit: Getty

"Therefore, there's going to have to be hearings that decide the order of events and most importantly the timing that is going to be allocated to each bit of the process.

"It would not surprise me, for example, if instead of five days of appeal for the liability part, we need four weeks minimum.

"These are very, very serious matters, very, very serious findings so far from the Independent Commission, but City will say that fairness demands they are given as much time as necessary in that appeal process to go through all of their arguments."

As for whether there is anything that could stop the Premier League handing out sanctions now, he concluded: "I think so. If it was something that is irreversible i.e. relegating them and then being corrected later, City would argue that was irreparable damage.

"Therefore I think it's unlikely any sanction is implemented before the expiry of the appeal process on sanction.

"So I do think that it seems to me that you have to go through the various stages, they do have to complete those appeals before the actual punishment is laid down on City. I just can't see any other way.

"City will say that until the appeal has been decided, there is risk of irreparable harm and I think that's something they will accept."

Sports.title: I agree with Graeme Souness – Bukayo Saka is a cheat and I refuse to watch Arsenal now
Sports.content:
I agree with Graeme Souness – Bukayo Saka is a cheat and I refuse to watch Arsenal now

Gabby Agbonlahor is officially fed up with Arsenal.

The Gunners laboured to a 1-0 win over Nottingham Forest on Sunday, marking the 32nd time they'd won by that scoreline in the league since Mikel Arteta's appointment in December 2019.

3 Arsenal's win over Forest ensured they kept pace with Manchester City in the Premier League Credit: Getty

It was far from a vintage performance by Arsenal as Noni Madueke's goal was their only shot on target despite boasting 74 per cent possession.

Gabby Agbonlahor's brutal verdict on Arsenal

Such was the nature of Sunday's snoozefest, Agbonlahor revealed on talkSPORT Breakfast he will actively avoid watching Arsenal games for the foreseeable future.

"I was bored, I was not entertained," Agbonlahor said.

"It was slow... that's not entertaining football.

"It makes me think to myself, the next time Arsenal are on, no thank you.

"Out of all the games this week in the Champions League, Arsenal is not the game I will be watching. For me, they're no closer to winning the Champions League."

Arsenal legend Martin Keown also hit back at the suggestion the Gunners are now the 'unwatchables'.

"Keown told White and Jordan: “It wasn't the best spectacle in the world, but ultimately Arsenal are different to the narrative being spun.

"But I would suggest that maybe it's the undeniables, because they will not be denied.

“They'll find a way to win a game. They've won 10 of the last 11 games and I can't even believe it's a topic. It's a topic because someone's trying to coin a phrase, basically.”.

Gabby Agbonlahor claims Bukayo Saka 'throws himself on the floor'

Agbonlahor was also highly critical of Bukayo Saka, who Graeme Souness labelled a 'cheat' for going down to easily.

However, the Aston Villa legend added it's a league-wide problem rather than being isolated to Saka.

"When I watch Saka, fantastic player, (but) I think he's limited and could never be an elite player like Lamine Yamal or [Michael] Olise," Agbonlahor said.

"But he does throw himself on the floor.

3 Saka consistently draws more fouls than the majority of his rivals Credit: Getty

"But he's not the only one. It's the majority of Premier League players now. Any little touch, rolling around on the floor.

"I am seeing more and more referees not giving it.

"But Saka, I agree with Graeme Souness, he does like to throw himself on the floor."

What are the stats behind Bukayo Saka being fouled?

Per Squawka, Saka is the second-most fouled player in the Premier League this term, having won 21 fouls.

Only Elliot Anderson (23) has been fouled more.

But Saka hasn't let the constant fouling stop him.

3 Saka has already scored nearly half of his league tally from last season (7) Credit: Getty

The silky winger, who signed a bumper contract extension in February, has scored three league goals for the Gunners this term.

It is a team-leading figure and one that underlines Saka's importance, especially with his strike against Aston Villa securing all three points.

Saka will now look to help preserve Arsenal's perfect Champions League record on Wednesday when they visit Bayern Munich, with kick-off scheduled for 8pm.

Sports.title: Cesc Fabregas would only leave Como in two major scenarios amid top club interest
Sports.content:
Cesc Fabregas would only leave Como in two major scenarios amid top club interest

Andy Brassell believes it would take a season on either end of the success spectrum for Cesc Fabregas to leave Como.

Fabregas' appointment as manager in July 2024 has proved transformative for the Italian club.



3 Fabregas has taken to managerial life like a duck to water Credit: Getty

After steering Como to 10th in their first Serie A campaign in 21 years, Fabregas oversaw a remarkable 2025/26 season in which they qualified for the Champions League by finishing 4th and reached the Coppa Italia semi-finals.

Fabregas' work has not gone unnoticed by clubs around Europe, as the likes of Bayer Leverkusen, RB Leipzig and Inter Milan all made approaches but were rebuffed.

With Fabregas' stock continuing to rise at a rapid rate, his name is almost certain to feature as a potential contender to take over at a faltering European behemoth.



But that's not the only scenario that could spark an exit from Como for Fabregas.

How Cesc Fabregas could end up leaving Como

"I think for him to leave Como next summer, one of two things is going to happen," European football expert Brassell told talkSPORT.com.



"Either it's going to go disastrously wrong, the calendar catches up with them and they bottom out in the league. By the way, I think that's a very unlikely scenario.

"Or scenario two, where it goes so well that they're still in the top four of Serie A and they get to the semi-finals of the Champions League playing dazzling football.



"So all of a sudden, a couple of absolutely enormous clubs come through the door and say, 'Right, you're the one for us.' When I say enormous clubs, I'm talking about maybe not Barcelona or Arsenal levels, of course they're happy with their current coaches, but that sort of level."

Ultimately, Brassell believes the likeliest scenario for Fabregas is that Como enjoy a berth in the Champions League knockout stages and perform well in Serie A, ultimately ending in the Spanish great remaining at the club for another term.

Although it may not represent an eye-catching season, Fabregas successfully juggling a domestic and European campaign at Como would be another step in the right direction for his managerial career.

3 Fabregas was named the Serie A Coach of the Year last season Credit: Getty



Why it could be difficult for clubs to prise Cesc Fabregas away from Como

Another element tying Fabregas to Como is his status as a shareholder in the club.

Fabregas became a shareholder in Como when he signed on as a player in August 2022.

It points to a relationship that runs deeper than Fabregas simply being a manager, as Brassell described the Spaniard being 'fully invested, emotionally and financially' in the project.

"He knows he's got time, he knows he's got patience, he knows he's got incredible resource," Brassell added.



"Why would you walk away from that if you were him?"

One club who may attempt to prise Fabregas away from Como, even amid his deep roots at the club, is Manchester United.

3 Could Carrick's dugout rival on Wednesday be his future replacement? Credit: Getty

Red Devils boss Michael Carrick is feeling the heat amid having overseen the club's worst-ever start to a Premier League campaign.

However, Carrick has the opportunity to claw back some momentum when he tests his managerial wit against Fabregas on Wednesday as United visit Como in Champions League action.



Both sides have begun their respective Champions League campaigns with a win and a defeat.

Yet a second defeat for United, especially against Fabregas' Como, could spark serious worries for Carrick's future.

Sports.title: Trent Alexander-Arnold reaches new Real Madrid low but warned against January transfer
Sports.content:
Trent Alexander-Arnold has been warned against leaving Real Madrid in January despite his struggles to break into the team.

The England international was an unused substitute at the weekend in Los Blancos' 4-1 win over Sevilla.



3 The dream move to Real Madrid hasn't quite worked out for Alexander-Arnold Credit: Getty

This was because Jose Mourinho selected midfielder Federico Valverde to play at right-back, with Endrick on the right wing.

Alexander-Arnold watched on from the substitutes bench along with Denzel Dumfries.

The former Liverpool star has started just three LaLiga games this season and has completed 90 minutes only once.



His one appearance in the Champions League saw him play in midfield, and he was left on the bench for the remarkable 3-2 comeback win over Roma.

Despite his lack of minutes and being benched for a midfielder, European football expert Andy Brassell isn't sure he should be considering a winter move away from the Bernabeu.



Speaking exclusively to talkSPORT.com, he said: "It is up to him, but so much of it depends on how much he plays between now and Christmas because if he only gets a couple of starts, he might think he's wasting his time.

"But no one often gets their dream move in January. You can probably count brilliant January signings on one hand.



"It is rare you get a player that hits the ground straightaway.

"But if playing time is that scant, I guess he will make a call in January."

However, the real concern is that Brassell believes Dumfries is the favoured right-back anyway.

"I think longer term, and when you think about their biggest game of the season [Barcelona], he's going for Denzel Dumfries.

"He is a very different attacking right-back to Trent and is much more Mourinho's cup of tea.



"So, he might have to think about things at the end of the season. Is he getting enough game time? Is he happy to be a bit-part player?

"The answer is probably no, so he needs to work out somewhere he really fits the tactics and the culture.

"He has had a lot of things go against him that isn't his fault because Valverde stepping in, though tactically viable, is an indicator of if there is ever some luck to be had, Trent is not the receiver of it."

3 Despite his lack of minutes and not making the World Cup squad, Alexander-Arnold was back in the England squad for the Nations League Credit: Getty



Why did Valverde play over Alexander-Arnold?

Valverde has played right-back before, but Brassell believes that the Uruguayan's role at the weekend was due to the presence of Endrick in the team.

He said: "I think you have to look at the shape of Real Madrid, and you've got to look at Vinicius Junior being out due to suspension.

"And for that reason, Endrick comes into the team, and I really like him as a right-sided winger, but there are off-the-ball implications, and you probably need a right-back who is a really good defender, and let's be honest, that is not Trent Alexander-Arnold or Denzel Dumfries.

"I think Valverde in, for this particular game, made sense. It is easy to look at it from the view of, 'if he can't get in ahead of a midfielder, what hope is there for him', but I think it is just the situation.



"I have never thought Trent defended as badly as some people say, but it is not his primary focus, and he gets caught out, so I think it is more than reasonable for Mourinho to make this call."

3 His Real Madrid contract expires in 2031 Credit: Getty

Alexander-Arnold's time at Real Madrid

After being with Liverpool his whole career, the right-back's contract ran down at Anfield, and Real Madrid agreed to sign him for nothing.

They then paid the Reds around £10million to get him in for the Club World Cup under Xabi Alonso.



He played five games but missed the 4-0 thrashing by Paris Saint-Germain due to injury.

And that was just the beginning, as last season, he only played in LaLiga 21 times.

Two separate injuries and the presence of Dani Carvajal ensured that he was in and out of the team.

And now that Mourinho is in charge, he's competing with Dumfries and Valverde for one position on the pitch.



Of course, he can play midfield, but again, there is a lot of competition for two positions.

Sports.title: What time is Como vs Manchester United? Red Devils winless in six as pressure builds on Carrick
Sports.content:
What time is Como vs Manchester United? Red Devils winless in six as pressure builds on Carrick

Manchester United take on Como this week in the Champions League's early slate of games, and it's live on talkSPORT 2.

The draw with Leeds United at Elland Road means the Red Devils are now winless in six, and it is their worst start to a Premier League season.



3 Michael Carrick has struggled to get a tune out of his side Credit: AFP

It was in the Champions League they recorded their last win, a 4-0 victory over minnows Sabah.

Last week, they were beaten 2-0 by Atletico Madrid, and overall, things aren't great for United.

Como are probably one of the last teams they want to face at this moment in time.



That is because Cesc Fabregas' side are an aggressive, athletic unit that are performing well in Serie A and have one Champions League win under their belt.

talkSPORT.com will also have updates in our live blog, and the game will be shown on TNT Sports as well.

Subscribe to the talkSPORT YouTube channel for news, views and analysis plus our regular goals show and for more, 

For the latest odds and bet boosts for every big event, visit talkSPORT BET.



3 Fabregas is widely seen as one of the best young managers in the game Credit: Getty

Como vs Man United team news

The visitors will be without Leny Yoro after he was sent off in the defeat to Atletico last week.

Luke Shaw and Kobbie Mainoo played no part at Elland Road and face late fitness tests.

Ayden Heaven should be available following illness, and he might come in for Lisandro Martinez.

3 Everything at Man United is stake at the moment Credit: Getty

Fabregas eyes 'extraordinary gift'

Fabregas can't wait to put his side up against Man United.

He said: "Getting ready for such wonderful games is fantastic but we must never forget that Serie A is the most important thing for us.



"For us, every day is an important step in our growth.

"We are a new club-not in terms of our history, but because we started from scratch three years ago. Consequently, we have to be careful in how we manage a great many situations.

"We've arrived here [Champions League] five years ahead of schedule.

"The Champions League is an extraordinary gift that came after last year's magnificent season.

"The Champions League is the toughest competition there is-at a higher level even than the World Cup or the European Championship."

Sports.title: Erik ten Hag eviscerates Cristiano Ronaldo with bombshell claims – ‘he let his team down’
Sports.content:
Erik ten Hag accused Cristiano Ronaldo of putting in minimal effort during his second stint at Manchester United.

Ten Hag launched the scathing attack on the Portuguese superstar's professionalism in a wide-ranging interview with The Athletic.



3 Ten Hag lasted over two years at Old Trafford before he was ultimately axed Credit: Getty

The pair's turbulent relationship lasted just 16 games at United as Ronaldo eventually fled to Saudi Arabian club Al-Nassr in December 2022.

Prior to Ten Hag's arrival in the summer of 2022, he held talks with Ronaldo in Portugal about how he planned to restore the club to its former glories.

But it took just two Premier League fixtures for the alarm bells regarding Ronaldo's professionalism to sound.



Following a 4-0 loss to Brentford, Ten Hag attempted to ram home his side's lack of effort by making them run laps.

However, Ten Hag, who ran the laps with his players, claimed Ronaldo finished one lap early.



Ronaldo's lack of effort soon became a recurring theme in training and, worryingly, during matches.

What did Erik ten Hag say about Cristiano Ronaldo's professionalism?

"I confronted him with this," Ten Hag, who is now the technical director at FC Twente, said.



"Many times I say, 'Ronnie, everyone wants to work for you to bring you in the right position, but if you can't bring yourself in the box, you can't score.'

"He was not capable to do this. It's the wrong idea to put this to me that I expected him to do the pressing, that he's exhausted. But he couldn't. He ran neither in possession nor out of possession.

"The reason was because he didn't prepare himself."

3 Ronaldo didn't do his United legacy any favours in the manner with which he left Credit: Getty

Ten Hag also claimed Ronaldo would tell his United teammates to 'save your legs at training' for matches.



"I understand it when you are top fit; you have sessions, you can save the legs," Ten Hag continued.

"But first you have to train yourself to get into the right fitness levels."

Did brutal stats prove Ten Hag was right about Ronaldo?

Ronaldo's alleged lack of professionalism under Ten Hag was exemplified by the fact he scored just three goals and registered two assists in the 2022/23 season prior to joining Al Nassr.

Two of the goals came against Moldovan club Sheriff Tiraspol in Champions League action.



3 At the time of Ronaldo's exit, he claimed he didn't have any respect for Ten Hag Credit: AFP

“He let the team down, and he let me down, because we planned with him,” Ten Hag said.

“I flew out to Portugal to speak with him about what I was aiming for before I came to United. Obviously, he’s one of the best in football history. I respected him a lot.

"But at that time, as a manager, I had to make a rational decision and keep the players I admire in.”

Sports.title: Piers Morgan disagreed with me but Martin Keown was wrong to question my motives in branding Arsenal 'The Unwatchables'... I have a duty to call it as I see it, writes TOM COLLOMOSSE
Sports.content:
Piers Morgan disagreed with me but Martin Keown was wrong to question my motives in branding Arsenal 'The Unwatchables'... I have a duty to call it as I see it, writes TOM COLLOMOSSE

It was around 2pm on Monday that I learned I was a lifelong Tottenham supporter who was desperate to move to London.

This certainly came as a shock to someone who follows another club entirely and has no plans to leave the Midlands. I also lived and worked in London for nearly 20 years.

Apparently, Martin Keown knows otherwise. Responding to my report of Arsenal’s 1-0 win at Nottingham Forest, Keown was quoted on talkSPORT’s X account as saying ‘I’m told he’s a Spurs fan… a journalist in the West Midlands looking to move to London.’

His anger was sparked by this paragraph in the piece. ‘Fans are disillusioned by the ongoing saga and the wider game needs a spectacular team to celebrate. Sadly, where once we had Arsene Wenger’s Invincibles, we now endure Mikel Arteta’s Unwatchables.’

Piers Morgan had his say later – with one crucial difference. Morgan disagreed with the article in every way but at no point did he speculate on my reasons for writing it.

Responding to my report of Arsenal’s 1-0 win at Nottingham Forest, Keown was quoted saying ‘I’m told he’s a Spurs fan… a journalist in the West Midlands looking to move to London'

Do Arsenal have a duty to entertain? No, and I expect them to win the title this year. Yet with their current approach, they are unlikely to be remembered in the same way the Invincibles were, or the way some of Alex Ferguson’s Manchester United teams or the Liverpool sides of the 1980s were.

Keown was a fine player and is a thoughtful pundit. He won 10 trophies in a hugely successful career with Arsenal and watches their progress with a keen eye. He disagreed with my analysis that the Gunners under Arteta are a tough watch – no problem.

When a journalist writes a forthright article, they know that criticism will follow. ‘You don’t know what you’re talking about’ or ‘What a load of rubbish’ – in the age of social media, these are some of the more polite responses.

Yet pundits should not try to guess why a journalist wrote a piece. A fair number of listeners might have heard that I was ‘a Tottenham fan’ and concluded I had written the piece because I was biased against Arsenal.

For the record, there are many Spurs fans in the media and none show bias, yet football is tribal and fans do not like their teams coming under attack.

That does not justify a pundit making statements – in this case incorrect – that could prompt listeners to doubt a reporter’s professionalism or credibility.

As always when we watch matches, we write about what we see. At Forest, I saw an Arsenal side put together at huge expense who registered a single shot on target, against a team who had yet to score at home this season and were without their best player.

In those circumstances, I thought they were disappointing and said so. But it will never be anything to do with the club I support - who, for the record, are not a member of the so-called big six, and nor do they play in London or the Midlands.

Sports.title: Erik ten Hag attacks Cristiano Ronaldo: Man United legend 'let the club down', failed heart rate tests, pulled out of training and was a bad influence, his old manager says
Sports.content:
Erik ten Hag attacks Cristiano Ronaldo: Man United legend 'let the club down', failed heart rate tests, pulled out of training and was a bad influence, his old manager says

Erik ten Hag has accused Cristiano Ronaldo of letting Manchester United down by failing to prepare himself for matches, with the former Red Devils boss claiming the forward pulled out of training sessions and encouraged team-mates to 'save their legs'.

Ronaldo left Man United by mutual consent in November 2022 after a bombshell interview with Piers Morgan, in which he claimed he had been 'betrayed' by Ten Hag.

The Portuguese star made just 16 appearances under Ten Hag, who had been appointed as Man United's head coach in the summer, with their relationship quickly unravelling.

Ten Hag, who was sacked as Man United boss in October 2024, has said he confronted Ronaldo over his preparation for matches.

Speaking to the Athletic, Ten Hag claimed Ronaldo did not get himself to the 'right fitness levels' after pulling out of training sessions and failed to get his heart rate raised to the required level when he did train.

'He let the team down, and he let me down, because we planned with him,' Ten Hag said.

Erik ten Hag has said Cristiano Ronaldo 'let the team down' at Man United after accusing him of failing to prepare himself for matches

Ten Hag said he confronted Ronaldo over his fitness levels as the former Man United boss claimed the star had pulled out of training sessions

'Obviously, he's one of the best in football history. I respected him a lot. But at that time, as a manager, I had to make a rational decision and keep the players I admire in.'

'Many times I say, "Ronnie, everyone wants to work for you to bring you in the right position, but if you can't bring yourself in the box, you can't score".

'He was not capable to do this. It's the wrong idea to put this to me that I expected him to do the pressing, that he's exhausted. But he couldn't. He ran neither in possession nor out of possession. The reason was because he didn't prepare himself.

'Every top team has to embrace the top player, but the top player has to work for the team.

'He was telling the players, "Save your legs at the training". I understand it when you are top fit; you have sessions, you can save the legs. But first you have to train yourself to get into the right fitness levels.'

The Dutchman reportedly claimed Ronaldo's stance ultimately rubbed off on other players in the Man United squad.

Ten Hag insisted that he had outlined his expectations for Ronaldo before he came to the club and that he had initially been a key part of his plans.

Ronaldo had clashed with Ten Hag earlier in the Dutchman's reign at Man United, with the forward having been warned about his conduct in pre-season having left Old Trafford at half-time after being substituted in a friendly.

Ten Hag dropped Ronaldo in October 2022 after he refused to come on as a substitute against Tottenham and walked down the tunnel before the end of the match

Ronaldo claimed he had been 'betrayed' by Ten Hag in an explosive interview in November 2022, which ultimately led to his Man United contract being terminated

He was dropped for a match against Chelsea in October 2022 after Ten Hag confirmed Ronaldo had refused to come on as a substitute against Tottenham three days earlier.

Ten Hag's former assistant Steve McClaren claimed earlier this year that there had been a standoff between the Dutchman and Ronaldo, which led to him trying to convince the star to follow the head coach's simple instructions to secure a place in the team.

Ronaldo's second spell at Man United ultimately ended after his explosive comments in November 2022.

'I don't have respect for him because he doesn't show respect for me,' Ronaldo said of Ten Hag at the time.

'Some people, they don't want me here - not only the coach but the other two or three guys. Honestly, I shouldn't say that. But listen, I don't care. People should listen to the truth. Yes, I feel betrayed.'

In 2024, Ronaldo doubled down on his disdain for the Dutchman, insisting he was too negative for a club of United's stature.

Ronaldo, now 41, last month became involved in another high-profile dispute with a manager after walking out of Portugal's squad, citing 'broken promises' from Jorge Jesus.

That came after he was left on the bench during their 2-1 Nations League win over Norway, with the Portuguese Football Federation subsequently suspending the forward for his actions.

Ronaldo said a plan had been drawn up for him to come off the bench for 30 minutes, but Jesus made him warm up without bringing him on because he 'didn't need Cristiano'.

Before Portugal's match against Denmark, football’s all-time leading goalscorer is understood to have agreed to an eight-point statement for Jesus to deliver at his press conference, aimed at quashing speculation that Ronaldo was demanding more playing time.

But Jesus veered off course, prompting Ronaldo to bail on the Portugal camp before releasing an extraordinary 1,996-word statement accusing the manager of twice backtracking on his word.

Ronaldo has since been fined £215 and banned for a month by Portuguese football chiefs, but the punishment is backdated to September 30.

It will ensure Ronaldo is free to return to Portugal's squad for their Nations League matches next month if he is called up by Jesus.

Sports.title: Erik ten Hag accuses Man United chiefs of breaking 'promises' that they would not sell Scott McTominay, made in infamous Ibiza contract summit, as he picks apart their transfer business
Sports.content:
Erik ten Hag has accused his former Manchester United bosses of breaking promises during his ill-fated spell at Old Trafford, claiming that they sold Scott McTominay against his wishes.

The Dutchman, 56, was sacked by Manchester United in October 2024 after a string of poor results, just months after leading the club to FA Cup glory and signing a one-year contract extension until 2026.

Ten Hag's future had been in doubt after he led United to a disappointing eighth-placed finish in the Premier League, but the club ultimately chose to stick by him after meeting for crunch talks in Ibiza that summer.

According to Ten Hag, United's chiefs made promises and failed to keep them, particularly in the transfer market.

He told The Athletic: 'I wouldn't go on with only one year left. So I said, "I need an extra year and we have to do it together".

'They promised me loyalty, they promised me backing, they promised communication, that we get aligned. We spoke about the issues. But the promises, they didn't keep.'

Erik ten Hag has accused his former Manchester United bosses of breaking promises

The Dutchman claims Man United's chiefs sold Scott McTominay to Napoli against his wishes

Keeping McTominay at Old Trafford was one of those promises, according to Ten Hag.

The Scot was sold to Napoli for £25million in the summer of 2024 and has since gone on to become one of the top midfielders in Italy, becoming a fan favourite at the Serie A club after steering them to the title in his first season.

He even earned a Ballon d'Or nomination and was compared to Argentina icon Diego Maradona by adoring Napoli fans.

On McTominay, Ten Hag said: 'That's why I got disappointed. In Ibiza, we agreed. I said, "No selling Scott McTominay". We would go aligned in the transfer window.

'I make an argument, a reason: we don't have scoring abilities. Scott brings scoring abilities and great mentality. He has United in all his veins. So when they bring up the subject, "No". And in the end they sold him. I got, of course, very embarrassed and disappointed.'

McTominay's transfer to Napoli was used by United's chiefs to raise funds for £42m midfielder Manuel Ugarte, who has struggled to impress since his arrival.

The Uruguayan, who is currently out injured with an anterior cruciate ligament tear he suffered at the World Cup, was mostly used as a squad player under Ruben Amorim and Michael Carrick last season.

Ten Hag's accusation against his former bosses comes just days after Lisandro Martinez explosively hit out at Manchester United's summer transfer strategy.

The defender accused the club's hierarchy of lacking ambition and singled out director of football Jason Wilcox for failing to build a competitive squad after Carrick guided the team to the Champions League as interim manager last season.

McTominay has flourished in Naples and played a key role in the club's 2024-25 title triumph

Asked if Carrick was backed enough over the summer after United's 2-0 defeat by Atletico Madrid last Tuesday, Martinez said: 'I don't think so. He does his best. You can't keep changing, changing, changing the manager.

'What about other areas? Tonight it is easy to say the coach and easy to say the players, but also we have to see other areas.

'I expect more (investment) 100 per cent. I expect more from our technical director. I have to control myself a lot but sometimes is a reflection of the mirror of how is our club at the moment.

'We did a fantastic season last season and now we expect more from the top; more players to compete because many teams bring many players as well.'

Sports.title: James Maddison apologises to Coventry fans over goal celebration - as Tottenham star explains why he kissed their badge after netting against his hometown club
Sports.content:
James Maddison has apologised to Coventry fans as he explained his decision to kiss the Tottenham badge after scoring against his hometown club. Maddison scored Tottenham's opening goal in their 3-1 victory over the Sky Blues on Monday night, which marked his first start in 18 months following an anterior cruciate ligament (ACL) injury. The 29-year-old netted with a curling effort from the edge of the Coventry box which arced into the top corner. Maddison initially appeared reluctant to celebrate against the club where his career began as he was pushed towards Tottenham fans by his team-mates. The midfielder eventually was seen performing his trademark darts celebration, before kissing the Tottenham badge. Maddison, who was jeered from the start by away supporters, had been criticised by some Coventry fans over his celebration having been vocal about his support of the club. James Maddison has apologised to Coventry fans after kissing Tottenham's badge after scoring against his hometown club Maddison insisted his goal celebration was to thank Tottenham for their support in his long recovery from an ACL injury I had already planned my first goal back I was kissing the badge of this club who has supported me and my family through the darkest days of my career over the past 18 months. I absolutely adore and love Coventry City. All my close friends and family know that. I’m a fan and… pic.twitter.com/heOFYobVSX — James Maddison (@Madders10) October 20, 2026 Maddison insisted in a social media post that his celebration was to reflect the support Tottenham have shown him through his long recovery from his ACL injury. ‘I had already planned my first goal back. I was kissing the badge of this club who has supported me and my family through the darkest days of my career over the past 18 months,' Maddison said. ‘I absolutely adore and love Coventry City. All my close friends and family know that. ‘I’m a fan and always will be and I will 100% apologise to anyone who thought the timing was bad as my first goal back just happened to be against my hometown club. ‘Good luck to Frank and the boys for the rest of the season. PUSB.’ Maddison's goal, his first in the Premier League for 610 days, helped Tottenham secure their first Premier League victory of the season. Second half goals from Omar Marmoush and Ben Davies secured a 3-1 win, after Jack Rudoni had cancelled out Maddison's opener. The result lifted Tottenham out of the Premier League's bottom three – above Coventry – and into 16th place.
