On the other, he will return to competitive racing in a world championship of the highest level, while playing an active role in developing an entirely new car.

Two different but complementary commitments through which McLaren will continue to invest in the young Italian, offering him a programme that combines driver development, technical experience and, perhaps most importantly for Fornaroli, the chance to race again.

Sports.title: Inside the competition building F1’s future engineering talent
Sports.content:
Six Saudi Arabian high school students, four boys and two girls, are excitedly pacing around the Singapore Formula 1 paddock.

They are known as Team Lynx Racing, the recently crowned winner of the annual STEM Racing World Finals, which was held in Singapore during the week leading up to the grand prix. Coming out on top of an international, four-day engineering competition, Lynx Racing received the 2026 trophy on the actual grand prix podium as they met the likes of two-time world champion Fernando Alonso and enjoyed an Aston Martin garage tour.

Some of them are hoping that it's not the last time they see an F1 garage up close - the next time, donning a team kit.

Since its inception in 2000 under the F1 in Schools moniker, STEM Racing has aimed to offer opportunities to talented children to pique their engineering curiosity and hone their skills through a demanding series of competitions.

Groups of three to six students are tasked with designing and manufacturing a miniature F1 car, powered by CO2 cartridges. The goal is to launch the car across a 20-metre track as quickly as possible, some reaching speeds of up to 70km/h. Winners of the regional and national competitions claim a place at the annual world finals to take on the best teams from around the world.

The 2026 edition in Singapore was the biggest one yet, with 91 student teams from 36 different countries represented, competing for a number of different awards judging their prowess.

STEM Racing World Final 2026 Singapore Photo by: STEM Racing

Despite the cars' miniature sizes, the competition itself bears more than just a passing resemblance to F1. Teams are free to design and manufacture the cars themselves using professional CAD software, putting their knowledge of aerodynamics to the test as they shave drag off their cars.

The end product is manufactured on a CNC router, with the front and rear wings being 3D printed before being assembled, painted and finally raced. Adhering to a strict rulebook, cars must all pass scrutineering like a real race car would.

But they are also judged on off-track skills. Teams have to build a marketing portfolio and sponsorship plan, create a brand, hold verbal presentations to judges and build a pit booth display to combine all of that into an impressive product. And with a maximum of six students per team, there is no place to hide.

The question of marketing and funding becomes especially pertinent for teams who make it to the World Final and face a trip to Singapore, which is not an inexpensive undertaking for a group of up to six members plus their teacher or adult guide.

STEM Racing World Final 2026 Singapore Photo by: STEM Racing

Strolling around the large ballroom of the Resort World Sentosa, where the 2026 finals are held, it's hard not to be taken aback by the level of competition, creativity and passion on display.

"I think it's important to gain experience, but I also love the competition element," says Noah of German team Spectrum, which would go on to take the third podium spot. "You really learn to work under pressure as a team."

Elsewhere, Aarav, team leader and design engineer at team Nebula from Singapore, said he enjoyed meeting and learning from his international peers. And like a true F1 designer, he was already stealing with his eyes as he checked on the competition. "The level here is so high," he said. "It is really interesting to see how other teams solve the same problems."

While there is no direct path to F1 given the age of most competitors, the initiative is supported by F1 and many of its teams. Many STEM Racing alumni have used the competition as a springboard to a relevant university degree and subsequently a place on an F1 team.

Greece's Kyriakos Theofanidis won the event in 2016 and is currently a mechanical engineer at Red Bull Ford Powertrains. James Mitchell from Australia competed at the World Finals as recently as 2023 before being snapped up by Aston Martin. Fellow STEM Racing alumnus Britain's Laurence Vines now works at Williams as a structural design engineer and still works for the event itself as a pundit, mentor and judge.

"I wanted to work in F1 and when I was 15 I wrote letters to all of the teams applying for work experience," Vines told Autosport. "Not having any connections in the sport, I just had no clue what the way in was until I discovered the competition by coincidence. In partnership with what was then called F1 in Schools, Williams ran its engineering academy where they'd support you through your studies, and I knew that was my way in."

Vines says the competition helped him because it familiarised him with tools and methods like CAD, CFD and FEA simulations much earlier. "Before I took part I didn't know what those things were. I wouldn't have touched them until university," he said. "At 15, I'm doing my first CAD, designing this miniature car. Under regulations which set you up so well to work in something like Formula 1. They're over 70 pages long with lots of detail.

"Since then, I've gone on to study Mechanical Engineering at University College London, which sponsored the competition and awarded me a full scholarship. I then did a placement at Williams."

STEM Racing World Final 2026 Singapore Photo by: STEM Racing

Amy Martin used the competition to pursue an engineering degree, before switching to the financial world. Those passions eventually collided as she joined Mercedes High Performance Powertrains as a financial controller.

"At the start I wasn't really that interested in F1," she said. "I just got my friends together in school and we were one of the few all-girl teams at the World Finals that year. After we won the Marketing Award, I got selected for the Williams Engineering Academy in 2016. They took us into the paddock where I met Nico Rosberg. That was when I decided I would do anything to get into F1.

"For a 16-year-old girl, it was genuinely electrifying to be there and look at what my future could look like."

When asked what she felt she got out of the competition, she replied: "Confidence is the main thing. When you're asking someone who's 15 or 16 to hold a presentation in front of world-class F1 engineers and judges, that's pretty tough. It instils a level of fearlessness.

"And the standard of some of the kids who compete... wow. They are not just so incredibly intelligent, but to be able to articulate themselves on a world stage, it's honestly great. It has created some really good all-rounders."

STEM Racing isn't just a boon for the students taking part, though, but it's also growing in importance for F1 teams themselves. In a budget cap world, identifying and attracting the next generation of engineering talent has started earlier and earlier, and it's no coincidence the majority of teams have established their own engineering academies, graduate schemes and other placement programmes.

"All teams realise the importance of young talent in the team. New ideas and people contribute so much," McLaren's racing director Randy Singh told Autosport. "We have a very established graduate scheme at McLaren and many of the people who've come off that scheme are here at track this weekend, like Oscar's performance engineer and our lead strategist. It's a really good way of getting super talent into the team.

"Things like STEM Racing are super useful for kids of that age because it teaches you a lot about how a Formula 1 team works. There's design, there's research, there's marketing and commercial aspects as well. That's all really useful experience."

Randy Singh, McLaren Racing Director Photo by: Peter Fox / Getty Images

When asked what his advice is to teenagers aspiring to work in F1 or the wider motorsport world, Singh replied: "As long as you're involved in some kind of deep technical endeavour where you work as a team, whether it's STEM Racing, Formula Student, rocketry, or even doing sports to a very high level can be in itself fairly technical, then I think that really equips you well to work in a fast-paced team environment like F1.

"I certainly wouldn't limit people to one route or another, but these kinds of things make a big difference to people's applications. Sometimes, dealing with the dysfunctions of a team is a key thing that you don't really experience at university until you get to a professional environment, so that's super useful."

Despite the event's long affiliation with F1 into its 26th year, founder Andrew Denford feels STEM Racing is only now starting to turn a corner following its 2024 rebrand. "You've got to educate people on why they need to teach STEM in school," said Denford, who is also the CEO of the family-run Denford company which supplies CNC tools to the education sector.

"We started this in 2000 to get kids interested in engineering and manufacturing, first as Jaguar F1 in schools and when they pulled out of F1, Bernie Ecclestone allowed us to keep using the F1 name. It's just consumed my life, really. We've now got 77 countries who are involved in the programme. The level keeps getting higher. I've got to be careful I don't start talking technical terms, because they'll just blow me out of the water."

STEM Racing World Final 2026 Singapore Photo by: STEM Racing

F1's popularity boom post-Netflix has also seen the programme's numbers go up, with STEM Racing now adding several entry-level school programmes to its pathway for children as young as six, with varying degrees of complexity.

When asked what he wants children to get out of STEM Racing, Denford said: "We want them to find out what their skill set is. If you look at all the job roles; team principal, aerodynamicist, manufacturing engineer, marketing or project manager, they'll find within that team of six what they want to do.

"Then they can develop what they've learned and take it into the wider world."

Wherever the future may take any of the 2026 finalists is up in the air. Some will make it to the F1 paddock, the aerospace industry, or take a wildly different and unrelated career path that hasn't even emerged on the horizon yet.

But whatever that path may be, they will take on the future supercharged by their Singapore experience and the skills they honed along the way.

Sports.title: Mercedes explains why its upgrade made its F1 car harder to drive
Sports.content:
If Mercedes left Sepang with more questions than answers, the Singapore Grand Prix weekend finally provided the engineering team with the first real clues to unlocking their new package. Although it was a sprint weekend, the reopening of parc ferme and the decision to split configurations between the two drivers offered a valuable opportunity to experiment and gather critical data.

The data will be analysed during the break ahead of Austin, with one key goal: understanding exactly why the package introduced in Malaysia hasn’t properly worked as expected, despite the potential to extract. Mercedes has now confirmed a crucial piece of the puzzle, explaining that the upgrades shifted the car's aerodynamic balance, making the W17 significantly more difficult to drive.

While the new package achieved its primary objective of increasing overall downforce, as shown through Malaysia’s high-speed sections, it also exposed an unexpected weakness. The upgrades shifted the W17’s aerodynamic balance too far forward, unsettling the car and significantly narrowing its operating window.

"I think, if you wanted to just take the first order of the problem, we wanted to deliver more performance with more downforce. And we have measured more downforce on the car," explained Mercedes deputy technical director Simone Resta on the team's Nu Silver Arrows Radio Show podcast.

"Unfortunately, it's not a black and white problem. It's not zero one. It's a very grey environment with multiple variables. And I think we delivered the downforce but perhaps we haven't delivered the same level of downforce in every single running point of the car on the track. And that is then starting to alter a little bit the balance of the car in the condition, and then the driver has to adapt."

The balance has shifted toward the front-end

To some extent, a shift in balance was to be expected given the extent of the floor and sidepod changes introduced in Sepang. The real issue, however, was that while Mercedes successfully unlocked the additional downforce it had been targeting, those gains were not delivered consistently across the full range of operating conditions, contrary to expectations. As a result, the engineers struggled more than usual to identify a set-up capable of extracting the full potential of the updated W17.

Andrea Kimi Antonelli, Mercedes Photo by: Alastair Staley / LAT Images via Getty Images

“There are a few things we need to sort out, especially because we tend to see a car with more balance than before. Stronger front, even perhaps a bit more than we expected. So therefore, you need to re-centre the window we operate the car. And it's taking some time,” added Resta, emphasising that there is still untapped potential in the new specification.

This means Mercedes now has to approach both set-up and driving requirements differently to unlock the car's potential, while the W17 has become less forgiving and harder to drive when operating outside its ideal window. There is more performance to unlock, but accessing it consistently has become a far more complex task and the shift in balance has also made the car harder to drive.

During the first half of the season, one of the W17's strengths was its stable rear end, particularly in traction-limited situations. That strength often made Mercedes competitive and the benchmark at stop-and-go tracks, not only thanks to its power unit but also because of its ability to put power down effectively on corner exit from low-speed corners.

The rear is less stable under braking and this change the approach

However, the balance shift has also forced changes in driving technique. Antonelli, in particular, has always favoured an aggressive approach to corner entry, aiming to minimise the distance through the corner, gain time at the apex and getting back on the throttle as early as possible.

That approach worked brilliantly up to this point, partly because the previous specification provided a stable rear end that remained settled under braking, allowing him to attack corner entry. The new package, however, changed some of the W17's key characteristics and that stability.

As a result, the drivers have had to adapt their approach both at turn-in and through the mid-corner phase. Unsurprisingly, Antonelli reported persistent mid-corner understeer during both the Malaysia and Singapore weekends, stemming from an inability to rotate the car as cleanly as he would like on entry. That compromised his line through the apex and delayed throttle application on corner exit.

Andrea Kimi Antonelli, Mercedes Photo by: Clive Mason / Getty Images

A narrower window, but there is more potential to extract

To compensate for that understeer, drivers are left with two choices: increase steering input, which places additional load on the front tyres, or use the throttle to rotate the car at mid-corner, something that was frequently visible in Sepang. However, on a hot and abrasive track, however, the latter approach comes at a cost, as it accelerates rear tyre overheating and degradation. As a result, the updated W17 struggled considerably more than usual in Sepang's low-speed corners.

It therefore came as little surprise that, once parc ferme restrictions were lifted after the sprint race in Singapore, Mercedes shifted towards a significantly different set-up compared to the first part of the weekend. The direction chosen for qualifying and the race ultimately paid off, trying to find a more stable rear end.

Early indications of this had already emerged during the wet sprint: “The car was overbalanced initially, quite oversteer-y, difficult to drive. As the front tyres wore down, suddenly we found a much happier car balance. And then from there, Kimi suddenly was popping up with green and purple sectors and starting to match the pace of the leaders," said deputy team principal Bradley Lord.

The improvement was also evident on the timing sheets. Despite slower track conditions on Saturday, Antonelli was one of only two drivers in the top 10, alongside Hamilton, to improve on his Friday qualifying time. Most of that gain was found in sector two, the most technical part of the lap, where the set-up changes gave him the confidence to push harder and unlock more of the updated W17's potential.

For Austin, Mercedes will re-introduce the front wing tested during Singapore practice, aiming to recalibrate the package, widen the operating window, and extract the potential from the car the car: "We just have to re-centre the window. We just have to rework mechanically the car, trying to tweak a few of the characteristics that we're seeing with these packets on the car,” said Resta.

Sports.title: The maths behind when Mercedes could become F1 world champions in 2026
Sports.content:
The 2026 Formula 1 season has seen Mercedes return to its dominant past as it is on course to claim its first double championship victory since the COVID-struck 2020 campaign.

Kimi Antonelli and George Russell top the drivers’ standings with the former holding a 102-point advantage, while Mercedes leads second-placed Ferrari by 134 points in the constructors’ table.

It is thanks to 11 victories in 17 grands prix that the Silver Arrows is in this position at the start of the new regulations, most of those wins coming early on as rivals subsequently closed the gap.

Regardless, Mercedes is set for its first drivers’ title since 2020 after a period of Max Verstappen domination and a crown for Lando Norris, with it being a similar story in the constructors.

The Silver Arrows last won that championship in 2021 before Red Bull and McLaren overtook it during the ground-effect era, but with six rounds remaining in 2026, Mercedes is set for glory.

Antonelli can clinch his maiden world title next time out in Austin, though is most likely going to do it a week later in Mexico, whereas Mercedes may have to wait a little longer to win the teams’ crown.

How many teams can still win the F1 2026 world title?

Andrea Kimi Antonelli, Mercedes, Lewis Hamilton, Ferrari Photo by: James Sutton / LAT Images via Getty Images

There are 258 points left on offer in the 2026 F1 world constructors’ championship table, provided Qatar and Abu Dhabi go ahead amid the ongoing Middle Eastern conflict.

That means there are four teams left with a mathematical shot, as Mercedes leads Ferrari by 134 points, McLaren by 239 and Red Bull by 246 - fifth-placed Racing Bulls is 478 behind.

Position Team Points 1 Mercedes 578 2 Ferrari 444 3 McLaren 339 4 Red Bull 332 5 Racing Bulls 100 6 Alpine 68 7 Haas 30 8 Audi 23 9 Williams 12 10 Aston Martin 7 11 Cadillac 0

Can Mercedes win the F1 2026 world title at the US GP?

When F1 greets the chequered flag in Austin next weekend, there will be 215 points left available in the 2026 constructors’ championship.

That means the United States Grand Prix is likely to see McLaren and Red Bull drop out of contention, as they would need to be within 214 points post-Austin.

It is because Mercedes has nine more wins than both squads, so if McLaren and Red Bull cut it to 215 in Texas, they would still be eliminated from the fight due to countback of victories.

Given that would require the reigning champions and Red Bull outscoring Mercedes by at least 25 and 32 points respectively, Ferrari is realistically the only threat to the German marque.

And because the Scuderia will leave the United States still within 214 points of Mercedes regardless of what happens, the constructors’ title will not be decided next weekend.

When can Mercedes win the F1 2026 world title?

Andrea Kimi Antonelli, Mercedes Photo by: Sam Bagnall / Sutton Images via Getty Images

The worst-case scenario for Ferrari in Austin is that it experiences a double non-points score with Mercedes finishing 1-2, which would leave a 177-point gap between them.

If that unlikely scenario happens, the German marque heads to Mexico City with a chance of claiming its ninth constructors’ title - moving level with Williams on the all-time list behind Ferrari (16) and McLaren (10).

Again, provided Qatar and Abu Dhabi go ahead, there are 172 points available in the four grands prix after Mexico. So, if the above scenario in Austin happens, Mercedes would just need to make sure that Ferrari doesn’t outscore it by at least six points in Mexico.

Yet at no point this season has Mercedes taken a full score from a grand prix with Ferrari taking nothing, as the below table indicates - excluding sprint races as there are none left in 2026.

Grand Prix Mercedes points haul Ferrari points haul Australia 43 27 China 43 27 Japan 37 23 Miami 37 12 Canada 25 30 Monaco 25 18 Barcelona 18 25 Austria 40 14 United Kingdom 18 40 Belgium 25 30 Hungary 21 22 Netherlands 33 22 Italy 43 8 Spain 35 12 Azerbaijan 35 20 Malaysia 18 27 Singapore 17 26

Looking at that, Mercedes has outscored Ferrari by an average of 7.6 points across the 17 grands prix so if that were to happen across the next two, it leaves a gap of 149 points.

So even for Mercedes to clinch the title in Mexico is a tough ask. F1 is most likely looking at the grand prix afterwards, in Brazil, where the Silver Arrows could become world champions.

Sports.title: What drives Bortoleto as his junior rivals hit new heights in F1
Sports.content:
Gabriel Bortoleto has watched Kimi Antonelli and Isack Hadjar celebrate their first Formula 1 podiums. Both are from his generation of drivers, having competed against him throughout the junior categories.

So he knows them well, having raced against and beaten them - but their respective F1 careers have taken different paths so far. While Antonelli and Hadjar have already enjoyed podium success, Bortoleto is helping Audi build a team that hopes to challenge at the front in the coming years.

It would be understandable if Bortoleto felt impatient, but the 22-year-old has accepted that his opportunity may take longer to arrive.

“They're the two drivers from my generation who are getting podiums,” the Brazilian told Autosport. “I've raced against them all my life. The truth is that I did well against them in the junior categories, and I know what I'm capable of. But I have to be patient. Everyone has their own path. Let's see where we all end up in 20 years."

Bortoleto has already achieved his childhood dream of reaching F1, but the experience has also brought new challenges. After years of fighting for wins and championships in the junior categories, he now has to judge his progress by different standards.

"I'm very happy to be in Formula 1,” he added. “It's the first step towards a dream I've always had. At the same time, to be honest, it's also difficult when you come from the junior categories, where you've been winning, and then arrive in Formula 1 knowing you can't fight at the front. It's been almost two years now. Today, the goal is to score points, and that's not easy."

Gabriel Bortoleto, Audi Photo by: Steven Tee / LAT Images via Getty Images

What keeps Bortoleto motivated is his belief in Audi's future. He doesn't see the team as a stepping stone to a seat elsewhere, or his current situation as an opportunity to attract the attention of an established frontrunner. He wants to be part of the project when Audi itself becomes a winning team.

"What motivates me and keeps me going is the project I'm part of,” said the 2023 F3 and 2024 F2 champion. “I'm not in a team whose ambition is to stay where we are today. I'm in a team that's improving every year and has a clear long-term plan. I hope that one day I'll look back and see that everything we've been through helped us reach the top."

Bortoleto is also aware that, given his age and potential, he is expected to play an important role in Audi's future. But he sees that as a source of pride rather than pressure.

"Pride, yes. Pressure, no,” he said. “There will be difficult moments, there will be times when you're not winning, and I have to keep working on my mindset, on myself, and developing as a driver. Because the day Audi gives me the opportunity to win, with a winning car and a winning engine - and it will happen, I don't think it will take that long - I'll have to be ready to show what I can do."

Bortoleto is convinced that Audi will eventually give him the machinery to compete at the front. He understands that it may take time, but he also knows how quickly the competitive order in F1 can change.

"Right now, Hadjar and Kimi are definitely closer to the ultimate goal, which is winning a world championship. But everything could change in a year. You never know. I just have to keep doing my best,” said Bortoleto, who is 15th in the drivers’ standings, with Audi eighth in the constructors’ championship.

‘Mattia Binotto is much more than a boss’

Mattia Binotto, Audi F1 Team Photo by: Joe Portlock / LAT Images via Getty Images

One of the people Bortoleto regularly turns to for advice about his situation is Mattia Binotto. The man leading Audi's F1 project experienced Ferrari's successful years from within the team and has worked through very different periods in its history. He is now involved in building a new operation with ambitions of reaching the front, and Bortoleto values that experience.

"I talk to Mattia a lot,” he said. “I often ask him for help with this situation because I know he has a lot of experience and understands what I'm going through now. He's already been part of a winning team, and now he's in a team that wants to win. He helps me a lot."

Their relationship has also developed beyond what Bortoleto initially expected from the person running his team.

"He's a mentor, a friend, a boss, but he's also very different from what I imagined,” claimed Bortoleto. “Because normally, when you have a boss, the relationship is a bit formal. But he's different. I don't just see him as a boss, but also as someone I can go to for advice about my personal life. That's a really nice aspect of our relationship."

Another person Bortoleto turns to for advice is Max Verstappen. The two are friends and share an interest in sim racing, which gives the Brazilian plenty of opportunities to ask questions. Rather than focusing exclusively on driving techniques or preparing for qualifying, Bortoleto is particularly interested in Verstappen's experience of Red Bull's development into a championship-winning team.

"I talk to Max often,” revealed Bortoleto. “Obviously, the details stay between us, but we often talk about how I'm feeling, how I'm developing, what I want from Audi and how we're progressing as a team. I ask him questions about what he experienced at Red Bull before winning the world championship: what things were like, how the team worked."

Max Verstappen, Red Bull Racing Photo by: Clive Rose / Formula 1 via Getty Images

And sometimes those conversations take place during a gaming session.

"These are things that sometimes come into my head while we're playing, so I ask him,” said Bortoleto.

Binotto and Verstappen can offer Bortoleto different perspectives on the same challenge. Binotto has experience of working within a successful organisation and helping develop a team with ambitions of winning, while Verstappen knows what it is like to spend years working towards a first world championship.

For Bortoleto, their advice is valuable as he tries to develop both as a driver and as part of a team that is not yet ready to fight for victories.

The boy who never wanted a Plan B

Bortoleto's willingness to be patient today contrasts with his attitude during his junior career, when he refused to consider any alternative to reaching F1.

"Never," he replied, when asked whether he ever had a Plan B.

"A lot of people told me it was wrong to think that way, and maybe it was, because there are many great categories in motorsport where you can become a professional and race at a high level. But I wanted to reach Formula 1 because that was what I'd dreamed of since I was a child."

As he progressed through the junior categories, people around him tried to make him consider the possibility that an F1 opportunity might never come. There were only so many seats available, driver turnover was limited and plenty of talented drivers had missed out.

Gabriel Bortoleto, Invicta Racing, Monza 2024 Photo by: Invicta Virtuosi Racing

"They would tell me, 'Even if you win Formula 3, and even if you're winning Formula 2, what are you going to do if it doesn't happen,” he said. "And I'd reply, 'I can't get that into my head. Don't even tell me that.' I'd get angry and walk away."

Bortoleto went on to win the F3 championship as a rookie before stepping up to F2 the following year. One of the defining moments of that campaign came at Monza in 2024.

He ended up in the gravel at the first Lesmo during qualifying, at a crucial stage of his championship battle. Title rival Hadjar was due to start third, while Bortoleto faced the prospect of starting from the back of the grid. For a few minutes, he feared the damage to his championship hopes could be considerable.

"I said to myself, 'I'm starting last, he's starting third. Even if I drive the race of my life, where can I finish? We all have the same cars, it's not as if one is much better than another. Even the engineers were saying it wouldn't be easy to overtake,” he said.

Bortoleto went on to win the race.

"With everything that happened during the race, winning was an incredible feeling for me. Something really special."

The result also came at a crucial point in his efforts to secure an F1 seat. Bortoleto had yet to sign a contract and knew that every opportunity to demonstrate his ability mattered.

"I had to show that I deserved an opportunity," he claimed.

Gabriel Bortoleto, Stake F1 Team KICK Sauber Photo by: Andy Hone / Motorsport Images

The phone call that made 20 years of work worthwhile

When confirmation of his F1 seat finally came, Bortoleto initially struggled to believe what he was hearing. Talks with Audi had been going on for some time, but he had not known whether the opportunity would be for 2025 or 2026. Then his manager called to tell him the date of the announcement.

"I said to him, 'What announcement? For 2026?' And he said, 'No, for 2025!' I replied, 'What are you talking about, 2025?' And he said, 'You'll be racing as a full-time driver in 2025.'"

Bortoleto was at his home in Milan with his girlfriend when he received the news. He immediately called his family in Brazil.

"I made a video call with my dad, my mum and my brother, and I said, 'I have something to tell you. Stop everything!' I remember my mum was crying, my brother was incredibly excited and my father didn't know what to say,” he said.

For Bortoleto, the moment was about more than securing an F1 contract. It was also an opportunity to reflect on the years of karting, travelling and sacrifices his parents had made to support his career - many of which he had been too young to fully appreciate at the time.

"It's impossible to explain what it means,” he said. “But it's the result of 20 years of work. I know how many days my father wasn't at home, how many races he couldn't come to watch when I was little because he had to work."

The Bortoleto family had no previous background in motorsport. His father worked in the internet and telecommunications industry before becoming involved in Brazilian motor racing, where he now runs the Stock Car series.

Rubens Barrichello in the Stock Car Pro Series Photo by: Duda Bairros

"They made so many sacrifices, including living away from me so they could keep working. And that day, when we had that video call, I think what went through my mind was that it was a huge achievement for me, but an even bigger one for my mum and dad. All those sacrifices had been worth it."

That family background also appears to have influenced Bortoleto's attitude towards money. Asked whether F1 drivers compare their salaries and compete over who earns the most, he smiles at the suggestion.

"I don't care how much other drivers earn,” he claimed. “What matters to me is having a winning car and a good project ahead of me. The money comes as a consequence. If you're a great champion, you'll never be short of money. If you're winning races, the last thing you should be worrying about is how much money you're making."

He also believes that earning a significant amount of money comes with responsibilities towards others: "If anything, the question is where to spend it or who to help. If you make all that money and don't help the people around you, you don't deserve it."

A mind that never switches off

Bortoleto admits that he finds it difficult to stop thinking about racing. Video games provide a way to relax, even when he is still spending his free time behind a virtual steering wheel.

"My mind is always on racing,” he said. “I need something that helps me switch off from what I do for the rest of the day. Sometimes it's still motorsport, but in a different way. I'm laughing, I'm having fun, it's not work. I don't have to chase perfection."

Gabriel Bortoleto, Audi F1 Team Photo by: Andy Hone/ LAT Images via Getty Images

Perfection is something Bortoleto believes no human driver can truly achieve, however close they might come.

"The perfect lap? No, I don't think it exists, because perfection would mean being able to say, 'There was nothing more I could have done.' But you can have a lap that's very close to perfection. Perfection isn't human. For me, perfection is what you get in computer simulations."

That attitude also shapes how Bortoleto approaches his own development. Rather than judging himself solely by his current results, he wants to make sure he continues learning and improving throughout his career.

"I study, I try to understand,” he said. “In the end, when I look back at my career in 20 or 30 years, I don't want to think that I didn't do everything I could."

It is another reference to the long-term perspective that runs through Bortoleto's approach to F1. He is prepared to wait and see where he, Antonelli and Hadjar stand in 20 years, just as he wants to look back on his own career knowing he made the most of his opportunities.

For now, that means accepting that other drivers of his generation are fighting for podiums while he helps Audi develop into a team capable of challenging at the front. He sees those years as part of the process of reaching his ultimate goal, rather than time lost waiting for a competitive car.

Before the interview ends, there is one final question: where does Gabriel Bortoleto hope to be in five years?

"Hopefully winning world championships, obviously with Audi."

Sports.title: What Verstappen knew about Red Bull’s big upgrade when he signed his new F1 deal
Sports.content:
While Max Verstappen was still seriously considering the possibility of ending this Formula 1 season without winning a single race at Monza, things now look considerably different.

Verstappen came remarkably close to victory in Baku before actually coming out on top in the subsequent races of the triple-header in Malaysia and Singapore.

It marks a huge contrast with the beginning of this year, when Red Bull was a distant fourth in the pecking order and at times even found itself fighting Haas and Alpine.

Unsurprisingly, that sparked plenty of speculation about Verstappen's future again, although he revealed at Zandvoort that, in reality, he had come much closer to an early F1 retirement than to switching teams.

Ahead of Verstappen's home race, the news finally emerged: the Dutchman's already long-term deal with Red Bull had been renegotiated and extended by another two years.

Now that the Milton Keynes-based squad has made a huge step forward and is fighting for victories again, the question arises whether he might already have known more when he signed.

In other words, did Verstappen already know that Red Bull would become competitive again with its next upgrade package?

“No, not really, it was more just talking about the future, and of course the ideas about how the team is moving forward,” Verstappen replied. “And I liked those ideas. It’s also not that they really needed to convince me or whatever, it's just the general chat that you have with the team.

Max Verstappen, Red Bull Racing Photo by: Jayce Illman / Getty Images

“And for me, it's been really enjoyable to work with this team. Naturally, yes, with the progress that we have had, it's a nice bonus, because fighting up front is a lot more satisfying, of course.”

Verstappen also added that the Baku upgrade is not just about outright performance. Perhaps even more important than the pure gains in load and lap time is the fact that the RB22 has become considerably more predictable again.

And that is precisely what allows the driver behind the wheel to make more of a difference again, at least as far as the limitations of the current power unit regulations allow him to do so.

“The big thing that has changed with our car is that has just become a lot more predictable and balanced, where in the beginning of the year many times I didn't know what was going to happen going into a corner,” Verstappen explained. “Back then, a lot of weird things did happen with the car.

“That's why you could never really run it to the limit, because you didn't know where the limit was, or suddenly the limit had shifted. That [change] has made it a lot better in the last few race weekends, just knowing a bit more where the limit is and having a more predictable balance.”

Team principal Laurent Mekies also dismissed the suggestion that Red Bull had already anticipated the huge progress in Baku and had been able to use it to convince Verstappen to put pen to paper.

“The short answer is no. We were not waiting for a magic upgrade that was supposed to bring us to the performance,” the Frenchman clarified.

Max Verstappen, Red Bull Racing, Laurent Mekies, Red Bull Racing Team Principal Photo by: Joe Portlock / Getty Images

“We knew that we had upgrades coming and we also knew that Baku would be the last one of this year. It was continuing the trend of the development of the car, and as I said earlier, at the time we actually felt that we would probably struggle to close those final three tenths.

“So it was certainly not an argument of convincing [Max] at the time of the discussions.”

Mekies stressed that Verstappen's contract extension was instead based on the longer term and on his confidence that Red Bull can continue to provide him with competitive machinery in the future.

In that respect, the Baku upgrade was not so much used to convince him, but is seen internally more as an example of what is possible when all the pieces of the puzzle fall into place.

“I think more globally, we knew that the dynamic was very strong in Pierre [Wache]'s team and in Ben [Hodgkinson]'s team, in terms of what we felt was still the potential of the car package, both on the chassis side and on the PU side,” Mekies continued.

“And yes, this is the sort of discussion we had with Max. It’s not about the Baku package or any other package, but about the underlying factors and where we felt the long-term opportunities were. But no, nothing specifically about the Baku package.”

As for those long-term opportunities, both Mekies and Verstappen continue to stress that the current situation is still not good enough. Red Bull is not there yet and still needs to address several underlying weaknesses.

With the current chassis and the limitations of the budget cap, that will no longer be possible in 2026, which is why Verstappen has repeatedly emphasised that further changes will be needed for the 2027 car if Red Bull is to compete consistently at the front again.

Sports.title: Colapinto urges fans to stop online abuse: “You’re not helping me or my future”
Sports.content:
Franco Colapinto has vocally asked Argentinian fans to stop online abuse after several incidents in the last couple of months.

Following the Zandvoort, Madrid and Baku races, hateful comments were directed at FIA stewards, Pierre Gasly and his family, and Lando Norris, among others. This has been a recurring theme in the 2026 Formula 1 season, prompting Alpine to regularly release statements to try and combat the vituperation.

Colapinto had previously been coy when it came to taking a stand on this matter; in Baku he meekly labelled the behaviour as “not nice to see”, and after causing the Turn 1 pile-up in Azerbaijan, he nuanced the situation.

“I think we miss that it doesn't come only from Argentinians,” Colapinto then said. “It comes a lot from them, I fully agree, [but] it doesn't just come from them. They are extremely passionate and they support me a lot. It's bad. They are bad many times.

“But it comes from all the world and from many other fanbases. I don't know if we are not seeing it. I get loads of it. No one ever talks about it.”

On Thursday, the Argentine went on to make his strongest statement to date in a bid to curb his fanbase’s frenzy – he directly told his fans that they ‘sometimes went too far’ and ‘were not helping him or his future’.

“Hello everyone, there’s something very important that I’ve needed to talk to you about for some time,” Colapinto said in a Spanish-language video posted on Instagram. “I probably should have spoken to all of you sooner, but this is something that needs to be addressed, something we need to change and improve.

Franco Colapinto, Alpine Photo by: Sam Bagnall / Sutton Images via Getty Images

“I will always be grateful, and I genuinely feel incredibly fortunate, to have had you all supporting me from the very beginning.

“I’m grateful for all the support you give me, for how you help me achieve results, and for how you constantly push me to aim higher. You help me and the team achieve our results, race after race, day after day, as we train and try to improve. And I’m genuinely grateful for all of that.

“I know it makes you incredibly proud when things go well for me, when I score points for myself and the team. And I have always been very grateful for that support.

“But sometimes, we go too far. Instead of supporting me, we end up criticising people and attacking other drivers, other colleagues, my team-mates, my mechanics, my engineers – people I work with every single day.

“I know you think you’re defending me, but you’re actually doing the opposite. You’re not helping me or my future.”

Colapinto’s immediate future is secure, with the 23-year-old having clinched a new Alpine deal for the 2027 season back in August. He currently lies 12th in the 2026 standings with 27 points to his name, while team-mate Gasly is 10th on 41 points.

Sports.title: Who will win this year’s ultimate F1 dream ticket? You decide…
Sports.content:
After hundreds of applications for the ultimate prize in grand prix racing, the Heineken x F1 Season Ticket is down to six finalists – and F1 fans can now vote to decide who wins.

The candidates – from the UK, New Zealand, Singapore, Czechia and the USA – have all put their pitches forward for the adventure of a lifetime, which will see one of them get free travel, accommodation and passes for every single F1 race next season.

The competition challenged F1 fans around the world to share their passion for the sport and explain why they, more than anyone, deserve to be gifted an unforgettable season of racing, experiencing unique events, connecting with fans and watching the action first hand.

The initiative was designed by Heineken to showcase the connections that can be formed through a shared passion for the sport, demonstrating that ‘Fans Have More Friends.’

F1 fan Brandon Burgess was the first recipient of the golden ticket and has been posting his stories to almost 150,000 followers on his social channels this season. His journey has now almost run its course – and now it is time to choose the next ‘star’ to take over his mantle.

Global shortlist

The list of entries demonstrates the sport’s global fanbase and the massive reach of the competition – and the final six all have a unique story to tell, with a different reason why they deserve that special prize.

Start action Photo by: Clive Rose / Getty Images

Callum, from Scotland, used to pretend to be Michael Schumacher in front of the TV when he was a toddler. He’s a keen film photographer and says: “I’d love to take you behind the scenes of the F1 season ticket and show you the people and places of F1 on film.”

New Zealander, Dale, says he wants to discover the “F1 world” behind every race, exploring the unique people, cultures and fans. “I want to meet the people who make it special and bring everyone along for the ride,” he says.

Lukas, who lives in Czechia, says winning the prize would “finally be some peace for my sofa” and promises fans they can “be the team boss” by choosing challenges for him to take part in each race weekend, sharing the results as the season goes on.

India, from the UK, describes herself as a “completely ordinary fan” looking to make next year “extraordinary” – and also asked other fans to set her fun challenges for each race, saying that winning would “bring together my two passions of F1 and seeing the world.”

Joy, whose home race in Singapore took place earlier this month, wants to use the opportunity to experience “the excitement and sportsmanship” of F1 around the world and to have a chance to “share the same passion” with those around her.

Jose, from the USA, is a fan not just of the racing but also of the strategy, technology and teamwork behind F1. He visited his home race in Las Vegas last year and said: “Travelling to every race in the 2027 would honestly be a dream come true.”

Singapore GP Photo by: Colin McMaster / LAT Images via Getty Images

Picking a winner

The opportunity to travel to every grand prix opens up unprecedented access to the sport and its fans. The current ticket holder Burgess has shown just how to get the best out of the experience this season and he was on the judging panel that picked the shortlist.

Speaking before the competition began, he said: “The key thing I'll be looking for is the passion for F1, because you have to be a true fan to make the most of this opportunity. It’s going to be hard to give it up and there’s quite a lot of pressure choosing who’s next.”

The competition was open to fans aged 25 or over, with entrants asked to name their favourite team and driver and select who they would take to a future race from a list of options provided by F1 and Heineken.

Fifty entrants were then selected at random and invited to submit a 90-second video on why they should become the next ticket holder – and the final six videos are now available to watch, so fans can determine who should win the adventure of a lifetime.

Sports.title: Formula 1’s move to shorter grands prix in 2027 will not be permanent | Formula 1
Sports.content:
Formula 1 will reinstate full grand prix distances in 2028 after shortening the races this year, the FIA has confirmed.

The championship announced last month it will cut 15 kilometres from the standard grand prix distance next year as a result of the new fuel flow limits which will come into force. Shortening the grand prix distances will reduce the number of components teams need to redesign next year.

The shortened distance of 290 kilometres will apply for all grands prix except Monaco, which has run to a shorter distance of 260km for many years and will continue to.

However the first edition of the 2027 Formula 1 Sporting Regulations published by the FIA notes the previous distance will apply again from 2028. “The distance of the race [i.e. grand prix], from the start signal referred to in Article B5.7.2 to the end-of-session signal referred to in Article B5.16.1, shall be equal to the least number of complete laps which exceed a distance of 305km,” it states.

Sports.title: Featured Comment: Budget cap not to blame for lack of winning teams in F1 | Brief
Sports.content:
This week’s poll asks whether Formula 1 needs to rethink its budget cap as the series’ top four team have pulled further away from their rivals this year.

But reader @Skydiverian suggests it might not be realistic to expect F1 to regularly have more than four race-winning teams:

Four competitive teams has happened before but it’s still not great and the problem is as it always is, money. And I’d like to see more teams in a season have a realistic shot of winning races. It’s unfortunate that the stats are not on my side.

Pretty much since the late 80s the problem has been that the best teams could throw more money at the problem to fix it. Now, teams that are significantly behind can’t throw more money at the problem to catch-up due to the cost cap, rather than simply not having the money in the first place as was common in the 80s. (This season is interesting. It seems that Mercedes blew most of it’s cap early to get and maintain their advantage, whereas Red Bull didn’t and that’s in part why Max has had a better car the last two races. But it’s not like Williams or Aston Martin can fix their problems by spending more money to fix the deficit).

The problem is that ultimately there’s no easy fix, but spending millions to be the so-called best of the rest basically seems pointless if there is a very unlikely chance of a team outside of the top four having a realistic shot at the podium or even a win. And that’s always been a problem going back decades.

Some number crunching by looking at the history books: the 500th race was 1990 Australia, 1,100th being Vegas 2023. In those 600 races I’ve found six that were won by drivers driving for teams who finished outside the top four in the constructors championship.

That’s six of 600 races over 33 years where we had a winner driving for a team who finished outside the top 4 in that years constructors championship, 1% of all races. Seven if you count Johnny Herbert’s win at the Nurburgring which to me was a genuine surprise at the time. To me those stats aren’t good enough.

Whether that’s the fault of teams with no money, teams with too much money or teams with a cash limit so they can’t design their way out is up for debate. But my point is that I’d like to see more teams have a reasonable chance of winning. F1 has never really had that and will continue not to unless something changes (maybe by letting teams further down have a bigger budget the following season rather than just more CFD time).

I’d rather that at least 70% of drivers have a realistic chance of winning, ideally 100% of teams. It’s the reason I preferred IndyCar before Alex Palou showed up, results were unpredictable and smaller teams have a chance of getting a win or two. That’s just so rare in F1 and the current cost cap rules will continue to make unlikely.

@Skydiverian

Sports.title: Early coronation for Antonelli? Five talking points for the United States Grand Prix | Formula 1
Sports.content:
Andrea Kimi Antonelli could win the world championship this weekend in only his second year as a Formula 1 driver. Here are the talking points for the United States Grand Prix.

Will Antonelli clinch the title?

The odds are stacked heavily in favour of Mercedes’ new star clinching the title at some point, but most likely not this weekend. That said it is not beyond the realm of possibility team mate George Russell could have another poor weekend and come away point-less while Antonelli takes his ninth victory of the season, putting him over the line.

The title has been won at this track twice before, and both times it was by a Mercedes druver: Lewis Hamilton won the championship there in 2015 and 2019. But regardless of whether Antonelli does clinch the title this weekend it is clearly a matter of ‘when’ not ‘if’.

Verstappen dominating again?

The driver most likely to delay Antonelli’s championship celebrations is not his team mate but Max Verstappen. Red Bull have made a breakthrough with their RB22 and as well as winning the last two grands prix plus a sprint race, Verstappen could have taken victory in Baku as well with better luck.

He arrives at this weekend’s race looking like the driver to beat, with every indication he could dominate the final rounds of the season, setting himself up for a shot at the title next year.

McLaren’s driver headache

McLaren arrive in Austin in a curiously similar situation to last year: a clash between their drivers at the previous race in Singapore has created an obvious tension. What’s more, Lando Norris and Oscar Piastri’s collision during the sprint race in Singapore was more costly than the one they had in the grand prix 12 months ago.

Norris’s radio messages during the grand prix gave the distinction impression he was looking for ways to make amends, having eventually accepted he was the one at fault for their collision. But above all the team will be anxious to avoid a repeat of the first-corner collision which wrecked their sprint race at the circuit 12 months ago. Particularly as a resurgent Red Bull are poised to relegate the reigning constructors’ champions to fourth place in the standings.

US teams’ driver decisions

Of the two teams competing in their home event this weekend, one has settled its driver plans for 2027. Haas has announced Rafael Camara as the replacement for Esteban Ocon, whose Formula 1 future is in serious doubt as few likely alternatives remain for next year.

Could Cadillac be one of them? F1’s new American team is yet to confirm its plans for next year. However its hopes IndyCar star Colton Herta would take Formula 2 by storm and make himself an obvious candidate for promotion have been dashed: he lies 19th in the standings, 181 points behind fellow rookie and championship leader Camara.

Are Colapinto’s die-hards paying attention?

Last week Franco Colapinto spoke out in criticism of the element of his fanbase which has sent vile abuse to his rival drivers, team members and FIA officials since he made his F1 debut this year. The Alpine driver told those attacking others in his name that they are not helping his cause in F1.

Will they take his words on board? We’ll get an indication the next time he is involved in any kind of incident on-track – however slight it may be.

Sports.title: On This Day: Ralf Schumacher wins Formula Nippon title despite spinning out | Brief
Sports.content:
30 years ago today Ralf Schumacher won the Formula Nippon title despite retiring two laps into a rain-lashed race.

Schumacher arrived at the final race at Fuji Speedway just two points ahead of team mate Naoki Hattori. But Schumacher spun out two laps into the rain-hit race (see 3’50 in the video below).

That left Hattori on course for the title, which looked increasingly secure as the laps ticked down. But conditions worsened, and seven laps from home he spun out too, handing Schumacher the 1996 title. Schumacher made his F1 debut the following year for Jordan (now Aston Martin).

Katsutomo Kaneishi won ahead of future Formula 1 driver Pedro de la Rosa. Another future F1 driver, Shinji Nakano, took fourth place behind Masahiko Kageyama. Just seven of the 26 starters were running at the finish.

Sports.title: O’Shaquie Foster Claims He Can Dominate Emanuel Navarrete
Sports.content:
O’Shaquie Foster insists he has Emanuel Navarrete completely figured out ahead of their October 24 unification bout in San Antonio. Foster plans to outclass him, take his belt, and force critics to treat him like an elite name at 130 pounds.

Foster claimed he could turn this into a one-sided blowout if he simply sticks to the outside and picks Navarrete apart.

“I believe not only that I can beat Navarrete, I believe that I can do it in a dominant fashion, a super dominant fashion,” Foster said to Bradley’s channel. “I can make it an easy night and just box his head off.”

At the same time, Foster called this matchup a nine out of ten in difficulty and admitted it represents the biggest threat of his career. Navarrete throws wild, looping bombs from angles nobody learns in the gym. Foster insists none of that will rattle him. He points to past rounds with Rey Vargas, Robson Conceicao, and Jon Fernandez as proof that he knows how to handle height, awkward attacks, and long-range pressure.

Navarrete brings chaos, not textbook mechanics. Surviving separate elements from past opponents does not guarantee Foster can absorb the non-stop pressure Navarrete brings from opening bell to the final seconds. Foster cannot afford to run and let rounds slip away on activity alone.

He claims he wants to dominate, yet talking about an easy night while hunting for a highlight reel finish creates immediate risk. If Foster gets trapped between cruising on points and trying to look spectacular, Navarrete will make him pay with relentless volume.

“I’m looking to come in to make a statement,” Foster said. “I’m coming in to put on a dominant performance, show the world who I really am.”

Trying to invent power and aggression at age 31 against Navarrete is playing with fire. If Foster wants to leave San Antonio with the belts, he has to accept who he is, ignore the crowd, use his legs, and be content with a disciplined, ugly points win. Anything else plays right into Navarrete’s hands.

Foster has his sights set on undisputed status before jumping up in weight. Talking about blowing through Navarrete is bold talk, but a flat decision win will not deliver the respect he expects. Foster made big promises, and on October 24, he has to back them up against a puncher who never stops coming forward.

Sports.title: David Benavidez Plans His Own Promotional Company
Sports.content:
David Benavidez is launching DB Promotions to guide his own career once his contract with Sampson Lewkowicz wraps up in December. Even with the change, he intends to keep working alongside PBC and his existing inner circle.

Benavidez revealed his upcoming December bout marks the end of his decade-long deal with Lewkowicz. He treated the decision as a natural progression, making sure to acknowledge the promoter who helped build him into an attraction.

“This is the last fight on my contract,” Benavidez said to Brian Custer. “You know, I’ve honored the contract. The contract has been 10 years.”

Benavidez spoke carefully about the shift, never downplaying Lewkowicz while making it clear he is ready for independence.

“Sampson, he’s did a wonderful job,” Benavidez said. “He’s one of the greatest promoters of all time. But, you know, it’s just my time to do my own thing.”

When questioned about the venture’s name, he confirmed it will be DB Promotions, serving as his primary promotional banner starting early next year.

Stepping out on his own gives him significant leverage over the business side of his fight nights. Still, key details like equity splits, bankrolling, and operational responsibilities remain unstated, meaning the precise financial upside is impossible to calculate right now.

Putting his name on the banner gives Benavidez a chance to pocket more of the promotional money. That’s an obvious reason to make the move. But he still wants Al Haymon and TGB running the show alongside him. Having his own company won’t make the television money his, and he’ll still need those partners to get fights funded and dates booked.

Benavidez also aims to look past his own headline slots, expressing interest in signing boxers who train alongside him and his father, Jose Benavidez Sr.

“There’s a lot of great fighters I could take under my wing and put them under the promotion company,” he remarked.

Signing prospects gives DB Promotions life after Benavidez hangs up the gloves, yet building an actual stable turns a fighter into a financier. The expenses add up quickly with club show site rentals, airfare, hotel blocks, and purse guarantees that rarely turn a dime. Promoting his own headlining dates is one thing, but bankrolling young talent is a financial drain that devours capital long before a prospect ever sniffs a television date.

The move could let Benavidez pocket more of the money from potential fights with Jai Opetaia, Artur Beterbiev or Oleksandr Usyk. But with Haymon and TGB still involved, putting DB Promotions on the banner hardly means he’s going it alone.

Sports.title: Lucas Bahdi Seeks Schofield Rematch Over Knockdown Calls
Sports.content:
Most Valuable Promotions has formally challenged Lucas Bahdi’s defeat against Floyd Schofield III, petitioning the WBA for an immediate rematch after claiming uncalled knockdowns cost their fighter the vacant lightweight world championship.

The promotional outfit submitted video footage alongside detailed documentation to the WBA following the October 10 clash in Chicago. MVP maintains that if the referee had correctly recognized and scored the disputed incidents, Bahdi would have emerged with a majority decision win instead of leaving the ring empty-handed.

Schofield took the vacant belt by unanimous decision, capturing wide margins on the official cards with scores of 116 to 110, 115 to 111, and a steep 119 to 108. Bahdi’s side now wants the sanctioning body to grant another title opportunity, arguing that multiple officiating blunders corrupted those final numbers.

“The video evidence demonstrates multiple significant officiating errors that directly impacted the outcome of the fight,” MVP said in its statement. “Our review shows that had these knockdowns been properly ruled and scored, Lucas would have won the WBA lightweight world championship by majority decision.”

That claim sounds bold on paper, yet MVP failed to provide the necessary receipts to back it up. The public release never identified which specific rounds contained the uncalled drops, nor did it offer an adjusted scorecard breakdown to illustrate how Bahdi overturned an eleven-point deficit on the widest card.

Rather than rehashing standard complaints about judges favoring the house fighter, MVP pinned the blame directly on the third man in the ring. The core of their protest argues that referee mistakes prevented the judges from scoring mandatory 10 to 8 rounds, skewing the overall totals.

“We have submitted our findings to the WBA and requested an immediate rematch,” MVP said.

Securing a second fight remains an uphill climb. A rematch forces Schofield to revisit an opponent he already officially conquered, and lodging a protest never guarantees the WBA will order the boxers back into the ring. The sanctioning body has not issued a ruling on the video review, leaving MVP’s victory claim as promotional posturing until officials deliver a verdict.

Sports.title: Does Oleksandr Usyk Need Daniel Dubois Again?
Sports.content:
Daniel Dubois’ second-round stoppage of Fabio Wardley gives Oleksandr Usyk another possible opponent for his farewell fight. It also raises a harder question: how much would Usyk gain by beating someone he has already stopped twice?

Dubois retained his WBO heavyweight title on Saturday in London, rebuilding interest in a third meeting with the unbeaten Ukrainian. Usyk stopped him in nine rounds in 2023 and five rounds in their 2025 rematch. Those results leave Dubois needing the fight far more than Usyk does.

At 39, Usyk is choosing how to finish his career rather than working his way toward another championship opportunity. He has already become undisputed champion at cruiserweight and heavyweight, with two victories apiece over Anthony Joshua, Tyson Fury and Dubois.

That leaves a shortage of unfinished business.

A proposed Deontay Wilder fight would have offered a recognizable opponent Usyk had never faced. However, those negotiations have reportedly collapsed, with Fury and David Benavidez emerging as alternatives for a possible final appearance.

Fury’s appeal depends heavily on his December 11 fight with Joshua. A strong victory would give promoters something fresh to sell: Fury returning from that British heavyweight clash to take another run at the man who beat him twice in 2024. A defeat would make a third Usyk fight considerably harder to justify.

Dubois has strengthened his own case by stopping Wardley twice this year. Yet beating Wardley does not answer the technical questions Usyk posed in their previous meetings. Dubois would still need to show he can land consistently against Usyk’s movement and avoid being drawn into a fight where the Ukrainian controls the pace.

Benavidez would offer a different opponent and a fresh style, although his ability to compete with Usyk at heavyweight remains untested.

Usyk’s next fight needs more than a famous name or another belt attached to it. A Dubois trilogy would give the younger man a chance to overturn two defeats. The challenge for its backers is explaining why Usyk should spend his final appearance giving him that opportunity.

Sports.title: Artur Beterbiev Targets David Benavidez In Risky Cruiserweight Jump
Sports.content:
Artur Beterbiev wants David Benavidez next. He has spent over twenty months sitting on the sidelines, hoping for a trilogy clash with Dmitry Bivol that never materialized. Jumping up to cruiserweight offers a fresh target, but it also threatens to drag out his inactivity even longer.

Beterbiev dropped fresh training clips online this Monday, poking fun at his age while calling out the new division player. He joked about his physique looking like a man of forty-five, scaring people off. In reality, he sits at 41, turning 42 this coming January. That birthday will likely pass before he steps inside a ring again, especially since talks for a clash with Benavidez point toward 2027.

“Hope nobody was scared off by my 45-year-old physique,” Beterbiev wrote on social media.

Benavidez revealed the interest himself on Inside The Ring earlier this month. The former undisputed light heavyweight ruler reached out to his camp about meeting at the 200-pound limit. Benavidez sounded open to giving him the shot.

Chasing Benavidez hands Beterbiev a sensible target after the Bivol pursuit hit a wall. His February 2025 rematch with Bivol stands as his last sanctioned outing. Wasting nearly two years on that stalled trilogy took away precious championship time he can never get back.

The workout clips prove his muscle hasn’t vanished, but raw power was never the concern. The real test is sharpness under fire. Sitting idle chips away at reflexes, punch rhythm, championship stamina.

Benavidez brings relentless punch output that gym sessions cannot duplicate. Stepping up to 200 pounds also forces Beterbiev to show his heavy knockout power can hurt naturally larger men.

At the same time, Benavidez cannot sleep on the veteran. Beterbiev still carries sledgehammer power on the inside, creating real danger for anyone willing to stand in the pocket.

Sitting around waiting for Dmitry Bivol is pure career poison at this stage. Beterbiev is burning daylight he simply doesn’t have.

Turning 42 in January means every single idle month takes a bite out of his remaining sharpness. If the Benavidez camp can actually nail down a firm date for early 2027, fine, he can target that window. But if those talks drag out into vague promises or get pushed deep into the summer, Beterbiev cannot afford to sit in a training camp doing nothing.

The Bivol ship has sailed. Bivol went through back surgery, took other obligations, and showed zero urgency to jump straight back into a grueling trilogy war. Beterbiev spent the better part of two years holding out hope for that rubber match while his prime years slipped right out from under him.

If Benavidez isn’t locked in for Q1 2027, Beterbiev needs a stay-busy fight by late spring at the absolute latest. Even taking a mid-tier cruiserweight test to acclimatize to the 200-pound frame would do wonders for his timing. Heavy bag work and sparring with headgear can never replicate live incoming fire, especially against relentless combination punchers like Benavidez

Sports.title: Shakur Stevenson Wanted $15 Million Per Fight From Zuffa
Sports.content:
Shakur Stevenson wanted $15 million per fight from Zuffa Boxing regardless of who stood across from him, according to reporter Sean Zittel. The reported figures explain why Stevenson parted ways with the promotion without stepping into their ring.

Zittel reports that Zuffa explored a January date against Jose ‘Rayo’ Valenzuela in Newark that would have paid Stevenson roughly $7 million, with an alternative December slot against an undetermined opponent carrying similar money. Stevenson turned both options down, holding out for top-tier compensation. Zittel added that Stevenson initially accepted $15 million to fight Haney before raising his demands even higher. The reporter did not disclose the final dollar amount Stevenson sought after moving the goalposts.

“He wanted $15 million no matter who was going to be put in front of him,” Zittel said on his channel about Shakur’s purse expectations.

Zittel clarified that the $15 million target was originally connected to a potential showdown with Devin Haney. Instead of treating that number as an opponent-specific purse, Stevenson reportedly wanted that guarantee for every outing. Zittel noted that while he reached out without receiving a response from Stevenson or his team, his sourcing did not come from Bill Haney or anyone in the Haney camp.

He described the split between Shakur and Zuffa as mutual, with the fighter unhappy about the available money and the company unwilling to meet his price. Walking away leaves Stevenson searching for a backer willing to exceed that $7 million mark. While launching his own promotional company grants him control over his schedule, another outfit or broadcaster still must step up to fund those purses.

High-profile opponents demand substantial guarantees of their own, quickly inflating the total cost of staging an event.

Shakur earned a defining victory over Teofimo Lopez in January, yet his tenure with Zuffa concluded without another appearance. Turning down the Valenzuela bout kept him on the sidelines during prime earning months.

Unless a network or deep-pocketed backer agrees to meet that 15 million asking price, Stevenson will struggle to balance his self-valuation with what the sport is willing to pay him. Standing firm on an inflated number risks keeping him on the shelf while the rest of the division continues to move forward without him.

Sports.title: Carlos Adames Zuffa Debut Draws Fan Criticism
Sports.content:
Carlos Adames’ reported Zuffa Boxing debut against Gerome Warburton is drawing criticism from fans who see the Welsh fighter as an underwhelming opponent for the WBC middleweight champion.

According to Dan Rafael, Adames will face Warburton in the November 14 main event in Riyadh, Saudi Arabia. The bout will take place above 160 pounds, with Adames’ WBC title not at stake.

For Zuffa, signing Adames brings an established champion into its middleweight roster. However, introducing him against Warburton gives fans little opportunity to judge him against one of the division’s leading contenders. It looks like an opportunity for Adames to collect a win and make an impression before moving toward a bigger fight.

Warburton, 31, has an 18-2-2 record with two knockouts. That limited knockout total helps explain the reaction to his selection. Adames is accustomed to facing world-level opposition, and Warburton has yet to prove he belongs in that company.

His fourth-round stoppage loss to Kieron Conway in May 2025 is another reason fans are questioning the matchmaking. Conway beat him at British and Commonwealth level. Now Warburton is being brought in to headline against a reigning world champion.

There is some recent form in Warburton’s favor. He has won three consecutive fights since that defeat, including victories over Nathan Heaney in March and September this year. Those results deserve recognition when discussing how he landed this opportunity.

Nonetheless, beating Heaney twice does not establish Warburton as one of the best middleweights available. Adames represents a much higher level, and the pressure will be on the champion to produce a performance that reflects that difference.

A quick stoppage would give Zuffa a highlight to promote. A long, competitive fight could bring more criticism of Adames and raise questions about what this debut achieved.

The matchup gives Warburton a major opportunity. Adames has considerably less to gain.

Sports.title: Shakur Stevenson Leaves Zuffa After Three Months
Sports.content:
Shakur Stevenson says Zuffa Boxing granted his release over the weekend, ending his three-month stay without a fight. The unbeaten four-division champion plans to start his own promotional company and pursue opponents at lightweight and light welterweight.

Stevenson announced the split in a video posted on his YouTube channel and shared on X. He described spending eight weeks in camp preparing for fights that never materialized.

“I requested to be released from Zuffa Boxing. Now over the weekend, my request has been granted, and now I am officially a free agent,” Stevenson said.

The 29-year-old signed with the Dana White-led company in July. He hasn’t fought since defeating Teofimo Lopez on January 31 at Madison Square Garden to win the WBO and Ring light welterweight titles.

Negotiations for a Devin Haney fight failed to produce an agreement amid disagreements over weight and rehydration conditions. Talks involving WBA light welterweight champion Gary Antuanne Russell also failed to produce a fight.

Stevenson insisted he wasn’t looking to blame anyone for his inactivity.

“This is the business of boxing. I’m not mad at anyone. I’m not pointing no fingers.”

Nevertheless, leaving so soon after signing shows how quickly his plans with Zuffa unraveled. The company secured a prominent unbeaten champion, but the relationship ended before he appeared on one of its cards. Zuffa declined immediate comment to The Ring.

Stevenson now wants control over how his next fights are arranged.

“I am now taking my career in my own hands and I’m starting my own promotional company,” he said.

He added that he is willing to work with other promoters and networks, opening the possibility of partnerships rather than another exclusive promotional deal. Shakur calling himself a promoter sounds empowering on social media, but acting as an actual bank is an entirely different business.

Starting a promotional banner without self-funding just means running an LLC to collect an extra operational fee while someone else assumes all the downside risk. If Stevenson expects a guaranteed purse in the multi-million-dollar range, that check has to clear through site fees, network licensing rights, ticket gates, and pay-per-view buys.

When an elite fighter possesses a purely defensive, safety-first ring style, the math turns hostile very quickly. Traditional promoters like Matchroom, Top Rank, or Queensberry understand what it takes to make an event profitable.

If external backers refuse to absorb those deficits, Stevenson will eventually face two stark paths: either accept realistic purses based on actual revenue generation, or find a wealthy benefactor willing to burn capital regardless of the balance sheet.

The moment Shakur put pen to paper with Zuffa and immediately waved off Jose “Rayo” Valenzuela, the whole premise of the deal fell apart. Dana White’s business model has always run on control, matching his roster internally, and fighters taking the bouts handed to them. Shakur treated the setup like a traditional boxing boutique where he could dictate terms, pick who makes financial sense, and snub the promoter’s own in-house assets.

Cutting bait after just three months was simply accepting the obvious. Shakur’s approach to the sport is completely incompatible with Dana White’s playbook.

“Give it maybe a year or two, we will get to 147 where everybody is pressing me to just be a 147-pounder,” Stevenson said. “I will get there, but on my term and not on nobody else’s.”

Ghana News.title: Former Manchester United forward Dwight Yorke confirms interest in Black Stars coaching job
Ghana News.content:
Former Manchester United forward Dwight Yorke has openly confirmed his interest becoming the next Black Stars head coach.

Yorke is among the notable names linked with the vacant role following the departure of former coach Carlos Queiroz.

The Portuguese mutually parted ways with the Ghana Football Association (GFA) following a difficult start to the 2027 Africa Cup of Nations (AFCON) qualifiers, which included a 2-0 defeat away to Côte d'Ivoire in Bouaké and a 4-2 loss at home to Gambia.

Speaking to The Guardian, Yorke stated that the team’s immense talent makes the role an attractive prospect, provided the right team culture and player commitment are established.

"It's a job I'd be interested in, given Ghana's history and the players available," Yorke said.

"You look at the squad, and your eyes open even wider. The conversation [I had with an agent regarding my interest in coaching the Black Stars] started there and then reached the media before I really knew it.

"The talent is there. Build the culture and get the players to buy in, and the football will follow."

Yorke served as the head coach of the Trinidad and Tobago national team from November 2024 to March 2026. Prior to joining Trinidad and Tobago, the former United striker coached Australian top-flight side Macarthur Football Club, penning a two-year deal in July 2022 before being sacked in 2023.

In the wake of Queiroz's exit, the GFA and the Ministry of Youth and Sports selected an interim technical team to manage the camp.

Black Queens head coach Kim Lars Björkegren has been placed in charge as interim head coach, supported by assistant coaches Ibrahim Tanko and Godwin Attram, alongside former national team goalkeeper Fatawu Dauda as goalkeeper trainer.

The interim team will guide the team for the 2027 AFCON qualifier doubleheader against Somalia in November.

The Black Stars currently find themselves at the bottom of the Group C table without a point after two matches.

Having missed out on the 2025 AFCON, the pressure is firmly on the team to win their upcoming matches.
