Ghana News.title: ‘My officers are suffering’ – Director-General of Prisons calls for welfare interventions
Ghana News.content:
The Director-General of the Ghana Prisons Service, Patience Baffoe-Bonnie, has described the conditions under which some prison officers work as “hell”, appealing for welfare interventions, including a contagious disease allowance, to improve their working conditions and protect their well-being.

She has appealed to the Public Accounts Committee t to improve conditions of service for prison officers, particularly through better remuneration and the introduction of a contagious disease allowance for officers exposed to potentially infectious inmates.

Speaking before the committee on Tuesday, October 20, Mrs Baffoe-Bonnie said prison officers endured difficult working conditions despite not having committed any criminal offence themselves.

“The Ghana Prison Service, working as a prison officer, is hell. It has a psychological effect, emotional effect, physical effect,” she said.

She explained that prison officers were required to work and live in the same environment as convicted persons, exposing them to many of the difficult conditions associated with incarceration.

“Everything about a prison officer is highly challenging, because the prison officer, who is not convicted of any offence, is compelled to live in the same space as somebody who is convicted,” she said.

According to her, the consequences of these conditions extend beyond the workplace, with the average prison officer facing considerable psychological pressure.

“What it means is that every bad condition in that environment is directly linked to the prison officer, who has not committed any offence. So the average prison officer is usually depressed,” she added.

Poor conditions threaten recruitment

Mrs Baffoe-Bonnie also raised concerns about the Ghana Prisons Service’s ability to attract qualified and motivated personnel, pointing to recruitment trends that she said suggested a lack of interest in joining the service.

She said the number of people who sought to purchase recruitment forms for the Prisons Service was significantly lower than the figures recorded for other security agencies during the last recruitment exercise.

She warned that the trend should concern policymakers, as it suggested that prospective applicants were increasingly reluctant to pursue careers in the service.

“The last recruitment that we did, when you look at the trend of how people purchase the forms, gave me a very serious implication, or a concern, because the people who wanted to buy the prison forms were far fewer than all the other agencies, which means that people are not ready to be prison officers,” she said.

The Director-General attributed the situation to the difficult working environment and what she described as inadequate salaries.

She argued that the country needed to recognise the risks and demands associated with prison work and provide additional compensation to make the profession more attractive.

“Because the environment is toxic, the salary is not too good, and we must begin to compensate for these things as part of salary as a country,” she said.

She added that improving remuneration and conditions of service was necessary to attract the right people to the service and ensure that officers could effectively carry out their responsibilities.

Mrs Baffoe-Bonnie expressed hope that her appeal to the committee would help the public and policymakers better appreciate the challenges facing prison officers and the need for urgent support.

Call for contagious disease allowance

A major concern raised by the Director-General was the long-standing demand for a contagious disease allowance for prison officers who face the risk of exposure to infectious diseases while performing their duties.

She said the issue had been under consideration for a considerable period, but argued that the current approach to the allowance did not adequately address the risks confronting officers across the prison system.

Mrs Baffoe-Bonnie noted that allowances were paid to personnel at Ankaful Prison because the facility had been designated as a contagious disease prison.

However, she maintained that the greatest risk could lie elsewhere, particularly in facilities where the health status of inmates had not yet been established.

She explained that prisoners sent to a designated contagious disease facility would generally have been diagnosed with a relevant illness before their transfer. Officers working in other prison facilities, by contrast, could be exposed to infectious diseases before the conditions of inmates were identified.

“For me, the biggest challenge is not those who are even working in the contagious disease prison. Because by the time we are taking a prisoner there, we would have diagnosed him as having a disease,” she said. “The danger, rather, is in the spaces where we are yet to know whether the prisoners have the contagious disease or not.”

She argued that officers working in these settings should also be considered for the allowance because they could face exposure while caring for inmates whose medical status remained unknown.

“They, rather, are not being paid that allowance. So it's a very humble appeal,” she told the committee.

Appeals for targeted financial support

The Director-General urged PAC to prioritise addressing this gap in the allowance system, arguing that the financial implications would be relatively small compared with the potential benefits for officers' welfare.

She said the government and relevant authorities could begin by resolving the issue of the contagious disease allowance before considering broader salary-related concerns.

“The margin is very little. I believe that before we look at all other salaries, if we can work on that, at least it will be a step in the right direction to ensure that my officers are somehow taken good care of,” she said.

Mrs Baffoe-Bonnie maintained that better welfare arrangements would not only improve the well-being of prison officers but also strengthen their ability to discharge their duties in accordance with the law.

She said providing officers with appropriate support would give her greater confidence in enforcing the law while ensuring that personnel were not left to bear the burden of difficult working conditions without adequate compensation.

“And I'll have the moral courage and justification to be implementing the laws as they are,” she said.

The Director-General reiterated her appeal to PAC to consider the concerns raised and take steps to improve the welfare of prison officers.

Ghana News.title: Ghana’s economic recovery: Distinguishing policy continuity from political propaganda
Ghana News.content:
George Domfe, President of APL

If the IMF commends Ghana for its economic recovery, such recognition should not automatically be interpreted as praise for the NDC government alone.

The 36-month Extended Credit Facility (ECF) programme was approved in May 2023, under the previous administration. By October 2023, IMF Managing Director Kristalina Georgieva had already acknowledged Ghana's recovery efforts, including progress in addressing the country's debt challenges.

International credit rating agencies have also recognised the contribution of debt restructuring to Ghana's economic stabilisation efforts.

The following assessments provide important evidence for understanding the origins and evolution of Ghana's economic recovery.

1. IMF: Debt Restructuring and Macroeconomic Stabilisation

In its 10 December 2024 Third Review of Ghana's Extended Credit Facility (ECF) programme, the IMF reported that economic growth was recovering faster than expected, inflation was declining, and the country's fiscal and external positions had improved considerably. The Fund also highlighted progress in domestic debt restructuring, the agreement with official creditors, and the successful Eurobond exchange. These developments demonstrate that significant elements of Ghana's economic recovery were already underway before the change of government in January 2025.

2. S&P Global Ratings: Debt Restructuring and Fiscal Space

In its 14 October 2024 assessment, S&P Global Ratings explained that Ghana's restructuring of US$13.1 billion in Eurobonds was intended to ease external debt-servicing pressures and restore public debt sustainability. The agency estimated that the restructuring, combined with the earlier Domestic Debt Exchange Programme (DDEP), would reduce interest expenditure to below 20% of government revenue in 2025, compared with more than 47% in 2022. It also estimated that the Eurobond restructuring would provide approximately US$4.4 billion in cash-flow relief over the lifespan of the IMF programme.

This relief was expected to ease the government's financing constraints, reduce debt-servicing pressures, and create fiscal space for economic stabilisation. Consequently, debt restructuring constituted an important component of the recovery process initiated before the current administration assumed office.

3. IMF: The Continuity of the Economic Recovery Programme

In its June 2025 Fourth Review, the IMF reiterated the importance of Ghana's comprehensive debt restructuring in restoring debt sustainability. The programme sought to reduce the present value of public debt relative to GDP and lower the external debt-service-to-revenue ratio.

The Fund also reported that Ghana's real GDP growth had increased from 3.1% in 2023 to 5.7% in 2024, although favourable international gold prices and other factors also contributed to the improved performance.

The IMF's assessment supports the conclusion that debt restructuring was a SIGNIFICANT component of the broader policy framework underpinning Ghana's economic recovery. The recovery, THEREFORE, should not be attributed exclusively to the new administration. That assertion is completely misleading!

INDEED, THE NEW ADMINISTRATION DIDN'T BRING ON BOARD ANYTHING EXTRAORDINARY! IT ONLY CAME TO CONTINUE WHAT WAS ALREADY BEING DONE!

4. Fitch Ratings: Debt Restructuring and Improved Creditworthiness

In June 2025, Fitch upgraded Ghana's long-term foreign-currency issuer default rating from Restricted Default to B− with a Stable Outlook. The upgrade reflected progress in debt restructuring, fiscal consolidation, and an improving macroeconomic outlook.

This rating action provides further evidence that Ghana's debt restructuring and broader macroeconomic adjustments contributed to an improvement in the country's credit standing.

Although the upgrade occurred under the current administration, the restructuring process and several associated policy measures had commenced under the previous government. The timing of the upgrade must therefore be distinguished from the period in which the underlying reforms were initiated and implemented.

THE EVIDENCE FROM THE IMF AND THE INTERNATIONAL CREDIT RATING AGENCIES CLEARLY INDICATES THAT GHANA'S ECONOMIC RECOVERY WAS ALREADY UNDERWAY BEFORE THE CHANGE OF GOVERNMENT IN JANUARY 2025.

The current administration inherited an ongoing IMF-supported programme that had been implemented for approximately 19 months, with measurable progress already recorded. Its contribution should therefore be evaluated within the broader context of policy continuity, while recognising that external developments may also have influenced certain economic outcomes.

The political propaganda surrounding Ghana's economic recovery is excessive! Economic analysis must distinguish between initiating a policy programme, implementing its principal reforms, and continuing an existing programme. A balanced assessment should acknowledge the contributions of both administrations and recognise the role of the IMF-supported programme in the recovery process.

Ghana News.title: ECG to begin nationwide meter audit to curb electricity theft
Ghana News.content:
The Electricity Company of Ghana (ECG) is set to commence a nationwide meter audit exercise across all its operational areas to reduce commercial losses, improve revenue assurance and combat electricity theft.

In a statement, ECG said the exercise would involve inspecting and verifying prepaid and postpaid meters, Special Load Tariff (SLT) installations and associated wiring “to confirm the integrity of metering systems and ensure accurate measurement and billing of electricity consumption.”

The company said the announcement served as official notice of the exercise, stressing that “no further prior notices, appointment letters, or advance notifications will be issued.”

It therefore urged customers, landlords, estate managers, property managers, facility managers and security personnel not to deny or delay access to authorised ECG personnel on the grounds that they had not received a separate notification letter.

ECG cited Regulation 4(h) of the Public Utilities Regulatory Commission (Customer Service) Regulations, 2020 (L.I. 2413), which requires consumers to grant utility employees or authorised agents safe and reasonable access to their premises, subject to the production of verifiable identification and compliance with the utility’s customer charter.

“All ECG employees and authorised agents participating in the exercise will carry official ECG identification cards,” the statement said, urging customers to verify the identities of field personnel before granting them access.

Ghana News.title: I’ll pursue all lawful avenues to clear my name – Embattled Obuasi SHTS headmaster
Ghana News.content:
The headmaster of Obuasi Senior High Technical School (SHTS), Zakaria Abdulai, says he will devote his attention and resources to clearing his name following allegations of sexual abuse involving female students at the school.

Mr Abdulai said this as he resigned as Secretary of the National Democratic Congress (NDC) in the Juaben Constituency and withdrew his candidature for the constituency chairmanship.

In an October 20 letter to the NDC General Secretary, he said his resignation and withdrawal from the forthcoming constituency elections took immediate effect.

“At this time, I intend to devote my attention and resources to pursuing all lawful avenues to clear my name and vindicate my position. I remain hopeful that, once these matters are resolved, I will be able to return to active political engagement and continue contributing to the ideals and aspirations of the NDC,” he stated.

The decision comes amid public concern over allegations that Mr Abdulai sexually abused more than 14 female students at the school. The allegations have triggered calls for accountability and a thorough investigation.

Mr Abdulai maintained his innocence and expressed gratitude to friends, relatives and supporters who have continued to believe in him.

“I wish to express my profound gratitude to my friends, relatives, and all well-wishers who have stood by me and maintained their faith in my innocence in the face of the allegations levelled against me and my office,” he said.

He also thanked the NDC for giving him the opportunity to serve the party and contribute to its growth and development.

Mr Abdulai did not provide details of the legal steps he intends to pursue or indicate when he expects the matter to be resolved.

His letter was copied to the NDC National Chairman and the party’s Ashanti Regional Chairman.

The allegations have also prompted the National Association of Graduate Teachers (NAGRAT) to call for the removal of the headmaster and Ghana Education Service (GES) officials in Obuasi over their alleged handling of complaints concerning the case.

NAGRAT President Jacob Anaba has claimed that concerns about the alleged misconduct were raised before the matter became public and questioned whether the relevant education authorities responded appropriately.

The allegations remain subject to investigation.

Ghana News.title: AIK chief scout Herish Sadi arrives in Accra for One World Sports Management’s West Africa Talent Hunt tournament
Ghana News.content:
The chief football scout at Swedish football side AIK, Herish Sadi, has arrived in Accra for the West Africa Ralent Hunt tournament.

Sadi arrives in Ghana for the three-day football tournament put together by One World Sports Management to unearth talent from the western side of the continent.

The 37-year-old was the scout behind the discovery of Brighton and Hove Albion forward Zadok Yohanna, taking him from Nigeria to AIK in Sweden.

The idea behind Sadi's arrival in Ghana is to watch and identify talented players who are capable of making the jump from Africa to Europe, with the scout working together with the administrators of One World Sports Management.

Speaking following his arrival in Ghana, Sadi asked young players to always be ready for the next step, as there are several opportunities.

"You need to always be on your toes because you never know when it's going to happen; people's lives change overnight," he said.

"You need to be sharp, be on your toes to do your bets all the time, and hopefully that is enough for somebody to recognise you and make the change that you want.

"You need to relax, enjoy the game, be proud and fight for what you want."

Six teams are involved in this year's West Africa Talent Hunt tournament, including Great Somas, Nice Ibrahim, Visio FC, Liberty Academy, Exulted FC and Sakibatti.

The final day of the tournament is scheduled for Wednesday, October 21.

Ghana News.title: GES directs Ashanti Regional and Obuasi Municipal education directors to step aside over Obuasi SHTS probe
Ghana News.content:
The Ghana Education Service (GES) has directed the Ashanti Regional Director of Education, Dr William Amankrah Appiah, and the Obuasi Municipal Director of Education, Kwamena Owusu-Nketiah, to step aside with immediate effect as investigations continue into allegations of sexual misconduct involving the headmaster of Obuasi Senior High Technical School (SHTS), Zakaria Abdulai.

In a statement issued on Tuesday, October 20, 2026, and signed by its Head of Public Relations, Daniel Fenyi, the GES said the directive was intended to ensure the investigation proceeds without interference or the perception of interference.

The two directors have been instructed to hand over their offices and all state property in their possession to the Deputy Ashanti Regional Director of Education, Thomas Kwame Boateng.

The GES also reaffirmed that Mr Abdulai remains interdicted, dismissing reports circulating that he had been cleared.

“The public is urged to ignore any news making the rounds that the headmaster has been cleared,” the statement said.

Management of the Service called for calm, support and cooperation as investigations into the matter continue.

The directive follows mounting pressure from civil society organisations, including RISE-Ghana, over the handling of the allegations against Mr Abdulai.

The National Democratic Congress (NDC) has also directed Mr Abdulai to step aside from the Juaben Constituency Chairmanship race pending the outcome of an investigation by the Criminal Investigations Department (CID) of the Ghana Police Service.

A JoyNews investigation by Manasseh Azure Awuni reported that municipal authorities, education officials and other influential figures had received reports concerning alleged sexual abuse by the headmaster months before his suspension.

The number of students alleging abuse has reportedly risen to 16.

The Education Ministry has directed the CID to investigate the allegations.

The decision to have the two education directors step aside comes as authorities face calls to establish how the allegations were handled and ensure the investigation proceeds without interference.

The GES has urged stakeholders to cooperate with the process as investigators work to establish the facts.

The allegations against Mr Abdulai have not been established, and he remains entitled to the presumption of innocence.

Ghana News.title: GoldBod targets bigger stake for Ghana in new mines through geological studies
Ghana News.content:
The Ghana Gold Board (GoldBod) is undertaking geological investigations in parts of the country to reduce investment risks and position Ghana to secure stronger equity stakes in future mining projects, Chief Executive Officer Sammy Gyamfi has announced.

Mr Gyamfi said the board was collaborating with the Ghana Geological Survey Authority under its Mining Support Programme to investigate mineralised areas at Funsi in the Upper West Region and Bensere in the Ashanti Region.

The studies are expected to provide reliable geological data, attract credible investors and support the responsible expansion of Ghana’s mining base.

Delivering a keynote address at the African Minerals Policy Forum – Mining in Motion 2026, Mr Gyamfi said the initiative was intended to address one of the major barriers to greater Ghanaian participation in the mining industry: the risk capital required for geological exploration.

He argued that mineral sovereignty must extend beyond legal ownership of resources to effective local participation in financing, technology, processing and mining operations.

“These studies will help build a reliable investment-grade asset portfolio, reduce investor risks and position GoldBod to negotiate stronger equity stakes in the resulting model mines for Ghana,” he said.

Mr Gyamfi added that the country needed to move away from overdependence on free-carried interests and royalties towards securing controlling equity interests in sustainable mines.

World.title: Trump pleads not guilty to 34 felony counts
World.content:
News outlets will not be allowed to broadcast former President Donald Trump’s arraignment on Tuesday in a New York state court, a judge said Monday night, but he will allow some photographers to take pictures in the courtroom before the proceedings formally begin.

Acting New York Supreme Court Judge Juan Merchan rejected the request by several media organizations, including CNN, for permission to broadcast the historic proceedings. Trump’s arraignment — like most arraignments in the Manhattan courthouse — is a public proceeding, but news cameras are not usually allowed to broadcast from inside the courtroom.

However, the judge is allowing five pool photographers to take still photos at the beginning of the proceedings “until such time as they are directed to vacate the jury box by court personnel.”

Earlier on Monday, Trump’s lawyers urged the judge to reject the media’s request for live cameras in the courtroom. The Manhattan District Attorney’s office told the judge they didn’t have a position.

The media outlets that tried to get cameras into the courtroom argued that “the gravity of this proceeding … and, consequently, the need for the broadest possible public access, cannot be overstated.”

Trump is now in Manhattan ahead of the arraignment. A grand jury indicted the former president last week.

The arraignment is also expected to bring the unsealing of the criminal charges against Trump, which have not yet been seen by his lawyers or the public.

The indictment stems from Manhattan District Attorney Alvin Bragg’s investigation into hush-money payments, made during the 2016 presidential campaign, to women who claimed they had extramarital affairs with Trump, which he denies.

Trump denies all wrongdoing and his lawyers said last week that they’ll fight to get the charges dropped.

World.title: Russian authorities detain suspect over St. Petersburg cafe blast
World.content:
A Ukrainian tank is seen near the frontline area amid the Russia-Ukraine war, in Bakhmut, Ukraine, on April 02. (Muhammed Enes Yildirim/Anadolu Agency/Getty Images)

The Ukrainian military has reported little change to the front lines but heavy fire from Russian forces at various parts of the front line in the Donetsk region.

The General Staff said that more than 45 enemy attacks had been repelled over the past day, with the focus on Lyman, Bakhmut, Avdiivka and Mariinka.

It said there were 17 air strikes and more than 20 strikes by multiple launch rocket systems.

“In the Bakhmut direction, the enemy is trying to take full control over the city of Bakhmut and continues to storm it,” the General Staff said.

West of the city, Ukrainian defense forces repelled about 20 enemy attacks, according to the General Staff.

Oleksandr Syrskyi, commander of Ukrainian Land Forces, posted on Telegram that in Bakhmut he had met with “soldiers and commanders who destroyed the myth of invincibility of the Wagner fighters and Russian paratroopers.”

“The enemy is weakening and trying to cover up its failures with new fakes about the capture of Bakhmut,” Syrskyi said.

Syrskyi referenced the possibility of a future counter-offensive, saying that “the forward movement of our entire army depends on what every soldier is doing right now on their section of the front.”

Some of the most intense fighting is to the northwest and west of the city of Donetsk – as the Russians continue months-long efforts to dislodge Ukrainian defenses in Avdiivka and Mariinka. The General Staff said that some 20 assaults had been repelled.

“There are also some operational successes of our military in the Donetsk area. Our military have taken some positions. They have taken a more strategic and favourable position,” said Oleksii Dmytrashkivskyi, spokesperson for the military in that zone.

He also noted that Russian special forces had been introduced in the area.

“The enemy is trying to attack our positions between Avdiivka and Marinka. These attempts do not stop. It should be noted that the enemy has suffered quite significant losses,” Dmytrashkivskyi said.

He also claimed that the Russians “don’t have the same amount of equipment and, as they themselves say, they are on a ‘diet’ of ammunition for assaults.”

Social media video showed both sides engaged in heavy fire in the Avdiivka area, which the Russians have surrounded on three sides.

Denis Pushilin, the leader of the self-declared Donetsk People’s Republic, claimed that Russian forces were still advancing in the Avdiivka direction.

“It is still premature to speak of encirclement, but the situation is being created, if not critical, then extremely difficult for the enemy… After clearing Kamianka, our units are moving further. There are difficulties both with the terrain, which must also be overcome, and there are also similarities with weather conditions. But these difficulties are mutual — both for the enemy and for us,” Pushilin said.

World.title: Suspected Chinese spy balloon was able to transmit information back to Beijing
World.content:
Washington —

The Chinese spy balloon that transited the US earlier this year was able to capture imagery and collect some signals intelligence from US military sites, a source familiar with the matter tells CNN.

The balloon was able to transmit information back to Beijing in real time, the source said, and the US government still does not know for sure whether the Chinese government could wipe the balloon’s data as it received it. That raises questions about whether there is intelligence the balloon was able to gather that the US still doesn’t know about.

Still, the intelligence community has not been overly concerned about the information the balloon was able to gather, the person said, because it is not much more sophisticated than what Chinese satellites are able to glean as they orbit over similar locations.

A US intelligence official told CNN on Monday that “although analysis of the wreckage of the High Altitude Balloon remains ongoing, thus far, its flight over the United States does not appear to have provided critical new insights to the People’s Republic of China.”

The US also knew what the balloon’s path would be and was able to protect sensitive sites and censor some signals before the balloon was able to pick them up, officials have said.

As CNN has reported, the US intelligence community last year developed a method of tracking what it says is a fleet of these Chinese balloons operating across the globe, controlled by the Chinese military.

The FBI is still examining the balloon, but so far officials have been able to glean additional information about how the device worked, including the algorithms used for the balloon’s software and how it is powered and designed.

CNN has reached out to the National Security Council at the White House and the Pentagon for comment. NBC was first to report on the new intelligence.

Video Ad Feedback Justin Trudeau on what the world needs to do to handle China's threats 1:33 • Source: CNN Justin Trudeau on what the world needs to do to handle China's threats 1:33

The balloon first crossed into US airspace over Alaska in late January before passing through Canada and down into Montana, where it hovered for a few days, leading the US to believe it was trying to surveil sensitive military sites, like Malmstrom Air Force Base in Montana. It was eventually shot down by the US off the East Coast on February 4, and the incident further escalated tensions between Washington and Beijing, including the postponement of a diplomatic visit by US Secretary of State Antony Blinken to China.

A senior State Department official said in February that, as the balloon floated across the US, it “was capable of conducting signals intelligence collection operations.”

Gen. Glen VanHerck, the commander of US Northern Command and NORAD, said at the time that the US “did not assess” that the balloon “presented a significant collection hazard beyond what already exists in actionable technical means from the Chinese.”

The surveillance program, which includes a number of similar balloons, is in part run out of the small Chinese province of Hainan, officials told CNN. The US does not know the precise size of the fleet of Chinese surveillance balloons, but sources tell CNN that the program has conducted at least two dozen missions over at least five continents in recent years.

Roughly half a dozen of those flights have been within US airspace, although not necessarily over US territory, according to one official familiar with the intelligence.

China has maintained that the balloon was actually just a weather balloon thrown off course, and the US has been assessing the possibility that it was not deliberately maneuvered into the continental US by the Chinese government, CNN has reported.

Still, China did maintain some ability to maneuver the balloon, officials believe. And once the balloon was over Montana, China appeared to take advantage of its position to loiter over sensitive sites and try to collect intelligence.

This story has been updated with additional reporting.

World.title: Beijing promised to 'fight back' over Taiwan leader's US visit. But this time it has more to lose
World.content:
Hong Kong —

An anticipated meeting between Taiwan’s President Tsai Ing-wen and US House Speaker Kevin McCarthy in California this week has sparked concerns of a repeat of the pressure campaign China launched last year when then-Speaker Nancy Pelosi visited Taipei.

At that time, Beijing encircled the island democracy with unprecedented military drills – firing multiple missiles into its surrounding waters and sending dozens of warplanes speeding across a sensitive median line dividing the Taiwan Strait.

It also cut off contact with the United States over a number of issues from military matters to combating climate change, in retaliation for what it viewed as a violation of its sovereignty.

This time, Beijing has already threatened to “resolutely fight back” if a Tsai-McCarthy meeting goes ahead.

Video Ad Feedback See why tensions are rising between US and China over Taiwan 2:32 • Source: CNN See why tensions are rising between US and China over Taiwan 2:32

It also slammed Washington for allowing Tsai to stopover in the US while en route to and from official visits in Central America, warning it could lead to “serious” confrontation between the two powers.

A defiant Tsai staked out her own ground, pledging as she took off on her 10-day trip not to let “external pressure” stop Taiwan from connecting with the world and like-minded democracies.

But the optics of the meeting, taking place in California and not Taiwan, and its timing – at a particularly thorny moment in China’s foreign relations and ahead of a presidential election in Taiwan that could reset the tone of its relationship with Beijing – may see Beijing tread more carefully this time, or at least not escalate further, analysts say.

“This puts the burden on China not to overreact, because any overreaction is only going to push China further away from the world,” said Yun Sun, director of the China Program at the Stimson Center think tank in Washington.

That doesn’t mean, however, that Beijing won’t be closely watching Tsai’s movements as it calibrates its response – and decides how much military might to flex over her meeting with an American lawmaker on American soil.

The opacity of China’s system – and the potential for competing interests within its vast bureaucracy – also make it difficult to accurately predict its response.

“Every time Taiwan does anything that China doesn’t like, the Chinese react with their own military coercion,” Sun said. But in the current situation, “they have to consider the consequences of overreaction,” she added.

House Speaker Kevin McCarthy talks to reporters at the Capitol in Washington on March 24, 2023. J. Scott Applewhite/AP

Rising pressure

The expected meeting, which McCarthy’s office announced earlier this week would take place on Wednesday, also comes at a precarious moment in US-China relations.

Washington and Beijing are struggling to stabilize their communication amid flaring tensions over issues from a downed suspected Chinese surveillance balloon to semiconductor supply chains – raising the stakes of potential damage to that relationship if Beijing lashes out as it did when Tsai met Pelosi.

Taiwan is still feeling the fallout of that response last August, with Chinese military forces now regularly making incursions over what had previously been an informal but largely respected border of control between Beijing and Taipei in the Taiwan Strait. Taiwan’s official Central News Agency also reported Monday that Tsai would meet with McCarthy, citing Tsai’s presidential office.

Video Ad Feedback See image of a Chinese balloon hovering over Taiwan 3:05 • Source: CNN See image of a Chinese balloon hovering over Taiwan 3:05

But a meeting between Tsai and the leader of the Republican majority in the US House of Representatives, who ranks second in line to the Presidency, would mark another symbolic moment for Taiwan and the US, which only maintain unofficial ties.

For Tsai, who is entering the final year of her two-term presidency, “it’s clearly a capstone event,” according to Wen-Ti Sung, a political scientist at the Australian National University’s Taiwan Studies Program. “She has this image as the Taiwanese president who has taken US-Taiwan relations to new heights, and who … has been able to give Taiwan almost unprecedented international visibility,” he said.

That increased visibility – and enhanced cooperation with the US – has followed China’s mounting pressure on the island, which sits fewer than 110 miles (177 kilometers) from the mainland coast.

China’s Communist Party claims the self-governing island democracy as its own despite never having controlled it, and has vowed to take the island, by force if necessary.

The party has undertaken a sweeping expansion of its military capabilities over the past decade under leader Xi Jinping – and ramped up its pervasive economic, diplomatic and military pressure on Taiwan.

That’s driven concerns, among some in Washington, that Beijing is preparing for an invasion, though China’s official language still suggests that scenario is not its preferred option for achieving the claimed goal of “reunification.”

It is those pressures – and how to support Taiwan against unilateral actions by Beijing – that are likely to be on the table when Tsai, McCarthy and a bipartisan group of US lawmakers sit down on Wednesday.

Congress has been a pillar of increasing American support for Taiwan in recent years. Lawmakers regularly visit the island and drive bipartisan legislation enhancing support and cooperation.

While the US switched its diplomatic relations to Beijing decades ago, it maintains unofficial ties with Taiwan and is bound by law to provide the democratic island with the means to defend itself.

Under Washington’s longstanding “One China” policy, the US acknowledges China’s position that Taiwan is part of China, but has never officially recognized Beijing’s claim to the island of 23 million.

Though McCarthy does not have Pelosi’s decades-long record of advocacy regarding China, the California Republican is now a leading voice pushing for closer scrutiny of Beijing, and meeting Tsai could help him to burnish that image.

Last month, McCarthy told reporters that meeting Tsai in the US would not impact whether he travels to Taiwan in the future – something he had earlier said he wanted to do.

Fighter jets of the Chinese People's Liberation Army Eastern Theater Command conduct joint combat training exercises around Taiwan on August 7, 2022 in this photo released by Xinhua News Agency. Gong Yulong/Xinhua/AP

Beijing watching

A meeting in California, on US soil, is widely seen as less likely to provoke Beijing than a McCarthy visit to Taiwan.

Pelosi’s trip – the first from a lawmaker of that rank to the island in 25 years – generated a fever pitch of nationalist and anti-US rhetoric in mainland China.

This time, so far, domestic conversation in China’s heavily controlled media sphere has been significantly muted.

But the stakes remain high – including for Beijing itself – over how it responds, analysts say.

As Taiwan prepares for a presidential election in January, a fierce response could push voters away from Taiwan’s main opposition party Kuomintang (KMT), widely seen as more friendly toward Beijing.

It could also jar with another high profile trip happening now: a tour of mainland China from former Taiwan president and senior KMT member Ma Ying-jeou, the first visit from a current or former Taiwan leader since the end of the Chinese Civil War in 1949.

Ma’s tour is a “once in a half a century opportunity to send a conciliatory message between the two sides, Beijing shouldn’t want to tank that,” said Sung, the political scientist.

China is also acutely aware that its actions toward Taiwan are under a significantly brighter global spotlight following the invasion of Ukraine by Russian President Vladimir Putin, a close diplomatic partner of Xi. Putin’s rhetoric over Ukraine has echoes of how Xi speaks of Taiwan.

Beijing has recently sought to position itself as an agent of peace in that conflict – especially as it aims to repair frayed ties with Europe.

This week, as Tsai is expected to meet with McCarthy, French President Emmanuel Macron and European Commission President Ursula von der Leyen will head to China – an important opportunity that Xi may not want to overshadow with military posturing.

An aggressive response also risks stoking confrontation with the US, not yet six months after Xi and US President Joe Biden called to enhance communication during a face-to-face meeting in Bali.

“(A less overtly aggressive response) would imply that Beijing does not wish to escalate tension with the US to a level that can risk getting out of hand,” said Steve Tsang, director of the SOAS China Institute in London.

“A reset in US-China ties is not on the agenda, but an easing of tension is not beyond the realm of possibility.”

World.title: ‘Horizontal revolt’: Why Albania’s young protesters want PM Rama to go
World.content:
From the ‘Flamingo Revolution’ to street clashes in Tirana, an inside look at a leaderless youth uprising challenging Edi Rama’s decade-long rule.

Share ‘Horizontal revolt’: Why Albania’s young protesters want PM Rama to go on social media

For several days, the streets of Tirana have witnessed a wave of antigovernment demonstrations, with demonstrators engaged in fierce clashes with security forces, while police have fired tear gas on thousands of young protesters to prevent them from scaling barricades.

Protests escalated last week after school and university students joined them, citing rising tuition fees and crumbling infrastructure.

What initially began as a targeted environmental protest in May has rapidly escalated into one of the most serious political challenges facing Prime Minister Edi Rama in his more than a decade in power.

Yet, as the unrest reaches a boiling point, a fundamental question remains: Who is behind this movement, and can it force systemic political change?

‘A horizontal rebellion’ spurred by social media

Contrary to claims by government officials that the unrest is being orchestrated by political opponents or external actors, analysts and journalists on the ground emphasise that the movement is largely decentralised and youth-driven.

Fatos Hakorja, editor-in-chief of TV Klan and Klan News, told Al Jazeera that the demonstrations have evolved organically into a broad coalition of high school students, university students, environmentalists, and aggrieved citizens.

“So far, what can be said with certainty is that the protests have been organised mainly by young people themselves,” Hakorja told Al Jazeera. “What began as the ‘Flamingo Revolution’ gradually developed into a broader student and youth protest… There is no clear evidence that a single consolidated structure stands behind the protests,” he said, referring to the May protest against a luxury resort that threatens the protected coastline.



Hakorja noted that coordination takes place dynamically across digital platforms such as WhatsApp, Telegram, and Snapchat, rather than through formal organisational hierarchies.

Albanian political analyst and publicist Ben Andoni echoed this view, describing the situation not merely as a standard protest, but as “a genuine, horizontal revolt”.

“The protest has turned into a rebellion for the past seven days. It was a protest before, but it has never taken on the character of a movement. If it were so, there would be a leadership group and some short-, medium-, and long-term goals,” Andoni told Al Jazeera.

“It is a horizontal movement, where people are mobilised by TikTok groups and social networks, but not by true cultural and political organisations. That is also a handicap or a source of pressure for Rama’s government, which seeks to negotiate, but finds no single counterpart standing in its way.”

From the ‘Flamingo Revolution’ to broad structural discontent

The roots of the current unrest are multifaceted, blending localised grievances with deep-seated frustration over governance, economic stagnation, and corruption.

The initial spark – dubbed the “Flamingo Revolution” – was ignited by environmental opposition to controversial luxury development projects, notably in the protected area of Zvernec and the planned resort investment on Sazan Island by the firm of Jared Kushner, United States President Donald Trump’s son-in-law.

The flamingo, native to these coastal lagoons, quickly became a symbol of resistance against the perceived commodification of public lands.

However, environmental concerns swiftly converged with student anger over high tuition fees, inadequate dormitory conditions, and low educational competitiveness. Beneath these immediate triggers lies a much deeper structural crisis.

“Problems of corruption, nepotism, and a lack of perspective are the main reasons that drove people to protest,” Andoni explained.

“The protest summarised the entire range of problems that Albania has, and brought them to the doorstep of a government that has crossed lines regarding corruption, inequality, and particularly a lack of empathy for the people.

“Among some protesters, especially on social media, there is also a narrative that Rama is placing the country’s interests at the service of private interests, his personal hold on power, or foreign interests, including Israeli interests. These claims have not been proven, but they seem to have increased the anger of some young people and part of the wider population,” Hakorja added.



Rama has strongly rejected the allegations, calling them conspiracy theories and dismissing them as manipulated disinformation spread through social media by “foreign hands”, aimed at destabilising the government and undermining the country’s public institutions.

Rejection of the entire political class

A defining feature of the uprising is the protesters’ explicit rejection of the ruling Socialist Party (SP) and the traditional opposition, including the Democratic Party (PD) led by Sali Berisha.

While Prime Minister Rama has accused the opposition of taking over the movement, and opposition supporters have joined the crowds on the ground, experts stress that opposition leaders exercise no direct control over the demonstrators. In fact, several opposition MPs who attempted to address the crowds faced open hostility and rejection.

“A large number of these young people seem to feel unrepresented by the whole political class,” Hakorja told Al Jazeera.

“They see the political system as disconnected from their reality and as a system that protects the interests of a minority more than it addresses the problems of the majority of citizens.”

This widespread cynicism has resulted in an uncompromising stance. Demonstrators have demanded the immediate resignation of Prime Minister Rama and the formation of a technical government, refusing official offers of dialogue due to a total breakdown of trust in state institutions.

The deep cynicism towards Albania’s political class stems from a widespread feeling that leaders are entirely indifferent to citizens’ daily struggles. Young people face rampant corruption, high unemployment, and an economy that drives huge brain drain.

This disconnect is further spurred by years of government apathy towards crumbling public education, high tuition fees, and poor dormitory conditions.

Furthermore, controversial state-backed developments – such as the planned luxury resort by Kushner’s firm – serve as prime examples for citizens who believe the political establishment consistently trades national resources and public goods for private and foreign interests.

Heavy-handed security and growing fatigue

Faced with a leaderless movement that refuses to negotiate, the Albanian government has increasingly relied on security forces to maintain control.

Police have been accused of brutality as they have used tear gas, water cannons, and rubber bullets to quell the protesters. At least 167 people have been arrested, including minors.

In a move that highlights the administration’s reliance on law enforcement, Prime Minister Rama announced a 2,500-euro ($2,800) bonus for police officers on the front lines, alongside substantial salary increases set for 2027.

Hakorja pointed out that the government is treating the crisis predominantly as a matter of public order and security.

He also highlighted troubling incidents, such as the appearance of unidentified civilians armed with wooden sticks inside the Socialist Party headquarters. While these individuals remained inside to protect the building as protesters hurled stones and attacked the entrance, their presence – including individuals holding public positions – led to fears of informal, non-state security responses operating alongside or outside official police forces.

What lies ahead?

As both sides brace for further escalation, the immediate outlook remains uncertain. Without clear leadership to negotiate terms, or intervention from international partners such as the European Union and the US, the deadlock threatens to prolong political instability.



According to Andoni, the Rama administration has used force as its main instrument, as it has suffered a severe loss of moral authority and legitimacy.

“Demonstrators remain persistent and aggressive, while Rama plays the card of force through the police,” Andoni told Al Jazeera, adding that “fatigue” is impacting the young protesters.

“It seems that young people may execute a tactical withdrawal first by temporarily stepping back from the streets due to exhaustion, leaving the weight and burden of proof on Mr Rama” – placing the ultimate responsibility on the prime minister to prove that his government has the legitimacy, capability, and sincere intent to carry out deep reforms and resolve a crisis that police force has only further escalated.

Whether this youth-led rebellion marks the beginning of a new political era in Albania or subsides under policing and exhaustion, it has irrevocably exposed the deep rift between Albania’s youth and its governing political establishment.

World.title: Why Rubio is visiting Reliance’s oil refinery in India, the world’s largest
World.content:
Reliance is central to Washington’s efforts to punish Russian energy buyers and contain oil prices amid the war on Iran with a crucial midterm election looming.

Share Why Rubio is visiting Reliance’s oil refinery in India, the world’s largest on social media

New Delhi, India — United States Secretary of State Marco Rubio has arrived in India for a two-day visit, during which he is set to tour the Jamnagar refinery complex in Gujarat, owned by billionaire Mukesh Ambani’s Reliance Industries, a major player in global oil markets.

Reliance’s crude refinery in Prime Minister Narendra Modi’s home state is the world’s largest single-site refinery. In many ways, Reliance Industries’ businesses sit at the crossroads of the ongoing global energy crisis.

The conglomerate is central to Washington’s efforts to punish Russian energy buyers, while also trying to contain oil prices amid the war on Iran, on top of rising diesel costs in the US, where a crucial midterm election looms. Reliance has also only recently committed to a major investment in the US, which President Donald Trump’s administration has cited as an example of its successes in luring global capital.

Rubio is skipping the capital, New Delhi, at a time when the US-India bilateral relationship has been rocky, strained by a string of friction points — and an elusive trade deal.

So why is the top US diplomat visiting the world’s largest single-site oil refinery?

Where is Rubio visiting?

After meetings in Mumbai, India’s financial hub in the western state of Maharashtra, Rubio will fly to Jamnagar in neighbouring Gujarat, near the Gulf of Kutch. Jamnagar opens into the Arabian Sea and is home to Reliance Industries’ refining complex, a major hub for crude processing and fuel exports, which processes 1.4 million barrels per day (bpd).



Rubio had visited India earlier this year too, but this trip “is a little more business-focused”, the US ambassador to India, Sergio Gor, told reporters last week. A readout from Rubio’s office noted that he would “meet with business leaders to promote opportunities for commercial investment and economic cooperation”.

“[At Jamnagar] he will meet some of the folks at Reliance,” Gor said.

What’s in Jamnagar?

The world’s largest single-site oil-refining complex has a combined crude-processing capacity of 1.4 million bpd. That is nearly 1.5 percent of global refining capacity, according to the company.

The complex comprises two refineries: the original facility, commissioned in 1999 with a capacity of 660,000bpd, and a second, export-oriented refinery commissioned in 2008, adding 580,000bpd, which operates in a special economic zone.

Jamnagar imports crude from international suppliers and exports refined products to global markets. The refinery can process heavy, sulphur-rich crude that many facilities cannot handle efficiently, converting oil into higher-value products.

Reliance said last month that the complex has processed more than 216 crude grades, claiming to be “perhaps the only refinery to achieve this feat”.

The Jamnagar refinery’s capacity is also driving a sharp revival in imports of Venezuelan crude — taken over by the US earlier this year after abducting then-President Nicolas Maduro — as Washington seeks to reshape global oil trade.

Reliance is expected to account for roughly 350,000bpd to 370,000bpd of the October intake, according to estimates from analytics firm Kpler. “We will talk with Reliance about refining more Venezuelan crude,” Rubio told reporters in brief remarks on Tuesday.

Why is the refinery significant for global energy supplies?

Reliance is a central player in keeping global oil markets stable, as one of the world’s biggest suppliers of refined petroleum products. In September, for instance, six of the seven large cargo ships that docked at European Union ports carrying oil products were bearing Reliance goods.

Reliance’s biggest export is diesel, which Trump has been particularly worried about, with prices reaching historic highs in the US ahead of midterm elections early next month.

Though the data on exports by category is not public, an analysis by the Reuters news agency from trade sources noted that Reliance Industries exported 21.66 million tonnes of refined petroleum products in the first half of 2025 from Jamnagar. Diesel accounted for the largest share at 9.81 million tonnes, followed by petrol at 6.14 million tonnes and jet fuel at 2.06 million tonnes.



Europe accounted for the biggest share of the company’s exports, making up 28 percent of Reliance’s refined products during the period. Buyers include BP, ExxonMobil, Glencore, Vitol and Trafigura.

The Jamnagar refinery also shipped about $143m worth of oil products to the US last month, according to data cited by the Centre for Research on Energy and Clean Air (CREA), a think tank in Finland.

CREA noted in its report that the EU’s ban on importing petroleum products made from Russian crude from January 2026 does not adequately prevent products from refineries in third countries from entering Europe when those refineries also process Russian crude. The Jamnagar refinery is a prime example of that loophole.

Rubio’s visit to the refinery also comes as Trump faces his worst approval ratings amid inflation and rising fuel prices ahead of the midterm election in November. Just about 31 percent of Americans are happy with Trump’s performance – the lowest-ever number in his two terms, according to a Reuters/Ipsos survey.

The Trump administration has also reportedly been pushing Ukraine’s President Volodymyr Zelenskyy to stop strikes on Russian energy facilities, which have rattled the global fuel markets.

Why the refinery is important for the Russia-Ukraine war

Reliance is also a critical actor in US efforts to influence how much oil Russia sells.

Since the start of Russia’s full-fledged war on Ukraine in February 2022, India has emerged as the second-largest buyer of Russian oil after China. And Reliance is driving that surge in imports. While only 3 percent of its oil was sourced from Russia before 2022, that share rose to 50 percent by 2025.

So when Trump imposed an additional 25 percent tariff on Indian goods in August 2025 to punish New Delhi for the purchase of Russian oil, Reliance was directly affected. It cut back on Russian crude imports significantly in subsequent months, but it still made up a third of the oil processed by Jamnagar’s refinery during the July-September 2026 quarter.

That was under threat when the Trump administration appeared poised to impose a 100 percent tariff on Indian goods because of continued Russian oil imports, under a new law passed last month.

But Trump has since suspended those proposed tariffs, easing concerns for India and Reliance.

Rubio has said India has been diversifying its import mix away from Russian crude, even as it still buys millions of barrels of Russian oil every day. “You’ve got countries like India, for example, that have voluntarily diversified their energy portfolio, but are still getting a substantial amount of energy from Russia because it’s hard to pivot from one day to the next,” Rubio said on Sunday.

“But they’re also an important ally and partner of the United States.”

Is Reliance also investing in the US?

Yes, India’s richest man, Mukesh Ambani, the chairman and managing director of Reliance Industries, is investing in the US, primarily through energy-related projects.

It is backing America First Refining’s planned oil refinery at the Port of Brownsville in Texas, also the first major US refinery in about 50 years, announced by Trump in March.



The refinery is expected to cost $3bn to $4bn and process about 60 million barrels of US crude annually. Reliance has signed a 20-year agreement to buy a large share of the facility’s output, with operations expected to start around 2029.

In November 2024, Reliance’s US subsidiary also acquired a 21 percent stake in helium explorer Wavetech Helium for $12m as part of its low-carbon energy strategy.

Last month, Trump announced that India’s Essar Group — an oil major with knee-deep ties to Russia — is planning an $18bn integrated steel investment in the US through its subsidiary, Mesabi Metallics.

Didn’t Trump’s ally just lock horns with Ambani?

Despite Reliance’s investments in the US and Rubio’s upcoming visit to the Jamnagar facility, Elon Musk, the world’s richest man who is also a key Trump ally, recently hit out at Ambani.

His Starlink space telecommunications firm has struggled for years to secure a licence to operate in India.

In ⁠a series of X posts recently, Musk accused Prime Minister Narendra Modi’s government of stalling Starlink’s entry to ⁠favour market leader Ambani’s telecom firm, Jio. Musk taunted Ambani directly, addressing ‌him as “Prime ‌Minister Ambani” and asking whether he would “consider allowing Starlink to compete”. Starlink, Musk wrote, was being blocked by “oligarchs” protecting their “monopolistic chokehold” on Indians.

In a statement issued on X, Reliance said it has “never feared competition” and has “grown in an India that welcomes investment and innovation, homegrown or international”.

World.title: Iran denies collapse is close as US claims IRGC running out of money
World.content:
Iranian authorities have remained defiant despite the financial strain, saying they want to lift the US blockade and pressure on their terms.

Share Iran denies collapse is close as US claims IRGC running out of money on social media

Tehran, Iran – Iranian authorities have rejected claims that Iran is unable to support its regional allies, but acknowledged that the United States’ sanctions and the war have created financial challenges.

US Central Command chief Brad Cooper claimed last week that a combination of military attacks and a naval blockade of Iran’s southern ports “has dealt severe blows” to the country.

The admiral said the US had prevented at least $25bn in Iranian crude exports and helped freeze approximately $350m in cryptocurrency assets. This means the Iranian Revolutionary Guard Corps (IRGC) are now unable to pay their soldiers and Iran-linked regional groups suffering from financial shortfalls.

“The financial strain on Iran’s military has become so significant that there are reports of Iran-aligned militia groups across the region withholding payments to their soldiers in order to funnel money back to the IRGC, which also is not paying its troops,” Cooper said.

This is being portrayed as a victory for the US in its war with Iran, which so far has shown very few tangible victories for Washington.

Michael Knights, head of MENA research at US-based intelligence and geopolitical risk advisory firm Horizon Engage, said Hezbollah in Lebanon and the Houthis in Yemen have suffered financially during the past few years.

“The national economies feeding the Hezbollah and Houthi movements are badly broken, so they continue to receive stipends and in-kind funding – in fuel products – from Iran,” Knights told Al Jazeera.

Funding the axis

For decades, the IRGC Quds Force has supplied money, weapons, components, training and manufacturing expertise to regional allied groups. It has enabled partners at loggerheads with the US and Israel to assemble or produce a number of weapons locally, according to United Nations experts and US officials.



The axis groups also draw on businesses, including oil exports, as well as donations and local resources to fund their operations. Some Iraqi factions have been integrated into the official security forces and receive government funding through the Popular Mobilisation Forces.

Allied commercial networks in Iraq are selling Iranian commodities and distributing proceeds through intermediaries and exchange houses, the US Department of the Treasury has claimed.

This has put them in a better financial position than their “poorer cousins” in Hezbollah and the Houthis, Knights said, with some money allegedly flowing from Iraq towards Iran in recent years.

“Some Iraqi militiamen and government civil servants are indeed paid late at the same time that Iraqi militias send funding overseas to help Iran, the Houthis and Lebanese Hezbollah,” he told Al Jazeera.

The US Treasury alleged in September that Kataib Hezbollah, a prominent Tehran-backed Shia Muslim armed group in neighbouring Iraq, siphoned Iraqi resources to support Iran.

The Treasury also described substantial earlier transfers from the Quds Force to Hezbollah, depicting flows in both directions.

A report by the Reuters news agency earlier this month cited unnamed sources as saying Hezbollah received $200m from Iran in September. The US State Department rejected the report at the time, saying Hezbollah was “trying to save face with fake stories about cash influxes from Iran”.

Iran says no ‘collapse’ imminent

Iran’s economy has taken hit after hit in recent years due to war, domestic mismanagement and sanctions.

This has led to runaway inflation, low-paying jobs, a depreciating national currency and isolation from the global community for 90 million Iranians.

There appears to be little sign of the situation improving, with the World Bank reporting earlier this month a projected 7.7 percent contraction of the economy in the fiscal year 2026-27.

The authorities emphasise that does not affect their resolve. They have also challenged US Treasury assessments that economic pressure could result in losing control within months.

“Despite all these pressures, the Iranian economy has demonstrated very good resilience, and the claim that Iran’s economy is collapsing is nothing more than an illusion,” Central Bank chief Abdolnaser Hemmati said earlier this month.



Financial problems

President Masoud Pezeshkian acknowledged on Sunday that military attacks and the maritime blockade had created substantial problems for the country. But he said his government was relying on domestic capacities to withstand the pressure.

He claimed consumption management had now removed the need for petrol imports that would otherwise cost $12bn, if US pressure allowed imports at all. The president promised to return revenues from recently increased fuel prices to households by modestly increasing their electronic food vouchers.

Knights said the Iranian authorities were “stuck in an aggressive cycle of escalation with the US government no matter what state Iran’s economy is in”.

“Trump is betting that being poorer will make Iran’s regime more flexible, but that has never been a good bet,” he said.

Negar Mortazavi, a senior fellow at the Washington, DC-based Center for International Policy, said she expected Tehran to continue prioritising its regional allied groups despite the financial strains involved.

“Economic pressure is certainly constraining Iran’s military resources, but that does not mean it will fundamentally change the IRGC’s strategic calculations or force Tehran to surrender,” she told Al Jazeera.

World.title: France PM promises more curfews as authorities seek to regain control
World.content:
Prime Minister Sebastien Lecornu says local authorities will coordinate with mayors to decide whether to impose curfews.

French Prime Minister Sebastien Lecornu has said new curfews will be imposed where necessary in parts of the country, as authorities sought to restore order after weekend demonstrations over the cost of living and issues in the education system descended into riots.

In a post on X on Tuesday, Lecornu said local authorities would coordinate with mayors to decide whether to impose curfews in their respective prefectures.

More than half a million people gathered across France on Saturday for demonstrations that brought together students demanding better education conditions and groups rejecting the high cost of living. The protests descended into looting and arson in numerous locations, with more than 2,500 people arrested.

Monday night passed without any major incidents across France, police have confirmed.

The government is due to hold a series of meetings as it intensifies efforts to contain the unrest, which followed weeks of student protests over education standards.

French Digital Minister Anne Le Henanff is due to meet social media bosses on Tuesday to discuss the protests. In a post on X on Monday, Henanff said goods looted over the weekend were being sold online and called on platforms to remove such listings.

Demonstrators have called for further protests this Saturday, but France’s main trade unions have not backed the call, with union officials due to meet Lecornu on Wednesday. On Thursday, Lecornu will hold talks with political parties about the protests, which come before presidential elections due to take place in April and May next year.



Marine Le Pen, the leader of the far-right National Rally, currently leads the polls. Far-left candidate Jean-Luc Melenchon, who leads La France Insoumise, is currently in second place. President Emmanuel Macron cannot stand because of France’s two-term limit.

Le Pen and Melenchon have both been accused of exploiting the protests before next year’s vote.

Alice Cohen-Morzadec, a spokesperson for the French Student Union, told Al Jazeera that the demonstrations were an “outburst” of anger in response to Macron’s policies, which she said had “destroyed” students’ living conditions.

“One student out of two cannot eat properly. One student out of three doesn’t have a permanent house to live in. We cannot study in these conditions,” Cohen-Morzadec said.

World.title: Is Russia stalking satellites which help Ukraine from space?
World.content:
Analysts say a Russian craft’s close pass of a commercial radar satellite is a first and a warning to Kyiv’s backers.

Share Is Russia stalking satellites which help Ukraine from space? on social media

A Russian military satellite has manoeuvred to within metres of a US-registered radar satellite believed to provide intelligence to Ukraine, according to space-tracking data reported by The War Zone, a US defence news site.

Cosmos 2612 may have passed ICEYE-X36, a satellite owned by the US arm of the Finnish company ICEYE.

LeoLabs, a US space-tracking company, put the closest approach at about 500 metres, according to Breaking Defence.

ICEYE has supplied radar imagery to Ukraine since 2022, Defence News reported.

So is Russia stalking satellites which help Ukraine from space? Al Jazeera spoke to analysts to find out:

What has happened?

A Russian satellite has deliberately positioned itself close to a Western one, after months of manoeuvring.

Cosmos 2612 is one of six satellites the Russian military launched in April, The War Zone reported.

In May, four of them moved close to an ICEYE satellite.

ICEYE-X36 is a commercial satellite, owned by a private company rather than a government, but ICEYE sells radar imagery to militaries and supplies data to the US and its allies.

ICEYE’s chief executive, Rafal Modrzewski, told the Reuters news agency the company then moved its own satellite, which appeared to prompt further Russian manoeuvres.

Then, between Thursday and Friday last week, Cosmos 2612 closed in from more than 320km (200 miles) from ICEYE-X36 to about 4.8km (3 miles), the space-tracking company LeoLabs told the news site Axios.

Over the weekend, it moved between positions ahead of and behind the ICEYE satellite, at times coming within roughly 500 metres, LeoLabs said in a report on Monday, adding that the estimate was uncertain and, by Monday, it had begun to move away.



A Ukrainian official told Axios that Ukraine’s military works with ICEYE and uses its capabilities, but said it was unclear whether ICEYE-X36 itself supports Ukraine.

Has Russia done this before, and what is the purpose?

In the past, Russia has mainly carried out such manoeuvres against Western military satellites, rather than commercially owned ones, Mark Hilborne, a senior lecturer in the defence studies department at King’s College London, told Al Jazeera.

In early 2020, two Russian satellites moved close to USA 245, a US spy satellite.

In September 2025, German Defence Minister Boris Pistorius said two Russian Luch-Olymp satellites were tracking two Intelsat satellites used by the German military.

Dr Marco Langbroek, a lecturer in optical space situational awareness at TU Delft Faculty of Aerospace Engineering, said: “At geostationary altitude, we have seen two Russian satellites (LUCH/OLYMP-K 1 & 2) repeatedly approach western communication satellites to distances of a few tens of kilometres in the past few years, likely with the intention to eavesdrop on communications and data transfers. And we have seen the Russians practising very close approaches in Low Earth Orbit – similar to what they now did to ICEYE-X36 – with their own satellites as test targets.”

However, this incident is different, because “approaching another satellite this close without the cooperation of the owner or operator of the other satellite, is widely considered ‘not done’ as it is dangerous, with a risk of collision or interference.

“It is equivalent to placing your car on the freeway within 10 cm of another driving car: highly unsafe.”

Langbroek said it is not known what the purpose of the Russian manoeuvre was, however, “it could be a dry run for a future attack, it could be provocation or scare tactics to ruffle the feathers of Ukraine and its allies, and/or a test to see how the satellite operators react to a threat like this.”

This sort of manoeuvre, therefore, falls into the pattern of “hybrid warfare” – “the same kind of provocations and inciting reactions like what Russia does when they fly a drone into Polish airspace or zoom a NATO warship at low elevation in the Baltic Sea”.

How common are these incidents?

Close approaches have happened for years, but not like this.

Hilborne said this is “the first time that a country has done such a manoeuvre … against the commercial satellite without any consent”.

It was also “incredibly close”, he said, with some reports putting the distance at less than 30 metres.



Far more common is interference that does not require going near a satellite at all. This is mostly done through jamming, which drowns out a satellite’s signals, often from the ground.

Western military officials told Reuters that Russian interference with Western space systems has increased significantly since its full-scale invasion of Ukraine in 2022.

What is the significance of this?

For Hilborne, the choice of target “is starting to indicate that Russia does not distinguish between commercial and military satellites as potential targets”.

That matters because militaries, including Ukraine’s, increasingly rely on commercial satellites for communications and imagery.

Moscow has warned about this.

In October 2022, a senior Russian foreign ministry official told the United Nations that “quasi-civilian infrastructure may be a legitimate target for a retaliatory strike”.

Juliana Suess, a space security researcher at the German Institute for International and Security Affairs (SWP) in Berlin, said Russia may be calculating that reactions will be less severe if it shadows a commercial satellite rather than a sovereign one, especially one not belonging to the US.

But ownership is not that simple.

ICEYE-X36 is owned by ICEYE’s US subsidiary and registered as a US satellite, Hilborne noted, adding, “this creates a complex problem”.

The distance matters too. A gap of less than 5km may sound far, Suess said, but “it’s essentially a hop and a skip in space”.

“It’s incredibly close and could potentially enable Russia to conduct nefarious activity, including intercepting data from the satellite or disrupting its service – temporarily via signal jamming, for example,” she added.

“A kinetic attack would also be possible but seems less likely at this point in time, in part because this would be an unprecedented measure taken against a satellite”, she explained.

Is Russia just sending a message, or escalating?

Probably both.

“It is sending a message that these platforms could be held under threat,” Hilborne said, adding that it also represents an escalation, suggesting Russia might be willing to attack, since any satellite could be used as a weapon simply by crashing it into another.

Suess added: “I think regardless of whether we see further manoeuvring or consequences, the political goal of intimidation should not be underestimated”.

“The manoeuvre is also a message that space assets cannot be considered wholly safe or removed from the war in Ukraine”, she said.

She pointed to November 2021, when Russia destroyed one of its own satellites with a missile, an event referred to in the European Union’s 2023 space strategy.

“We have long known what Russia is capable of in terms of disrupting or even destroying space assets. This manoeuvre is also a reminder of those previously demonstrated capabilities,” she said.

Moscow calls such spacecraft “inspector satellites”, and in 2020 described such manoeuvres as common practice “by many countries”, Radio Free Europe/Radio Liberty reported.



Hilborne described the approach as “another example of activity that sits below the threshold of conflict”.

An outright attack on ICEYE-X36 looks unlikely for now, Hilborne said.

“With the current balance in the conflict, and this being an American-registered satellite, it would seem unlikely that Russia would actually attack the satellite, as the response would be unpredictable”, he said.

An attack could also create a large amount of space debris, which would be a problem for everyone, he added, warning that “it’s hard to second-guess where Russia draws the line”.

How has Ukraine fought to keep its eyes in space?

Ukraine’s access to satellites has come under pressure before, at times from its own allies.

In March 2025, as Washington paused intelligence sharing with Kyiv, the US National Geospatial-Intelligence Agency “temporarily suspended” Ukraine’s access to the main portal for US government-purchased commercial imagery.

If ICEYE-X36 were disrupted, Ukraine would not necessarily go blind, Suess said, because the ICEYE constellation has more than one satellite, and sovereign radar satellites, such as Germany’s, could also provide data.

But speed is the issue. According to ICEYE, the expanded access agreed this year meant faster access, Suess explained.

“The question is whether a similarly fast transfer of data could be enabled with a new provider, whether commercial or sovereign in nature,” she said.

Now, Ukraine faces another squeeze. Last week, the order to limit Starshield – the military-grade version of SpaceX’s Starlink service – for Ukraine came from inside the White House, two US officials and a Western official told Reuters.

On Saturday, US Secretary of State Marco Rubio said Starshield is currently unavailable to Ukraine, but that Kyiv’s request to use it for attacks deep inside Russia is “under discussion”.

World.title: Yemen: Maps show 10 years of changing control
World.content:
A decade of war has shifted Yemen’s front lines, but the Houthis still hold the capital, Sanaa, and no side controls the country.

Looking at maps of who controls which areas of Yemen over the past 12 years of war reveals changing alliances and coalitions, all while the country faces poverty and malnutrition.

The Houthi armed group, also known as Ansar Allah (Arabic for Supporters of God), seized the capital, Sanaa, on September 21, 2014, after advancing south from their heartland of Saada in northern Yemen.

The Iran-allied group used antigovernment grievances to gain support after July 2014 fuel subsidy cuts triggered anger.

The Houthis mobilised protests demanding the reversal of the government’s decisions, and subsequently its resignation. They allied with forces loyal to former President Ali Abdullah Saleh, which helped them capture military positions and state institutions.

Then-President Abd-Rabbu Mansour Hadi fled to Aden in February 2015. When forces aligned with the Houthis and Saleh advanced towards the southern port city, Hadi took refuge in the Saudi capital, Riyadh. In March 2015, Saudi Arabia launched a military intervention to restore his internationally recognised government.

Over the next decade, alliances broke and front lines shifted. In this visual explainer, AJLabs uses seven maps to track how Yemen has been fragmented, and how no side has been able to control the whole country.

October 2016

By late 2016, two years after the Houthis seized Sanaa, Yemen was split into rival zones of control.

The Houthi-Saleh alliance controlled Sanaa and much of the northern and western heartlands, home to most of Yemen’s population.



Pro-government forces held territory across the south and the east, supported by Saudi Arabia and the United Arab Emirates.

Al-Qaeda in the Arabian Peninsula (AQAP) also challenged government authority across parts of the south.

December 2017

The antigovernment alliance in Yemen went through its most significant fracture after Saleh appeared close to switching sides in the conflict, leading to a short outbreak of fighting with the Houthis, who then killed Yemen’s former longtime president in Sanaa in December 2017.

This left the Houthis, a primarily Zaidi Shia group, in sole charge of much of northwestern Yemen, including Sanaa and the port city of Hodeidah.

Some pro-Saleh forces switched sides, and pro-government and anti-Houthi forces controlled territory across the south and the east while AQAP retained pockets of influence.

Nearly three years into its intervention and despite a heavy air campaign, the Saudi-led coalition had failed to restore the internationally recognised government of Hadi in Sanaa.

March 2019

The Houthis continued to hold Sanaa and much of the northwestern highlands. Government-aligned forces held extensive territory across the south and the east while AQAP maintained pockets of influence.

The December 2018 Stockholm Agreement halted a pro-government offensive against Houthi-held Hodeidah, a major entry point for food, fuel and aid.

Neither side had been able to achieve a decisive victory. Divisions among the Houthis’ opponents further weakened efforts to establish government authority.

2022

The UAE-backed Southern Transitional Council (STC), which seized Aden in 2019, held territory separately from government forces. Despite officially being part of the anti-Houthi, Saudi-led coalition, the STC fought the government several times.

Hadi was forced to transfer his powers to an eight-member Presidential Leadership Council (PLC), ending his presidency without reclaiming the capital.

April 2023
