Saudi-Houthi negotiations raised hopes of a settlement and led to a truce in April 2022, but Yemen remained divided as it had been for years.

While the Houthis retained their control over Yemen’s northwest, the STC continued to undermine Yemen’s internationally recognised government as it tried to increase its own power in the south in the hope that this would eventually lay the foundations for an independent state.

Government forces controlled broad areas of the east, which separatists also wanted to claim for any future state.



The Hadrami Elite Forces, a UAE-backed group, controlled coastal Hadramout. The National Resistance Forces (NRF), led by Saleh’s nephew Tareq Saleh and supported by the UAE, held part of the Red Sea coast.

March 2025

By 2025, the Houthis had held Sanaa and most of Yemen’s northwest continuously for more than a decade.

Government-aligned forces operated across the south and the east.

Houthi attacks on shipping, which the group said were launched in solidarity with Palestinians in Gaza, drew attacks from Israel, the United Kingdom and the United States.

Yemen’s coastline and the Bab al-Mandeb strait became central to a confrontation whose consequences reached far beyond the country.

January 2026

Government forces regained Hadramout and al-Mahra from the STC, which had seized the governorates in December 2025.

Saudi air attacks and a government advance fractured the STC’s leadership. A delegation in Riyadh announced the STC’s dissolution, but coalition officials in Yemen rejected the announcement, and its leader Aidarous al-Zubaidi fled the country.

The map above shows contested authority across parts of southern Yemen and Socotra. Tareq Saleh’s forces remain separately marked along the western coast while the Houthis retained Sanaa and the northwest.

The PLC sought to unify anti-Houthi formations. Regaining territory strengthened its position, but establishing a single command remained unfinished.

September 8, 2026

In early September, Houthi forces attacked west of Taiz in an attempt to cut road access to the Red Sea coast.

Government forces initially claimed gains in Hais and western Taiz, but the port city of Mocha fell on September 10 as Tareq Saleh’s NRF withdrew and repositioned.

By September 11, government sources reported Houthi advances into Dhubab and Mayyun Island, completing their reported takeover of Yemen’s Red Sea coast.

By September 25, nearly 130,000 people, including 71,000 children, had been displaced in three weeks, according to UNICEF.

PLC Chairman Rashad al-Alimi called for a general mobilisation and offered amnesty to Houthi fighters who defected.

Government forces intensified their air and ground operations in Taiz towards the end of the month while Saudi Arabia sought support from Pakistan and Turkiye amid continuing Houthi attacks.

October 13, 2026

After announcing Operation Dawn of Yemen on October 4, the internationally recognised government launched a major offensive on October 5 with the stated aim of retaking areas that included Sanaa. The Southern Giants Brigades fought alongside government troops and former STC-affiliated units.

The same day, the government said its forces had recaptured positions around Dhubab and Bab al-Mandeb, but the full extent of their gains on the coast could not be confirmed. It also said it had seized mountain positions in Haifan, western Taiz and around al-Waziiya.

Fighting also spread to Marib, where government forces claimed heights around the Maas camp and positions north of Harib by October 13.



But while the government claimed these gains, it also lost territory in Taiz governorate, leading to a siege on the city of Taiz, one of the most important government-held areas of the country, with the major road linking it to the south controlled by the Houthis.

The escalation deepened Yemen’s humanitarian crisis, and by October 7, more than 200,000 people had been displaced, including more than 3,700 who fled by sea to Djibouti, according to the International Organization for Migration.

Government and Saudi-led coalition air attacks increased, including on Sanaa. The Houthis, meanwhile, attacked Saudi Arabia repeatedly with ballistic missiles, including an October 10 attack on Riyadh’s airport that killed 13 people.

World.title: Yemen’s critically ill are trapped as war closes the country’s airports
World.content:
A re-ignition of Yemen’s war has left the chronically sick and needing treatment trapped in the country.

Sanaa, Yemen – Rajaa Ghirsan, a 50-year-old seamstress from Sanaa, Yemen’s Houthi-controlled capital, can barely speak or breathe due to obstructions in her airway.

Her vocal cord paralysis and severe complications in her larynx have left her dependent on a device fitted around her neck to keep air flowing and stave off suffocation. The device has to be replaced every two months and costs $100 each time.

She has undergone six operations in Egypt and India since 2006 in an attempt to try to help her breathe normally, but she now needs another complex operation abroad to open her airway. As Yemen’s conflict-weakened health system lacks the infrastructure and specialist care required, she will need to head overseas for treatment.

After registering with the Higher Medical Committee in Sanaa, the body responsible for arranging medical treatment abroad, she spent seven years trying to secure a seat on a once-weekly flight to Amman, where Yemeni patients have been treated.

But repeated closures and air attacks have kept that flight out of reach, and she cannot afford the long overland journey to Aden airport, which is her only alternative out of the country.

“The device helps her breathe a little, but it has worn her out and taken away her rest for years,” says Nouran al-Salawi, 28, Ghirsan’s daughter, who has cared for her mother for the past decade while raising two children of her own. “She is waiting for the moment she can have the last operation and be free of it, or she is waiting for death instead.”



Ghirsan is among the many Yemenis who depend on Sanaa International Airport to get the medical care they need abroad. The airport is the main air link for millions living under Houthi control in the north, but it has been repeatedly shut since the Saudi-led coalition fighting the Houthis closed it to commercial traffic in August 2016.

A United Nations-brokered truce allowed a limited number of flights to resume in May 2022, but Israeli air attacks in 2025 damaged the airport and destroyed aircraft. In July, Yemeni government forces backed by Saudi Arabia struck its only working runway to prevent an Iranian plane with a Houthi delegation from landing.

As of today, no regular flights leave the capital, while Aden, the seat of the internationally recognised government and the main alternative for patients in the north, has also come under attack.

Anis al-Asbahi, spokesperson for the Houthi-run Ministry of Health in Sanaa, told Al Jazeera that repeated closures of Sanaa airport over the past decade have affected about 400,000 patients, including 250,000 who need treatment abroad. The flight disruptions have also affected more than 125,000 people with cancer who face shortages of medicine.

“It has led to shortages of more than 1,600 types of medicine, including 12 cancer drugs that are barred from entering the country,” he said. “Additionally, more than 40,000 patients with thalassemia and haemolytic anaemia face shortages of iron chelation drugs and the intravenous solutions needed for their treatment.”

Yemen’s Houthis have unilaterally released 159 war prisoners loyal to the Saudi-backed government of Yemen, according to a statement by the head of the Houthi Prisoner Affairs Committee, Abdul-Qader al-Murtada [Yahya Arhab/EPA]

Paying with money and lives

Fighting between government and Houthi forces has reignited in recent months, leading to new restrictions on the movement of aid and people.

This month, UN envoy Hans Grundberg told the Security Council that the country had slid back into full-scale war. Aden’s airport has been hit twice this month, most recently on October 16, when two missiles landed about 500 metres (550 yards) from a Yemenia plane preparing to take off for Cairo.

With Sanaa airport out of operation, Aden’s under attack, and unrest this year in Seiyun, a city in the eastern province of Hadramout that hosts another airport, patients in northern Yemen have limited options.

Mohammed Shajara, 30, tried to reach Tehran for treatment for his paraplegic five-year-old daughter in June. But he was left stranded in Tehran when the government blocked Iranian flights to and from Sanaa in July, so they returned without treatment. Aden was his next option, but the journey from Sanaa takes about 14 hours and involves crossing dozens of checkpoints on both sides of the front lines. With the airport coming under repeated attack, he is holding off for now.



Abdulkarim Abdullah, 60, had kidney failure and relied on weekly dialysis in Sanaa. The regular treatment has strained his family’s finances, so they have looked for a treatment to fix the problem. Abdulkarim had been due to fly from Sanaa to Amman for this, but the subsequent suspension of flights to Jordan left him with no way out of the capital. With Seiyun airport also out of service, the family turned to Aden.

To get there, Abdulkarim’s brother, Mohammed Abdullah, had to pay about $2,300 to cover the journey and prepare for the flight.

“Hiring a car from Sanaa to Aden cost $200, a hotel stay before the flight $500, security clearances for the two brothers $400, and plane tickets $1,200,” Mohammed says. To raise the money, he sold his brother’s wife’s gold, and then his own car.

“Despite all of our efforts, my brother never made it to the airport. He died on the road to Aden in January,” Mohammed says.

Trapped by the war

Fouad al-Haddad, director of al-Jumhuri Hospital in the southwestern city of Taiz, said other patients have died waiting to receive treatment abroad or due to domestic travel restrictions.

“[The] closure of main roads around Taiz has forced travellers onto longer detours through mountain bends and rugged terrain, journeys that take more time and effort and that many patients are too sick to endure, on top of the security risks along routes close to the fighting,” he said.

Nearly 147,000 people were displaced across Yemen in September, more than 80,000 of them to Taiz, according to government figures. Taiz is hosting most of the Yemenis recently displaced by fighting elsewhere in the country.

Nadia al-Rashidi, head of the Hayat Jadida (New Life) organisation, a local NGO in Hadramout, said flights from al-Rayyan airport in Mukalla to Aden, and from there to Cairo, now run only once a week. Al-Ghaydah airport, in neighbouring al-Mahra, is also closed, while both al-Rayyan and Seiyun have only partly resumed operations since forces linked to the Southern Transitional Council (STC) were pushed out of the south in January.

Travellers flying to Egypt and Jordan also need security clearances. This can take about half a month to issue through the regular process and cost $200 to fast-track, al-Rashidi said.

No side spared

Aref al-Hawshabi, director general of the National Centre for Health Education and Media at the Health Ministry in Aden, said 1,170 patients from government-held governorates have submitted medical files to travel abroad for treatment under the ministry’s free grants programme.

“The real need is far higher, because many patients are unable to submit their files at all,” he said.

The conditions that most often require treatment abroad include cancers and blood diseases; bone marrow, liver, and kidney transplants; cochlear implants and corneal transplants; heart disease; scoliosis; and congenital malformations of the reproductive system.



Flight disruptions and airport closures delay these patients and put them at serious risk, al-Hawshabi adds, particularly those with fixed appointments at hospitals abroad.

“Some who manage to leave then struggle to get home, staying abroad longer than planned on money they do not have, while others face problems entering India and Jordan even after clearing the obstacles at home.”

In September, the government’s health minister, Qasim Buhaibeh, warned that some areas could lose health services entirely if funding continues to fall. He said 19.3 million people in Yemen need health assistance while the response has received only 17 percent of the funding it requires, and that dialysis and cancer treatment are among the services most at risk.

There is currently no medical evacuation programme in either part of the country.

Doctors in hospitals across Yemen are seeing the impact of these travel restrictions, and the race against time for patients to receive treatment.

“I see the price that Yemenis pay every day in the wards,” said Fouad al-Haddad from the al-Jumhuri Hospital. “What we have now are bodies exhausted by disease and medical needs that cannot be postponed.”

This story is produced in collaboration with Egab.

World.title: UK to deploy Typhoon jets to help defend Saudi Arabia from Houthi attacks
World.content:
Ministry of Defence says warplanes will operate in ‘defensive role’ and not be used to attack Yemeni group.

Share UK to deploy Typhoon jets to help defend Saudi Arabia from Houthi attacks on social media

The United Kingdom has said it will deploy fighter jets to help protect Saudi Arabia from attacks by Yemen’s Houthis.

In a statement on Tuesday, the British Ministry of Defence said the Typhoon warplanes would operate in a “defensive role” and not carry out attacks against the Iranian-backed armed group.

“The UK will fly defensive counter air missions to support the protection of Saudi cities and critical national infrastructure against aerial attack, using RAF Typhoon fighter jets,” it added.

The support includes an extension of air-to-air refuelling support for Saudi air operations, the ministry added.

The announcement comes amid heavy fighting between the Houthis – also known as Ansar Allah, Arabic for Supporters of God – and Yemen’s internationally recognised government, which is backed by Saudi Arabia.

In recent weeks, the Houthis have carried out missile and drone strikes against the kingdom, including oil facilities and Riyadh’s main airport, while the Saudi-led coalition supporting the Yemeni government has launched air attacks on Houthi positions.

“The continuing attacks from the Houthis on our ally Saudi Arabia are absolutely despicable. The targeting of the airport in Riyadh in particular shows the lengths the Houthis are going to escalate the situation in the region,” UK Defence Secretary Wes Streeting said.

“That’s why today I have approved further UK military support. RAF Typhoons will fly defensive air missions to help protect Saudi airspace from drones and missiles. This builds on the UK equipment and personnel we already have in the country to defend against Houthi air attacks,” he added.



Reporting from London, Al Jazeera’s Camille Nedelec said the UK government’s decision was partly driven by growing concerns over rising energy prices.

“What’s happening in the Gulf has a direct impact on people’s homes,” she said, adding that the move “shows increasing engagement by the UK” in the region.

The UK announcement came a day after Egypt’s parliament delayed for a second day a vote on President Abdel Fattah el-Sisi’s request to authorise military support for Saudi Arabia, if the kingdom asked for its support.

State media said the new session would be held on October 26.

World.title: Zelensky prepares for Oslo talks with US envoys as Rubio denies withholding intelligence
World.content:
US special envoy Steve Witkoff has arrived in Norway ahead of talks with Volodymyr Zelensky with relations on the slide between the Ukrainian leader and US President Donald Trump.

Norwegian Prime Minister Jonas Gahr StÃ¸re said Zelensky had asked Oslo and neighbouring Finland to organise the meeting with the US and European allies "at a critical time for Ukraine".

Ahead of the meeting, US Secretary of State Marco Rubio rejected as "scandalous" and "outrageous" accusations that Ukrainians were dying because the US was withholding intelligence from Kyiv.

He was speaking after Zelensky's military technical adviser, Serhii "Flash" Beskrestnov, told the BBC that the lack of reliable US warnings meant lives were being lost.

"This looks very strange," said Beskrestnov. "Sometimes we receive this information before the attack, another time we [do] not."

Relations between Kyiv and the US have soured in recent weeks to the extent that Trump has said it is time for Ukraine to get a new president, and most recently "for somebody else to negotiate on behalf of Ukraine".

StÃ¸re said the aim of the Oslo talks were to steer relations towards "a more constructive path". He told reporters at the parliament in Norway that they wanted to ensure that the war ended diplomatically with a lasting and just peace.

Zelensky said earlier he had had a "constructive discussion" with Rubio about the need for US early warnings, missile interceptors and SpaceX's Starlink internet network.

Last week a bipartisan group of US senators called for an urgent investigation into disruptions to the Starlink network in Ukraine, and unconfirmed reports on Tuesday said the transfer of more Patriot interceptors had not yet been approved.

The US secretary of state is currently on a visit to India and admitted to reporters that it may be true that Patriot interceptor missiles had not yet arrived in Ukraine, although nothing had been denied to Kyiv intentionally.

World.title: North Korea publishes photos of Kim Jong Un - why do rumours of his death keep coming back?
World.content:
Kim Jong Un has appeared in North Korean state media looking remarkably healthy for a man rumoured to have died from a brain haemorrhage.

Photographs published by state newspaper Rodong Sinmun show the 42-year-old dictator touring what the paper said was a clothing and footwear exhibition with his daughter.

The images emerged hours after a Chinese dissident who lives in the US claimed, without evidence, that Kim had been taken to a hospital in Beijing in a coma and had died.

For those who watch North Korea closely, this kind of rumour has become almost routine.

In one of the world's most secretive states, facts are often difficult to verify, creating fertile ground for speculation.

This latest claim originated with Wanjun Xie, who identifies himself as chairman of the Chinese Democratic Party, a group banned by Chinese authorities. He has previously circulated unverified claims, including speculation about the death of Chinese leader Xi Jinping.

Xie alleged that Kim suffered a severe brain haemorrhage and was transferred to Beijing because North Korea lacked the medical facilities to treat him.

He claimed Kim later died and that his body had been secretly returned to North Korea, with the regime concealing his death.

Yet the photographs tell a different story.

Kim is seen examining displays, accompanied by Kim Ju Ae and his usual entourage of officials.

While there is no way to know exactly when the images were taken, there are other reasons to doubt the claim.

World.title: Man charged with attack on Australian MP as suspect's father says she is family friend
World.content:
A 43-year-old man has been charged after Australian MP Helen Haines was hit by a car in the state of Victoria on Monday.

The suspect will appear in court on Wednesday to face charges of dangerous driving causing serious injury, intentionally causing serious injury and the federal offence of causing harm to a public official.

Local media earlier named the alleged attacker as environmental activist Brendan Nugent. His father and his partner said they had been friends with Haines "for more than 20 years" and thanked residents and officers who helped her after the "shocking and horrific crime".

Haines remains in a critical condition after surgery and is reported to have lost one of her legs.

"Helen Haines is a deeply respected, valued and much loved member of our local community," Rod Nugent and his partner Christine Cunningham said in a statement.

"All of our love and all of our thoughts are with Helen and her family and friends."

They promised to assist Victoria Police "in any way we can".

Police say they will allege the incident was targeted.

Haines, 65, the independent member for Indi, is in a critical but stable condition after undergoing surgery at a Melbourne hospital.

World.title: Suspect arrested after historic town hall set alight - French media
World.content:
A suspect linked to a far-left movement has been arrested in France after a 19th Century city hall was gutted by a fire over the weekend that broke out during mass disorder, French media reports.

The clock tower and parts of the roof of the ornate city hall in the central city of Limoges were engulfed in flames before collapsing on Saturday.

The 34-year-old suspect is known to police for acts of violence against public officials and is on the "S" list, a French national security watchlist, FranceInfo and BFMTV reported.

Meanwhile in Marseille, a curfew for young people will be introduced on Tuesday evening.

The city's mayor BenoÃ®t Payan said that the prefect had decided to introduce the curfew in Marseille "starting this evening and for days to come".

He said the measures apply to minors and will only be in commercial areas of the city, which were particularly affected by looting which took place last weekend.

French Justice Minister GÃ©rald Darmanin told BFM Television that 149 people were in detention following widespread demonstrations over the weekend.

Hundreds of thousands of demonstrators took to the streets to protest against rising fuel prices, the cost of living and deteriorating public services, including schools.

Darmanin previously said he asked prosecutors to be "extremely firm" and "ruthless towards those who attacked police officers, gendarmes and firefighters, who looted shops and who attacked public buildings".

The justice minister insisted France did not need to be put into a state of emergency which would "deprive all French people of their individual freedoms".

But French Prime Minister SÃ©bastien Lecornu earlier said he had not ruled out imposing a state of emergency.

World.title: Tourist found guilty after stealing Las Vegas flamingo from enclosure
World.content:
A Canadian man has been found guilty of animal cruelty after he took a flamingo from its enclosure in Las Vegas and brought it back to his hotel room during an alcohol-fuelled bender.

Mitchell Fairbarn, who was visiting the US city, took the Chilean flamingo named Peachy from the Flamingo Las Vegas Hotel and Casino in March.

Videos shown at his trial showed a smiling Fairbarn carrying the bird by the neck as he took a lift to his room. He testified that he had drunk 30 to 40 beers before the incident and said he never meant to harm the animal. He faces nearly five years in prison.

Animal experts testified the flamingo had feathers torn out and suffered blood loss due to Fairbarn's actions.

A lawyer for Fairbarn said his actions were intended as a harmless prank, and blamed alcohol for his "bad decisions".

"He should not have done that, should not have gone into the habitat, shouldn't have touched a bird, shouldn't have taken Peachy inside," said his lawyer Josh Tomsheck, external.

"The truth is, Mitch was drunk. Mitch was stupid. He made bad decisions."

His lawyer added he had received death threats since his arrest.

Testifying in his defence, Fairbarn, 34, said he thought it would be "funny" to take the bird.

He said he had been up drinking all night and had just gotten off a call with a colleague when he made the decision to abscond with the bird.

The Flamingo Las Vegas, located along the famous Las Vegas strip, features a wildlife habitat inside its hotel and casino that is free to walk through. It features a flock of Chilean flamingos, other birds, fish and turtles.

During the trial, the jury heard from 14 witnesses and reviewed more than 112 pieces of evidence, according to CBS, the BBC's US partner.

It took a jury around five hours to convict him on felony and misdemeanour animal abuse charges.

Fairbarn has been unable to leave the US since his arrest. He remains on house arrest in Las Vegas, with a sentencing hearing due to take place in December.

A veterinarian for the state said that Peachy has largely recovered since the event but has a now has a more anxious demeanour around humans.

World.title: Why Israeli Gen Z voters are drawn to the far right
World.content:
More than half a million first-time voters will cast their ballots in this election, which many Israelis see as existential for Israel's future security and identity.

Polls suggest it will be a tight race, and the new young voters could help decide the result.

More than 16% are planning to support far-right parties - either Ben Gvir's Jewish Power or the Religious Zionism party of his far-right ally Bezalel Smotrich - according to a poll for one of Israel's most popular newspapers, Yedioth Ahronoth.

And almost three-quarters see themselves as "right or centre-right", according to another survey for Israel's leading Channel 12 television network.

"Itamar Ben Gvir gives me a sense of security," said 20-year-old Mordechai, one of the young fans accompanying the politician to Ramle.

"Like everyone in history, from Trump to Moses, there are slips of the tongue that are a bit less good. So what? 90% of the things by Itamar are amazing."

"Itamar will give us safety, and when we go to the army, someone will have our backs and be behind us," said 18-year-old Nadav.

"I think he's trying to show that we're a strong country. For many years, we couldn't show we're strong in our beliefs. We couldn't express our ideology."

Meir Schreiber, an ultra-Orthodox 23-year-old who grew up in London, said the Hamas-led 7 October 2023 attacks on Israel, which triggered the Gaza war, also convinced him that Ben Gvir was the right choice.

"Young people understand that peace isn't something we can do," he told me, "because what happens to you when you're young shapes your personality - we saw October 7."

World.title: Marseille braces for more unrest after protests give way to 'apocalyptic' disorder
World.content:
Thunder and lightning have boomed across Marseille following the weekend's mayhem, illuminating the cracked windows and boarded-up doors of hundreds of businesses that were smashed as protests gave way to disorder.

France's second city saw some of the worst violence as chaos gripped the country on Saturday. Local business leaders say more than 500 premises were damaged, and the majority looted.

A police union boss told the BBC that the weekend had been an "apocalyptic" hell for his colleagues. 118 officers were injured, representing more than a tenth of the national figure.

So far, 101 arrests have been made in the port city, a quarter of them children.

But by Monday, it was police who were most conspicuous on the city's streets, not protesters. For eight hours, demonstrations and gatherings were banned in an effort to avoid a third consecutive day of disorder.

World.title: Seventh day of violent clashes between Albanian protesters and police
World.content:
Outside the cafe in the park, when the gas has cleared, 27-year-old activist Sidorela Vatnikaj, a masters student, describes her typical day. In a movement without leaders she is one of the more experienced, with eight years in the forefront of anti-government protests behind her.

"In the morning, you try to co-ordinate with all the groups - where they are, and where the protest is taking place. If any lawyers are needed, if any first aid kit or any kind of equipment is needed. And you also have to make sure all your friends, your family members in the protest are OK."

The day is spent going from protest to protest, much of it running from police, she said.

She is uncomfortable with the violence towards the authorities from her fellow protesters, but blames the police for starting and fuelling it.

"When I see people throwing stones at the police, I understand their anger. I don't judge them. I'm not happy, but they have no other way to be listened to," Vatnikaj said.

"They come from families whose family members had no other choice than to leave the country - a million in the past decade. They have not only been robbed, they have been bullied, ignored and now they they have also been beaten up."

At the weekend, the prime minister asked rhetorically what would happen if he stepped down.

"We need a technocratic government for one year, to prepare the country for real, democratic elections," Vatnikaj replies. She has accused Rama of rigging previous elections, and of being hand in glove with rich foreign investors and organised crime groups.

Young people in Albania feel encouraged by their fellow Gen Z protesters around the world, Vatnikaj said.

"I have seen my mother and father's generation, working all their lives and dreaming of having a democratic society where they could live with dignity. That never happened," she said.

Rama has been in power for 13 years, and has been a dominant figure in Albanian politics since the turn of the century. He has promised EU membership by 2030, and said he is the only one who can deliver it.

World.title: Bauchi NDC governorship candidate resigns, may join APC
World.content:
The governorship candidate for the Nigeria Democratic Congress (NDC) in Bauchi State, Ibrahim Kashim, had resigned from the party.

Mr Kashim, a former Secretary to the Bauchi State Government (SSG), officially resigned his membership of the NDC in a statement dated 16 October.

In the statement, Mr Kashim disclosed that his decision came after careful reflection.

However, he said stepping down from the NDC does not diminish his commitment to advocating for political reform and socio-economic advancement in Bauchi State.

“Our conviction remains that our dear state deserves purposeful leadership, a stronger economy, greater opportunities for our youths and women, improved security, and a future in which every citizen can live with dignity and hope,” Mr Kashim stated.

He also assured his followers that the political movement remains active.

He said consultations were ongoing with relevant stakeholders and groups who share a common vision with him for a peaceful and prosperous Bauchi State.

Stay Ahead with Premium Times 

He urged his supporters to remain calm, steadfast, and united, adding that details regarding the next phase of his political movement will be announced in due course.

Although Mr Ibrahim Kashim has yet to announce his next political move, speculation is mounting that he is likely to defect to the All Progressives Congress (APC).

​Mr Kashim served as the Secretary to the State Government (SSG) under current Governor Bala Mohammed, having been appointed to the role in June 2021.

​He resigned in December 2024 amid the rift between Governor Mohammed and the Minister of the Federal Capital Territory (FCT), Nyesom Wike.

​At the time, his departure—officially announced by the governor—fueled speculation that his allegiance lay with Mr Wike, ultimately prompting his exit from office.

NDC reacts

Responding to the development, the Bauchi State Chairman of the NDC, Abdullahi Misau, said the party was disappointed and unhappy with the development.

“Honestly, we are not happy with this development. We are deeply disappointed, but since it is beyond our control, we can only pray that it turns out to be in the best interest of all parties involved.

“In politics, everyone seeks what they believe is best for them. Every individual has the right to choose their own path and decide how they want to contribute to society and the nation, while also pursuing their personal interests,” he said.

“Under the electoral framework, the governorship candidate and the running mate contest together. Since we have a running mate, it cannot be said that we are no longer in the race,” Mr Misau stated.

The chairman explained that the party would seek legal advice on the implications of the candidate’s resignation, including consultations with relevant legal authorities of the Independent National Electoral Commission (INEC).

“We will consult our legal team and seek guidance from INEC’s legal counsel on the appropriate steps to take. However, I can assure you that we are still in the race,” he added.

Mr Misau further assured party members and supporters that the NDC leadership would continue mobilising support across Bauchi State.

World.title: Police fire teargas to disperse #EndSARS memorial at Lekki Toll Gate
World.content:
Police officers fired teargas at the Lekki Toll Gate in Lagos on Tuesday, dispersing participants at a memorial to victims of the #EndSARS protests and preventing them from laying wreaths.

The Punch newspaper reported that residents, journalists and political figures had gathered for the event organised by the Enough is Enough movement when officers fired teargas canisters.

Among those affected were Gbadebo Rhodes-Vivour, the African Democratic Congress governorship candidate in Lagos State, and Funso Doherty of the Nigeria Democratic Congress.

A video sighted showed participants scrambling for safety as the teargas spread across the area, according to the report.

A PREMIUM TIMES reporter who visited the toll gate at 11: 15 a. m. on the day saw police officers at the scene but could not find any of the organisers. The reporter also percieved a smell of teargas but could not establish its source at the time.

The organisers had scheduled a wreath-laying ceremony for 11 a.m. to honour people who died or went missing during the 2020 protests.

They planned to lay 15 wreaths: nine for people listed as dead in connection with the Lekki incident, four for those listed as missing and presumed dead, one for journalist Pelumi Onifade and another for other unidentified victims.

Stay Ahead with Premium Times 

The nine people listed as dead were Victor Sunday Ibanga, Abuta Solomon, Jide, Olalekan Abideen Ashafa, Olamilekan Ajasa, Kolade Salami, Folorunsho Olabisi, Kenechukwu Ugoh and Nathaniel Solomon.

Those listed as missing and presumed dead were Abiodun Adesanya, Ifeanyi Nicholas Eji, Tola and Wisdom.

Rights groups demand accountability

The incident occurred as civil society organisations renewed calls for justice for victims of police abuses and the implementation of recommendations arising from investigations into the Lekki incident.

The Rule of Law and Accountability Advocacy Centre (RULAAC) said the disbandment of the Special Anti-Robbery Squad (SARS) had not ended allegations of police brutality, torture, extortion, unlawful detention and extrajudicial killings.

In a statement on Tuesday, the group called for the enforcement of the Police Act 2020 and the Anti-Torture Act 2017. It also urged authorities to investigate allegations of abuse, prosecute officers found culpable and strengthen civilian oversight of the police.

RULAAC also raised concerns about alleged abuses at police detention facilities, including Tiger Base in Owerri, Imo State. It called for detainees to have access to lawyers and relatives and urged the police to keep proper records of arrests and transfers and comply with court judgements.

Corporate Accountability and Public Participation Africa (CAPPA) called on the federal and Lagos State governments to apologise for the Lekki shootings and provide redress for victims.

In a separate statement on Monday, the organisation urged the authorities to conduct independent investigations, prosecute those found responsible and compensate people killed or injured during the crackdown.

CAPPA said the Lagos State Judicial Panel of Inquiry’s report implicated security personnel in deaths and injuries at the toll gate. It criticised the federal government’s rejection of the panel’s findings and the Lagos State Government’s White Paper, which disputed aspects of the casualty records.

The group also called for the implementation of a July 2024 judgment of the ECOWAS Community Court of Justice which, according to CAPPA, found Nigeria liable for human rights violations and ordered compensation and fresh investigations.

CAPPA renewed its call for justice for Pelumi Onifade, a journalist arrested by officers of the Lagos State Task Force on 24 October 2020 while covering events at the Ministry of Agriculture Abattoir in Oko-Oba, Agege. It called for an investigation into his death and the prosecution of anyone found responsible.

The organisation also urged the authorities to preserve the Lekki Toll Gate as a national memorial and introduce safeguards, including body-worn cameras for police officers.

Recurrent violations

Tuesday’s dispersal brings back the memory of abuses of past #EndSARS memorial attendees by the police.

In July 2025, the Federal High Court in Lagos ordered the Inspector-General of Police and the then Lagos State Commissioner of Police Moshood Jimoh to jointly pay N10 million in damages to protesters whose rights were violated during a memorial procession at the toll gate on 20 October 2024.

The judge Musa Kakaki held that the arrests violated the protesters’ constitutional right to peaceful assembly and association.

The applicants told the court that police officers used teargas and live ammunition to disperse them, assaulted some participants and detained them before releasing them without charge.

The judge also ruled that an earlier Lagos State High Court order restricting protests to designated parks could not be applied retrospectively to the gathering.

The suit was filed by 22 individuals and three organisations: the Education Rights Campaign, Take It Back Movement and Campaign for the Defence of Human Rights.

Police arrested demonstrators during anniversary events in 2021 and arrested protesters and journalists in 2022.

Six years after #EndSARS

The #EndSARS protests began in October 2020, when young Nigerians took to the streets to demand an end to police brutality, particularly abuses attributed to SARS.

The federal government announced the unit’s disbandment on 11 October 2020, but demonstrations continued as protesters demanded accountability.

The shooting at the Lekki Toll Gate on 20 October 2020 became one of the defining moments of the protests. Investigations into the incident and demands for justice have continued in the years since.

World.title: IReV uploads different from results transmission for physical collation – Ex-INEC commissioner Okoye
World.content:
Former National Commissioner of the Independent National Electoral Commission (INEC), Festus Okoye, on Tuesday, distinguished between transmitting election results to the next stage of collation and uploading polling unit results onto the INEC Result Viewing (IReV) portal.

Mr Okoye, speaking on Channels Television’s Morning Brief on Tuesday, called on INEC to intensify public education on the distinction ahead of the 2027 general elections.

He said more education on key aspects of the electoral process was important to avert confusion as the nation heads to its general elections in a few months.

“So I think that the commission should do a lot to educate people aggressively on some of these issues because failure to understand these provisions could fuel confusion about the electoral process,” he said.

According to Mr Okoye, while section 60(3) of the Electoral Act 2026 provides for electronic transmission to IReV, section 60(5) separately addresses the transmission of results to the next level of collation.

INEC introduced the IReV technology in 2020 in its bid to make the process more transparent, and deployed it for the general elections for the first time in 2023.

However, contrary to INEC’s promise, only a fraction of the polling unit results were uploaded promptly. A large percentage of the results from the polling units came only after election day and after INEC had declared President Bola Tinubu the winner of the poll.

Stay Ahead with Premium Times 

INEC would later explain that the system suffered a glitch preventing prompt uploading of the results. The explanation did little to convince many Nigerians that INEC did not manipulate the results during the downtime to suit the ruling All Progressives Congress. Two frontline presidential candidates, Atiku Abubakar of the Peoples Democratic Party and Peter Obi of the Labour Party, went on to challenge the election outcome up to the Supreme Court which affirmed Mr Tinubu’s victory.

Three and a half years after the election and with just three months before the next general elections cycle, INEC has yet to recover from the confidence crisis that resulted from the 2023 IReV delays.

Mr Okoye, whose time in office as INEC commissioner coincided with the introduction of the IReV tool and the 2023 IReV crisis backlash, said on Monday that the results on IReV were only for transparency, while the results used for collation were those transmitted by presiding officers and assistant presiding officers to the next level, where collation officers examine the original Form EC8A from each polling unit.

He also explained that the collation officer examines the results recorded on the physical form and resolves discrepancies where necessary.

Mr Okoye, who served as INEC commissioner between July 2018 and August 2023 (months after the 2023 election), said the distinction between the two processes was important to public understanding of elections and urged INEC to explain the relevant legal provisions more clearly.

‘Technology can malfunction’

Revisiting the 2023 elections on Monday, Mr Okoye noted that technical difficulties affected the real-time uploading of presidential election results.

He said INEC had prepared for the election and that the uploading of results for the House of Representatives had been progressing well before problems arose with the presidential election results.

“Technology can malfunction at any time. Technology can disappoint you,” he said.

He said the central problem was that the presidential election results were not uploaded in real time, rather than not being uploaded at all.

He added that the perception that the results had not been uploaded at all created a credibility problem for the election.

Mr Okoye also said the results were eventually uploaded.

He maintained that the experience demonstrated the importance of distinguishing between the electronic publication of results and the process used for their collation.

Political elite, not electoral laws, are the problem

Asked if the problem was the law, Mr Okoye said Nigeria’s electoral challenges could not be resolved simply by introducing new laws, since political actors who benefit from electoral manipulation did not want elections to be free and fair.

“The law alone cannot conduct elections. Even if we amend the law 100 times, it may not conduct elections. The human element is also very important. It is very, very fundamental,” he said.

He maintained that the Electoral Acts of 2010, 2022 and 2026 could provide a basis for conducting credible elections, but that their effectiveness depended on how political actors behaved.

Mr Okoye, lamented that “what is missing is that at each point, those who benefit from election rigging and election manipulation want to manipulate the process”.

According to the former INEC commissioner, political parties often fail to campaign on clear ideological positions and instead focus on ensuring that voters’ choices do not count.

He said the practice of vote-buying had intensified and become more sophisticated.

Drawing on his experience observing the Ekiti and Osun governorship elections, he said those involved in vote-buying had adopted methods designed to monitor how voters cast their ballots.

“They have gone digital, they have upgraded their act, they have optimised the way they do vote-buying,” he said.

He said those involved sought to control the positioning of voting cubicles so they could see how voters marked their ballots before directing them to collect money.

Mr Okoye stressed that he had not seen anyone prosecuted for vote-buying in connection with the two elections, despite the deployment of security agents.

He urged Nigerians, the media and civil society organisations to look beyond INEC when assessing the credibility of elections, arguing that political actors also bear responsibility for electoral failures.

“INEC has paid staff, but they are limited to polling units. The poll workers include corps members and students of tertiary institutions, university lecturers and professors, and government workers,” Mr Okoye said. “Elections are a multi-stakeholder venture.”

Electoral law amended ahead of 2027 elections

The Electoral Act 2022 was repealed and replaced by the Electoral Act 2026, signed by President Bola Tinubu in February, following weeks of controversy over electronic transmission of election results and protests at the National Assembly.

The Senate initially rejected a proposal to make real-time electronic transmission of polling-unit results to IReV mandatory, prompting protests by civil society groups and other stakeholders.

Following further deliberations, the final law provided for electronic transmission but retained a fallback: where electronic transmission fails or becomes impossible, the signed Form EC8A serves as the primary source for collation and declaration of results.

Mr Okoye’s argument that INEC needs to educate voters about the law and how results are processed comes as preparations for the 2027 general elections gather pace.

INEC’s revised timetable scheduled the presidential and National Assembly elections for 16 January 2027, with governorship and state assembly elections to follow on 6 February 2027.

Campaigns for the presidential and National Assembly elections have since started.

World.title: Dauda Lawal: Political patronage or public service? By Bala B Bitrus
World.content:
No administration should be beyond criticism; if anything, criticism is necessary to keep it on its toes. In Zamfara State, however, the nature of the current debate is revealing. At a stakeholders’ meeting, members of the All Progressives Congress (APC) voiced frustration over Governor Dauda Lawal’s apparent preference for the state’s development over political patronage. Their grievances raise a fundamental question: should public resources serve the interests of political loyalists or the collective good?

The complaints of some party members suggest, in simple terms, that Governor Dauda Lawal is too frugal in managing the state’s resources and insufficiently generous in meeting the demands of politicians who helped bring him to power. Perhaps a banker’s instinct for financial prudence has something to do with it. But the distinction between being financially responsible and being politically indifferent is an important one.

It must be stressed that Governor Lawal acknowledges that party members deserve to be patronised, and available evidence indicates that some have received contracts worth billions of naira. The disagreement, therefore, is not necessarily about whether party members have benefited, but about the extent of those benefits and the expectation that party members should have continuous access to public resources, with or without rendering any service.

At its heart, the dispute is about entitlement and the desire to sustain a system of political patronage that prevailed under previous administrations.

The timing of these complaints is also significant. With the 2027 general elections approaching, some party members appear to believe they can arm-twist the governor into returning to the old order. One must concede that some grievances may be genuine, particularly among party members who cannot meet the requirements for contract awards. Others, however, may reflect frustration with an administration unwilling to accommodate the expectation that public resources should be distributed among political loyalists.

Governor Lawal debunked the allegations of contract marginalisation while acknowledging a communication gap that had made it possible for some beneficiaries to deny benefiting from the administration. He consequently promised to publicise contract awards, including their values and the names of beneficiaries. With this decision, the governor has effectively killed three birds with one stone.

First, greater transparency will make it harder for beneficiaries to deny receiving contracts or sustain unfounded allegations of marginalisation. Second, it will raise the standard of accountability by allowing citizens to scrutinise the award of public contracts. Finally, it will enable Governor Lawal to continue focusing on the important task of delivering development to the people of Zamfara State.

Stay Ahead with Premium Times 

To ensure that more party members can compete for contract opportunities under the Rescue Mission administration, Governor Lawal should complement his financial inclusion programme with a capacity-building initiative to familiarise interested members with public procurement procedures, tender documentation and eligibility requirements. This would give them a fairer opportunity to compete for contracts on merit, without compromising transparency or lowering the standards required for public expenditure.

The controversy in Zamfara State extends beyond the state and presents an opportunity for Nigerians to reflect on a longstanding problem in the country’s politics: the tendency to measure a government’s success by its generosity towards political supporters, particularly the number of appointments and contracts awarded to them. Political parties exist to win elections and implement policies that improve people’s lives, not to serve as platforms for the enrichment of their members. Competent party members have every right to compete for contracts and appointments, but such opportunities must be governed by merit, due process and the public interest.

Politicians must be told in clear terms that their financial and political contributions do not confer an automatic claim to the public treasury. The success of a government should instead be measured by its performance and the benefits it delivers to the citizens it was elected to serve. This principle is particularly relevant in Zamfara State, where the administration inherited serious challenges in security, education, healthcare and infrastructure, all of which demand that scarce public resources be deployed in the wider public interest.

The real question, therefore, is this: by refusing to distribute public resources indiscriminately among party members while awarding contracts to those with the capacity to deliver, has Governor Lawal developed Zamfara State? There answer is a resounding yes.

The primary purpose of government is to protect lives and property and promote the welfare of citizens. Section 14(2)(b) of the 1999 Constitution of the Federal Republic of Nigeria (as amended) affirms that “the security and welfare of the people shall be the primary purpose of government,” while Section 14(2)(a) establishes that sovereignty belongs to the people, from whom government derives its authority. These provisions underscore the obligation of government at all levels to serve the public interest and protect the people.

Although the police and armed forces operate principally under the federal authority, Governor Lawal has refused to remain passive in the face of the security challenges confronting his people. Governor Lawal has responded by funding security operations, strengthening local security initiatives and collaborating with the military and other security agencies to combat terrorism and banditry. His administration’s interventions demonstrate that, even within the limits of state authority, a government can take practical steps to protect its citizens and support the restoration of peace.

The government has recruited and equipped more than 2,000 Community Protection Guards and provided operational vehicles to support security agencies. These interventions form part of its efforts to strengthen local security capacity and improve security conditions so that people can return to their homes and engage in economic activities. Security remains a work in progress. However, the debate should recognise these concrete interventions.

Agriculture is central to Zamfara State’s economic recovery because the livelihoods of many residents depend on farming. Recognising this, Governor Lawal’s administration has supported farmers through the distribution of agricultural inputs and equipment. In July 2025, the government launched a wet-season support programme targeting 59,205 smallholder farmers, with fertiliser, rice and maize seeds, herbicides and insecticides.

In February 2026, further inputs were distributed to dry-season farmers, while a larger intervention announced in July included 72,000 bags of fertiliser, 200,000 litres of herbicides, 100 crop-residue crushers, 100 grass choppers and 100 feed-milling machines. These measures are intended to improve productivity, strengthen food security and support rural livelihoods.

The administration has also pursued agricultural mechanisation. In August 2026, Zamfara began receiving 100 tractors under the Federal Government’s Renewed Hope National Agricultural Mechanisation Programme, following state approval of ₦6.271 billion for participation. The tractors come with implements to support land preparation and cultivation. These interventions demonstrate an effort to move agriculture beyond subsistence production, but their ultimate success will depend on farmers’ access to their fields, effective distribution of inputs, safe transportation of produce and access to markets.

In infrastructural development, Governor Lawal’s administration has prioritised roads, schools and healthcare facilities as part of its broader effort to rebuild Zamfara State and improve the living conditions of the people. The construction and rehabilitation of urban and rural roads have improved transportation. In education, the administration has rehabilitated and constructed more than 800 schools across the state’s 14 local government areas, creating a more conducive learning environment. These investments are particularly important in a state where insecurity and neglect had constrained economic activity. Their value lies in improving economic opportunities and restoring public confidence in government.

Healthcare infrastructure has also received significant attention, with the remodelling and upgrading of the Ahmad Sani Yariman Bakura Specialist Hospital in Gusau standing out as a flagship intervention. The project includes modern diagnostic facilities such as MRI and CT scanners, alongside improvements to specialist departments, laboratories and other essential services. The administration has also intervened in general hospitals, including facilities in Gusau and Anka, while undertaking the construction of a 200-bed facility at Talata Mafara General Hospital. These investments are designed to strengthen specialist and secondary healthcare, expand access to diagnosis and treatment, and reduce the need for residents to seek medical care outside the state.

The administration also understands that well-constructed healthcare facilities alone cannot deliver care without adequately remunerated personnel. In September 2026, Governor Lawal approved a 95 per cent salary increase for health workers, effective September 7, under a revised remuneration structure aligned with the Federal Government’s Consolidated Health Salary Structure (CONHESS). This intervention is aimed at improving staff welfare, attracting and retaining skilled medical professionals, and strengthening healthcare delivery across Zamfara State.

The government has also paid more than ₦16 billion in pension and gratuity arrears owed to retirees and settled approximately ₦1.4 billion in outstanding WAEC fees accumulated between 2018 and 2022. It has also cleared the liabilities that led to the withholding of university results for some indigenes of the state. These were significant obligations that had imposed real hardships on affected families. Settling such liabilities may not generate the immediate political visibility associated with distributing money to party supporters, but it addresses longstanding responsibilities that previous administrations should never have ignored.

These interventions bring the central issue into focus: the difference between deploying public resources to meet legitimate obligations and treating the treasury as a source of discretionary benefits for politically connected individuals. Governor Lawal’s administration has prioritised infrastructure, education, healthcare, security and economic development while emphasising financial discipline. The question is not whether politicians should benefit from government, but whether such benefits should take precedence over the needs of the wider population.

There is no doubt that political parties need members and that competent party loyalists deserve opportunities for appointments and contracts. However, such opportunities must be earned through competence, merit and due process; public resources cannot be treated as the exclusive preserve of party members. In a democracy, the people remain the ultimate beneficiaries of public resources, while elected officials are their temporary custodians.

History will ultimately judge the Lawal administration positively for choosing the public interest over political patronage and for prioritising the welfare of the people over the distribution of their collective patrimony among politicians.

Bala B Bitrus is public affairs commentator

World.title: JP Morgan to secure Nigerian banking licence after N50 billion deposit with CBN – Report
World.content:
American multinational banking institution JP Morgan Chase & Co. is on track to obtain a banking licence in Nigeria, having deposited N50 billion ($38 million) with the Central Bank of Nigeria (CBN), Bloomberg reported Tuesday, citing sources with knowledge of the matter.

Paying the deposit marks part of the last regulatory hurdles to be cleared by the bank before it can be granted approval to run a merchant banking business in Nigeria, the news outlet said, quoting insiders who spoke on the condition that their identity will not be disclosed, given that the process is still private.

Earlier this month, Dapo Olagunju, the managing director of JP Morgan West Africa, had revealed during the Nigeria-Asia Financial Connectivity Dialogue in Singapore the bank’s plan to set up a merchant banking subsidiary in the country.

The CBN teamed up with JP Morgan, the Nigerian Exchange Group and FMDQ Group to convene the dialogue.

According to Bloomberg, JP Morgan, the biggest bank in the US, hopes to receive the permit by year-end or in early 2027, provided it is able to obtain all the requisite approvals.

The expansion push forms part of JP Morgan plan to broaden its presence in Africa, where it is looking to scale up its share of payments, lending, trade finance and corporate banking business.

At the moment, JP Morgan operates a representative office in Lagos, meaning the licence, if issued, will enable it to enlarge its services, which it provides through its asset & wealth management and commercial & investment banking business, in the country.

Stay Ahead with Premium Times 

JP Morgan’s presence in Nigeria dates back to 1961, when Chase Manhattan Bank, which later evolved into JP Morgan Chase & Co., opened a branch in Lagos, providing a wide range of commercial banking services to local businesses and individuals.

A year earlier, Chase International Investment Corporation, a unit of Chase Manhattan Bank, served as the lead partner in organising Nigerian Textile Mills in Lagos, regarded as the first major private industrial project with an American interest in Nigeria.

World.title: FIFA Women’s World Ranking: Super Falcons suffer massive fall as Malawi make biggest leap
World.content:
Nigeria’s Super Falcons have dropped seven places to 43rd in the latest FIFA Women’s World Ranking, recording the biggest loss in ranking points among all nations in the October update.

The Nigerian team lost 83.54 points following a difficult international period that included the 2026 Women’s Africa Cup of Nations (WAFCON), African Olympic qualifying fixtures and international friendlies.

The latest rankings, released after 183 international matches, highlight contrasting fortunes in African women’s football, with several teams improving their positions while others suffered significant setbacks.

For Nigeria, the decline raises fresh concerns about the team’s consistency as preparations for future international competitions gather momentum.

The Super Falcons remain Africa’s most successful women’s national team, with a record 10 WAFCON titles, but their latest ranking setback underlines the need to translate that history into stronger performances.

Malawi record historic rise

While Nigeria lost ground, Malawi emerged as the biggest climbers in the latest rankings, rising 49 places to 104th in the world.

The Scorchers gained 158.44 points, the highest increase recorded by any nation in the update, following their impressive performances during the recent international period.

Stay Ahead with Premium Times 

Their rise reflects the progress of a team increasingly making its mark in African women’s football and contrasts sharply with Nigeria’s decline.

Cameroon also made significant progress, climbing nine places to 62nd after emerging as African champions. Tanzania rose 11 places to 111th, while Burkina Faso moved up nine positions to 109th.

These gains underline the growing competitiveness of women’s football on the continent, where more countries are improving their performances and challenging established teams.

Egypt suffer biggest African ranking drop

Egypt recorded the largest fall in ranking positions among African teams, dropping 14 places to 113th after losing all three group-stage matches at WAFCON.

Zimbabwe fell nine places to 136th, while the Democratic Republic of Congo dropped eight positions to 114th.

Nigeria remain Africa’s highest-ranked team at 43rd, followed by South Africa in 59th, Cameroon in 62nd and Morocco in 64th.

Ghana occupy 65th position, with Zambia 70th, Côte d’Ivoire 72nd, Algeria 73rd, Senegal 76th and Mali 86th.

The rankings illustrate the contrasting progress of African teams and the pressure on established powers to maintain their positions through consistent results.

Spain retain global lead

At the top of the world rankings, Spain maintained first place after winning their first encounter with the United States before drawing the second. The results helped the European champions extend their lead over the Americans to almost 80 points.

The United States remain second, while Germany are third after winning both of their home friendlies.

Denmark were the only team to change positions within the global top 10, climbing two places to 10th after recording a win and a draw away to Canada. The Danes returned to the top 10 for the first time since August 2010, pushing the Netherlands down to 11th and Korea DPR to 12th.

For the Super Falcons, the fall to 43rd is a setback that places renewed emphasis on improved performances and consistency. With the 2027 FIFA Women’s World Cup in Brazil approaching, Nigeria will need to regain momentum to strengthen their global standing and maintain their position among Africa’s leading teams.

World.title: PluggedIN 2026: Aproko Doctor, Taaooma, Layi Wasabi, Osas Ighodaro, others to feature
World.content:
Nigerian entertainers and digital creators, including Aproko Doctor, Taaooma, Layi Wasabi and Osas Ighodaro, will feature at the second edition of PluggedIN, an event aimed at strengthening commercial partnerships between creators, brands and advertising agencies.

Scheduled for 22 October in Victoria Island, Lagos, the event will bring together content creators, brand executives and industry professionals to explore opportunities for turning digital content and original ideas into sustainable creative businesses.

Organised by Woof Studios Africa in partnership with Insight Redefini, a Publicis Groupe-affiliated business in Nigeria, the event will be hosted by actress and media personality Bisola Aiyeola.

Other creators expected at the gathering include Biodun Stephen, Afropolitan, Bolaji Ogunmola, Folagade Banks, Geena Foodies n Spice, Ify’s Kitchen and Shank Comics.

Highlights

The event will also feature discussions on content ownership, audience retention, brand partnerships and the commercial opportunities available to creators beyond individual social media posts.

A panel comprising Craze Clown, Jay On-Air, Kiekie and Winifred Nwania of Zeelicious Food will examine the practical realities of building sustainable creative businesses.

Another discussion, titled Beyond the Post: What Brands Really Want to Build with Creators, will bring together brand and agency executives to explore how businesses can develop longer-term partnerships with creators through original content and integrated storytelling.

Stay Ahead with Premium Times 

The panel will include Adeyinka Jemi-Alade, Head of Integrated Marketing Communications at TGI Group; Bolaji Popoola, Media and Consumer Experience Manager at Mondelez International; Chisom Bikawei, Media Communications Manager at Nestlé Nigeria PLC; Esosa Osagiede, Group Creative Director at Insight Redefini; Francis Obiajulu, Senior Brand Manager for Amstel Malta and Hi-Malt; and Sam Okolie, Head of Mainstream Spirit at Guinness Nigeria.

Creative economy

The event comes amid growing interest in the creator economy, as digital platforms give Nigerians opportunities to build audiences and reach international markets.

According to figures cited in the announcement, Nigeria had more than 1,500 YouTube channels with over 100,000 subscribers in 2024. Collectively, the channels generated more than $10 million in advertising revenue on the platform.

However, the announcement also cited research showing that more than 56 per cent of Nigerian creators earn less than $100 monthly, highlighting the challenge of turning online visibility into reliable income.

Woof Studios Africa founder and Creative Director Adetutu Laditan said the partnership with Insight Redefini would help creators access brand relationships and the production support they need to develop their ideas.

“Nigerian creators are thinking bigger, and that is exactly what forward-thinking brands want to be part of,” Ms Laditan said.

She added that the studio’s role was to manage the business and production complexities of funding, producing, and distributing creative ideas.

According to her, the partnership would give creators greater access to advertising strategy and brand partnerships, helping them move from viral success to long-term commercial sustainability.

Chief Executive Officer of Insight Redefini Group, Babatunde Olaifa, said creators had become central to how businesses engage with consumers.

“The creator economy is no longer a secondary channel; it is the absolute frontline of consumer engagement in Africa today,” Mr Olaifa said.

He added that PluggedIN 2026 would connect the agency’s brand portfolio with creators while offering opportunities for strategic support and commercial collaboration.

PluggedIN

The 2026 edition follows the inaugural PluggedIN event, which was held in partnership with YouTube in 2025.

This year’s partnership with Insight Redefini builds on the event’s focus on connecting creators with businesses and agencies that can help develop and commercialise their ideas.

Rather than focusing solely on influencer campaigns, the organisers say the initiative aims to encourage collaborations that extend to original formats, digital series, communities and intellectual property.

Creators and industry stakeholders are expected to explore ways to build commercially viable projects from Nigeria’s expanding digital content landscape at PluggedIN 2026.

World.title: New ECOWAS Court judges pledge judicial excellence, integrity, effective justice
World.content:
The new college of Judges of the Community Court of Justice, ECOWAS, have pledged to uphold judicial independence, integrity and impartiality, strengthen collegiality and promote timely and effective delivery of justice.

Hon Justice Charlyne Brumskine, President of the Court reiterated the commitment of the Honourable Judges in her opening speech delivered on 19 October 2026, to mark the beginning of a five-day orientation programme for the newly appointed Judges, held under the theme, “Becoming an ECOWAS Judge: Judicial Excellence, Institutional Integration and Effective Adjudication.”

Congratulating her colleagues on their assumption of office on 13 October 2026, Justice Brumskine emphasised that serving at the regional Court required a thorough understanding of the ECOWAS legal order, the Court’s jurisdiction and procedures, and its jurisprudence developed over more than two decades.

The Hon President identified three priorities for the new college of Judges: independence and integrity; collegiality; and effectiveness. She stressed that “public confidence in the Court depends on the fairness, impartiality and integrity demonstrated in every case.” She emphasised the importance of rigorous deliberation, mutual respect and consistency in judicial decisions. She highlighted the need to tackle delays and improve the timely delivery of justice and align judicial work with the Court’s Strategic Plan 2026–2030. She further underscored the need for sustained engagement with Member States to strengthen compliance with the Court’s judgements.

Justice Brumskine acknowledged the Acting Chief Registrar, Dr Ousmane Diallo, the facilitator, Professor Friday C. Nwoke, former Vice-President of the Court, and the Court’s staff for their contributions to the organisation and delivery of the programme.

The other Judges participating in the orientation programme are: Hon Justice Désire Henri AIHOU (Vice President), Hon Justice Henrietta Uzoamaka DIDIGU (Member), Hon Justice Yaouza OURO-SAMA (Member) and Hon Justice Awa BAH (Member).

In an earlier welcome address, Dr Ousmane Diallo, Acting Chief Registrar, outlined the objectives and expected outcomes of the programme. He described it as an opportunity to facilitate the smooth integration of the newly appointed Judges and their Executive Assistants into the Court’s institutional and operational environment.

Stay Ahead with Premium Times 

Dr Diallo explained that the programme would familiarise the participants with the Court’s organisational structure, departmental responsibilities, administrative procedures and coordination mechanisms. It is also intended to clarify the respective roles of judicial, legal, administrative and other support services, while strengthening communication and collaboration among Judges, Executive Assistants, heads of departments and staff.

Among the expected outcomes of the orientation programme are: improved understanding of the Court’s structure and support systems; and stronger professional relationships built. The programme will promote institutional continuity, operational efficiency, and staff preparedness to support the new Judges for the effective discharge of their functions.

World.title: Eniola Badmus apologises to Laide Bakare, calls for end to feud
World.content:
Nollywood actress Eniola Badmus has apologised to her colleague, Laide Bakare, following the backlash over her reaction to Bakare’s name during a recent podcast appearance, expressing a desire to put their differences behind them.

Badmus tendered the apology in a statement shared on Instagram on Tuesday, days after a clip from her appearance on Isbae U’s Curiosity Made Me Ask podcast went viral on social media.

During the interview, the host mentioned Bakare as one of his favourite actresses, prompting Badmus to hiss and change her facial expression. The moment attracted reactions online and revived discussions about the strained relationship between the two actresses.

Reflecting on her reaction via her Instagram page, Badmus admitted that it could have been perceived as dismissive and expressed regret over how it came across.

“On reflection, I realise my reaction when Laide Bakare’s name was mentioned during my recent interview could have come across as dismissive, and for that, I sincerely apologise,” she wrote.

Addressing Bakare directly, the actress added, “Laide, whatever our differences, I choose peace and I genuinely wish you well.”

Badmus said maturity involves learning from past experiences and choosing to move forward rather than holding on to disagreements.

“We’re all growing, learning and becoming better versions of ourselves. Sometimes maturity is simply knowing when to let go and move forward,” she stated.

She concluded her message with a plea for peace, writing, “Joo maa binu. No negativity. No grudges. Let love lead and peace reigns.”

The apology comes amid a history of public disagreements between the actresses, whose relationship has been marked by exchanges on social media and confrontations at public events.

In March 2024, Badmus appeared to mock Bakare’s outfit at the latter’s book launch. Bakare had attended the event in a white outfit with an orange cape, which generated mixed reactions online.

Badmus subsequently took to Instagram and wrote, “Ewo ninu yin lo wo Aso Pastor Ajidara. Abeg who??” The remark was widely interpreted as a dig at Bakare’s outfit.

Bakare expressed disappointment over the incident, questioning why a colleague she regarded as a childhood friend from their University of Ibadan days would publicly criticise her instead of celebrating her achievement.

World.title: No plot to kill Atiku, APC campaign council declares
World.content:
.Says, ex-VP’s details not withdrawn

By Omeiza Ajayi

ABUJA: The All Progressives Congress Presidential Campaign Council APC-PCC has declared that there is no plot to assassinate former Vice President Atiku Abubakar, the Presidential candidate of the African Democratic Congress ADC, insisting that his security details have not been withdrawn.

The council said the claim, made by a member of the ADC, Timi Frank, was false and must be proved.

In a statement on Tuesday, the Spokesperson of the APC Presidential Campaign Council, Dele Alake, said: “We categorically reject the claim that the presidency of Nigeria or the APC Campaign Council is involved in any plot to assassinate former Vice President Atiku Abubakar or any opposition figure.

“This is a grave allegation that Mr Frank must prove. We thus urge security agencies to invite him to substantiate the allegation, given its gravity and the urgent need to preserve life,” the statement said.

The council also dismissed reports that Atiku’s security cover had been pulled. “The narrative that the security personnel attached to former Vice President Atiku have been withdrawn is totally false. The former Vice President is well protected by the police and the Department of State Security DSS.

“Contrary to the falsehood promoted by Timi Frank, President Tinubu recently directed security agencies to reinforce and increase protection for all presidential, vice-presidential, governorship, and Deputy Governorship candidates across the country.

“The security around the ADC Presidential candidate has never been compromised. As a former Vice President of Nigeria, he enjoys two levels of state-funded security protection. President Tinubu has increased security protection for Alhaji Atiku Abubakar as a Presidential candidate ahead of the 2027 general elections.”

The campaign council, however, said it would not treat any real threat lightly. “We also urge Mr Frank not to hesitate to provide any information in his possession that will enable prompt investigation. Any credible threat to life must be treated seriously, irrespective of political affiliation,” the statement said.

It described the allegation as a familiar tactic of opposition figures. “Mr Frank’s claim is typical opposition rabble-rousing meant to heat the polity. Many opposition figures, including Timi Frank, have made it a habit to write open letters and tag foreign leaders and international organisations in social media posts to draw undeserved attention to themselves,” it said.

The council also pointed to the President’s own record in opposition politics. “President Bola Tinubu, as a statesman and an avowed democrat, recognises opposition politics as an essential part of our 27-year-old democracy. For 16 years in Nigeria, President Tinubu was the face of opposition, and he galvanised the opposition movement to defeat the Peoples Democratic Party as a governing party in Nigeria in 2015.

“As we go deeper into the campaign season, politicians and supporters will continue to make outlandish statements and frivolous allegations to gain political advantage.

“We urge candidates, political parties, and supporters to be factual and responsible in public statements and avoid utterances that can trigger avoidable tension in the polity. Let our political competition be peaceful, lawful, and focused on the big issues that matter to Nigerians, not character assassination or wild, baseless allegations”, Alake said.

former Deputy National Publicity Secretary of the All Progressives Congress APC, Comrade Timi Frank, has raised alarm over alleged plots to intimidate and arrest the Presidential Candidate of the African Democratic Congress ADC, Atiku Abubakar, using the Economic and Financial Crimes Commission EFCC.

In an open letter addressed to United States President Donald Trump and other international leaders, Frank appealed for diplomatic intervention over alleged threats to the life and political freedom of the former Vice President.

Frank, who is Ambassador for East Africa and the Middle East of the United Liberation Movement for West Papua (ULMWP) and Senior Adviser to the Global Friendship City Association, United States, said the allegations required urgent and independent investigation.

“These allegations must be independently and urgently investigated. Given their gravity, however, they cannot be dismissed or ignored until it is too late to prevent harm,” he said.

He voiced particular concern that the EFCC could be used to initiate proceedings against Atiku in circumstances that might lead to his arrest and prolonged detention during the election campaign.

“The concern is not that Atiku Abubakar should be placed above the law. The concern is that the law must never be placed at the service of political persecution.

“The protection of political opposition is not a favour that any government grants at its discretion. It is a fundamental obligation of every democratic state,” he said.

World.title: #EndSARS: No Nigerian should be punished for demanding good governance – Obi
World.content:
Peter Obi

By Adegboyega Adeleye

Presidential candidate of the Nigeria Democratic Congress (NDC), Peter Obi, has said no Nigerian should be punished for demanding good governance, as he marked six years since the October 20, 2020, incident at the Lekki Toll Gate.
