World.title: Cameroon: Online Fraud Is Becoming a Gateway to Human Trafficking in Cameroon
World.content:
analysis

Criminal networks exploit job seekers' aspirations, turning promises of employment abroad into schemes involving detention, extortion and forced recruitment.

The discovery in September of 15 underage girls in a barricaded compound in Yaoundé's Essos neighbourhood, followed days later by 20 people (including two children) in a basement in Ngousso, has reignited concerns about human trafficking in Cameroon. The two mixed-use neighbourhoods in the capital's northeast are home to working- and middle-class residents.

These are not isolated incidents. Reports from 2025 reveal that criminal networks have been exploiting desperate citizens in Yaoundé and the central Adamawa Region by luring them with false job promises.

Keep up with the latest headlines on WhatsApp | LinkedIn

In May this year, an operation in Dibombari in the Littoral Region led to the rescue of 17 youths recruited through fake job offers posted on digital platforms. The victims had paid an average of 550 000 CFA francs (US$942) in the hope of travelling to Malaysia, only to be held captive while awaiting departure. Four suspects were arrested.

A few weeks later, the National Gendarmerie announced the dismantling of a vast network in Yaoundé operating under the guise of multi-level marketing on behalf of the businesses QNET, IGNITE and UNIMEC. QNET has denied any involvement, and the positions of the other two companies are not yet clear.

An investigation launched on 16 May resulted in 13 arrests and the identification of around 6 000 victims of fraud and human trafficking nationwide, according to National Gendarmerie data given to the Institute for Security Studies (ISS). The criminal networks involve recruiters, intermediaries, logistics and accommodation providers, coordinators and masterminds - some operating from outside the country.

The large scale of these illicit operations confirms the shift towards digitalisation, with networks no longer relying on in-person contact or local recruiters. Social media, digital platforms and fake job or training offers make it possible to quickly reach individuals seeking employment or opportunities abroad.

Human trafficking facilitated by cybercrime is expanding globally. In Africa, cyber-recruiters have for years been exploiting the continent's growing connectivity. But in Cameroon, large-scale recruitment and fraudulent migration schemes via platforms like WhatsApp and Facebook are relatively new and increasing. In response, the Ministry of Public Service and Administrative Reform has issued official warnings about the threat.

In the recently dismantled Yaoundé network, the primary targets were vulnerable youth, job seekers, students and those seeking to migrate, drawn by the prospect of lucrative employment or skills development abroad.

Once recruited, they paid expensive fees and were then held in compounds - some for months - until authorities discovered the sites. Captors exerted constant psychological pressure on their victims, forcing them to extort money from their loved ones and recruit new targets online in order to secure their release.

Some victims from southern Cameroon were transferred via Garoua in the North Region to Nigeria. Deprived of their travel documents, they were confined and forced to raise money from their families.

The distinction between recruitment scams and the forced detention of victims is crucial. The Palermo Protocol against transnational organised crime defines human trafficking as recruitment or harbouring combined with deception, fraud, abuse of vulnerability or coercion, for the purpose of exploitation. In Cameroon, the initial scam does not involve human trafficking. It is the confiscation of documents, confinement, threats and coercion used to recruit others that mark the shift to trafficking.

The National Gendarmerie data also reveals a transnational dimension. The network's ringleaders are allegedly based in Malaysia, with offshoots in West and Central Africa. Two people sought in connection with the investigation have been located in the Democratic Republic of the Congo (DRC) and Central African Republic.

Cameroon also serves as a destination for foreign victims, including Chadians recruited by networks operating in Yaoundé. In March 2025, police rescued 13 people held in a house in Yaoundé - seven from Madagascar, six from the DRC.

The common factor across all these cases is the exploitation of economic and social vulnerability by criminal networks. In the QNET-IGNITE-UNIMEC case, the existence of multiple accommodation sites across different regions shows how criminal networks employ a web of clandestine houses or dormitories to isolate victims, confiscate their phones and keep them under constant surveillance.

Recent interventions show that security forces are able to identify and dismantle some of the networks. However, the vast distances between recruitment and trafficking sites and the transnational nature of the criminal networks call for enhanced cooperation within Cameroon and between the countries involved. This should include intelligence sharing and the designation of dedicated contact points to centralise alerts, prevent administrative obstacles and enable immediate intervention.

Close 

Cameroonian authorities also need to undertake rigorous monitoring and documentation of collective housing facilities, premises rented to groups, and informal shelters to identify suspicious gatherings before they become detention sites.

The government should redouble efforts to establish formal protocols between digital platforms such as Facebook and WhatsApp and the National Gendarmerie, enabling the rapid removal of fake job offers and the tracing of the accounts that disseminate them.

These measures may seem obvious, but coordinating such efforts is rarely easy. Cameroon's ability to curb the expansion of this hybrid criminal phenomenon will depend on whether authorities have the political and budgetary will to act.

Aicha Pemboura, Researcher, Central Africa Observatory on Organised Crime and Violence, ISS

World.title: Africa: All of Africa Today - October 20, 2026
World.content:
Rwandan Govt Critic Found Beheaded in Uganda

Robert Kabera, a 50-year-old former Rwandan army sergeant major and outspoken critic of President Paul Kagame, has been found beheaded on the outskirts of Kampala, Uganda. Kabera had fled Rwanda and sought asylum in Uganda, citing political persecution. He later gained a following through his YouTube channel, which featured criticism of Kagame's government. Ugandan police said his head had not been recovered. His widow expressed fears for her family's safety. The opposition Rwanda National Congress has called for a thorough investigation, as his killing renews concerns about the safety of Rwandan dissidents living in exile. Other critics of Kagame have been killed abroad, including former intelligence chief Patrick Karegeya, who was found dead in Johannesburg in 2014.

Keep up with the latest headlines on WhatsApp | LinkedIn

UN Condemns Deadly Drone Strikes Across Sudan

Drone strikes across Sudan have killed and injured civilians, including children, as fighting between the Sudanese Armed Forces and the paramilitary Rapid Support Forces continues to intensify. The attacks injured at least 19 people at a market in Abyei and targeted locations in Khartoum, including an area near the airport. The strikes reportedly killed at least 19 people, including 10 children, across several states. The United Nations condemned the attacks and raised concerns over the targeting of humanitarian workers, with 25 Sudanese Red Crescent volunteers reportedly killed since the conflict began in April 2023. An estimated 20 million people face acute hunger, with famine risks rising in parts of Darfur and Greater Kordofan. Despite the insecurity, aid agencies continue delivering assistance, including restoring water supplies to thousands of people in Central Darfur. Sudan's humanitarian response plan remains just over 43% funded.

Zimbabwe's Ruling Party to Discipline MPs Who Missed Constitutional Amendment Vote

Zimbabwe's ruling Zanu-PF party plans to discipline Members of Parliament who failed to attend crucial parliamentary sittings during consideration of Constitutional Amendment No. 3 Bill. Party legal secretary Ziyambi Ziyambi announced the sanctions at the party's annual conference in Chinhoyi, naming several senior officials and deputy ministers among those who did not vote, although their reasons remain unclear. The disciplinary move comes as Zanu-PF advances resolutions to postpone its next elective congress from 2027 to 2029, potentially keeping President Emmerson Mnangagwa at the helm until 2030. Provincial leaders defended resolutions supporting his continued leadership and called for constitutional alignment and greater national self-sufficiency in areas such as medicine, technology and industrial production.

Thabo Mbeki Denies Blocking Apartheid-Era Prosecutions at Inquiry Commission

Former South African president Thabo Mbeki has denied allegations that he held secret meetings with former apartheid-era military and police generals to prevent prosecutions for human rights abuses. Testifying before the Khampepe Commission of Inquiry into delayed Truth and Reconciliation Commission (TRC) prosecutions, Mbeki said the generals approached him in 1996 seeking a meeting with the ANC over amnesty applications. He argued that former president FW de Klerk and his cabinet should also apply. Mbeki said the ANC subsequently pursued collective amnesty for some of its leaders to encourage the apartheid leadership to do the same, but the courts later overturned the decision. He maintained that his administration never directed the National Prosecuting Authority to halt or suppress investigations, arguing that prosecutions were the NPA's responsibility. He also defended his 2003 parliamentary speech and later arrangements involving pardon requests, saying these aimed to encourage truth-telling rather than grant blanket immunity to those responsible for apartheid-era crimes.

Close 

Nigeria and Rwanda Seek to Strengthen Defence Cooperation

Nigeria's Chief of Army Staff, Lieutenant General Waidi Shaibu, has arrived in Rwanda for a five-day official visit aimed at strengthening defence and security cooperation between the two countries. Shaibu held talks in Kigali with Rwanda Defence Force Chief of Defence Staff General Mubarakh Muganga and Army Chief of Staff Major General Vincent Nyakarundi. The discussions focused on implementing existing agreements covering military training, exchanges of instructional and logistics personnel, and other shared security concerns. Shaibu and his delegation also visited the Kigali Genocide Memorial to pay tribute to victims of the 1994 Genocide against the Tutsi and toured the Campaign Against Genocide Museum to learn about the genocide and Rwanda's post-conflict recovery. The visit is scheduled to conclude on October 23.

World.title: South Africa: From First Jab to the Next - The Data System Tracking South Africa's LEN Roll-Out
World.content:
South Africa's LEN roll-out isn't just about getting six-monthly HIV prevention jabs into people's arms. We also need to know whether people return for their next dose, whether clinics have enough stock and who is being left behind. A digital system linking LEN clinics will help us find out.

South Africa's LEN roll-out isn't just about getting six-monthly HIV prevention jabs into people's arms. We also need to know whether people return for their next dose, whether clinics have enough stock and who is being left behind. A digital system linking LEN clinics will help us find out.

Giving someone their first LEN jab is easy to count. Knowing whether they return six months later is what tells us whether the programme is really working.

A digital system called SyNCH connects LEN clinics in all provinces outside the Western Cape, which uses a different system, allowing health workers to see information about a person's previous LEN doses when they visit another participating clinic.

The information feeds into a dashboard that helps health officials see who is using LEN, where uptake is low and where clinics may need more support.

South Africa still doesn't have a comprehensive national electronic patient record. The LEN system shows what becomes possible when health information can follow a patient between clinics.

Giving someone an HIV prevention injection is one thing. Knowing whether they come back six months later for their next one is another.

That difference matters.

Keep up with the latest headlines on WhatsApp | LinkedIn

South Africa started rolling out lenacapavir, or LEN, a twice-yearly injection that prevents HIV, in June . But the success of the programme cannot be measured simply by counting how many people receive their first injections.

The health department also needs to know whether people return for their second and third doses. By 15 October just under 79 000 people had received their first LEN dose, and the first group of people who will receive their second dose, will have to do so in early December .

The department needs to see which clinics have high or low uptake, which groups of people are being reached — and which are being missed. And it needs to know whether clinics have enough stock to give people their next injections when they are due.

Without good data, health officials are effectively trying to manage a national programme without being able to see clearly what is happening on the ground.

That is why one of the less visible parts of South Africa's LEN roll-out could turn out to be one of its most important: the digital system behind it.

SA's HIV prevention medicine dashboard (screen grab)

Following a LEN user from one clinic to another

LEN is currently available at 360 public clinics in South Africa. Most of these clinics are connected through an electronic system called SyNCH, short for the Synchronised National Communication in Health system .

SyNCH was developed by the public health intelligence organisation, Health Systems Trust (HST) and ASG Technologies in partnership with the national health department. It was originally built to help manage medicines for stable patients with chronic conditions who collect their treatment from pick-up points outside clinics. It has since been expanded to include HIV prevention medicines — both the daily HIV prevention pill and LEN.

For LEN users, this means something remarkably practical.

When someone receives LEN, their visit is recorded electronically. If they later go to another LEN clinic connected to SyNCH, a healthcare worker can see information about their previous LEN visit, including when they received their last dose.

So a person does not necessarily have to return to the same clinic every six months to continue using LEN.

That matters in a country where people move between towns and provinces for work, study or family reasons.

The exception is the Western Cape, which uses a different electronic patient-record system. LEN users there can move between participating clinics within the province, but their records are not connected to SyNCH clinics elsewhere in the country.

South Africa has spent years trying to build a comprehensive national electronic patient record. We are not there yet. SyNCH is not such a record either. But what is happening with LEN shows what becomes possible when clinics can share important information about an individual patient's care.

A first dose doesn't tell you whether a programme works

The system does more than help individual LEN users.

The information entered at clinics feeds into a LEN dashboard that allows health officials to see what is happening with the roll-out without waiting months for reports to work their way up through the health system.

Officials can see how many people are choosing LEN or the daily HIV prevention pill and break the figures down by age, gender and area — from province all the way down to individual clinics.

That can answer important questions.

Are young people taking up LEN? Are some districts doing much better than others? Are particular groups not being reached? Is a clinic attracting many LEN users while another nearby is seeing very few?

Those differences matter because a national total can hide local problems.

A headline figure might show that thousands of people have received LEN. But it won't necessarily tell officials that uptake is low in one district, that a particular age group is being missed or that a clinic needs extra support.

More detailed data can.

And as the roll-out continues, another number will become increasingly important: how many people come back for their next injection?

LEN protects someone for six months at a time . If large numbers of people receive their first dose but don't return for later injections, the programme will not have the impact we hope for.

Because SyNCH keeps a person-level record of LEN use, the health department can track whether people return for subsequent doses rather than simply counting injections given.

That turns data from a record of what has already happened into a tool for improving what happens next.

Data can also help prevent stock problems

There is another crucial part of the picture: medicine stock.

A successful campaign can create its own problem if demand grows faster than the supply of medicine to clinics.

Digital information can help health officials see how LEN is being used and where stock is running low. That gives managers an opportunity to respond — for example, by moving stock or replenishing a clinic — before shortages interrupt people's prevention.

This is especially important for a medicine that must be given on a schedule.

Someone who has made the effort to return for their next injection should not discover that the clinic has run out.

The dashboard isn't the achievement on its own

It is tempting to think of a dashboard as the innovation. But a dashboard is only as useful as the information underneath it.

Close 

The bigger achievement is connecting what happens to an individual LEN user at a clinic with information that nurses, doctors and programme managers can use.

HST has worked with the national health department and other partners for years to build and support some of the digital systems on which this work depends. LEN shows how that infrastructure can be adapted for a new public health programme rather than building a separate system from scratch each time.

There is a broader lesson here.

South Africa has many ambitious health policies and programmes. But launching an intervention is only the beginning. We need to know whether people are actually getting it, whether they continue using it, whether clinics have enough stock and whether the people who could benefit most are being reached.

That requires good data.

The same principle applies far beyond LEN. A health system needs to be able to follow people through care, whether they are using HIV prevention, collecting HIV or TB treatment, or receiving long-term care for conditions such as diabetes or high blood pressure.

Technology on its own won't fix South Africa's health system. Nor will another dashboard.

But when health workers can see the information they need to care for someone, and managers can see problems early enough to do something about them, data becomes more than numbers on a screen.

It becomes part of healthcare itself.

Ntombi Sigwebela is the chief executive officer of Health Systems Trust.

This story was produced by the Bhekisisa Centre for Health Journalism.

World.title: Uganda: Police Break Silence On Murder of Rwandan Dissident Beheaded in Mpigi
World.content:
Police have launched investigations into the murder of a Rwandan dissident whose headless body was discovered in Mpigi District, with the victim's missing head yet to be recovered.

Sgt Maj Robert Kabera, 50, a former Rwanda Defence Forces (RDF) soldier who was critical of President Paul Kagame's leadership, was found dead on Saturday morning, October 17, in Luwala Village, Kammengo Sub-county.

Police spokesperson Kituuma Rusoke told journalists on Monday that officers had registered a murder case after the discovery of the body.

"We acknowledge that we registered murder of male adult averagely 50 years whose head was cut off and up to now it hasn't yet been recovered. We recovered the body minus the head. He was identified as Robert Kabera by his relatives," Rusoke said.

Keep up with the latest headlines on WhatsApp | LinkedIn

He said police received the report on Saturday, although investigators believe the killing could have occurred either during the night of October 16 or in the early hours of October 17.

According to Rusoke, local residents discovered the remains and alerted police. Kabera's relatives had also become concerned after he failed to communicate as he usually did.

"The remains were discovered by locals who informed police. Incidentally relatives were concerned about their person who usually wouldn't take long to communicate," he said.

Police officers who visited the scene found the headless body, which was subsequently taken to Mulago City Mortuary as part of the investigation.

Rusoke said investigators were examining the circumstances surrounding the killing and other details that could help establish what happened.

"We are investigating that murder and any other details relevant to the murder or any circumstances surrounding his life," he said.

Kabera reportedly fled Rwanda for Uganda around 2020 after raising concerns that his life was in danger.

His killing comes against the backdrop of his reported criticism of the Rwandan leadership. However, police have not publicly established a motive for the murder or indicated whether his political views were connected to his death.

Investigations are ongoing, with the recovery of his missing head among the outstanding details in the case.

World.title: These numbers show just how fraudulent Notre Dame has been during the Marcus Freeman era
World.content:
Marcus Freeman is 49-13 overall as the head coach of Notre Dame since taking over the Fighting Irish at the end of the 2021 season. It's a respectable record, but when you take a slightly deeper dive into the numbers, the situation turns into an utterly embarrassing one.

Notre Dame's best season under Freeman came in 2024 when the Irish finished the regular season at 11-1, rattling off 10 straight wins after losing at home to Northern Illinois, before ultimately losing in the national championship game to Ohio State. That campaign was unquestionably great and very respectable, but when you peel back the curtain and focus solely on the regular season, not even 2024 could be labeled impressive.

On the heels of the Irish losing on the road to BYU in Week 7, the team's first noteworthy opponent of the season, Notre Dame has been in the crosshairs yet again as a program that simply can not win the rare meaningful game it actually schedules during the regular season, and it turns out that there is some very real legitimacy behind that idea.

COLLEGE FOOTBALL FACES ANOTHER CLOCK CONTROVERSY AFTER BYU UPSETS NOTRE DAME

Chris 'The Bear' Fallica of Fox Sports did some digging into Notre Dame's record under Freeman to find out if the narrative about the Fighting Irish was as bad as some in the college football world have made it out to be, and the numbers paint quite the picture.

THE CRAIG CARTON SHOW–UNFILTERED, UNAPOLOGETIC AND UNMISSABLE. DOWNLOAD HIS DAILY PODCAST NOW!

Notre Dame has won 16 games dating back to the start of the 2025 season, and according to Fallica's findings, those 16 teams have posted a combined record of 62-91 against FBS opponents. If you take those 16 teams and look at their record against Power Four schools, it drops to a stunning 32-78 mark.

While those numbers reflect how soft Notre Dame has made its schedule over the years, it somehow gets even more alarming.

WEEK 7 AP TOP 25 POLL FEATURES A COMPLETE SHUFFLE AFTER CHAOTIC WEEKEND, WITH MIAMI TAKING OVER THE TOP SPOT

Freeman has posted a 44-11 regular-season record while in charge of the Irish, and of those 44 wins, a whopping five have come against teams that finished the season ranked. Two of those five ranked opponents happened to be service academies.

Looking ahead at the remainder of Notre Dame's regular season slate, the Irish play host to No. 1 Miami on Nov. 7 and No. 23 SMU two weeks later.



Things will fall into place as they always do, but it's relatively safe to assume that if the Irish finish the year at 10-2, they will punch a ticket into the College Football Playoff.

If Notre Dame finishes inside the Top 12 in the final CFB Playoff rankings, it automatically qualifies for the Playoff no matter the teams or resumes in a similar position.

World.title: Fox News Power Rankings: Trump country at a crossroads
World.content:
NEW You can now listen to Fox News articles!

Republicans have had their share of good and bad election nights this century, but they’ve usually been able to count on the heartland.

Once evenly divided, rural voters have become substantially more Republican over the last two decades. Nearly two-thirds of these voters backed President Trump in the 2024 election.

REPUBLICANS FACE BRUTAL MIDTERM HEADWINDS. SIX FORCES COULD HELP THEM DEFY HISTORY.

Today, just under half of rural voters say they’ll support the GOP again in November.

Like other groups, rural Americans are concerned about paying the bills. Nineteen percent said the rising cost of living is their biggest economic problem in a recent survey, with gas and energy costs not far behind.

The Trump administration has, in part, tried to counter those anxieties by talking about job growth and the AI boom, but rural voters are frustrated about those issues too.

Less than a quarter of rural voters say the economy is in good shape, and unemployment is a focal point: 8% called a lack of jobs and unemployment their biggest economic issue, and only 28% thought there were good or excellent job opportunities in their communities.

DAVID MARCUS: ON THE GROUND IN MIDDLE AMERICA, FOUR ISSUES WILL DECIDE THE SENATE, AND NONE ARE AFFORDABILITY

Data centers are part of the story too. Only 2% called it their biggest economic problem, but that number is larger than it seems. For 1 in 50 rural voters, data centers are a bigger problem than housing, the cost of living, or getting a job.

These factors have put the Republicans in a tough spot all over the map.

They are a reason why heartland states like Ohio and Iowa have been competitive most of the year and why more rural districts, including some that Trump won by double digits, are becoming margin-of-error races.

Even setting the polls aside, there are signs that the rural vote is on shakier footing. TV viewers in Wyoming will see ads this week for Republican candidate Chuck Gray that don’t mention Trump or the GOP. Two years ago, Trump won 71.6% of the vote there — his best performance in any state, in any election.

Low rural turnout or party switching would make many races closer than the GOP would like, including in Florida, Mississippi and South Carolina.

Four states are worth singling out thanks to another complicating factor.

TRUMP-ALIGNED CONSERVATIVE EMERGES FROM CROWDED PRIMARY TO DECIDE WHO FILLS WYOMING’S LONE HOUSE SEAT

This year, prominent independent candidates are running for Senate against a Republican in four rural-heavy states: Idaho, Montana, Nebraska and South Dakota.

They are pushing anti-establishment policies like congressional term limits and lobbying bans and have a heavy focus on corruption, the top voter concern in last week’s Fox News poll .

And all four say they won’t caucus with either party or would form their own independent caucus if they were elected.

With the Democratic brand still relatively weak around the country and abysmal in these states, the party has stepped out of the race entirely in three of the four (in Montana, a Democrat is staying on the ballot, though support for her has declined).

Normally, frustrated partisans stay home in scenarios like these, leaving the incumbent party to win by a more modest margin. This year, those voters have the ability to turn out for a different candidate, so the margin may get narrower.

FOX NEWS POWER RANKINGS: AS THE HOUSE FALLS, THE SENATE STAYS IN PLAY

All these states have been competitive over the last decade or so. Former Sen. Jon Tester, a Democrat, held on to his seat in Montana in 2018; Republicans have scored single-digit victories in South Dakota and Nebraska (where the same independent is running again this year), and even Idaho had a gubernatorial race that came within 15 points back in 2014.

These states could be close again.

In this week’s Power Rankings, two gubernatorial races get more competitive as the final two weeks of campaigning begin.

Florida

The Sunshine State is the beating heart of the "MAGA" movement. Trump and Gov. Ron DeSantis have posted stronger results each time they’ve run, with the latter winning his last re-election bid by nearly 20 points.

Thanks in part to those performances, Republicans have carved out structural advantages, including a 1.5 million registered voter gap and a resilient get-out-the-vote operation.

But DeSantis’ first win came within around 30,000 votes (or 0.4 points) and in a similar environment to the one we’re in now.

Here, Hispanic voters will play an outsized role, and polls suggest that a large chunk of them have shifted away from the GOP. In last week’s national Fox survey, 31% of Hispanic voters said they preferred the Republican candidate over the Democrat. That’s down 12 points from their support for Trump in 2024.

The Republican candidate, Rep. Byron Donalds, will be pleased to have the endorsement of DeSantis. He remains popular in the state. Donalds still has the edge against Democrat and former Rep. David Jolly, who is hoping former President Bill Clinton can shore up his support when they appear together for the first time today.

Still, this race is no sure thing for the GOP. Florida moves from Likely R to Lean R.

Nebraska

In Nebraska, Republican Gov. Jim Pillen is looking for a second term in office. He cruised to victory the first time with a 23-point win, but with both suburban and rural voters wavering on Trump this cycle, this could be a tougher battle.

Three other factors are playing a role.

First, the presence of Dan Osborn, one of the four notable independents on the ballot in Senate races this year, could boost Democratic turnout for challenger Lynne Walz in a governor’s race that would otherwise attract less attention.

There’s Pillen himself, who has faced some local pushback over a 5% budget cut and hiring freeze within state government.

CLICK HERE TO DOWNLOAD THE FOX NEWS APP

Finally, the ballot, which will feature third-party challenger Brett Lindstrom, a former state lawmaker who lost to Pillen in a Republican primary four years prior. He’ll appear on the ballot as an "America First" candidate. The party was founded in July.

World.title: DOJ sends grand jury subpoenas to Philadelphia DA Krasner after judge's referral, sources say

The Justice Department sent grand jury subpoenas to Democratic Philadelphia District Attorney Larry Krasner's office in recent days, Fox News has learned.

Two sources briefed on the subpoenas say they are related to potential obstruction of justice relating to the handling of cases before federal judges. The sources said the subpoenas came as a result of a federal judge referring Krasner and his top deputy to the DOJ for possible criminal investigation.

Krasner's office did not immediately respond to a request for comment. The DOJ declined to comment.

FEDERAL JUDGE REFERS PHILADELPHIA DA LARRY KRASNER TO DOJ FOR POSSIBLE CRIMINAL INVESTIGATION

Reports of the subpoenas come more than a month after U.S. District Judge Paul Diamond referred Krasner and his deputy, Matthew Stiegler, to the DOJ, saying evidence uncovered in a murder conviction case could constitute false statements, perjury, obstruction of justice and conspiracy.

Neither man has been charged.

DELETED EMAIL DETAILS ALLEGED TRUMP-TARGETING PUSH INSIDE LETITIA JAMES’ OFFICE: ‘FIND AND PURSUE CRIMES’

Diamond also disqualified Krasner and Stiegler from the case but declined to disqualify the entire DA's office.

The judge alleged that Krasner and Stiegler sought to pressure prosecutors into presenting a false narrative to the court and that Krasner warned of "consequences" if staff alerted the court to an internal conflict.

BIDEN-ERA FEDERAL PROSECUTOR HIT WITH CRIMINAL INVESTIGATION REFERRAL OVER ALLEGED FALSE STATEMENTS TO FBI

"I have thus reluctantly concluded that Philadelphia’s highest law enforcement official and one of his top assistants may have violated the law," Diamond wrote.

The dispute stems from the case of Dennis Johnson, who was convicted in 2009 of killing Kenyatta Smith.

SOROS NETWORK REBUILDS PROGRESSIVE PROSECUTOR PUSH AFTER STRING OF ELECTION LOSSES

The DA’s office said in a 2022 filing that Johnson was entitled to habeas corpus relief based on ineffective assistance of counsel, according to The Associated Press.

Prosecutors later raised potential conflicts involving Stiegler and urged that the matter be referred to the Pennsylvania Attorney General’s Office.

PHILADELPHIA DA SAYS HE'LL KEEP PIECE OF TRUMP'S WHITE HOUSE BALLROOM 'AFTER WE ALL BLOW IT UP'

According to the opinion, Krasner opposed that move and repeatedly said someone from his office needed to remain involved to "protect the office."

"I respectfully and vigorously disagree with the court’s findings of fact and conclusions of law," Krasner said in a statement at the time. "I look forward to appealing to the higher court as soon as the law allows. This remains a pending matter, which limits for now my and my office’s ability to respond in the media."

World.title: Carmelo Anthony thinks Knicks are the 'team to beat' as long as they do this following NBA title win
World.content:
Carmelo Anthony can’t wait for Tuesday night at Madison Square Garden, as he watches Jalen Brunson and the rest of the New York Knicks receive their long-awaited NBA title rings, and even better, watching a banner fly to the rafters for the first time in 53 years.

In fact, Anthony, who will be working the NBC Sports desk as part of their NBA crew, has to stop himself from prepping like he’s the one on the court wearing his No. 7 jersey again for the Knicks.

This page may contain affiliate links to legal sports betting partners. If you sign up or place a wager, FOX News may be compensated. This content was created by a team that works independently from the FOX newsroom.

"A game like tomorrow – opening night, ring night, banner night. Like right now, I’m preparing myself to get ready for the game like I’m about to go play," he told OutKick, while highlighting his partnership with DraftKings ahead of the 2026-27 NBA season.

CLICK HERE FOR MORE OUTKICK SPORTS COVERAGE

"And I have to pinch myself, like, ‘Yo bro, you ain’t getting back out there. You’re good on this side.’ Just the fact that I can still be in tuned to the game of basketball like that, and more importantly, to moments and still feel what those moments actually feel like.

"I can imagine what will be going through those guys’ minds tomorrow, the adrenaline that will be pumping through them. Because winning one is a dream – we all dream of winning one. You don’t play this game without dreaming of winning a championship."

This past summer felt like a dream for millions of New Yorkers and others in the surrounding area who were all pulling for the Knicks to break their championship drought. It felt like destiny, from the OG Anunoby tip-in to win Game 4 against the San Antonio Spurs in the NBA Finals, to the other key moments in their playoff run that Anthony and many other former Knicks had great seats for at The Garden.

But now, Anthony knows what comes with the title territory: everyone is hunting for the crown.

THE CRAIG CARTON SHOW–UNFILTERED, UNAPOLOGETIC AND UNMISSABLE. DOWNLOAD HIS DAILY PODCAST NOW!

"Defending it is a job," Anthony said. "So, nobody’s sneaking up on anybody anymore. That banner is going up there and the target goes on [the backs of the Knicks] instantly. Every team is going to circle the Knicks on the schedule, so that price of being champs in New York. You better embrace it and it’s going to be a fun ride."

The ride this past season was one Anthony didn’t want to get off. He admitted watching the team at first felt like he was a player all over again – until he realized he needed to just enjoy the moment like the rest of his peers and all Knicks fans hoping things would end with the Larry O’Brien Trophy being hoisted.

"I was putting myself into those moments and kind of thinking from a mental standpoint like, ‘What would I do here? What play?’ I was playing those games in my head, and then after a while I was like, ‘No, Melo, what are you doing? Just be a fan,’" he said. "So, I started to turn that part of my brain off and operating that way. To be a fan of basketball and the New York Knicks and of the players that were out there representing. It’s a beautiful thing, because as a former player, I love those moments. I live for those moments. The tip-in was like – ah! That was a moment! Jalen Brunson’s three was a moment. So, I understand what the Garden feels like in those moments, but that moment right there was special."

A new season brings new opportunity for not just the Knicks, but every NBA team hoping this will be their year. The Knicks have the crown, but teams like the Philadelphia 76ers, who will have LeBron James and Jaylen Brown suiting up for their first regular-season game with them in Madison Square Garden on Tuesday night, gunning for the title.

"When you know you have the crown, you’re not going to let anybody knock that crown off," Anthony said. "No matter what we gotta do, no matter how we gotta do it, no matter how hard it is to maintain this crown, we gotta do what we gotta do. And I think that’s the mentality coming into this season. Also, I think each individual player had to get better at something and get stronger in their weaknesses this offseason. If they did that, again, that’s the championship mindset.

"If they’re coming back like that, New York is the team to beat."

JOEL EMBIID REJECTS IDEA 76ERS STARS MUST 'TAKE A BACK SEAT' AS NBA REGULAR SEASON LOOMS

STAYING MELO WITH DRAFTKINGS

While Anthony is looking forward to what the Knicks do this season, he’s excited for his partnership with DraftKings and being a part of its campaign ahead of the season.

"We got a great campaign, man. Myself, Kevin Hart, Nick Jonas. We really came together, and I got to give a shoutout to DraftKings and that creative team for putting that concept together," he said. "The beauty in that is the fact that we can have more fun with DraftKings because it’s in all 50 states now, which is major. I just love the fact that more people are involved, and more people can have fun with the game of basketball in this sense, and just sports in general. I love that."

Anthony called it a "beautiful thing" being able to work alongside Hart and Jonas for the campaign, which he is excited for fans to see.

With DraftKings available in all 50 states, the campaign revolves around Hart and Jonas traveling throughout the country, where car troubles can happen. As the tow truck figures out their situation, Anthony is waiting with his own car problems in the clip as he tries to get the word out about DraftKings.

World.title: Iran regime under pressure as rebel groups escalate attacks in volatile southeast
World.content:
NEW You can now listen to Fox News articles!

A new coalition of Iranian opposition groups in the restive southeastern provinces of Sistan and Baluchistan and Kerman in the Islamic Republic have launched a string of armed attacks against the clerical regime in the region.

The six strikes claimed by the coalition known as the People’s Fighters Front (JMM) have contributed to instability in the provinces, raising pressing questions about whether armed resistance against the clerical regime in Tehran will spread and if the regime can retain control over Sistan and Baluchistan, which is a majority Iranian Sunni province.

Iran is largely a Shiite Muslim country, and the minority Iranian Sunni population has faced discrimination over the decades. Sistan and Baluchistan is the second largest of the 31 Iranian provinces.

MOJTABA KHAMENEI DEFIES ‘MALICIOUS’ ATTACKS AS US ARMY ZEROES IN ON IRAN’S 350,000 TROOPS

Mardo Soghom, an Iran expert who has written extensively about the Islamic Republic, told Fox News Digital, "The Sunni unrest can stretch the regime's military and internal security capabilities and have a psychological impact on its forces, in addition to what they experienced during the 40-day operation by the U.S. and Israel. The armed groups would not be able to establish control of the south-east, but they can seriously weaken the regime's control."

He added, "Whether these forces are receiving assistance from the Islamic Republic's adversaries — being that the Gulf Arab states or even Israel and the U.S. — remains an open question."

According to an October Human Rights Activist News Agency (HRANA) report, "The pace of violence accelerated significantly in recent weeks [in the provinces] with 18 incidents recorded in just the final 18 days of the reporting period, surpassing the total for any previous full month."

JMM coalesced as an opposition coalition in Dec. 2025 through an amalgam of Baloch nationalist organizations with the militant Sunni group Jaish al-Adl.

HRANA documented "at least 63 armed incidents were recorded across Iran’s southeastern provinces of Sistan and Baluchistan and Kerman between March 31 and Oct.10, 2026, amid a sharp escalation in armed violence in the region."

The armed resistance resulted in "at least 94 people dead and 33 injured, while official sources reported 87 fatalities and 10 injuries."

IRAN INSTALLS NEW WAR CHIEFS AS TEHRAN SIGNALS ‘PROLONGED CONFRONTATION,’ EXPERT WARNS

The Baloch coalition stunned the regime on Oct. 14 with the assassinations of women members of the Basij paramilitaries, including a commander and a police officer in Sistan and Baluchistan Province. The Basij has been designated a terrorist entity by the U.S. government because it falls under the American-classified terrorist movement Islamic Revolutionary Guard Corps (IRGC).

Just days before the attack on the female Basij commander, Iranian regime-controlled media reported that Nosrat Eftekhari, deputy for Cultural and Social Affairs of the Provincial Law Enforcement Command, was killed by a roadside bomb in Zahedan, Sistan and Baluchistan provinces.

Jason Brodsky, policy director at United Against Nuclear Iran (UANI), told Fox News Digital that "There have been periodic cycles of unrest in Sistan and Baluchistan Province over the years. What we are now witnessing is an uptick in such activity. The current commander of the IRGC’s Ground Forces, Mohammad Karami used to be governor of the province and commanded IRGC forces there. His experience in the province was one of the reasons Karami was elevated to the post in 2025 given the sensitive security situation in the country."

Brodsky continued that "I don’t see any imminent threat in terms of such a seizure of control, but a red line for Iranians, especially in the opposition, is preserving the territorial integrity of Iran. That needs to be understood in Western capitals."

MOTORCYCLE PATROLS SWARM IRANIAN CITIES, CHECKPOINTS RISE AS REGIME BRACES FOR UNREST

Khalilullah Balochi, who is a Baluch activist and journalist, told Iran International that "The activities of these groups are not new; what is new is the intensification of attacks."

JMM’s devastating attacks targeting the brutal Iranian regime have generated attention from Iranian dissidents and experts.

Navid Mohebbi, who worked as a Persian media analyst for the State Department's Public Affairs Bureau, told Fox News Digital "The newly formed popular Fighters Front has carried out a series of relatively successful attacks against mid-level regime officials and security personnel in Sistan and Baluchistan province in recent months, drawing a degree of public attention. At a time when the regime is executing protesters on a daily basis, the killing of certain mid-ranking security and military operatives has been met with some satisfaction among segments of Iranian society."

He warned, however, that "Nevertheless, the Iranian public remains deeply cautious and largely distrustful of such groups. Two major concerns underpin this distrust: the possibility of separatist ambitions and the influence of radical Islamism, which is fundamentally at odds with the increasingly secular outlook of Iranian society."

AFTER 6 MONTHS OF WAR, US MUST PREPARE FOR A FUTURE AFTER IRAN’S GOVERNMENT FALLS

Mohebbi sees encouraging signs from the JMM, including "the coalition’s recent statements, unlike the rhetoric traditionally associated with similar groups, contain no explicit references to Baluch separatism. Instead, the coalition has identified its primary objective as dismantling the system of Velayat-e Faqih (Guardianship of the Islamic Jurist) and liberating the country from its oppression. It has explicitly declared that it seeks ‘an Iran for all Iranians."’

He continued that "The reality is that these groups lack the capacity to confront the regime in conventional warfare. Through guerrilla operations, however, they can inflict significant psychological blows on the regime and its security establishment. Whether their activities can gain traction beyond Sistan and Baluchistan will depend largely on their ability to sustain what appears to be an effort to earn broader public trust."

Beni Sabti, an Iran expert at the Institute for National Security Studies (INSS) in Israel, told Fox News Digital the coalition has "a lot of guns" and created an "armed rebellion" against the Iranian regime in the provinces. He said, however, the armed upheaval is limited to the region Baluchistan.

Sabti, who was born in Tehran, said the clerical regime in the capital Tehran does not exercise solid control over the provinces, which resembles parts of South America where some governments lost sovereignty to militias.

CLICK HERE TO DOWNLOAD THE FOX NEWS APP

He said that there are no reporters in the restive region. As a result, it is difficult to secure accurate news. Sabti said the "IRGC has a headquarters there to fight against these Baluchis." The JMM coalition "can only continue to harm the soldiers and, from time to time, kill a commander. There are a lot of these local commanders in Iran. It is not like an air force commander."

World.title: Sports journalists stay silent on WNBA national anthem protest and high school cross country dispute
World.content:
Activists or cowards?

That's the question I often ask about members of the media when they go radio silent on a hot-button issue.

Do they avoid asking tough questions because they fear the answers might undermine a cause they support? Or do they stay quiet because they're scared of the blowback they'd get from their peers?

DREAM AND VALKYRIES SKIP NATIONAL ANTHEM AGAIN IN WNBA FINALS GAME 2 DESPITE RULEBOOK REQUIREMENT

Look no further than the past two weeks, when three major stories captured public fascination while traditional newsrooms responded with either deliberate silence or toothless coverage.

Story No. 1: The WNBA's national anthem walk-offs.

Before Games 1 and 2 of the WNBA Finals, both the Atlanta Dream and the Golden State Valkyries walked off the court before the singing of the Star Spangled Banner, only to return as soon as it was over. Yet, besides OutKick, I couldn't find a single instance of credentialed media covering the Finals even mentioning this. The San Jose Mercury News lauded Alanis Morissette's rendition before Game 2, but didn't appear to care that players weren't on the court for it. And a writer from SF Gate decried how "conservative media can't stop complaining" about personnel deciding to leave the floor.

JEMELE HILL IS RIGHT: WNBA FANS EXPECT JOURNALISTS TO BE 'CHEERLEADERS,' AND THAT'S NOT HOW THIS WORKS

Sorry, but this story matters to people. And apparently, mainstream reporters have no interest in asking players or coaches about it. OutKick's Dan Zaksheske has been ready with questions at press conferences but hasn't been called upon. Perhaps WNBA public relations officials are concerned he'll make the people he covers uncomfortable. They certainly don't seem worried that the other journalists in the room will.

Story No. 2: Valkyries fans' open hostility toward attendees wearing XX-XY shirts at Game 1.

Jennifer Sey, founder of XX-XY Athletics, posted disturbing video from Chase Center on Saturday. In it, a woman calls Sey "disgusting" and tells her to "f---ing kill yourself" for donning a shirt advocating for female-only sports. The clip got four million views on X, but virtually no mainstream media coverage — and certainly no condemnation. Yahoo! Sports ran a story that originally appeared on Basketball Network, but the author, Yakshpat Bhargava, seemed to be siding against Sey.

"What Sey should truly understand is that if her goal is to help women's sports take the next leap forward, why ignite controversies that are already in the past?" he wrote. "At this point, all attention should be on the Valkyries and Dream's play on the hardwood."

No, the issue of males in female sports is not a controversy that's in the past. It's alive and well. Need proof? Then look at...

WOMEN’S SPORTS MEDIA OUTLET BACKS TRANS ATHLETES, THEN AVOIDS QUESTIONS FROM REPORTER WHO DISAGREES

Story No. 3: A high school cross country runner who switched from the boys to the girls team midway through the season.

I've been covering this one for a couple weeks now. After finishing 76th in a boys JV race in September, a sophomore boy from Camas High in Washington state decided he was going to compete against the girls. Since making the switch, he has won a varsity meet and finished second in another race. In September, two girls from Skyview High protested by walking off the start line after the gun went off, and last week, about a dozen of his own teammates did the same thing.

As you might imagine, this has gotten national attention. Several Fox News Channel shows have covered the story, as have the likes of Clay Travis and Riley Gaines. But ESPN? The Athletic? Crickets. And though papers in Washington State such as the Seattle Times have mentioned the protests, nobody in legacy media is criticizing the boy's participation.

A couple months ago, I wrote about a new category that The Associated Press Sports Editors added to their annual writing contest: Excellence in Transgender Sports Coverage. But if you read how the category was introduced, you'd see that the only stories that have a chance at winning are hagiographies to trans athletes. There is no room for pushback — only acceptance.

CLICK HERE TO DOWNLOAD THE FOX NEWS APP

I've said before that journalists should be judged on two criteria — what they write, and what they don't write. And too many sports journalists have decided that certain stories are better left untold. The reason is simple — they care more about what their peers think about them than the public. And whether that's born out of activism or cowardice, the result is the same: The public gets cheated.

World.title: Lawmaker reportedly loses leg as car ramming stuns Australia
World.content:
An Australian lawmaker was in critical but stable condition Tuesday after being hit by a car in what authorities said was a deliberate attack, shocking a nation where political violence is extremely rare.

Helen Haines, a 65-year-old independent member of Parliament, was struck Monday by a white Toyota Land Cruiser outside her electoral district office in Wangaratta, a town of about 30,000 people in the southern Australian state of Victoria. She underwent surgery overnight after being airlifted to a hospital in the state capital of Melbourne, about 150 miles away.

Local media reported that one of Haines’s legs had been amputated and that she was fighting to keep her other leg. The Alfred Hospital in Melbourne did not respond to an NBC News request for comment on the reports.

00:47 Australian lawmaker in critical condition after car ramming 00:00 00:00

Police charged the driver, who they said was a 43-year-old local man, on Tuesday with intentionally causing serious injury, dangerous driving causing serious injury and causing harm to a federal official.

Prime Minister Anthony Albanese said earlier Tuesday that according to eyewitnesses, the driver had passed Haines and then performed a U-turn, hitting her as she was standing by the trunk of her parked car.

“It’s clear that there was a deliberate act here. This wasn’t an accident, someone, you know, just skidding off the road,” he told the Australian Broadcasting Corp., adding that the motivation was not yet clear.

Home Affairs Minister Tony Burke told the ABC that witnesses had described seeing the driver reverse and then hit Haines a second time.

The suspect’s father said the family knew Haines well.

She was a “deeply respected, valued and much loved member of our local community,” Brendan Nugent’s father Rod Nugent and Rod’s partner Christine Cunningham said in a statement Tuesday.

“Helen has been our friend for more than 20 years and what happened to her yesterday is devastating and unfathomable,” the statement added.

World.title: Tampa Bay Rays advance to World Series, will face Milwaukee Brewers
World.content:
Tampa Bay will face the Milwaukee Brewers in the World Series after the Rays on Monday won the American League Championship Series over Cleveland.

It will mark the third World Series berth for the Rays, who are searching for the franchise’s first MLB title after appearances in 2008 and 2020.

Cleveland took a 2-1 ALCS lead before Tampa roared back with successive wins in Game 4 and Game 5 to set up Monday’s clinching 7-3 win in Game 6.

Tampa jumped to an early lead after a double by Richie Palacios drove in two runs in the second inning. One inning later, a sacrifice fly by Jonny DeLuca brought in another run for a 3-0 lead. When Cleveland trimmed the lead to 3-1 in the sixth inning, Tampa answered with a two-run homer by Junior Caminero in the seventh.

Tampa Bay Rays' Richie Palacios reacts after a single during the sixth inning at Tropicana Field on Monday. Julio Aguilar / Getty

Cleveland applied pressure again by scoring two runs in the eighth to cut the lead to 5-3, but Tampa was ready for another answer in its next at-bat. A two-run homer by Yandy Diaz extended the lead to 7-3.

When the Brewers and Rays meet in Game 1 of the World Series on Friday, a first-time champion will be guaranteed. The Brewers are making their first World Series appearance since 1982. It will be a showdown of the teams that finished with the best records in the National and American leagues. Milwaukee finished with an MLB-high 103 wins, while Tampa had 98. The teams played three times in the regular season with Milwaukee winning twice, but all three games occurred during the first week of the season.

Tampa Bay Rays' Junior Caminero celebrates a two-run home run against the Cleveland Guardians on Monday. Phelan M. Ebenhack / AP

The Rays have advanced to baseball’s biggest stage despite building a roster using the third-lowest payroll. Milwaukee wasn’t a big spender, itself, ranking 19th in payroll. Yet the clubs from small markets with relatively low payrolls found ways to play the best baseball in each of their respective leagues this season en route to the World Series.

Tampa entered Monday’s Game 6 allowing just 1.0 walks and hits per inning pitched while sweeping the New York Yankees in the divisional round, then facing Cleveland. The Rays’ postseason star has been pitcher Drew Rasmussen, who has allowed three earned runs combined in his three appearances.

Few would have expected this season from Tampa after the franchise finished its 2023 and 2024 seasons in fourth place in the AL East while finishing lower than .500 each year. Making matters even more difficult was that the team didn’t even have its home stadium available for much of that stretch, after Hurricane Milton tore the roof off of Tropicana Field in downtown St. Petersburg in October 2024. It took until August for the Rays to host games in the stadium again, following a $60 million roof renovation.

World.title: Powerful nor’easter churning up the East Coast
World.content:
A powerful nor’easter is churning up the East Coast and is on track to bring several days of heavy rain, flooding and strong winds.

The storm is expected to stay far enough offshore that the heaviest rain will likely affect only the easternmost parts of the country. While the rain will stay mostly offshore, gusty winds and coastal flooding are still possible, especially across the Outer Banks.

Flood advisories are in place from the Jersey Shore to the Outer Banks for 1-2 feet of inundation from onshore winds.

The storm, still offshore, is intensifying. Coastline cities from New Jersey to Cape Hatteras can expect coastal flooding, beach erosion and gusty winds.

Rain and coastal flooding are expected to impact Cape Cod and Nantucket in the coming days. By Thursday, rough surf and rip currents will hit those areas.

The nor’easter could become a tropical storm but, if it does, it will only intensify as it continues east and away from the coast. It has a 40% chance of formation in two days, and 40% in seven days. If it develops, it will be named Josephine.

Winds will have the biggest impact, with 44 mph winds forecast in Nantucket. Virginia Beach could see 32 mph winds, and Cape Hatteras is expected to have 39 mph winds.

Meanwhile, a storm in the Pacific Ocean is expected to bring heavy rain, flooding and mountain snow. A flash flood risk is in place from Southern California to the Rockies.

A flood threat is in place for California and parts of the Southwest through Thursday, specifically in Southern California from San Luis Obispo to Santa Barbara, and across the Four Corners states.

Six million people across Arizona are also under a flood watch, including Phoenix and Flagstaff.

World.title: Zelenskyy meets with Trump envoys as U.S. blasts ‘scandalous’ accusations on withdrawn support
World.content:
U.S. envoys were expected to meet with Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy in Norway on Tuesday, as Kyiv scrambles to respond to an American pressure campaign that has been allied with moves aimed at courting the Kremlin.

President Donald Trump’s negotiators, son-in-law Jared Kushner and special envoy Steve Witkoff, have so far had little success finding a diplomatic solution to the war. Their latest meeting comes with Washington’s backing in doubt as Kyiv accused the U.S. of withdrawing support crucial to its defense against Russia — a suggestion that Secretary of State Marco Rubio called “scandalous.”

Witkoff will be meeting with Zelenskyy in Oslo on Tuesday, with Kushner joining via videoconference, the Norwegian government said. Norwegian Prime Minister Jonas Gahr Støre and Finnish President Alexander Stubb will also join the talks, it added.

Officials from the U.S. and Ukraine had been expected to meet in Norway this week for another round of negotiations, sources familiar with the matter told NBC News, as a series of recent actions by Trump in favor of Russia left both Congress and U.S. allies questioning U.S. mediation efforts.

Kremlin spokesman Dmitry Peskov told reporters he hoped that it would be possible for Trump’s envoys to hold a meeting in Russia “in the near future,” though he gave no firm indication on when this might be.

Zelenskyy met with Witkoff and Kushner in Kyiv last month. Genya Savilov / AFP via Getty Images

Trump has waived sanctions and agreed a diesel deal with Russia, in an apparent bid to lower fuel prices ahead of the Midterm elections. He called Monday for Zelenskyy to “get somebody else to negotiate,” his latest rebuke of the Ukrainian president.

Trump also appeared to downplay the impact of Russian attacks on Ukraine, a near-daily reality for the last 4 ½ years that have killed scores of civilians and flattened towns.

“Russia, frankly, has been fine on Ukraine,” Trump told reporters. “They haven’t been doing much.”

It was the latest public sign of his shift away from Ukraine.

Kyiv said it had once again received no early warning from the U.S. before the capital came under attack by Russian ballistic missiles on Sunday, the third time in recent days.

In addition to the withholding of intelligence, Ukraine said it was still facing speed restrictions on Starshield, the military version of the SpaceX service, with no explanation from the American side.

“All of this suggests that some political decision has been made to slow down support for us,” Zelenskyy said Monday in a virtual address to a bipartisan Congressional delegation. He also said the U.S. was delaying the delivery of crucial ballistic missile interceptors, and that Ukraine has nearly run out of its supplies.

Zelenskyy said early Tuesday he held “a substantive conversation” with Rubio, focusing on missile interceptors, early warnings of ballistic attacks and Starshield restrictions. He thanked Rubio and “everyone in America who supports fair approaches.”

Men carry away the body of a one-year-old girl, killed by Russian drone strike outside Kharkiv on Monday, while sat in her stroller. Sofiia Gatilova / Reuters

Rubio told reporters later that he told Zelenskyy in the 45-minute call that nothing had changed in U.S. support for Ukraine.

“There’s nothing being deliberately denied to Ukraine,” he added, speaking at the start of a trip to India.

When it comes to missile interceptors, Rubio said the U.S. has to strike a delicate balance between its obligations to other partners and its own requirements when it comes to what he called “the most in-demand product” in the defense industry right now.

“When a country doesn’t get interceptors from the United States, it’s not because we are denying,” he added. “We have our own needs too.”

Ukrainian officials including Zelenskyy have made clear their accusation that the U.S. has imposed restrictions that have disrupted military operations and hampered Ukraine’s ability to intercept Russian missiles, making the attacks more deadly.

“That’s scandalous, that’s outrageous, that’s just simply not true. That’s not accurate,” Rubio said Tuesday.

Officials in the eastern Kharkiv region shared images Monday of a dead child in a stroller — a one-year-old girl they said was killed alongside her mother in a Russian attack on a public park in the region.

“The world has enough strength to stop the war. That strength must finally be used — against the murderers,” Zelenskyy said in a post decrying the strike.

World.title: Vance declines to endorse Netanyahu after Trump offers full support for re-election
World.content:
Vice President JD Vance declined to endorse Israeli Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu on Monday, a day after President Donald Trump publicly backed Netanyahu as he seeks re-election this month.

“I’m not getting involved in the Israeli elections,” Vance said in an interview on Mark Halperin’s show “2WAY Tonight.”

“I’m not anti-endorsing him; I’m not pro-endorsing him,” Vance added.

Trump weighed in on the election Sunday, strongly backing Netanyahu’s re-election bid.

“If Israel has the wrong Leader, which would be anyone other than Bibi, America will have to do this work ourselves, and I am not inclined to do so,” Trump wrote on Truth Social.

“Bibi Netanyahu has been Strong, Brave, and Brilliant in the face of tremendous opposition, including that coming from even Israel, itself,” he said, adding that the post represents his “Complete and Total Endorsement of Bibi Netanyahu.”

Vance said Monday that Trump has “the most effective endorsement in American or international political history.”

He further defended his refusal to get involved in the race by saying he endorses “American candidates,” adding “that’s what I’m focused on” as the midterm elections approach.

While Vance declined to endorse Netanyahu, the vice president did travel to Hungary in April to stump for then-Prime Minister Viktor Orbán, who was ultimately voted out after 16 years in power.

Vance also reiterated Monday that he has not decided whether he will run for president himself in 2028. But should he do so, Vance said, he thinks Trump will endorse him.

“I really have not made up my mind about what to do in 2028. I just haven’t focused on it,” Vance said. “I think if I run, the president will endorse me right away, right at the beginning.”

Trump’s endorsement of Netanyahu comes as the Israeli leader faces mounting backlash over the U.S. ally’s deadly assault on Gaza and intensifying settler violence in the occupied West Bank, where attacks on Palestinian farmers, activists and journalists flared over the weekend.

Secretary of State Marco Rubio said Saturday that the Trump administration was “very disturbed” by the images that emerged after American journalist Heidi Levine, a photographer working for The Washington Post, was among those attacked just days before Trump offered his support for Netanyahu.

Netanyahu cast doubt on the attack, calling it “alleged.”

U.S. Ambassador to Israel Mike Huckabee welcomed the arrest of 10 suspects Monday after what he called a “despicable act of terror carried out by masked cowards.” Levine remains in the hospital.

Vance has previously taken a more skeptical stance toward Israel than many on the right.

In June he warned Israel against opposing American efforts to negotiate an end to their joint war with Iran.

“Donald J. Trump is the only head of state in the entire world who is sympathetic to the nation of Israel at this moment in time,” Vance said at the time. “If I was in the Cabinet of the Israeli government, I might not be attacking the only powerful ally that I have anywhere left in the entire world.”

Polling shows a decline in support for Israel among the American public over the past few years.

Favorable views of the Israeli government fell from 47% in 2022 to 32% in 2026 in 2026, according to polling conducted in May by the Pew Research Center.

World.title: Christina Applegate reveals she was misdiagnosed with MS
World.content:
Christina Applegate announced Tuesday that she was misdiagnosed with multiple sclerosis, more than five years after announcing she had been told she had the chronic condition.

Applegate, 54, shared the news in a double episode of her podcast MeSsy, where she and co-host Jamie-Lynn Sigler discuss life with multiple sclerosis. Applegate had taken a break from the podcast in recent weeks. She said Tuesday she had taken that time to process the new information.

Applegate said that "all of a sudden, a few years ago," her doctor wanted to take her off an infusion treatment and see how her B cells reacted. The cell count didn't increase or decrease after the treatment stopped, which began "kind of a study into my diagnosis," Applegate said. Eventually, her doctor had surprising news: Applegate had never had multiple sclerosis at all.

"She came into my room and said, 'Congratulations, you don't have MS,' " Applegate said. "I was, like, not happy at all. Everybody else was so happy."

Multiple sclerosis, or MS, is a disease where the body's immune system attacks the central nervous system. Symptoms vary from person to person, according to the National Multiple Sclerosis Society, and there are multiple types of the disease. The condition has no known cause, and its progression is impossible to predict.

Dr. Marwa Kaisey, an associate professor at the Cedars-Sinai Medical Center department of neurology, said on the podcast that almost one in five people who have been told they have multiple sclerosis "didn't actually have it." Misdiagnoses with the condition are "fairly common," she said, because there is no one test for it.

Applegate said at the time of her initial diagnosis, she underwent tests including a spinal tap and MRIs. Scans showed lesions on her brain, she said.

Applegate said that she continues to have debilitating symptoms that affect her daily life and mobility.

"You don't get misdiagnosed and then all of the sudden I'm better," Applegate said. "If anything, I've gotten worse. So I'm back at square one where I don't know what's going on with me. And that's going to be an online investigation that my doctors are going to be getting into just to find out what has been going on since 2021, why did this happen?"

The investigation will begin next week, she said.

Applegate has previously described living with symptoms including numbness, an off-balance feeling, and a tingling sensation in the limbs. She said in a 2022 interview with The New York Times that she "can't walk without a cane."

In the same interview, she said she used a wheelchair during filming of the Netflix hit "Dead To Me," and the show's script was adjusted to accommodate her symptoms. In 2023, Applegate said her symptoms might lead to her giving up acting on camera. She said Tuesday that she has physical therapy three times a week.

After she was officially diagnosed with the disease, she became an outspoken advocate for MS. On Tuesday, she said the misdiagnosis made her feel "like I let everybody down."

"It's very unnerving and it's really confusing for me," Applegate said.

World.title: 3 more Democrats slated to join summit on political future
World.content:
Nine days after next month's midterm elections, three prominent Democrats who are widely believed to have presidential ambitions will join other potential 2028 party contenders in Denver to discuss the future of the party.

Sens. Cory Booker of New Jersey and Chris Van Hollen of Maryland, as well as Rep. Ro Khanna of California, are among the latest additions who plan to join the "What's Next" summit, according to an updated list of attendees first shared with CBS News.

All three lawmakers identify as progressives, and all three have drawn national attention over their political ambitions in recent years. Booker ran for president in 2020 but dropped out before the first primary contests. Khanna has described himself as a "long-shot presidential candidate," and Van Hollen has acknowledged that he is "kicking the tires" on a possible 2028 run.

The three have also introduced tax plans that could be precursors to 2028 platforms.

The meeting will take place from Nov. 12 to 14, and is being hosted by Majority Democrats, a group formed last year by largely moderate elected officials and other high-profile Democrats who say they are "committed to reshaping and growing the Democratic Party."

Chaired by Rep. Jake Auchincloss of Massachusetts, the organization says it aims to take lessons from the 2026 races into the upcoming presidential election, in part by bringing together leading voices from across different factions within the party.

"Democrats have talked a big game about building a 'big tent' that can hold onto a majority. The sad reality is, we were all hat, no cattle when it came time to live up to those ideals," said Matt Corridoni, a spokesperson for Majority Democrats. "What's Next is an opportunity for Democrats from every wing of the party to have the open and often difficult conversations we need to win in 2028."

The three latest entrants join an initial lineup of other possible presidential candidates including former Transportation Secretary Pete Buttigieg and Sens. Raphael Warnock of Georgia, Ruben Gallego of Arizona and Chris Murphy of Connecticut.

Govs. Abigail Spanberger of Virginia and Mikie Sherrill of New Jersey plan to attend, as well as other members of Congress and political strategists.

Democrats hope to win control of the House in November's midterm elections and carry the momentum into the 2028 presidential race.

Many feel the party has not settled on a political identity after losing the White House in 2024, and moderate and progressive Democrats disagree on the party's direction.That split has not helped the party win over voters: In a February CBS News poll, most voters described the Democratic Party as "weak."

Presidential contenders could begin launching their campaigns in the coming months, and some possible 2028 candidates have sought to raise their profile on the midterm trail, appearing alongside Democrats in key states. New York Rep. Alexandria Ocasio Cortez and former Vice President Kamala Harris have both visited Michigan this fall to campaign with Senate nominee Abdul El-Sayed. California Gov. Gavin Newsom campaigned in New Hampshire last weekend with Rep. Chris Pappas, who is in a tight race for Senate.

Organizers chose to hold the inaugural What's Next summit in Denver as it is one of the cities under consideration to host the 2028 Democratic National Convention. Over 2,000 people are expected to attend, according to a person familiar with the planning.

"Winning in 2028 will require us coming together to take the best ideas from every corner of the Democratic Party and forging them into an agenda that can build a durable majority and deliver for the American people," said executive director of Majority Democrats Rohan Patel.

Good morning. You're reading the Up First newsletter. Subscribe here to get it delivered to your inbox, and listen to the Up First podcast for all the news you need to start your day.

Today's top stories

The Justice Department has charged 28 green card holders in California with election crimes for allegedly illegally registering to vote or voting in U.S. elections. This marks a significant escalation in the Trump administration's feud with the state over its voting system as the midterm elections approach. The DOJ also filed an emergency request to prevent California from processing ballots returned by people on the voter rolls that the federal government says are "likely noncitizens." California has sought clarification on the federal government's conclusions but has not received any. Last week, the DOJ sued California and Los Angeles County after local officials refused to investigate allegations made by the administration about noncitizen voting.

Research shows that in many cases, when legal permanent residents register to vote, it is due to a misunderstanding of the rules. Cold and flu season in the U.S. starts this month and lasts through May, according ot the Centers for Disease Control and Prevention. Cooler temperatures and drier air can increase our vulnerability to illnesses like the common cold, flu, RSV and COVID-19. Get ahead of the game now by putting together a cold-and-flu prep kit. 🤒 Over-the-counter medications are good options, but always follow the recommended dosage to avoid risks or side effects.
