World.title: Lieutenant-governor will skip Quebec cabinet's swearing-in at incoming premier's request
World.content:
The audio version of this article is generated by AI-based technology. Mispronunciations can occur. We are working with our partners to continually review and improve the results.

Wednesday will mark a historic moment for Quebec and its ties to the monarchy.

It will be the first time that the lieutenant-governor — a representative of the monarchy — will not preside over the swearing-in ceremony of a new government's cabinet at the National Assembly.

According to Radio-Canada sources, Lt.-Gov. Manon Jeannotte has accepted a written request from Quebec premier-designate Paul St-Pierre Plamondon not to attend the event, and will watch the event on a screen from her nearby office . She will sign the necessary appointment documents behind the scenes so the secretary general can administer the oaths without her.

This will allow the newly appointed ministers to begin their work immediately.

In a letter sent Monday to Jeannotte, the Parti Québécois leader stated his incoming government will not allow a representative of the monarchy crowto preside over the event.

"We firmly intend to abolish this monarchy in Quebec, both within our democratic institutions and in our civil society," St-Pierre Plamondon wrote.

“We thank you in advance for the co-operation you will demonstrate to ensure that this important day for our democracy unfolds without hindrance and with respect for the will of the elected members of the National Assembly of Quebec,” he added.

St-Pierre Plamondon made it clear that he does not want the lieutenant-governor present.

Jeannotte is obliging with that request, and will sign the documents in real-time to legitimize the appointments.

In a statement obtained by Radio-Canada, the lieutenant-governor's office said she doesn't want to become the centre of attention and "is exercising discretion and restraint so that the attention remains focused on democratic institutions."

To swear or not to swear allegiance

Meanwhile, the new government's anti-monarchy agenda is facing an immediate legal roadblock.

One of the lawyers challenging the 2022 Quebec law that made the mandatory oath to the King optional for elected officials says his case for an emergency injunction will be heard in court Tuesday.

Lawrence David said in an email he expects a quick decision from Judge Ian Demers, but "we will 100 per cent appeal the judgment if we do not win."

Earlier this month, David, founder of the Public Interest Litigation Institute, filed an emergency injunction in an attempt to force the incoming Parti Québécois (PQ) government to swear allegiance to King Charles.

The injunction asks the court to immediately suspend a 2022 provincial law, known as Bill 4, that made the oath to the monarch optional for members of the National Assembly. David already filed a lawsuit in August over the same matter .

Bill 4 added a clause to the Constitution Act of 1867 stating that the oath to the monarch no longer applies to Quebec legislators.

The bill was tabled by the Coalition Avenir Québec government after facing pressure from the PQ. Several members of the PQ had refused to swear allegiance to King Charles III and were barred from sitting.

Will the PQ be barred from their seats?

The legal challenge comes on the heels of the provincial election, which handed the Parti Québécois a minority government. St-Pierre Plamondon has already stated he will once again refuse to swear allegiance to King Charles.

If the stay is granted, incoming MNAs who refuse the oath could be legally barred from taking their seats when the legislature reconvenes in mid-November.

At the heart of the lawsuit is the argument that Quebec unilaterally altered the 1867 Constitution Act without the required unanimous consent of the House of Commons, the Senate and all of the country’s provincial legislatures to abolish the mandatory oath.

It also alleges the law violates Section 3 of the Canadian Charter of Rights and Freedoms, which guarantees the right to effective representation, because politicians who do not take the oath are not qualified to serve as an MNA.

David has warned that if the newly elected government attempts to unilaterally abolish the office of the lieutenant-governor, he is prepared to launch additional legal challenges.

World.title: A contractor left this Toronto man without a roof. His insurance company is denying his claim
World.content:
The audio version of this article is generated by AI-based technology. Mispronunciations can occur. We are working with our partners to continually review and improve the results.

What began as a simple knock on the front door last spring has resulted in an elderly Scarborough man living out of a suitcase, his home roofless and in ruins.

Police are now investigating a possible fraud, while the man's home insurance company has denied most of his claim.

Lawrence Huang was approached in late May by representatives of a company called Super Dry Roofing and Masonry, who told him his roof was infested with rodents, seriously damaged, and in need of replacement.

The 76-year-old, whom his niece Katie Semple describes as “on the spectrum,” signed a roof replacement contract and gave a salesman for the company a $25,000 advance on the $50,000 job.

The contractor went to work, completely removing the roof of Huang�’s two-storey Guildwood Parkway home, leaving the contents open to the elements.

Lawrence Huang says he has been living in motels since a contractor walked off a project at his Scarborough home, leaving it without a roof, after his bank became suspicious and refused to honour a cheque made out to the company. (Submitted by Katie Semple)

And the price began to rise. Semple says her uncle then handed over $1,800. Within weeks he gave the contractor another cheque, this time for $64,000 — at which point employees at his bank became suspicious, and refused to honour the large cheque. They also contacted police, the city and Semple, his only surviving relative.

Within days, the workers abruptly abandoned the site, leaving his home with no roof and a massive pile of scrap lumber in the driveway.

Semple says she has tried to contact Super Dry, but the phone number appears to be disconnected.

CBC Toronto has also attempted to contact the company using phone and email contacts listed on the contract. The phone number is not assigned and an email was returned as undeliverable.

Insurance won't cover 'faulty ... workmanship'

After Super Dry left, Huang initially tried living in the basement, but city engineers and Toronto Fire Service ordered him to leave. Since then, Semple says, he has been living in motels and trying to figure out how his home can be rebuilt — and how it will all be paid for.

The contents of his home, including valuable books and family mementoes, are now a sodden mess, destroyed by trespassers, rain and animals.

“It’s a lifetime of memories,” Semple said. “It’s terrible. I lost sleep. I don’t know what to do. I’m the only one he has left.”

The kitchen of Lawrence Huang's home, four months after contractors left the job site, with the home's roof removed. TD Insurance has said it will cover the cost of the home's ruined contents, but not the structural damage. (Mike Smee/CBC)

Semple says her uncle’s insurer, TD Insurance, is refusing to cover most of the damage, including Huang’s rebuild, which he cannot afford to do on his own.

In a Sept. 9 letter to Huang, shared with CBC Toronto, TD Insurance’s adjuster wrote: “We do not insure the cost of correcting faulty design, material or workmanship.” Damage caused by animals, vandalism or rain also isn't covered in Lawrence Huang's policy, according to the letter.

Semple argues that, in her opinion, the damage to the home was caused by a fraudulent company — but, she says, TD Insurance still isn’t budging on paying for the damage to the roof.

TD Insurance wouldn't speak with CBC Toronto about Huang’s case, citing privacy concerns. But in an email, the company wrote: “TD Insurance recognizes how distressing this situation has been for our client and his family and continues to work directly with them regarding the claim."

Katie Semple stands in what was once the living room of her uncle's Scarborough home. She says trespassers have done damage, as has the weather. (Mike Smee/CBC)

Semple says she hired her own adjuster to communicate with the company and some progress has been made. In a follow-up letter dated Sept. 28, TD Insurance said it will cover the damage to the contents after all, but remains adamant that it will not pay for the home’s rebuild.

Until that happens, Huang will continue to live in a motel. Semple says he is covering those costs, but he doesn’t have enough money to rebuild the house.

Luis Seco, a University of Toronto professor who studies the insurance industry, says it’s common for insurers to balk at covering some types of damage, typically structural, which is the most expensive to repair.

He says ultimately an insurance company can deny any claim, and the onus is then on the homeowner to take them to court, if they believe the company is violating its policy contract.

But that can be expensive, and he suggests that homeowners first apply to a non-profit insurance industry mediator, the General Insurance Ombudservice, whose members include most Canadian insurance companies.

Police investigating, say roofing scams common

Toronto police acknowledged in an email that it is investigating a fraud complaint at Huang’s property.

Det. David Coffey of the financial crimes unit told CBC Toronto he couldn't comment on Huang’s case specifically, but he said roofing scams are common in the city.

“We’ve been dealing with roofing scams for as long as I've been a police officer, and that’s 29 years,” he said.

Det. David Coffey is with Toronto Police Services' financial crimes unit. He says confidence schemes have cost Torontonians $50 million so far this year. (Mike Smee/CBC)

He said the roofing scam is considered a con game, in which a fraudster builds up a person’s confidence before talking them out of their money.

Typically the scam begins with a salesperson’s knock on the door. The homeowner is warned that a leak in his or her roof is imminent and urgently needs fixing. “They present themselves as the answer to that emergency,” Coffey said. “Your roof is going to leak and the city is going to condemn your house.”

He said most scammers begin by asking for relatively small sums — in the low thousands — and then they escalate the demand until they're convinced the homeowner has nothing left to give.

“It’s really the urgency and the fear they’re generating,” Coffee says. “We’re not reacting intellectually; we’re reacting emotionally.”

So far this year, Coffey says cons of all types have cost Torontonians about $50 million. And that only covers reported scams. TPS figures only about five to 10 percent of victims actually report the crime.

'Bring yourself down off that ledge'

Coffey says the damage done to the Huang home — if it is a fraud — would be “on the higher end” of the typical roofing scam.

His advice? “You need to bring yourself down off that ledge they’ve put you on … Pause and verify. Slow it down and do your own due diligence into that company.”

But he says the best defence is to simply not do business with contractors who come knocking.

“Personally, as a citizen, I wouldn't hire anyone who knocks on my door," Coffey said.

“Urgency these days doesn't mean hurry up. Urgency these days has to mean stop, and verify and talk to your family, talk to other people. Those are the keys.”

World.title: Winnipeg teacher stripped of certificate after sending hundreds of messages to student in 'serious breach'
World.content:
The audio version of this article is generated by AI-based technology. Mispronunciations can occur. We are working with our partners to continually review and improve the results.

A Winnipeg teacher has been stripped of his licence over a years-long "inappropriately close relationship" with a student that began in a middle school and continued after the student went on to high school.

Robert Gregoire texted the student hundreds of times from his personal phone and over 1,000 times over Microsoft Teams between 2022 and 2024, referring to her variously as "ma belle," "my beautiful," "muffin" and "princess," according to an Oct. 6 disciplinary decision from Manitoba's independent teacher commissioner.

Gregoire fostered "an increasingly personal relationship" and prioritized "his own emotional needs" over the student's well-being, states the report.

"This conduct represents a serious abuse of the trust."

Gregoire's is one of two new disciplinary decisions posted publicly on the commissioner's disciplinary decision dashboard, which was launched earlier this year.

In 2022, Gregoire began an "inappropriately close relationship that crossed professional boundaries" with a Grade 8 student at the middle school where he worked in the River East Transcona School Division.

Gregoire eventually left his post as a teacher at the middle school to follow the student to her new high school in the division in 2024, the decision states.

Between 2022 and 2024, he and the student exchanged over 1,000 Microsoft Teams messages, including during school breaks and vacations, "late at night and in the early hours of the morning," the report states.

Gregoire referred to her as his "favourite student" who was "très spéciale," or very special, according to the discipline report.

He told her he missed her and that getting a message from her after a bad day gave him a smile, and repeatedly requested she visit him at the middle school after she left.

Gregoire invited the student to meet him outside school at restaurants near her high school. He also invited her for ice cream after school, and to meet with him on weekends and on winter break for skating, the report said.

Cautioned by principal

The principal of the middle school where Gregoire worked cautioned him in June 2024 against messaging students and reminded him to only communicate with those he was instructing for educational purposes.

The principal pointed to the division's code of conduct for child protection, which prohibits writing personal text messages to students and offering special treatment, as well as spending time with students outside of school hours, the disciplinary decision says.

Gregoire ignored the principal and kept texting the student, it says.

He notified the student he would pursue a job opportunity at her school. Later, he messaged her that he was happy to learn he would be teaching one of her classes.

In December 2024, Gregoire hugged the student goodbye at the high school, according to the report. The division put him on administrative leave that month.

River East Transcona School Division filed a complaint with Manitoba's independent education commissioner on April 20 of this year. The commissioner's office ordered an investigation the following day and Gregoire was fired.

He subsequently agreed to the facts surfaced through the commissioner's investigation and agreed they constituted professional misconduct.

Gregoire surrendered his teaching certificate in May. It was permanently cancelled after the investigation wrapped.

"The thousands of messages exchanged over several years, together with Mr. Gregoire’s failure to disclose the relationship, demonstrate a sustained and deliberate pattern of misconduct rather than isolated lapses in judgment," the report concludes.

Gregoire took responsibility for his behaviour and expressed remorse, the report adds.

2nd teacher loses licence

Brady Nurse also lost his teacher certification in a recent decision by Manitoba's teacher commissioner for inappropriately communicating with a student, in what was described as "a fundamental breach of a teacher’s duty of care to students."

Nurse was employed in the Portage la Prairie School Division when, between October and December last year, he exchanged texts with a student.

The commissioner's report characterized the messages as "inappropriate communications" involving "a student experiencing circumstances of heightened vulnerability," which Nurse was aware of.

The division launched its own investigation after being approached by RCMP about Nurse on Dec. 9.

Nurse provided copies of texts between him and the student the next day.

A week later, the division asked if there were any other messages that hadn't been disclosed.

Nurse claimed he had provided all of the messages, but when asked specifically about text messages exchanged on Nov. 18, he retrieved more messages that had been deleted.

He was put on leave two days later.

In an interview with division staff in January, Nurse admitted he didn't share every text initially out of concern that some "might be perceived as inappropriate," the report states.

Nurse admitted to his conduct. He resigned in March and surrendered his teaching certificate in May. It has since officially been cancelled.

World.title: How did a deadly fire spread so quickly at CFB Wainwright during training?
World.content:
The audio version of this article is generated by AI-based technology. Mispronunciations can occur. We are working with our partners to continually review and improve the results.

A grass fire at CFB Wainwright in Alberta reportedly travelled one kilometer in just 36 seconds. A powerful cold front swept across the region that afternoon, bringing a dramatic drop in temperature, strengthening winds and a sudden shift in wind direction.

How did this deadly Alberta fire spread so fast?

A dangerous combination of weather conditions was at play Saturday afternoon when a deadly fire engulfed a training exercise at CFB Wainwright in east-central Alberta, killing four soldiers and severely injuring dozens more, weather and wildfire experts say.

That morning, Environment Canada had issued yellow alerts for much of southern and eastern Alberta because of strong winds forecast to reach up to 100 km/h and an incoming cold front that could cause abrupt changes in wind direction.

Before the cold front reached the area, the temperature in Wainwright climbed to nearly 20 C under sunny skies.

"Conditions were extreme," said Mike Flannigan, a professor of wildland fires at Thompson Rivers University in Kamloops, B.C., who runs the Canada fire weather outlook. "Things were dry. Any fires that started would have spread rapidly and would be intense and that's pretty well what happened."

Flannigan said NASA satellite data indicate a fire was burning near the base by around 2 p.m. The Canadian Forest Fire Weather Index shows that fire conditions across the Canadian prairies, including southern and central Alberta, ranged from very high to extreme.

Around 4 p.m., a cold front moved through the area, bringing a roughly 10 C drop in temperature and a sharp shift in wind direction, Flannigan said. He said the shift pushed the fire northwest toward the training area.

Canadian Armed Forces Maj.-Gen. Wade Rutland, inaugural commander of the revitalized 1st Canadian Division, told reporters Sunday that the fire began as a grassfire and spread rapidly around 4 p.m. as the wind direction changed.

Rutland said range control at the base were aware about a fire for several hours but decided training could carry on "for a certain amount of time."

That day, soldiers were throwing hand grenades on a grenade range, he said, while others were conducting a "section attack," in which 10 soldiers attack a simulated enemy.

Rutland said it is not yet known what exactly caused the fire. "Quite frankly, it could have been any of that or none of it," he said.

The major-general said troops described the fire as covering a distance of a kilometre in under a minute, with the fire suddenly "right on top of them."

"This was uncommon, rapid, and I certainly hadn't seen anything like it," he said, adding that conditions for most of the day were "within standard procedures to conduct training exercises" with wind gusts below 50 km/h.

Heavy winds were forecast

However, meteorological and wildfire experts say the combination of dry fuels, low humidity and strong winds created conditions favourable to rapid fire spread. Heavy wind gusts of over 80 km/h had also been forecast for the area later that day.

"This was a very dangerous setup," said Jonathan Porter, chief meteorologist for AccuWeather, a commercial weather forecasting company.

Porter says the company issued a warning to its business customers in the Wainwright area about a risk for high winds around 2:30 p.m. MT.

In addition to the strong wind, Porter said humidity was low, at about 20 per cent, creating "an ideal setup for wildfires to spread."

Flannigan of Thompson Rivers University had a similar assessment of the day's conditions, noting any fire ignited at the time would have spread quickly and intensely.

But those conditions were forecast and were not necessarily unusual for the area at this time of year, he said.

"You do get windy conditions and fall is the time for them," Flannigan said. He added that heavy rain this spring had caused abundant grass growth, which, after drying this month, created a large amount of fuel for fire to spread.

Reported speed difficult to assess

While grass fires spread more quickly than forest fires, it's unlikely the fire at CFB Wainwright travelled one kilometre in under a minute, Flannigan said — unless it merged with another fire or ignited unexploded ammunitions.

According to Natural Resources Canada , grass fires can travel up to 12 km/h and their flames can reach up to 10 metres high.

Flannigan noted their speed typically reaches roughly 10 per cent of the speed of the wind that carries them.

A Wainwright Fire Rescue vehicle is seen in Wainwright, Alta., on Sunday as crews continued responding to the aftermath of the deadly fire at CFB Wainwright. (Jennifer Gauthier/Reuters)

In response to questions from CBC about the weather conditions and the response at CFB Wainwright at the time of the fire, the Department of National Defence said in an emailed statement that military police and the Canadian Forces National Investigation Service are conducting investigations in Wainwright and elsewhere in Alberta.

"The investigation remains active, and commenting on specific details at this stage would be inappropriate," spokesperson Kened Sadiku said.

Flannigan said he hopes the incident leads to better wildfire warning systems in Canada and within the military.

"One thing I can say is that grass fires are dangerous," he said. "Any fire we have to treat with respect."

Porter said he expects the Armed Forces' investigation to examine what actions were or were not taken in response to weather warnings "issued well in advance" and whether those warnings reached the people making decisions about the exercise.

"A key part of this investigation is going to be what actions were taken based upon the high wind warnings that were issued in that area," he said.

Fires at base not uncommon, says retired major general

It's not uncommon for troops to continue training even after flames spark nearby, says Scott Clancy, a retired major-general in the Royal Canadian Air Force and Canadian Armed Forces.

WATCH | Fires often start during military exercises: Retired major-general weighs in on what may come next after deadly fire on military base | Duration closed caption 5:39 Retired major-general Scott Clancy spoke to CBC News Network Monday about how training exercises are conducted, fire risks and what might happen next after a deadly blaze at CFB Wainwright in Alberta.

Clancy told CBC News that soldiers will often continue field training exercises when fires start, noting that fires are routinely managed by military range control.

He said Wainwright is a very large base and a decision to "carry on" would have been made by range control officers who were managing exercises on site Saturday.

The investigation to come will "look at the leadership, the culture that was created around that leadership, the orders, the safety regulations [and] the specific decisions to carry on training," he said.

"Wildfires ... can be smouldering low and then a few minutes later be wild blazing fires," Clancy said.

World.title: Manitoba man, 84, who lost legs to MS is knitting tuques on custom-made cot
World.content:
The audio version of this article is generated by AI-based technology. Mispronunciations can occur. We are working with our partners to continually review and improve the results.

Before Leonard Foidart starts knitting, he lies face down on his custom-made cot, reaches down to adjust the light, grabs two knitting needles and selects the wool he feels will be just right.

Foidart, 84, loves to knit but is unable to sit for more than a few hours at a time. He lost his legs in the early 1990s due to complications from multiple sclerosis.

"The bones don't like me sitting on them too much," Foidart said from his home in Notre-Dame-de-Lourdes, Man., about 110 kilometres southwest of Winnipeg.

He said he has knitted and donated more than 1,000 tuques to numerous charities in the last five years, including Winnipeg's Siloam Mission and Central Plains Cancer Services in Portage la Prairie. Much of the wool is donated.

Foidart was diagnosed with bone and prostate cancer a few years ago. His wife, Tharsile, died last year after suffering a stroke.

"She taught me how to knit. So, every time I knit a tuque, she is right here beside me. In the 20 years, we never had a single argument. We had a good life," he said as his voice broke with emotion.

That's why, Foidart said, he refuses to give up knitting. After his cancer diagnosis, Foidart decided to build a cot. It sits on four wheels and has a comfortable body cushion, and a leather headband so he can rest his head.

Foidart shows off one of many baskets of donated wool. (Michele McDougall/CBC)

"I was a letter carrier for 19 years, and in my spare time I did carpentry work. And because I've been in this chair for 35 years, whenever a problem came along, this guy solved it," Foidart said as he tapped the side of his head.

He keeps meticulous records of each donation, with photos of labelled bags showing the date and number of tuques.

"You're here to help people, and that's my goal, to do the best I can to help people wherever they are and whatever shape they can be in," Foidart said.

His most recent donation of 200 tuques was to the Portage la Prairie Community Revitalization Corporation last week. The corporation supports and advocates for vulnerable people in the community.

Kimberly Sharp, left, and Tawnee Kowerchuk from the Portage la Prairie Community Revitalization Corporation hold some of the 200 tuques Foidart delivered last week. (Michele McDougall/CBC)

Co-ordinator Tawnee Kowerchuk said they got an email from Foidart's niece preparing them for delivery but she was shocked when he delivered the tuques himself.

"It was really special. When he showed up and we saw exactly what we were dealing with and how many, we were totally beside ourselves. It was just amazing," Kowerchuk said.

"And he was adamant they go to people who are in need. And they will."

Foidart is already working on the next batch of tuques. He said he doesn't set a goal of how many he wants to make in a month or a year but never strays from his schedule.

"I do the best that I can do today, and maybe tomorrow, even better. And mistakes now are very rare. After 1,200 tuques, they better be rare," he said as he laughed.

World.title: Canadian who stole a Las Vegas flamingo after drinking '30 to 40' beers convicted of animal cruelty
World.content:
The audio version of this article is generated by AI-based technology. Mispronunciations can occur. We are working with our partners to continually review and improve the results.

What happens in Vegas stays in Vegas. Unless you drink "30 to 40 beers" and steal a flamingo — because that will make international news.

A Las Vegas court convicted an Ontario man of animal cruelty charges Monday for snatching a flamingo named Peachy from its habitat at an iconic Las Vegas hotel in what prosecutors called a drunken and malicious act.

Mitchell Fairbarn was accused of "willfully, unlawfully, maliciously and feloniously" injuring the flamingo in the early morning hours on March 3, according to the indictment viewed by CBC News. He pleaded not guilty and his trial started last week.

After jurors returned convictions on felony and misdemeanor animal cruelty counts, Fairbarn remained in custody pending a Dec. 1 sentencing hearing. He faces up to four years in prison for the felony conviction, plus six months of jail time for the misdemeanor conviction.

"I thought it was something that we could joke about for the rest of our lives," Fairbarn, described by various Las Vegas media outlets as a contractor from rural Ontario, said in court Friday.

The façade of the Flamingo hotel in Las Vegas is seen at night on Las Vegas Boulevard in this file photo. (Pascal Le Segretain/Getty Images)

Fairbarn told the court that on the day of the incident, he drank "30 to 40" beers over the course of 24 hours while he was in Las Vegas for a construction expo, he said in video footage of the trial posted by multiple media outlets.

Fairbarn entered the flamingo habitat at the Flamingo Las Vegas Hotel and Casino around 5 a.m. on March 3, according to the Las Vegas Review-Journal, and took the bird because he thought it would be a "silly joke" with his friends.

"I thought it would be, at the time, funny," Fairbarn said.

The Flamingo's wildlife habitat, which the hotel says spans four acres and is certified by the National Wildlife Federation, is home to the resort's namesake Chilean flamingos, among other birds, turtles and fish.

Peachy was shaking, bleeding: witness

Video played at the trial showed Fairbarn holding the flamingo by the neck in an elevator and carrying it down a hotel hallway. He spent about 15 minutes with the bird, and two-to-three minutes with it in his room, reported 8NewsNow, citing police evidence heard in court.

Two of Fairbarn's friends testified earlier this week that they had been out drinking, then woke up in their hotel room to find the flamingo there before moving it to the hallway, notes Fox 5 Las Vegas.

A hotel facilities engineer searching for Peachy eventually corralled the bird into a corner with a towel, and told the court Peachy was shaking and bleeding.

The flamingo was injured during the incident, suffering seven to eight missing feathers, broken feather shafts and blood loss consistent with trauma, the bird's treating veterinarian testified in court, according to Fox5 Las Vegas.

Peachy, who is 27 years old, needed antibiotics, anti-inflammatories and weeks of pain medication, the news outlet reported.

CBC News has reached out to the Las Vegas Justice Court for access to court filings and has not yet received them. But multiple local media outlets present in court have aired footage from court where Fairbarn doesn't deny his actions — just his intent.

His lawyer Joshua Tomsheck said Monday it was a drunken act and no harm was intended. When Tomsheck asked Fairbairn Friday if he had any malicious intent "in your mind or your heart when you picked up that bird," Fairbarn shook his head and answered, "no."

CBC News has reached out to Tomsheck, but has not yet received a response.

Fairbarn testifies during his trial at the Regional Justice Center on Friday in Las Vegas. He says he didn't intend to hurt the flamingo he took up to his hotel room in March. (Benjamin Hager/Las Vegas Review-Journal/The Associated Press)

Justice delivered: animal rights advocate

Prosecutors said Fairbarn willfully caused the bird physical pain, noting feathers were found on the hotel floor and video showed the bird squawking while Fairbarn handled it. But Tomsheck said his client regrets his actions while intoxicated and never meant to harm the bird, a key element in the felony charge.

"He should not have done that, should not have gone into the habitat, shouldn't have touched a bird, shouldn't have taken Peachy inside," Tomsheck said in court Monday.

"The truth is, Mitch was drunk. Mitch was stupid. He made bad decisions."

Fairbarn told the court Friday that he has remained under house arrest in Nevada since the incident. Court records viewed by CBC News show he had to surrender his passport as one of his bail conditions.

Jurors began deliberations after both sides presented closing arguments Monday morning.

Nevada animal rights advocate John Waudby, who recently helped strengthen the state's animal cruelty laws, told The Associated Press he believes justice was delivered on Peachy's behalf.

"I hope this sends a message to anybody else that wants to mess with our animals, that you're not going to do it in Nevada," he said outside the courtroom after Monday's verdict.

The Flamingo Las Vegas Hotel and Casino is home to the resort's namesake Chilean flamingos, which reside at the hotel's wildlife habitat. (Ceasars Entertainment)

Peachy has since recovered, according to Fox 5 Las Vegas. But the flamingo is just one of several recent cases involving animal cruelty at Las Vegas casinos, reports the Las Vegas Review-Journal.

In June, a woman was charged after allegedly jumping into the fountain at The Venetian and grabbing a duckling named Daffy. In May, a teen girl was arrested and accused of stabbing three horses the the South Point Arena & Equestrian Center so they couldn't compete in a barrel race.

World.title: Stelco's U.S. owner says steelmaker had 'strongest' quarter since acquisition as massive layoffs underway
World.content:
The audio version of this article is generated by AI-based technology. Mispronunciations can occur. We are working with our partners to continually review and improve the results.

Cleveland-Cliffs says Stelco's third quarter this year was its "strongest" since it was acquired by the U.S. company in 2024.

At the same time, hundreds working for the steelmaker in Ontario are set to lose their jobs in Hamilton and Nanticoke. Layoff notices started rolling out earlier this month and are continuing.

"Third quarter was Stelco’s strongest ... since we acquired the company two years ago. The Canadian hot-rolled market has improved substantially," Cleveland-Cliffs CEO Lourenco Goncalves said in a statement Monday.

"However, more needs to be done by the Canadian government to correct a clearly oversupplied market for galvanized steel in Canada."

Stelco Holdings Inc. said on Sept. 28 it planned to idle part of its Hamilton plant in order to "ensure the survival" of the company as U.S. tariffs has squeezed its sales.

Ron Wells, president of United Steelworkers Local 1005, told CBC that 333 layoffs were expected in Hamilton. USW Local 8782 president John McElroy said up to 50 layoffs are expected at the Lake Erie Works in Nanticoke.

During an earnings call Monday, Goncalves said all of Cleveland-Cliffs's major profit drivers increased.

He praised U.S. President Donald Trump's trade policies, saying they are "helping create the conditions needed for companies like ours to continue investing in [local] communities and expanding domestic production," despite Stelco citing tariffs as a key reason for economic struggles.

Steel sales under 'best price environment in 3 years'

In June, Trump signed an executive order applying up to 50 per cent tariffs to certain steel and aluminum imports from Canada.

"We are currently selling steel under the best price environment in three years," said Goncalves.

"These are the prices we need to run a thriving business that grows employment, pays its workers well, reinvests in people and equipment, and protects our critical supply chains and national defence."

Goncalves said the success of the hot-rolled steel business was a direct consequence of the Canadian government's system tariff-rate quota, which limits the amount of product that can be imported.

The federal government has said Cleveland-Cliffs's purchase of Stelco included promises to employ "at least the same number of unionized employees and the vast majority of non-unionized employees" as there were in 2024 and through 2029.

Federal Industry Minister Mélanie Joly said "a business decision or even a change in market conditions cannot be used to not follow their commitment."

Goncalves reiterated Stelco's position that the layoffs are a temporary measure until Canada and the U.S. reach a trade agreement.

Stelco steel works in Hamilton are pictured on Oct. 9. The U.S.-based steelmaker announced 300 to 350 layoffs amid the Canada-U.S. trade war. (Evan Mitsui/CBC)

He said the Canadian market is "exposed" and that he has been asking the government to block or "severely reduce" the importing of galvanized steel into the market.

If that happens, he said, "Stelco can immediately bring back all the temporarily laid-off workers."

He also said he's willing to sell Stelco and is prepared to fight the Canadian government in court to preserve the plan to lay off workers.

Earlier this month, Joly said Ottawa is considering a range of legal options against Cleveland- Cliffs.

The minister said the government is examining its options under Section 40 of the Investment Canada Act. They could include financial penalties, a court order forcing the company to comply with its commitments or an order requiring it to sell its Canadian assets.

CEO's messaging 'confusing,' union rep says

Wells told CBC Hamilton on Monday that workers are feeling "underappreciated" as layoffs proceed.

"They're dedicated, loyal employees" he said. "They work weekends, they work holidays, they missed their kids' hockey games, graduations, and that loyalty isn't being repaid."

Wells also called Goncalves's messaging "confusing."

"He said Stelco's Q3 results were good, they're profitable. If they're profitable, why'd he shut down our [cold-rolled] and coated [steel] departments?" Wells said.

He also noted that Cleveland-Cliffs is advocating for a reduction in foreign imports, adding that "the U.S. [and] Cleveland-Cliffs might be part of that problem" as a large steel importer to Canada.

"We still hope Minister Joly follows through with her commitment to enforce the Investment Canada Act," Wells said.
