90 degree heat and thunderstorms expected across Belize today

By Breaking Belize News Staff (HP): Belizeans can expect a warm Tuesday with a few showers and possible isolated thunderstorms as relatively moist weather conditions continue across the country.

The National Meteorological Service says a relatively moist northeasterly airflow is prevailing over Belize, bringing sunny skies with cloudy intervals today and cloudy conditions at times tonight.

A few showers and possible isolated thunderstorms are expected mainly over central and southern areas this morning before shifting toward inland communities during the afternoon.

By late tonight, rainfall activity is expected to develop mainly along the northern coast, while showers elsewhere will remain generally isolated.

Temperatures will reach 90 degrees Fahrenheit inland, 86 degrees along the coast and 78 degrees in the hills.

Marine conditions will be relatively calm, with slight seas and waves between one and three feet. Winds will blow from the northeast to east at up to 10 knots.

Looking ahead to Wednesday, cloudy spells are expected with a few showers and possible isolated thunderstorms mainly over northern and some central areas.

Rainfall activity will shift toward coastal communities Wednesday night, while showers elsewhere will remain isolated, if any.

The tropics remain quiet, with no tropical cyclone formation expected over the region during the next 48 hours.

World.title: Coast Guard member Lionel Logan dies following shooting in Corozal; police investigation continues
World.content:
Coast Guard member Lionel Logan dies following shooting in Corozal; police investigation continues

By Breaking Belize News Staff: Police have confirmed that 35-year-old Belize Coast Guard member Lionel Logan has died after being critically injured in a shooting along the Philip Goldson Highway near Carolina Village, Corozal District, on Sunday evening.

Assistant Superintendent of Police Stacy Smith confirmed during Monday’s police press briefing that Logan succumbed to his injuries earlier that day. His death comes less than 24 hours after gunmen opened fire on a vehicle carrying Logan and several other passengers.

Logan, a resident of Libertad Village, was travelling in a black Chevrolet Equinox with 35-year-old Julian Dyer, a construction worker from Corozal Town, and other passengers after leaving a football game in Carolina Village.

According to initial reports, a black van carrying approximately four men pulled alongside their vehicle, and its occupants opened fire, striking Logan and Dyer.

Logan suffered multiple gunshot wounds, including injuries to his abdomen and the back of his head. He was transported to the Karl Heusner Memorial Hospital in Belize City, where he remained in critical condition before succumbing to his injuries on Monday.

Dyer sustained injuries to his right forearm and lower abdomen and was treated at the Corozal Community Hospital. A nine-year-old girl travelling in the vehicle also suffered a minor injury reportedly caused by shattered glass.

The bullet-riddled Chevrolet Equinox was subsequently discovered abandoned in the San Antonio Village area.

Police are continuing their investigation into the deadly attack. A motive has not been publicly established, and the police have not announced any arrests in connection with the shooting.

World.title: Police investigate whether improperly parked car contributed to fatal bus crash that killed Sherri Mejia and 4-year-old Taleenie Garbutt
World.content:
Police investigate whether improperly parked car contributed to fatal bus crash that killed Sherri Mejia and 4-year-old Taleenie Garbutt

By Breaking Belize News Staff: Police are investigating whether a car parked partially in the path of oncoming traffic contributed to Saturday evening’s fatal collision between a National Bus Company bus and a Toyota Corolla on the Thomas Vincent Ramos Highway.

The accident, which occurred between Miles 37 and 38 near San Juan Village, claimed the lives of Sherri Mejia and four-year-old Taleenie Garbutt.

During Monday’s police press briefing, Assistant Superintendent Stacy Smith said investigators believe the car had stopped along the highway to allow a passenger to relieve themselves.

According to preliminary findings, the bus was travelling in the opposite direction when its driver apparently attempted to swerve to avoid the parked car but was unable to prevent the collision.

Smith said an examination of the scene and the vehicle suggested that the car had not been parked completely off the roadway and may have been partially obstructing the lane used by oncoming traffic.

Mejia died at the scene, while Taleenie later succumbed to her injuries while receiving medical treatment. Four other occupants of the car were injured.

According to public reports, Taleenie’s father, Walton Garbutt, sustained a broken foot and a knee injury requiring surgery.

Police have obtained a urine sample from the bus driver and served him with a notice of intended prosecution.

Investigations continue to determine the precise circumstances of the collision and whether traffic violations contributed to the deaths.

World.title: Police launch internal investigation into chokehold used during arrest in Unitedville
World.content:
Police launch internal investigation into chokehold used during arrest in Unitedville

By Breaking Belize News Staff: The Belize Police Department has launched an internal investigation into a viral video showing an officer placing a man in a chokehold during an arrest in Unitedville, Cayo District.

During Monday’s press briefing, Assistant Superintendent of Police Stacy Smith explained that chokeholds are classified as deadly force under the department’s policies and procedures manual, comparable to discharging a firearm or striking someone in the head with a baton.

Smith said such force should only be used as a last resort when there is an imminent threat of death or grievous bodily harm. The internal investigation will determine whether the officer’s actions were justified under those circumstances.

She also suggested that less-lethal alternatives, including pepper spray, could have helped de-escalate the confrontation, but noted that the officers involved did not appear to have that option readily available.

The man involved has been identified as Samuel Parham, whose family has publicly questioned the officers’ actions following the October 16 incident.

Police confirmed that Parham has since been charged with grievous harm after an officer reportedly suffered a broken arm during the confrontation.

Smith said investigators had obtained additional footage showing an officer being thrown to the ground, an incident that was not visible in the shorter recording she initially reviewed.

The Professional Standards Branch is investigating the matter, and police are encouraging witnesses to cooperate as investigators seek to establish whether the use of force was justified.

World.title: Belize City man accused of raping ex-girlfriend in her home with her son present despite restraining order, remanded to prison
World.content:
Belize City man accused of raping ex-girlfriend in her home with her son present despite restraining order, remanded to prison

By Breaking Belize News Staff: A 26-year-old Belize City construction worker has been remanded to the Belize Central Prison after being charged with allegedly raping and assaulting his former girlfriend despite an existing protection order against him.

Shadron Gillett, of Iguana Street, appeared in the Belize City Magistrate’s Court on Monday, October 19, where he was charged with rape, harm and damage to property in connection with an incident involving a 28-year-old woman on July 2, 2026.

According to the allegations, the woman was resting on her verandah around 3 p.m. when Gillett approached her and insisted on speaking with her. She reportedly reminded him of the protection order and demanded that he leave.

The woman told police that when she attempted to record him with her cellphone, Gillett grabbed the device and smashed it. During a subsequent struggle, he allegedly damaged another cellphone before the confrontation moved into her bedroom.

The complainant alleged that Gillett grabbed her by the neck, ordered her to stop screaming for help and struck her in the head with a surge protector before sexually assaulting her.

During the alleged attack, the woman’s son reportedly knocked on the door. Gillett allegedly ordered him to leave, but the woman urged her son to remain. She further alleged that Gillett punched her in the mouth before fleeing the residence.

Police subsequently charged Gillett with rape, harm and damage to property involving two cellphones valued at a combined $1,300.

No plea was taken on the rape charge, which is an indictable offence to be tried before the High Court.

Gillett was offered bail of $5,000 with one surety of the same amount or two sureties of $2,500 each. His bail conditions prohibit him from interfering with the complainant or her family and require him to remain at least 100 yards away from her.

However, he was unable to meet bail and was remanded to prison until he can do so. His next court appearance is scheduled for December 28, 2026.

World.title: Augustine sisters acquitted of burning down mother-in-law’s $32,000 home in Crooked Tree
World.content:
Augustine sisters acquitted of burning down mother-in-law’s $32,000 home in Crooked Tree

By Breaking Belize News Staff: Two Belize City sisters accused of burning down their former mother-in-law’s home in Crooked Tree Village more than four years ago were acquitted of arson on Monday after a nine-member jury returned a unanimous not guilty verdict.

Janiene Augustine, 27, and her younger sister Janiece Augustine, 23, broke down in tears as the verdict was delivered before Justice Nigel Pilgrim in the High Court. The jury, comprising six women and three men, deliberated for approximately two hours before reaching its decision.

The sisters were accused of intentionally setting fire to a woman’s home on July 16, 2022, destroying a wooden structure valued at $30,000 and household contents worth an additional $2,000.

Prosecutors alleged that Janiene, who had been living at the property with her then common-law husband and their children, was motivated by a dispute that resulted in the common-law husband putting her out of the house two days before the fire.

The prosecution relied on circumstantial evidence, including testimony that the sisters had entered the property shortly before the blaze. However, no witness testified to seeing either woman start the fire.

In his summation, Justice Pilgrim highlighted the absence of scientific evidence establishing that the fire had been deliberately set. He reminded jurors that the burden rested entirely on the prosecution to prove guilt beyond a reasonable doubt.

Both sisters denied setting the house ablaze, maintaining that they had visited the property only to collect Janiene’s belongings.

The women were initially charged in April 2024, nearly two years after the fire, following directives from the Director of Public Prosecutions.

Janiene was represented by attorney David McKoy, while Janiece was represented by attorneys Leeroy Banner and Lesly Mendez.

Monday’s unanimous verdict brings the lengthy criminal proceedings against the sisters to an end, with both women cleared of the arson charge.

World.title: Where is the outrage?
World.content:
Minister of religion Lisean Gordon delivering the sermon during the Heritage Week Thanksgiving Service at the Greater Highway Church of Christ Apostolic in Caterwood, Trelawny, on Sunday. Looking on are Mayor of Falmouth C Junior Gager (left) and moderator Leisa Dawson. (Photo: Horace Hines)

CARTERWOOD, Trelawny — Minister of religion Lisean Gordon has criticised what she described as the public’s readiness to demand justice when police officers use force, but silence following the killing of two members of the Jamaica Constabulary Force (JCF) last Friday.



Preaching under the theme ‘Let the Children Know’ during a Heritage Week Thanksgiving Service at the Greater Highway Church of Christ Apostolic in Caterwood, Trelawny, on Sunday, Gordon said the lack of comparable demonstrations demanding justice for the slain cops reflects a troubling imbalance.

“They may be somebody’s father, somebody’s son. Nobody came out because we have placed in the heart of ungodly people that we are allowing them to take over this country, all in the name of politics,” said Gordon as she addressed the service hosted by the Jamaica Cultural Development Commission (JCDC) in Trelawny and the Trelawny Municipal Corporation.

Two members of the JCF’s Special Operations Branch, Corporal Trevoy Shaw and Constable Devoney Rose, sustained fatal gunshot wounds during a firefight with men who had barricaded themselves inside a house in the Five Miles area of St Catherine on Friday.

Three civilians, Errol Hussey, his son Malique Hussey, and nephew Javoun Cogle, also died in the incident while a 10-year-old girl was left nursing a gunshot wound.

Delivering the sermon, Gordon condemned the tendency to vilify members of the police force without knowing the circumstances surrounding an encounter, and charged that media coverage and circulating recordings often fuel premature judgements.

Gordon linked the hostility towards law enforcement personnel to a broader erosion of respect for authority, and contended that political allegiance is encouraging Jamaicans to excuse behaviour they might otherwise condemn.

“There is something called the hidden curriculum, which we sometimes forget about. The hidden curriculum: What they see us do is what they will do,” said Gordon, who is also an educator.

She also took issue with verbal attacks against political leaders, including Prime Minister Dr Andrew Holness and Opposition Leader Mark Golding, warning that adults risk normalising disrespect among children who observe and absorb their behaviour.

“This disrespect that we put up with…because we are affiliated to a party, and to politics, it must stop. Disrespect is disrespect, and everybody who leads us needs to be respected, whether they are on the Opposition side or they are on the ruling side,” declared Gordon.

She argued that while children are taught to assert their rights, adults are neglecting the importance of responsibility and accountability.

“But we teach them about their rights, but no longer teach them about their responsibility,” Gordon said as she insisted that parents and other adults must uphold discipline, principles, and respect rather than retreat from the challenges of raising the younger generation.

She warned that Jamaica faces a dangerous escalation of disorder if the erosion of these values continues, describing the threat as a storm more severe than Hurricane Melissa.

“I am afraid of what is coming to Jamaica. There is a storm coming that is worse than Melissa… It’s called a storm of lawlessness, it’s called the storm of disorder, and it’s coming towards us. It’s worse than a Category 5,” said Gordon.

The minister of religion urged Jamaicans to reflect on the values they are passing on to their children as she argued that a meaningful inheritance extends beyond material possessions.

Meanwhile, mayor of Falmouth C Junior Gager, in his remarks, called on Jamaicans to preserve the legacy of the national heroes through their everyday actions rather than limiting remembrance to speeches and ceremonies.

“Our national heroes stood firm in the face of adversity, injustices, challenges, and paved the way for the freedom and opportunities we enjoy today,” Gager said.

He urged citizens to serve their communities, stand up for what is right, invest in young people, and work together to build a better Jamaica.

Gager also underscored the Church’s role in strengthening families and communities through prayer, mentorship, compassion and outreach, helping young people embrace their heritage and recognise their potential.

World.title: Ochie ‘Lovers Rock’ gets Hollywood pop-in
World.content:
Jimmy Fallon, host of The Tonight Show Starring Jimmy Fallon on NBC, hangs out with promoter of Lovers’ Rock: A Night of British Reggae on Friday in Ocho Rios, St Ann.

A Hollywood power player showed up at Lovers Rock: A Night of British Reggae last Friday.

Jimmy Fallon, host of The Tonight Show Starring Jimmy Fallon on NBC, surprised the packed house at Ocean’s 11 Bar and Restaurant in Ocho Rios, St Ann.

Fallon popped into the venue with Wayne Jobson, the Jamaican impresario who is an influential figure in the Southern California reggae scene.

Steve James, who started ‘Lovers Rock’ in 2025, was surprised when the American comedian appeared.

“I was very shocked! We had received an indication that he might attend, but there is a big difference between hearing that someone may show up and actually seeing them there,” he told the Jamaica Observer. “When we saw him we were pleasantly surprised and delighted. His attendance was certainly an unexpected highlight of the evening.”

James said Fallon mingled with patrons, most of whom are fans of lovers’ rock, the genre that emerged in the United Kingdom during the late 1970s and early 1980s.

Since 2014 Fallon has hosted his late-night talk show, which is consistently one of the top-rated in the United States.

Beres Hammond also attended Lovers Rock: A Night of British Reggae, which saw a performance from singer/bassist Lloyd Parks.

The South Florida-based James, who hosts the Real Rock Radio show, led the line-up of selectors who played songs that defined the lovers’ rock movement. Others manning the turntables were Martin Mitchell; Twinn Spinn from Fetedayzradio.com; DJ Jacko from King Jammy Sound System; Buppy C from Vibes FM London; and Lady Gee, formerly of Choice FM London and Vibes.

“The atmosphere was fantastic! Many patrons expressed how much they had missed hearing this kind of music. For them, it was more than just a night of entertainment; it was a nostalgic journey that transported them back to their days in the UK,” said James, who is considered an authority on lovers’ rock.

The genre produced several stars, most of whom were born in the United Kingdom to Jamaican parents. They include Janet Kay, Peter Hunnigale, and Maxi Priest.

Lovers Rock: A Night of British Reggae was first held during Reggae Month last February at Pon Top Seafood Grill and Bar in Kingston. The second staging took place at the same venue in May.

The fourth is scheduled for Kingston in February.

World.title: Netball Jamaica boss talks up Sunshine Girls’ chances in Horizon Series
World.content:
Jamaica’s Sunshine Girls will face England’s Roses in the four-Test Horizon Series, with the first two games set to be played in England on November 21 and 22 at the Copper Box Arena. The Sunshine Girls will then welcome England to Jamaica on December 5 and 6. (Photo: Naphtali Junior)

NETBALL Jamaica (NJ) President Karen Baugh has promised entertainment galore as the Sunshine Girls look to tackle England’s Roses in the Horizon Series next month.

The four-Test series was announced at a press conference held at S Hotel in New Kingston on October 13, 2026. The first two games are to be played in England on November 21 and 22 at the Copper Box Arena.

The Sunshine Girls are set to welcome the Roses to Jamaica on December 5 and 6.

“When Jamaica and England meet on a netball court you can expect intense competition, a bit of drama, excitement, and if Jamaica has anything to do with it, a little extra flair,” Baugh said.

“…This is much more than just two netball matches… it is an international sporting event, a celebration of our Sunshine Girls, and an opportunity to showcase the best of Jamaica netball and Brand Jamaica. This is definitely a rivalry worth watching.”

The Horizon Series — contested in honour of netball icons Molly Rhone of Jamaica and Jean Hornsby of England — began in 2024 with a classic.

Baugh recalled her favourite match, one she ranks alongside the 2026 Commonwealth Games win over Australia.

“That first match here against England, [in] the last second, we were leading by one and Shanice [Beckford] literally ran down the clock to prevent them from scoring again — and we won in the last second to tie the series. We went on to win the last game and won the series 2-1,” she said.

That Jamaica team had trailed 1-0 after the England leg — drawing the first, losing the second — before coming home to win the series.

In 2025 Hurricane Melissa forced the cancellation of the Jamaica leg, and England won the two matches played in England.

“The trophy, our trophy, is currently in England so we have a question to settle in 2026: Will the Rhone Hornsby Trophy be coming home?” Baugh asked.

In a historic first, Jamaica’s men’s team, The Suns, have been invited by England Thorns to play the curtain-raiser in London.

“It is a great opportunity for the male players to showcase their talent, and we wish The Suns every success in what is promised to be an exciting contest,” Baugh said.

Baugh said that for the home leg of the series, fans will get two matches for the price of one. England’s Roses Pathway team will tour Jamaica for a three-match series against the Jamaica Development Squad.

The first match will be on December 3, with the other two serving as curtain-raisers on December 5 and 6.

“You want to come really early. You want the place to be electric,” Baugh said.

Baugh said that the series forms part of preparations for the 2027 World Cup in Australia and comes on the back of a stellar year.

At the 2026 Commonwealth Games in Glasgow, Scotland, the Sunshine Girls won silver, stunning world number one Australia 46-45 in the semi-final before going down to New Zealand in the final.

“That was a statement to the world that Jamaica is among the very best in world netball,” Baugh said.

World.title: READY TO COMPETE
World.content:
Jamaican winger Jamone Lyle (centre) is expected to feature prominently for Jamaica at the FIFA Under-17 World Cup in Qatar in November. Here he is seen dribbling away from Canada’s Eloi Breton (right) and Ulrich Zamble during the Concacaf Under-17 Qualifiers encounter between Jamaica and Canada in Costa Rica on February 11, 2026. (Photo: JFF Media)

WITH the FIFA Under-17 World Cup now less than 30 days away, national under-17 Head Coach Wendell Downswell says the group have had to make the most of a less-than-ideal preparation period as they look to ensure they’re ready to compete at the tournament.

The young Reggae Boyz are set to make their third appearance at the global eventwhen it kicks off in Qatar on November 19. Jamaica have been drawn in Group E with European giants Italy, Ivory Coast and Uzbekistan.

The team booked their spot back in February at the 2026 Concacaf U-17 Qualifiers. However, they haven’t been able to secure international matches since.

Downswell, though, says they have made the best of the options available to them.

“It’s not been the ideal preparation that we have had because we were not able to get an international game; we were exploring at least two international games,” he

told the Jamaica Observer.

“However, we have been having camps — probably about four to five with the core of the players — which is good. And what we do is we prepare them in such a way that we use the Premier League teams and the Tier 2 teams as part of the measuring stick to see where we are in terms of the necessary preparation, and the boys have been responding very positively.”

“The coaching staff have explored all the possibilities to stretch these players somewhat similar to opposition that we’ll be up against in the tournament itself. So, hopefully this level of preparation, this kind of limitation that we have, will be of utmost significance for us going forward.”

Downswell says the technical staff have been closely keeping track of all the players they intend to select for the squad. However, he says several factors, including the ongoing ISSA Schoolboy Football, season haven’t made life easy.

“We release them and then some of them come back, [and] some come back with injuries here and there, knocks here and there,” he said. “[But] we have been having conversations with them. We have another camp coming up on the 6th and we have been having dialogue with the schools, so they won’t be released from the 6th up to our departure on the 14th.”

Downswell, who previously guided Jamaica’s U-17 team to the 2011 World Cup, says the players have been put through extensive preparation on and off the field, ahead of the tournament.

“We’ve put in place tactical preparation and the mental aspect of the players to get them fully focused regarding this task ahead. We have placed a lot of emphasis on the mental aspect of preparation, and the players have been responding in a positive way,” he said.

“Also, the whole preparation going in[to] international [games] — how we play the first 10 minutes, 5 minutes, the various tactical manoeuvres that we have done for the players to assimilate and adapt from a tactical standpoint — these are some of the things that we have been working on.”

Jamaica struggled in their two previous World Cup appearances, exiting at the group stage in 1999 and 2011 without recording a win in six matches.

Donwswell, though, is confident these young Reggae Boyz can break that trend and create history for the country. “I’m very upbeat, very enthusiastic about going, and at the same time our intention is to compete,” he said.

“Our first game’s against Italy [so] what we will do, the fact that we haven’t gotten much international exposure, so to speak, since February, [the plan] is using each game as part of our preparation and hoping that it lends itself in such a way that we are able to come out of the zone and take it from there.”

The squad, which is expected to feature new senior Reggae Boyz Jahmarie Nolan and Jamone Lyle, is set to be finalised by the first week of November.

World.title: When Granny’s Jamaican House Becomes the Mood Board
World.content:
Crochet, embroidery and handmade textile details bring texture and unexpected craftsmanship to the table.

Remember Granny’s house? The mahogany furniture that was built to last several lifetimes. The crocheted doilies strategically placed on every available surface. The lace and eyelet curtains. The tufted sofas and chairs that were definitely not for everyday sitting. The cabinet filled with the “good” glasses and patterned china that nobody was allowed to touch. And, of course, those decorative lampshades.

For years, many of us would have looked at these things and thought: old fashioned. Today? Put them on a mood board and suddenly they’re vintage, layered and chic.

Welcome to the wonderful cycle of design, where what was once considered old can become the next big trend.

Take mahogany, for example. In an old Jamaican home, dark, heavy wooden furniture was everywhere — dining tables, sideboards, coffee tables and those formidable chairs that seemed almost indestructible. After years of lighter woods dominating event design, deeper wood tones are beginning to feel sophisticated again. Pair mahogany with contemporary florals, beautiful linens and modern lighting and it takes on an entirely different personality.

Then there’s eyelet and lace. We remember them as curtains blowing at the window or perhaps a tablecloth brought out when company was coming. Now those same textures can inspire gorgeous linens, napkins and decorative details for weddings. Styled correctly, they feel romantic and intentional rather than old-fashioned.

And let’s talk about lampshades. Those decorative fabric shades that were once a fixture in Jamaican living rooms are finding their way back into stylish interiors and event design. Table lamps are appearing on dinner tables, bars and lounge areas, creating a warm, intimate, residential feeling that overhead event lighting simply cannot replicate.

Then there are the tufted sofas and chairs. Once associated with formal living rooms and furniture that children were warned not to climb on, tufting is having another moment. Used selectively in a contemporary lounge setting, a beautiful velvet tufted sofa or statement chair can add richness, character and just enough old-world glamour.

Even patterned china is having its moment. Remember those beautiful plates displayed behind the glass doors of the cabinet? Mix-and-match floral china, coloured glassware and vintage silver pieces can now transform a tablescape and make it feel collected rather than rented straight from a catalogue.

And yes, even crochet deserves another look. Perhaps we don’t need a doily under every vase, but crochet, embroidery and handmade textile details can bring texture and craftsmanship into an event in a way that feels personal and unexpected.

That’s really what this return to nostalgia is about.

We spent years trying to make everything sleek, minimal and perfectly matched. Now there’s something refreshing about a room that feels as though it has a story. The Jamaican homes many of us grew up visiting were layered. Things were collected over generations. Furniture was kept, repaired and passed down. The “good” pieces had meaning.

The trick is not to recreate Granny’s entire living room at your wedding.

Choose the memory, then reinterpret it.

A mahogany table with contemporary flowers. Eyelet linen with modern tableware. Patterned china against an unexpected tablescape. A beautiful lampshade incorporated into a bar or dinner setting. A tufted velvet sofa paired with contemporary coffee tables.

Suddenly, it isn’t old-fashioned. It’s nostalgic Jamaican style with a modern point of view.

So perhaps the next time you walk into an old Jamaican home and see that lampshade, embroidered cloth, tufted chair or piece of mahogany furniture you once thought was terribly outdated, don’t be so quick to dismiss it.

You might just be looking at your next event mood board.

Shikima Hinds

World.title: Fi Wi Land: Beyond the duppy stories, discover the value of Jamaica’s bats
World.content:
Often misunderstood and surrounded by folklore, bats are among nature’s hardest-working environmental protectors, helping to control insect populations, pollinate plants and disperse seeds. Discover more about these fascinating creatures as the Jamaica Observer in association with the National Environment and Planning Agency (NEPA) premieres ‘Fi Wi Land’ on Monday.

In the debut episode, host Carlysia Ramdeen is joined by NEPA Environmental Officer Damany Calder who shares insights about bats, their importance to Jamaica’s ecosystems and why they deserve greater appreciation.

The new 12-week environmental series by the Jamaica Observer and NEPA explores Jamaica’s unique wildlife, ecosystems and natural resources while highlighting efforts to protect the island’s environment for future generations.

Catch the premiere on the Jamaica Observer’s YouTube channel and other digital platforms.

World.title: Proud moment for Barnswells as husband and wife conferred with national award
World.content:
Councillor Scean Barnswell and wife Danielle pose for a photograph after receiving their Badge of Honour for Gallantry at the 2026 Ceremony of Investiture and Presentation of National Honours and Awards at King’s House on Monday, October 19. 2026. (Photo: Llewellyn Wynter)

It was a historic and proud moment for the Barnswell family from Clarendon, when the husband and wife team of Councillor Scean Barnswell and Danielle Anna-Marie Barnswell stood on the dais at King’s House Monday morning to accept their national award – the Badge of Honour for Gallantry, from Governor General Sir Patrick Allen.

The occasion was the 2026 Ceremony of Investiture and Presentation of National Honours and Awards.

The Barnswells were among 149 Jamaicans who were honoured for outstanding contributions in various fields.

The two were recognised for their “quick and courageous” actions that led to the rescue of a six-year-old girl who was reportedly abducted from the St Thomas More Preparatory School in May Pen Clarendon on December 9 last year.

“In growing up you’re told to mind your business but in Jamaica, the children are all our business so in this case I’m happy we did that and I wouldn’t change anything,” said Mrs Barnswell during rehearsals for Monday’s ceremony.

Scean Barnswell is the councillor for the Hayes division in the Clarendon Municipal Corporation and a former Mayor of May Pen. He is looking to return to that position as the balance of power in the corporation recently swung from the Jamaica Labour Party (JLP) to the Opposition People’s National Party (PNP).

This came after the JLP-elected councillor for the May Pen North division, Tanya-Lee Williams, resigned from the JLP, giving the PNP a clear 12-10 majority in the corporation. The PNP has stated that this gives it the right to appoint the mayor and deputy mayor but a court injunction granted last Friday has stalled those plans. The PNP has said it will be going back to court.

According to reports from December 2025, Barnswell and his wife spotted a man walking with a small child along Bustamante Highway and, sensing something was wrong, immediately intervened. Their actions resulted in the safe recovery of the child and the capture of the suspect, who was arrested by the police.

In a statement at the time, the PNP described the incident as an act of humanity, noting that Councillor Barnswell showed decisive, selfless leadership in a moment of crisis. The party said his response reflected the values of community vigilance and public service and urged others to do likewise.

WATCH: Barnswell honoured for rescuing abducted six-year-old

The PNP also expressed gratitude to members of the public who raised the alarm and commended the Jamaica Constabulary Force for its swift response.

“It emphasised the importance of strong community–police partnerships in protecting children and preventing crimes of this nature,” the party said.

-Lynford Simpson

World.title: Don’t be Liz Truss, Badenoch tells Burnham
World.content:
Truss — Britain’s shortest-serving prime minister, who spent just 49 days in Downing Street — announced Tuesday she is publishing a new book setting out “what really happened” during the mini-budget in 2022, according to a press notice issued by her spokesperson.

“Bank Job: A short book on how the Bank of England broke the bond market and brought down the government” will be published later this month.

The ex-PM has blamed the mini-budget’s consequences on the Treasury, the Bank of England and the Office for Budget Responsibility watchdog.

Badenoch told a press conference in London she does not believe Labour is paying attention to the consequences of that Conservative budget by failing to reduce spending: “They are the ones who want to repeat the mistakes of four years ago, we are not going to be making that mistake again.”

“We need to live within our means,” she said. “We have to stop borrowing so much, but instead, Labour are taking out more loans to pay the interest on our existing loans.”

Questioned on why the public should trust her judgement on economic competence, Badenoch, who served as Truss’ international trade secretary, told POLITICO: “I am not Liz Truss and I think that the public can tell the difference.”

Badenoch said she only saw the mini-budget when it was presented and collective responsibility “doesn’t mean that you agree with all of the decisions that are made.”

“She needs to take responsibility for it, one way or another,” Badenoch said. “That is her issue.”

World.title: UK to deploy fighter jets to help Saudis against Houthi attacks
World.content:
U.K. Defence Secretary Wes Streeting said the “continuing attacks” on the U.K.’s ally are “absolutely despicable.”

“The targeting of the airport in Riyadh in particular shows the lengths the Houthis are going to escalate the situation in the region,” he added, referencing the attacks earlier this month that killed 14 people and injured hundreds more.

Streeting said that the fighter jets will be used to protect Saudi airspace from drones and missiles. The U.K. will also send an Atlas A400M aircraft, used to transport the equipment, as well as military advisers.

“This builds on the UK equipment and personnel we already have in the country to defend against Houthi air attacks,” Streeting said.

The MoD stressed there is a link between the conflict in the Persian Gulf and the situation domestically, pointing to disrupted energy supplies and a subsequent rise in the cost of living.

Since Prime Minister Andy Burnham arrived in Downing Street in July he has offered more support to Saudi Arabia. In September, he agreed to a request for air-to-air refueling of the country’s jets.

World.title: Ryanair’s O’Leary warns of ‘biggest increase’ in EU airfares next year
World.content:
But O'Leary said most European airlines lack significant hedging next year. “As we go out into next year, we're only 15% hedged at $85 a barrel. Basically, we're unhedged into the summer of 2027,” O'Leary told POLITICO in an interview ahead of a press conference in Brussels.

Ryanair's hedging contracts expire in April 2027. “We will still be profitable, although less profitable than currently, if oil prices remain high,” he said.

O'Leary warned that fewer available seats and higher fares could become the new normal as more airlines face financial struggles. “You're going to see dramatically less capacity this winter and into the summer of 2027.”

Ryanair itself is cutting 20 routes from Belgium this winter as a response to an increase in national aviation taxes, from €2 in 2025 to €7 from January.

The fuel price hike is also intensifying the airline sector's opposition to EU climate policies, which many carriers argue are adding to their already rising operating costs.

Ryanair had long advocated extending the EU's Emissions Trading System to all flights to and from the EU, a call O'Leary reiterated on Tuesday.

World.title: Spain’s conservatives in talks with far-right Vox over election deal
World.content:
Conservative leader Alberto Núñez Feijóo said it would be a “mistake” to allow Socialist boss Pedro Sánchez to lead again.

The leader of Spain’s conservative People’s Party, Alberto Núñez Feijóo, confirmed Tuesday that he is negotiating with the far right ahead of the Nov. 29 snap election to secure a majority in the Senate.

“Vox knows how far we can go; they know we have a sense of state,” Feijóo said Tuesday morning in an interview on Spanish radio station COPE, alluding to an alliance with the far-right party. “It would be a mistake to hand control over to Sanchismo,” he added, in reference to Pedro Sánchez’s Socialist government.

Feijóo, who is eyeing the premiership, said he was negotiating with Vox to coordinate Senate lists and counter a potential coalition between the governing socialists and other left-wing parties.

World.title: AfD’s Alice Weidel to unveil plan to downsize the EU
World.content:
“I’m not fooled by what the European Commission wants to do. The European Commission wants to turn itself into a state; we do not. And so we will stand in its way,” Le Pen said.

The AfD policy paper, obtained by Brussels Playbook, says the AfD would not seek to leave the EU or eurozone at first. Instead, it wants to renegotiate the EU treaties and cut the bloc’s powers, institutions and budget. Weidel will present her strategy at an event on Wednesday afternoon entitled “Our new deal for Europe.”

The party wants to replace direct European Parliament elections with delegates appointed by national parliaments, reduce the Commission’s role to purely administrative and transfer decision-making to national capitals. It also wants to replace the EU’s top court with an arbitration tribunal.

The plan calls for slashing and capping the EU budget, freezing staffing numbers and abolishing agencies. The AfD would use its veto power to scrap revenue from VAT and plastics taxes, and threaten to halt Berlin’s contributions to the common budget to force through the reforms it demands.

“If Brussels refuses the path of reform, this veto will be used to block future EU financing legislation and drastically reduce Germany’s contributions,” the AfD plan says.

The AfD also wants to give larger eurozone economies more voting power at the European Central Bank — giving Germany a say in monetary policy — and reject the digital euro.

World.title: Chancellor reveals Budget secrets early – but why?
World.content:
John Healey’s first budget is shrouded in secrecy so how come we know he won’t be touching capital gains tax?

Sam Coates and Anne McElvoy ponder whether the Treasury is worried about growth and discuss how Kemi Badenoch is trying to get the Conservatives on an economic front foot.

Plus, they pull apart the weekly polling numbers, and Sam’s got a story about the wait times for parents of special educational needs and disabilities (SEND) children.

World.title: Macron and Merz edge closer to a budget deal
World.content:
The Arctic is becoming a geopolitical battleground — and the EU wants a bigger role.

The European Commission is unveiling a new strategy focused on security, as Russia builds up its military presence, China explores new shipping routes, and Donald Trump’s Greenland ambitions raise tensions.

Also on the show, hosts Zoya Sheftalovich and Nick Vinocur discuss signs of progress in the EU’s long-term budget negotiations: Emmanuel Macron and Friedrich Merz appear to be finding common ground, while Kaja Kallas warns that proposed cuts could undermine Europe’s global influence.

And finally, could that designer handbag on Vinted be stolen? France investigates suspicious listings following a weekend of riots and looting.

World.title: French riots lay bare risks and opportunities for 2027 election candidates
World.content:
Police officers stand near a fire during an unauthorized demonstration marked by riots and clashes with law enforcement in Paris on Oct. 18, 2026. | Gauthier Bedrignans/Hans Lucas/AFP via Getty Images

PARIS — Looting and rioting across France over the weekend are threatening to reshape the contours of the French presidential race.

Far-right front-runner Marine Le Pen is seizing on the crisis to cast herself as the candidate of law and order, but there are risks for her too. Many voters see her as a highly divisive leader whose 2027 victory would only deepen the societal fault lines exposed by the riots.

Far-left firebrand Jean-Luc Mélenchon, widely tipped to challenge Le Pen in the second round next year, is also treading carefully as rivals accuse him of encouraging the rage on the streets that has morphed into pillaging and arson.

World.title: Power outage hits Google Cloud services disrupting UK banks
World.content:
A power outage at a Google Cloud data centre near London caused serious failures to services on Tuesday, the US technology giant said, as several UK banks reported widespread disruptions.

 

Google said in a service update that its Cloud services suffered an outage "due to a power event", adding that a full recovery was expected at around 1300 GMT on Tuesday.

Services for the digital bank Revolut, including withdrawals from ATMs, bank transfers and bank card top-ups, were disrupted, which a source close to the matter attributed to the Google Cloud failures.

UK lenders Lloyds and HSBC also confirmed customers were facing issues with their banking services.

Google said the incident began at 0608 GMT on Tuesday.

"Multiple Google Cloud services are experiencing elevated errors and intermittent network failures in europe-west2 region," Google said in an earlier update, referring to its London data centre.

Internet service tracker Downdetector indicated that hundreds of reports had been made of problems affecting other businesses, including the property website Rightmove and the Royal Mail postal service.

Lloyds said it was aware "some customers are having issues with our app and online banking".

HSBC confirmed that customers were experiencing "difficulties accessing our services" and said that it would "monitor the situation, which is also affecting other organisations".

A Revolut spokesperson said the bank was "working to fix the issue since it was identified" and offered its apologies "to anyone affected and for any inconvenience caused".

"We can confirm that all our customers' money and data are safe," the spokesperson added in a statement.

World.title: 'Everything is destroyed,' Paris pharmacy owner says after protests
World.content:
France was rocked by some of its worst rioting in recent years on Saturday, just six months before the country elects a successor to President Emmanuel Macron.

 

Images of clashes and public buildings set on fire or vandalised circulated around the world, prompting several countries, including the United States, China and Germany, to issue travel advisories for their citizens in France.

And closer to home there has been anger among locals after it emerged that at least 3,000 shops across the country had been vandalised or looted.

“The scale of the damage is immense. Everything is destroyed, everything. I have no stock left, they burned it all,” Odelia, a pharmacy owner in Paris, told Euronews.

“I don't even understand how someone could set on fire the building when there are homes above it.”

“They behaved like animals. They ripped out my water heater. They tore down my light fixtures. Is this how you protest the high cost of living?”

Meanwhile, France will impose new curfews in areas where needed on Tuesday, Prime Minister Sébastien Lecornu said, adding that the measures introduced in several cities the previous day had "helped keep the night calm".

Under pressure, the government scheduled another series of emergency meetings on Tuesday, including talks involving representatives of major social media platforms.

World.title: Airbnb introduces weather protection that will pay out if it rains too much on your holiday
World.content:
With the clocks set to go back this weekend, dark, miserable nights are drawing in for most of us.

 

Our only hope for escape (aside from the seasonal depression-busting daylight lamps) is an actual escape for a spot of winter sun.

Imagine you go all that way in search of Vitamin D and to swim in the sea only for it to rain the entire time. Heartbreaking.

It would undoubtedly feel like a waste of money (why didn’t I just stay at home?) – but this new announcement from Airbnb could lessen the blow somewhat.

The holiday home rental company is now offering optional weather protection insurance that will payout travellers on days it rains during their trip.

“Rain can cast a shadow over a trip guests have been looking forward to, but it shouldn't define it,” Justin Brouse, Airbnb’s director for strategic partnerships, AirCover and insurance, said.

“We're excited to work with Chubb to introduce weather protection, so guests can get value back when it rains spending less time dealing with a disruption and more time enjoying their trip.”

How Airbnb’s weather protection works

Airbnb guests who live in Austria, Denmark, France, Germany, Italy, Ireland, the Netherlands, Poland, Spain or Sweden will have the option to add on weather protection when booking.

The policy covers both domestic and international trips, although it isn’t available for trips in every country.

Underwritten by Chubb, the policy will have a daily payout of between €50 and €1,000 if there is rain of at least 1.5 mm in an hour between 8 am and 8 pm at your Airbnb stay’s location for the minimum number of hours shown in your insurance policy. The number of hours, and payout, will vary from country to country.

The rain monitoring is automatic and is taken from sources such as NASA, the European Centre for Medium-Range Weather Forecasts (ECMWF) and the National Oceanic and Atmospheric Administration (NOAA), so you won’t need to submit evidence for a claim, you’ll just be notified if you can make one.

Other options for weather-related insurance

Founded in 2022, WeatherPromise also offers insurance that covers your trip if it rains.

Working on a similar premise, the policy will payout automatically if it rains more than the specified amount agreed upon.

All you need to do is enter the hotel address where you are staying, the dates of the trip, and the covered amount, i.e. the cost of the trip.

World.title: Lisbon police arrest 55 housing protesters and clear Rossio tent camp
World.content:
Protesters who in recent days have been camping in the centres of Lisbon and Porto to demand the right to housing were forced to remove their tents and banners after the authorities intervened.

 

Just before 06:00 local time (07:00 CEST) on Tuesday morning, police vans arrived at Rossio and Praça D. João I and gave demonstrators five to ten minutes to bring the protest to an end. Police said the gatherings were no longer legal. In the capital, there was resistance to the order to disperse, with protesters forming a human chain. Objects were even thrown at officers from the Public Security Police (PSP), who resorted to using batons.

In a forceful operation, the PSP Special Unit expelled all protesters from Rossio Square. Police said they arrested 55 people and seized 228 camping structures. Protesters said about 30 demonstrators were injured and arrested.

Some of the protesters moved on to Praça da Figueira, where they continued to voice anger at the police action, demanding the return of their belongings and the release of those detained.

More than a hundred protesters sang “Grândola, Vila Morena”, the anthem of the 25 April 1974 Revolution that restored democracy in Portugal, and threatened to occupy the home of Prime Minister Luís Montenegro.

In Praça D. João I in Porto, the operation unfolded more calmly, with no clashes reported and the dozens of people camping there leaving of their own accord. There was some initial resistance as officers approached, but the orders were eventually obeyed.

The Porto protesters say they want to return to Praça D. João I and, in response, police have started installing metal barriers to block access to the square.

With the squares in Lisbon and Porto now cleared, cleaning operations are under way.

Staying on site

The lawyer representing the protesters has said they may stay on at the site where they have been holding demonstrations since last Saturday.

“I think so, yes,” the lawyer replied, quoted by the newspaper Observador.

The legal representative stressed that he cannot speak on behalf of everyone present and said that, for now, all that remains is “to wait” to find out the physical condition of those detained and how their belongings can be returned.

The group voted unanimously, in a Popular Assembly, to remain in Praça da Figueira until the whereabouts of their detained colleagues are known.

“The individuals taken into custody were brought to police facilities and will be brought before the competent judicial authority as soon as possible,” the police said in a statement.

New protest planned

Meanwhile, a new protest has been scheduled for Rossio Square in Lisbon, starting at 19:00 local time on Tuesday.

The organiser of the Popular Assembly, quoted by Observador, underlined the need to draw more people to this demonstration and to those planned for the coming days.

Despite this morning’s police operation, the activist insists that the movement will not slow down until all its members have a home to live in.

World.title: Fireworks, petrol bombs and water cannon as unrest escalates in Albania
World.content:
Violent clashes erupted in Albania’s capital, Tirana, on Monday as protesters threw Molotov cocktails, fireworks and stones at police, who responded with water cannon.

 

Demonstrators also set rubbish bins on fire as riot police advanced through the streets. The unrest comes amid months of anti-government protests fuelled by anger over corruption, demands for better university conditions and calls for Prime Minister Edi Rama to resign.

Rama accused demonstrators of crossing a “red line”, saying protests were a right but violence was a crime. Authorities said around 300 people had been injured in the clashes, more than half of them police officers.

World.title: France arrests man believed to be connected to town hall fire in Limoges
World.content:
French security forces arrested a man on Tuesday believed to be connected to the ultra-left over the burning down of a historic town hall in central France during rioting at the weekend on the sidelines of nationwide protests.

 

Anti-terror police have also been called in to investigate the suspected arson on the town hall in the central city of Limoges, a building dating back to 1883 whose roof and belfry collapsed when it was engulfed by fire on Saturday.

The destruction of the building has become a symbol of the violent rioting that erupted on the margins of a day of protests on Saturday that were called in a show of anger against grievances including the rising cost of living and conditions in schools.

The scenes of the building collapsing as it was hit by fire also brought back memories in France of the April 2019 fire that ravaged Notre-Dame cathedral in Paris which investigators believe started by accident but horrified the country.

The man, believed to be aged 40, was arrested by officers from the specialised RAID police unit in the nearby town of Val d'Issoire, the office of the Limoges prosecutor said.

In this image taken from Lucas Destrem's video flames engulf the 19-century City Hall in Limoges, 17 October, 2026 AP Photo

He had previously been flagged as someone requiring surveillance as a potential threat and is linked to ultra-left movements, a source close to the case said.

Meanwhile, France's Counter-Terrorism Sub-Directorate (SDAT), a branch of the judicial police, has been called in to investigate the case further, another source close to the case added, asking not to be named.

French Justice Minister Gérald Darmanin said late on Monday that anti-terror prosecutors would soon decide whether to investigate the incident as a suspected terror attack.

"If they take up the case, it means it is a terrorist act, implying that certain individuals, notably from the far left, clearly organised this destruction of the town hall," Darmanin told French TV channel TF1.

The right-wing mayor of Limoges, Guillaume Guerin, has lambasted the response by police, who he said "lacked the necessary resources" and "backed down" in the face of rioters.

Policemen patrol during an overnight curfew in Paris, 20 October, 2026 AP Photo

He called on the government to "inject millions" to rebuild the town hall, adding that "the state has failed." Prime Minister Sebastien Lecornu is due to visit Limoges on Friday, his office said.

Around 5,000 people, including 700 individuals described by the authorities as "radicalised and extremely violent," took part in the demonstration in Limoges on Saturday.

Some 7,000 people then took part in a protest to denounce the violence on Sunday evening.

World.title: Neanderthal remains dating back 46,000 years identified in Abauntz cave, Navarra
World.content:
An international team has identified the first Neanderthal remains in Navarre. They are six bone fragments recovered during previous campaigns in the Abauntz cave which, according to the analyses, belonged to a man who lived around 46,000 years ago.

 

The discovery was presented on Monday (19 October) at an event led by the president of the Government of Navarre, María Chivite.

The assemblage includes three metacarpal bones and a middle phalanx from the right hand of an adult individual. These are joined by two other fragments that have been identified as human through protein analysis. Genetic studies confirm that the remains come from a male Neanderthal.

Some of the bones preserve carnivore bite marks; those traces offer clues about what happened to the body after the individual’s death and how the bones ended up inside the cave.

The fossils were found in an archaeological context with stone tools and animal remains, some showing signs of having been processed and eaten by the human groups that occupied the cavity. That context helps to situate Neanderthal presence at Abauntz and to understand what activities were carried out there.

Archaeological excavation in the area where the bones were found Gobierno de Navarra

A Neanderthal in Navarre that fills a gap in the western Pyrenees

Until now, there were no fossils that could directly confirm that Neanderthals passed through this area.

"For the first time we have human remains that allow us to directly identify the presence of Neanderthals in Navarre," explains Andion Arteaga, who co-directs the project, in a press release issued by the team.

The date matters.Forty-six thousand years ago Neanderthals were still living in different parts of Europe. A few millennia later, around 40,000 years ago, the species disappeared from the continent, in a period also marked by the expansion of Homo sapiens.

The location of Abauntz adds further interest, as the cave lies in a natural corridor connecting the Iberian Peninsula with the rest of Europe, making it a good place to study mobility and possible contacts between human groups on both sides of the Pyrenees.

Ancient DNA and direct dating

Recovering ancient DNA from remains tens of thousands of years old is not common. Genetic material degrades over time and its preservation depends on the conditions in which the fossils have remained.

The team has combined palaeoproteomics, genetic analyses and radiocarbon dating to identify the bones, determine the individual’s sex and establish their chronology precisely. This work is being carried out together with the University of Vienna and the Max Planck Institute for Evolutionary Anthropology in Leipzig. The clearest precedent is El Sidrón, in Asturias, where genetics has shed light on kinship, social organisation and the evolutionary history of Neanderthals.

"Being able to recover ancient DNA and obtain direct dates for the fossils is particularly significant," stresses Mikel Arlegi, also co-director of the project.

Genetic analyses are ongoing and could provide more information about the evolutionary history and demographic dynamics of these populations.

Reconstruction of the hand incorporating the original bones Iphes-Cerca

The research originated at the Institut Català de Paleoecologia Humana i Evolució Social (Iphes-Cerca), based in Tarragona, which remains involved through Lucía López-Polín, Andreu Ollé and Aitor Burguet. The project is co-directed by Arteaga, from the Centre for New Technologies at the University of Warsaw and associated with Iphes-Cerca, and Arlegi, a postdoctoral researcher at the Musée de l'Homme in Paris.

The team brings together more than 25 specialists from different disciplines and institutions, including the National Centre for Research on Human Evolution (CENIEH) and the Institute of Archaeology of Mérida (IAM, CSIC–Government of Extremadura).

The project is supported by the Government of Navarre, through the Directorate-General for Culture–Príncipe de Viana Institution, by the Council of the Ultzama Valley, the Arraitz-Orkin local council and the Palarq Foundation. Members of the team taking part in the new excavation campaign, which is still under way in the cave, also attended the presentation event.

World.title: Albania's PM Edi Rama blames 'hybrid war' for fuelling unrest across the country
World.content:
Albanian Prime Minister Edi Rama blamed a "hybrid war" for fuelling unrest in his country on Tuesday, after a week of violent anti-government demonstrations in the capital Tirana.

 

Demonstrators have repeatedly clashed with police since Tuesday as months of protests escalate, driven by fresh demands for better university conditions, anger over corruption and renewed calls for Rama's resignation.

During the demonstrations, which have drawn thousands, police have regularly used water cannon, tear gas and rubber bullets to disperse crowds that have targeted government buildings and smashed stores in several parts of the capital.

Protesters have hurled stones, petrol bombs and fireworks at police.

Around 300 people have been injured in the clashes, more than half of them police, according to authorities.

On Tuesday, Rama repeated earlier accusations that "foreign actors" were to blame for the violence, previously accusing both Russia and Iran of driving online misinformation.

"This has now been recognised and is becoming a major issue across Europe," he said in a statement broadcast live while visiting the education ministry.

Albania's Prime Minister Edi Rama speaks during the United Nations General Assembly in New York, 25 September, 2026 AP Photo

"It is a hybrid war that gains traction precisely because it is rooted in genuine grievances, not mere fantasy," the prime minister added, citing the rising cost of living, housing affordability and concerns for the future.

He also hinted at a possible ban on social media for children under 16 and flagged changes to the age of criminal responsibility.

Since protests began, high school students have also attended protests alongside their university counterparts, with police and authorities regularly condemning the involvement of minors in violence.

On Tuesday morning, hundreds of university professors marched in solidarity with the demonstrators to condemn police violence targeting students, according to an AFP reporter.

Carrying a banner reading "Stop violence against students", the marchers called for Rama to resign.

Riot police respond during clashes at an anti-government protest in Tirana, 19 October, 2026 AP Photo

The week-long demonstrations have badly damaged several government buildings, including the education ministry, which remains a focal point.

The anti-government protests in the Balkan nation began over a controversial resort development in an ecologically protected area linked to US President Donald Trump's family.

But anger over the development has morphed into a broader push against corruption amid ongoing demands that Rama step down.

World.title: Shipping attacks threaten Turkey's resolve to keep warships out of Black Sea
World.content:
A wave of deadly attacks on cargo ships in the waters of NATO members Bulgaria and Romania has jolted the alliance into calling an emergency meeting on Black Sea security. Yet any move to send NATO ships hinges on Turkey reversing its steadfast refusal to allow warships into the Black Sea.

Advertising

Thursday saw two chemical tankers struck by drones close to a Romanian port.

It follows two similar attacks in Bulgarian waters in the past week. More than 20 sailors have been killed or remain missing.

“The war has come in full force to the Black Sea now,” said Yoruk Isik, a maritime analyst who runs the Istanbul-based Bosphorus Observer consultancy. “With the change in technology compared to the beginning of the war, drones really disrupted maritime traffic.”

According to Isik, the latest attacks underscore the growing spread of the conflict between Russia and Ukraine. “Russian ports and Ukrainian ports are heavily targeted, but now even in NATO waters ships are getting hit, in Bulgarian waters, Romanian waters.

“We are at a point where there is no safe place.”

The latest strikes targeted vessels along a key Ukrainian shipping route, casting Russia as NATO’s prime suspect as Moscow intensifies its assault on Ukrainian trade.

After meeting on Thursday with the leaders of Bulgaria and Romania, both NATO members, Secretary-General Mark Rutte said the military alliance would “continue to work closely with our allies in the Black Sea, adjusting our deterrence and defence posture as needed”.

Romanian President Nicușor Dan said NATO would hold a crisis meeting next week to discuss the situation.

Gatekeeper to the Black Sea

NATO could deploy air defence systems against drones to protect Bulgarian and Romanian waters.

But any deployment of naval ships will depend on NATO member Turkey, which controls access to the Black Sea through the Turkish Straits under a long-standing international treaty, the 1936 Montreux Convention.

Since Russia invaded Ukraine in February 2022, Ankara has blocked entry of Russian and Ukrainian warships or military vessels belonging to NATO members without a Black Sea coast, arguing for a diplomatic solution.

In recent weeks the Turkish government has sought to broker a ceasefire on commercial shipping, without success. Isik claims that failure, coupled with the latest escalation in attacks, is increasingly calling into question Ankara’s reliance on diplomacy alone.

“Either they’re going to have a breakthrough and the Kremlin is going to de-escalate, or Ankara is going to accept the reality that there needs to be a more credible force here – bigger vessels have to come,” the analyst said.

He pointed out that the navies of Romania and Bulgaria are not equipped to handle such an operation alone, with Cold War-era ships nearing the end of their lifespan.

“So Turkey's engagement is key to any successful NATO planning in the Black Sea.”

Russian leverage

Despite Turkish-owned cargo ships coming under attack in recent weeks, and Turkey’s deep reliance on Black Sea trade, Ankara has so far kept its powerful navy on the sidelines.

International relations expert Huseyin Bagci, of Ankara’s Middle East Technical University, says Turkey fears an escalation in the conflict and will be wary of allowing NATO ships into the Black Sea.

“I do not think the government would dare,” said Bagci. “Probably the government considers this a provocation to drag Turkey into the war... Turkey is afraid of getting involved in the Black Sea against Russia, this is somehow a trauma in the Turkish mind.”

Moscow also retains powerful leverage over Ankara, he suggested.

Russia’s state nuclear company Rosatom is about to complete a multi-billion-dollar nuclear power station in Akkuyu, southern Turkey. Ankara sees it as vital to the drive to reduce its heavy dependence on imported energy. “It is illogical to oppose Russia now while you let the Russians complete the nuclear plant,” said Bagci.

Erdogan hints at larger nuclear partnership with Russia, unsettling Turkey's allies

Ankara also knows that letting NATO vessels in while barring Russian warships could provoke Moscow into contesting Turkey’s prized status as the gatekeeper to the Black Sea.

However, retired Turkish diplomat Selim Kuneralp, an expert on the Montreux Convention, warns Turkey’s control over Black Sea access is likely already in Russian President Vladimir Putin’s sights.

“This has probably had an impact on Russia’s ability to conduct the war, and I doubt that Putin is very happy with the situation,” said Kuneralp. “So if he were to win the war, there is a very strong risk that he will take the initiative of saying: ‘this is unacceptable and we want to have free passage of warships from now on, regardless of whether there is a war’.”

As a signatory, Moscow has the right to call for a revision of the Montreux Convention every five years.

For centuries, Russia fought repeated wars with the then Ottoman Empire for control of the Turkish Straits. In the early years of the Cold War, even Joseph Stalin tried his hand, but the United States intervened and thwarted him.

Now Ankara walks a tightrope between Moscow and its NATO partners to avoid a resurrection of those historical rivalries.
