World.title: Germany: Google must have consent to publish property images
World.content:
A court in the western German state of Hesse has said Google is "spying" on people and has no right to publish information about their property on its Maps and Earth sites. The case stems from images taken from the air.

A state court in Hesse, Germany, has ruled in favor of a Frankfurt man who sued US tech giant Google over the publication of images on Google Earth and Google Maps that he argued invaded his privacy.

The man had previously sued to have images of his Frankfurt home and property scrubbed from Google's Street View site as well as from Apple Look Around.

Resistance to Google Street View has resulted in homes being scrubbed from the site as well as attacks on cars and cameras Image: Gelhot/Fotostand/picture alliance

Court finds privacy rights were violated

The court found that Google had infringed on the privacy of the man and his family by publishing aerial images of their property on Google Earth, saying: "Nobody must accept the worldwide publication of aerial images of their property without their consent, at least when concerning areas of a property hidden from public view."

"The plaintiff's personal space extends across the whole of the home's parcel. The only data to be gleaned here are personal, giving clues to private lifestyle, such as the size and design of the property. Beyond this, potential weak points in the property's security perimeter are also laid bare."

The court also accused Google of acquiring the images by "spying" because it does not notify property owners that their properties will be filmed.

The court additionally found that although Google says it contributes to the democratization of knowledge, it nevertheless has no right to invoke freedom of information to justify invading private spaces.

The ruling may still be appealed.

Edited by: Louis Oelofse

World.title: North Korean workers treated as 'slaves' at Russian drone factory, says new report
World.content:
A new report reveals the plight of North Korean workers at a drone factory in Russia. It also raised concerns that Pyongyang could gain hands-on knowledge of advanced weapons systems through the workers it sends there.

As many as 12,000 North Koreans working at a Russian drone factory are victims of "gross human rights abuses and human trafficking," according to a new report.

The figures were part of a joint report published on October 14 by the Washington-based Center for Strategic and International Studies (CSIS) and the Dallas-based George W. Bush Institute. It analyzes how Russia, North Korea, China and Iran are involved in expanding unmanned aerial vehicle (UAV) production at the Yelabuga plant in Tatarstan, and what each country stands to gain.

While Moscow gets access to more than 5,500 drones a month for its war against Ukraine, China benefits from being the main supplier of dual-use components, including batteries, internal electronics, engines and navigation systems.

Iran has supplied Russia with Shahed drones, which has helped Moscow produce upgraded domestic variants, known as Geran.

Meanwhile, North Korea is earning money by retaining as much as 90% of the wages of the laborers, the report stated.

"The geographical locations of these four countries… means that any kind of international interdiction is impossible," Dan Pinkston, a professor of international relations at the Seoul campus of Troy University, told DW.

North Korea gains critical intel by aiding Russia in Ukraine To view this video please enable JavaScript, and consider upgrading to a web browser that supports HTML5 video

Russia and North Korea defy UN resolutions

The joint report says Russia and North Korea are defying United Nations Security Council Resolution 2397, of December 2017 , which requires any UN member state to send North Korean workers home within two years.

"The North Korean regime… is selling the labor of its citizens under a state-to-state arrangement, controlling whether they may leave and collecting most of their wages," it said. This, according to the report, "is the definition of forced labor."

Song Young-Chae, a Seoul-based academic and human rights activist with the Worldwide Coalition to Stop Genocide in North Korea, says Pyongyang is "effectively conducting slavery of its own people and for its own profit."

"This is just a terrible situation, and we know that it is not happening only at Yelabuga," he told DW. "We know there are construction workers in the occupied Ukrainian territories, North Koreans in lumber camps and, of course, tens of thousands of soldiers have been sent to fight — and die — on the front lines in Ukraine," Song added.

"Life in North Korea is not easy, but these people are being sent to Russia as slaves, with no freedom, and they are only allowed to keep a fraction of the money they earn," he said.

The challenge, he admits, is to find a way to halt this "trade in humanity."

North Korea expands role in Russia's war with Ukraine To view this video please enable JavaScript, and consider upgrading to a web browser that supports HTML5 video

How much can realistically be done?

"These countries share a border, so it is easy to transport workers, and no other agency can intervene," Song said. "Russia and China are both permanent members of the UN Security Council but are ignoring its resolutions on this issue. There is very little that can be done."

Song's rights organization is attempting to highlight the plight of North Korean workers and to create a "coalition of like-minded nations and agencies" to protect laborers — although he admits to being "pessimistic."

Pinkston shares those concerns, as well as fears over the emergence of a powerful bloc that appears to be "ripping up the post-World War II order on the rule of law and human rights" and is intent on taking a confrontational approach to other nations.

The weapons being manufactured at Yelabuga will assist in achieving those aims, he said.

"UN Security Council resolutions on North Korean workers, on weapons proliferation, on the sale of dual-use technologies are all being ignored, so I think we can say that the UN's sanctions regime is pretty much dead," Pinkston added.

North Korea developing its drone capabilities

It is clear that both Russia and Ukraine have gained important insights into the modern battlefield through their ongoing conflict, Pinkston said, with the emergence of drone technology arguably one of the most critical advances.

"And like everyone else, North Korea has been watching closely, 'learning-by-doing' and innovating its own drone capabilities," Pinkston said, adding that there are "serious implications" for the South Korean military as it also attempts to keep up its defensive capabilities against a new generation of drones in the North.

Why Russia and North Korea can't quit each other (for now) To view this video please enable JavaScript, and consider upgrading to a web browser that supports HTML5 video

To curb the deployment of North Korean laborers to Russia and the proliferation of weapons, the joint report calls on the US State Department to work with other countries to disrupt human trafficking networks and sanction those responsible.

It also urges the UN to work multilaterally to investigate the Yelabuga complex and to catalogue the abuses that have taken place. Moreover, it demands accountability for those who have carried out abuses and for victims to be protected.

The report adds that foreign companies that are operating as part of the Yelabuga special economic zone — there are "several" European companies and at least one US firm with a presence at the site — should be pressured to leave.

Edited by: Emmy Sasipornkarn

World.title: Why US investors are snapping up Germany's famed Mittelstand
World.content:
Increasing amounts of US capital are flowing into Germany's traditional industrial firms and family-owned businesses. As many business owners struggle to find successors, more companies are becoming acquisition targets.

What do the long-established German companies Birkenstock, Viessmann, Linde and ebm-papst have in common? All have fallen into American hands.

Traditional German family-owned businesses and small-to-medium-sized enterprises (SMEs) have become increasingly attractive to US companies and investors.

Last year, US investors were involved in 76 acquisitions and investments in German industrial and manufacturing companies, according to an analysis by financial data provider PitchBook. The transactions were valued at about $29.5 billion (€26.3 billion) in 2025, nearly double the 2022 total. As of August 19, 2026, the figure stood at $23.9 billion.

No successor, but an investor instead

"From what we are seeing in the market, the interest from US investors in German companies is definitely still there," said Samar-Ahmad Albrecht-Mahmood of Veracity Capital Investments, which advises companies looking to invest in Germany.

German companies, particularly those in the industrial and manufacturing sector, remain attractive, "because many of them are highly specialized, have strong customer relationships and very good technical know-how," he told DW. "In many cases, these are businesses that have built up a strong position in their niche over decades."

At the same time, many German business owners are reaching an age where they are thinking about selling their business, Albrecht-Mahmood underscored, pointing out that "there is often no successor within the family."

"This brings companies onto the market that might not have been available for sale a few years ago," he said.

Notable takeovers this year include ebm-papst, the Mulfingen-based manufacturer of electric motors and fans, which was bought by US company Madison Air for $5.4 billion in August.

In June, the long-established Augsburg-based company Everllence, formerly MAN Energy Solutions, was sold to Bain Capital, with the US investment firm acquiring a 51% stake in the company.

Fewer acquisitions, but more investments

According to Die Deutsche Wirtschaft (DDW), a German business information network focused on the Mittelstand (medium-sized and family-owned companies), no country owns more German firms than the United States. Of the total 7,861 companies identified in the database "German Companies Under Foreign Ownership," 1,750 are currently held by US investors.

Young startups — Germany's next tech champions? To view this video please enable JavaScript, and consider upgrading to a web browser that supports HTML5 video

PricewaterhouseCoopers (PwC), one of the world's leading auditing and consultancy organizations, also underscored the growing US investor interest in acquiring German companies. In a report, titled Destination Germany, PwC said that while the number of acquisitions and equity investments has not increased, the financial volume of the deals has jumped.

The report highlighted, in particular, the acquisition of BASF Coatings by the US investment firm Carlyle, in partnership with the Qatar Investment Authority (QIA), for around €7.7 billion.

The deal was struck on October 26, 2025, and closed on June 30 of this year.

Waiting for reforms

According to a recent survey by the American Chamber of Commerce in Germany, about 62% of the US companies active in the country are expecting business conditions to improve over the next three to four years.

Meanwhile, some 52% of them are planning to expand their operations in Germany, up from 49% in 2024.

Where are all of Germany's inventors? To view this video please enable JavaScript, and consider upgrading to a web browser that supports HTML5 video

At first glance, however, the increase in US acquisitions and equity investments does not seem to align with the decline in US investment flows to Germany last year.

According to the Bundesbank, significantly less investment capital flowed from the US to Germany in 2025 than in the previous year.

While foreign direct investment in Germany has risen overall — from €57.4 billion in 2024 to a total of €86.1 billion last year — investment from the US amounted to only €11.8 billion, nearly 44% less than in 2024.

In contrast, investment from the United Kingdom rose to around €26 billion.

"I would say the trend is continuing, although perhaps not simply in terms of higher deal numbers every year," Albrecht-Mahmood said. "The general interest in good German industrial companies, especially strong Mittelstand businesses, remains high."

Relatively low valuations also play a role, the expert argued. "Compared to the US, we still see situations where German companies are valued more moderately, particularly in the SME segment. This can make acquisitions quite attractive for international buyers."

This article was originally written in German.

World.title: Brutal, revolutionary empire builder: Genghis Khan's legacy
World.content:
Berlin is host to a major exhibition on the founder of the Mongol Empire and his successors. Here's how Genghis Khan disrupted the course of history.

Genghis Khan is one of history's most radical figures. A blood-thirsty invader whose conquests caused the deaths of an estimated 40 million people, he was also a visionary political thinker who established the largest contiguous land empire in history.

The founder of the Mongolian Empire died in 1227. Ahead of the 800th anniversary of his death, Berlin's James-Simon-Galerie explores his legacy and the "Mongol Century" (1250–1350) in the exhibition "Genghis Khan and the World of the Mongols ."

The power of a disruptive individual

The ruler remains "incredibly relevant" to this day, says Matthias Wemhoff, the director of the exhibition project.

"What the era of Genghis Khan — the 'Mongol century,' if you will — vividly demonstrates is how quickly established structures can collapse, how rapidly vast empires can vanish from the map and how swiftly the entire landscape can be utterly transformed," the archaeologist tells DW.

The charismatic leader's unprecedented impact on the world also evokes present-day disruptive individuals who are triggering sudden, unpredictable societal shifts, says Wemhoff: "There's always been this question: Are world politics shaped by individuals or rather by groups and sociological processes?"

In this case, the answer is clear, says the museum director, who also co-wrote a 2026 book on the nomadic leader.

"If Genghis Khan hadn't existed, the course of world history would truly have been entirely different — so much of it is inextricably linked to his person," Wemhoff says.

Genghis Khan is revered in Mongolia as the founding father of the nation who united the warring steppe tribes. This statue is in the Parliament Building in the country's capital, Ulan Bator Image: Mark Ralston/AFP/Getty Images

The founder of the world's largest empire

Genghis Khan was born as Temujin around the year 1162. His father, a Mongol chieftain called Yesugei, died when he was still a child. His family was abandoned by its tribe. To secure his familial position, Temujin killed his older half-brother, Bekter, when he was still a young teenager.

Thanks to his charismatic personality, he built alliances and found followers who helped him become the sole ruler on the Mongolian steppe. He formally adopted the title of Genghis Khan in 1206.

At its peak, the Mongol Empire covered approximately 24 million square kilometers (about 9.3 million square miles), stretching from China and Korea to parts of Eastern Europe and the Middle East, and accounting for over 16% of the Earth's total land area.

Nomadic culture, with yurt tents, traditional costumes and music instruments is celebrated here in Mongolia's 'Mongols Nomadic Winter Festival' Image: AFP

Wemhoff lists various innovations under his rule: For one, Genghis Khan transformed warfare. Commanders were promoted for skill, discipline and loyalty rather than based on aristocratic rank or tribal loyalties. Soldiers were organized into decimal units of 10, 100, 1,000 and 10,000.

Despite being illiterate by modern standards, he also pushed for the introduction of the first written script for the Mongolian language, which allowed to build a state bureaucracy, track population and tax registers, record decrees, issue legal decisions and handle diplomacy.

A set of laws were established that replaced fragmented tribal customs with a unified legal system.

Trade was simplified through his adoption of a paper currency.

A policy of religious freedom was also established across the Mongol Empire, allowing all individuals to practice their chosen faith without state coercion.

Before the Mongol Empire, the Silk Road was fragmented by local conflicts and heavy taxes. Mongol rule placed the entire route under a single authority, making long-distance travel vastly safer.

The 'paiza' acted as the world's earliest form of passport, granting official travelers protection and safe passage across Eurasia Image: Uuganbaatar Otgonbaatar/Chinggis Khaan National Museum, Ulaanbaatar

The Mongol Empire is known as a period of relative political stability, economic growth and cultural exchange, an era historians call the "Pax Mongolica."

But "it all came with incredible levels of cruelty. The millions of people who fell victim to the Mongols — the mass executions, the abuse of women — this happened on a scale previously unheard of," notes Wemhoff.

Shifting centers of power

The exhibition opens with a raid that happened after Genghis Khan's death, but took place just 260 kilometers (around 160 miles) away from Berlin: the 1241 Battle of Legnica, in Silesia, Poland.

It embodies the brutality and intensity of the Mongols' methods.

There came the "highly mobile, agile Mongols on small horses — lightly armored in lamellar gear, wearing helmets that left the face exposed, and wielding bows capable of firing 20 or more arrows in a single minute," points out Wemhoff.

European knights, heavily armored and mounted on large, massive warhorses, didn't stand a chance against their enemies.

"When a hail of arrows rained down on them, the horses eventually went down, and the knights ended up lying on the ground, stuck on their back, much like a June bug," he adds. "The two styles of combat were simply mismatched."

The Mongols also used deception to confuse and trap their opponents Image: Staatsbibliothek zu Berlin – Preußischer Kulturbesitz, Orientabteilung, Diez A fol. 71 S. 58

The Mongols' western campaigns shifted historic power centers in a way that still impacts world politics today.

For example, after the Mongol invasion of Kievan Rus', which was the first East Slavic state, its thriving capital Kyiv was reduced to a depopulated ruin. Moscow became a key regional power, partly because it chose to cooperate with the Mongols rather than pursue resistance.

"In our Western European collective memory, the Mongol invasion plays hardly any role. It's something of an anecdote," says Wemhoff, noting that the era of Genghis Khan and his immediate successors is barely mentioned in standard Western European school curricula.

Germans are mainly familiar with the name of the empire's founder through the 1979 Euro-disco pop band Dschingis Khan, which represented West Germany at the Eurovision Song Contest with a campy song of the same name that reduced complex history to extreme tropes.

But in eastern Europe, the Mongol invasions "changed everything fundamentally," says Wemhoff. "And so fundamentally that we still feel the consequences of it today."

The exhibition "Genghis Khan and the World of the Mongols" runs from October 21, 2026, to April 18, 2027.

Edited by Helen Whittle

World.title: French authorities impose partial curfews in Paris, Nice
World.content:
10/20/2026 October 20, 2026 Dott, Lime count losses after Paris protesters burn shared e-Bikes

Piles of e-bikes ​burnt amid protests around France Image: Jack Taylor/REUTERS

In Paris, sights of e-bikes thrown into burning piles became a common sight over the weekend, prompting bike makers Dott and Lime to asses their losses.

Shared mobility operator Dott, in a statement to Reuters on Monday, said that about 300 of its electric bikes were destroyed and 120 severely damaged in Paris, during the nationwide anti-government protests on Saturday. The company has about 6,000 bikes int he city.

Dott also said 80 vehicles, including bikes and scooters were destroyed in Bordeux and another 30-40 Scooters in Lyon. It estimates the damage at about €400,000 ($450,000).

Lime, another entity for shared electric bikes, said 6% of its Paris fleet was destroyed or damaged.

Ahead of demonstrations, Lime said it worked with the police to remove vehicles from designated protest routes and restricted parking or riding in high-risk areas.

Smovengo, operator ​of the Vélib' Métropole bike-sharing service in Paris, told Reuters that some 300 of its 20,000 bike fleet were damaged or stolen over the weekend.

E-bikes often use lithium-ion batteries that can ignite and produce intense fires and toxic smoke.

There was no indication that e-bike operators were specifically targeted during the protests. Rather, their ready availability likely played a role as protesters used them to build barricades or build fires.

World.title: Germany news: Investment summit draws billions in commitments
World.content:
Merz delivered an upbeat and humorous speech in a bid to attract investors Image: Fabian Sommer/dpa/picture alliance

Chancellor Friedrich Merzhas indulged in an abundance of the most common cliches about his country and compatriots while trying to portray Germany as the ideal place to do business at an investment summit.

"Germans are hardworking, going to bed early, rising before dawn," he told the domestic and international guests at the Invest in Germany Summit.

"Worst traffic is in the morning between 6 and 7," he said.

"On holidays, we are first on the beach, spreading towels before breakfast. If we agree on delivery dates, we stick to it. If you invite friends from Germany for dinner at 7, we will arrive at 6:58.

"We are reliable, predictable, precise, and unsurprising," the chancellor continued. "We are, in short, what investors like most."

Finance Minister Lars Klingbeil also used blunt humor in his appeal to potential investors, saying in his speech simply: "I want your money."

Both pitches appear to have succeeded, with investment commitments worth billions made at the summit.

World.title: Japan probe sets course for Mars moon
World.content:
The MMX spacecraft is on its way to Mars' moon Phobos to collect surface samples that could help answer long-standing questions about the formation of the Solar System.

A Japanese spacecraft successfully set off on a journey to one of Mars' moons late Monday in a race to become the first mission to return samples to Earth and potentially unlock the mysterious origins of the Solar System.

The uncrewed Martian Moons eXploration (MMX) mission is expected to reach Mars in August 2027. It will attempt to collect samples from Phobos, the larger of the planet's two moons, and deploy the German-French rover IDEFIX to explore the surface.

Pioneering mission heads to Mars moon — and back To view this video please enable JavaScript, and consider upgrading to a web browser that supports HTML5 video

The flagship H3 rocket carrying the MMX probe lifted off into a pitch-black sky from the Tanegashima Space Center at 4:41 a.m. local time (1941 GMT Monday), the Japan Aerospace Exploration Agency (JAXA) said.

Flight controllers burst into applause and jumped to their feet as the spacecraft blasted into space, shaking hands and embracing. Thousands of people tuned in to watch the livestream despite the early hour.

An hour later, JAXA announced that the probe had successfully separated from the H3 rocket and was "beginning its journey towards the Martian system."

"I'd dreamt of this day, so I'm incredibly happy," said JAXA scientist Mari Aida. "Right now I feel really relieved."

The agency also received signals from the spacecraft as expected, confirming it was operating normally.

Making way for science

Scientists hope the probe's discoveries will help lay the groundwork for eventual human exploration.

"The samples from MMX will bring forth paradigm-shifting science on the Mars system for generations to come, especially as NASA prepares to send the first humans to Mars," Nicky Fox, administrator of NASA's Science Mission Directorate, said in a message broadcast on the JAXA live stream.

The mission is a collaboration with US and European space agencies, as well as numerous universities and tech companies Image: Kyodo/REUTERS

JAXA also hopes the mission will reveal how Mars and its two moons formed, unlocking a key piece of knowledge about the formation of the Solar System.

One theory holds that Mars' two moons formed after a giant celestial body collided with the planet. Another hypothesis suggests the moons are asteroids captured by Mars' gravity. Confirming either theory would help scientists determine "how a habitable environment for life might have arisen on the terrestrial planets," JAXA said, referring to the four rocky planets closest to the sun.

Probe to reach destination in August 2027

The probe is due to arrive near Mars around August 2027, where it will orbit one of the planet's two natural moons, Phobos.

A French-German rover named IDEFIX, after the dog from the Asterix comic series, will be the first vehicle to travel across Phobos to conduct surface observations and help ensure a safe landing for the Japanese probe. It is no bigger than a microwave oven.

Once MMX arrives on Phobos, it will spend about two hours collecting at least 10 grams of material from the moon's surface before launching back into space. It will also study Mars' other natural moon, Deimos, during a series of flybys before leaving the Martian region in 2030.

Phobos, the larger of the two Martian moons, orbits the planet three times a day Image: JAXA/DLR/dpa/picture alliance

Another objective of the mission is to explore the possibility of using Phobos as a "natural space station" by establishing the requirements for a round trip.

Phobos is a lumpy, potato-shaped rock measuring about 22 kilometers (14 miles) across.

The mission, which aims to complete the first round trip to the Martian region, is a collaboration involving US and European space agencies along with several private technology companies.

US and Chinese space agencies have also been competing to become the first to return rock samples from the surface of Mars to Earth. NASA's Perseverance rover, which has been exploring the planet since 2021, has already collected samples. The return mission, however, was canceled by US President Donald Trump's administration after a congressional vote in January.

Edited by: Louis Oelofse

The Meitei villagers were cutting and transporting firewood when the alleged attack took place, Lhari Dorjee Lhatoo, a senior police official, told reporters.

Bordering Myanmar, Manipur is home to various ethnic communities. The hilly state has witnessed ethnic violence between its mostly Hindu Meitei majority and largely Christian Kuki minority since 2023 over economic benefits and job quotas.

World.title: El Supremo amnistía la malversación a Junqueras y tres exconsejeros con fuertes críticas al Constitucional
World.content:
El Tribunal Supremo ha aplicado la amnistía al exvicepresidente de la Generalitat Oriol Junqueras y a los exconsejeros Raül Romeva, Dolors Bassa y Jordi Turull. Dos semanas después de que el Tribunal Constitucional estableciera que la Sala Penal debió otorgar la medida de gracia al delito de malversación que atribuyó a los exdirigentes independentistas, el Supremo ha cumplido ese mandato y ha amnistiado a los cuatro antiguos miembros del Govern a los que juzgó y condenó por ese delito en 2019. La amnistía deja sin efecto la pena de inhabilitación que aún pesaba sobre ellos, por lo que los cuatro podrían ya presentarse a las próximas elecciones u ocupar un cargo público. En el auto en el que expone su decisión, el Supremo lanza al Constitucional un reproche insólito, por extenso y contundente. “Su innecesaria grandilocuencia revela el deseo de adornar un razonamiento invasivo del ámbito jurisdiccional que corresponde al Tribunal Supremo”, recalcan los jueces.

La decisión de la Sala Penal pone fin a una causa abierta hace nueve años que implicó el encarcelamiento preventivo de los principales encausados, entre ellos los cuatro ahora amnistiados, lo que, en pleno desafío secesionista, acabó siendo clave para neutralizar política y jurídicamente a la cúpula independentista. Desde entonces, el proceso ha vivido todo tipo de avatares, desde un juicio retransmitido en directo que acabó con condenas de hasta 13 años de cárcel, reformas penales para derogar el principal delito que se les atribuía (sedición), indultos y, finalmente, una amnistía completa que el Supremo ha frenado hasta que el Constitucional le ha obligado a aplicarla.

El indulto aprobado por el Gobierno en 2021 perdonó a Junqueras, Romeva, Bassa y Turull la pena de cárcel que les quedaba por cumplir, pero seguían teniendo una condena que les inhabilitaba hasta los años 2030 (Romeva y Turull) y 2031 (Junqueras y Bassa). La medida de gracia acordada ahora implica el olvido de todos los delitos que se les atribuyeron, lo que, además de dejar sin efecto la pena de inhabilitación, supone el borrado de los antecedentes penales. El Supremo ha acordado además poner en conocimiento del Ministerio de Justicia el auto de este martes para que elimine los antecedentes penales de los exconsejeros Joaquim Forn, Meritxell Borrás y Josep Rull y la expresidenta del Parlament Carme Forcadell, que no fueron condenados por malversación y, tras la reforma legal que eliminó el delito de sedición, solo estaban condenados por desobediencia, que ahora queda amnistiada.

La medida no afecta por ahora al expresidente Carles Puigdemont y sus exconsejeros Toni Comín y Lluís Puig, a quienes el magistrado Pablo Llarena levantó este lunes de forma definitiva las órdenes de detención e ingreso en prisión que les impedían volver a España sin riesgo de ser detenidos. Pero su amnistía definitiva tardará unos días más porque la decisión de Llarena es recurrible. Una ve que los recursos -si los hay- se resuelvan, el paso definitivo de aplicar la amnistía a Puigdemont, Puig y Comin corresponde al tribunal que juzgó, condenó y ahora ha amnistiado al resto de líderes independentistas a los que se atribuyó malversación.

De los siete magistrados que juzgaron el procés, actualmente solo tres están en activo: Manuel Marchena, Andrés Martínez Arrieta y Antonio del Moral. Ellos han suscrito el auto de este martes, en el que declaran extinguida la responsabilidad penal de Junqueras, Romeva, Turull y Bassa al asumir la doctrina acordada el pasado 6 de octubre por el Constitucional sobre la concesión de la amnistía a ese delito. Pero como ya hiciera Llarena este lunes, el tribunal dirige fuertes reproches al Constitucional, que consideró que el Supremo ha caído en una “drástica contradicción” y se ha distanciado del “sentido común” y de la “lógica” de la finalidad de la ley de amnistía sin un elemental “nexo de coherencia”.

Desde la izquierda, Raül Romeva, Dolors Bassa y Jordi Turull. Europa Press

Los magistrados del alto tribunal devuelven el envite y censuran que el Constitucional ha enriquecido su decisión con consideraciones “absolutamente innecesarias para el respaldo de lo resuelto”. “La corteza de esos vocablos, su innecesaria grandilocuencia revela el deseo de adornar un razonamiento invasivo del ámbito jurisdiccional que corresponde al Tribunal Supremo con expresiones llamadas a camuflar la intensidad de la injerencia”, añade el auto, del que ha sido ponente el expresidente de la Sala Penal, Manuel Marchena.

El Supremo se extiende en sus reproches para advertir que la sentencia suscrita por los siete magistrados del ala progresista del Constitucional encierra “una descalificación que alcanza a otros catorce magistrados que han defendido la interpretación que ahora se considera vulneradora del derecho a la tutela judicial efectiva”, en referencia a los cinco del tribunal de garantías que discreparon de esa decisión y los nueve del Supremo que se negaron a aplicar la medida de gracia a ese delito o rechazaron los recursos presentados por los condenados contra esa decisión. Para el alto tribunal, este “significativo” número de magistrados que han expresado su coincidencia con la tesis que ahora rechaza la mayoría del Constitucional “hace muy difícil aceptar con naturalidad la irracionalidad que se atribuye a la decisión recurrida”.

No es usual que una resolución del Supremo ni de ningún otro tribunal contenga críticas tan expresas y directas a las resoluciones de otro, aunque, en este caso, no se trate de un órgano jurisdiccional sino del tribunal de garantías. Pero dentro del Supremo, especialmente en la Sala Penal, muchos magistrados censuran desde hace años que el Constitucional se haya convertido en una especie de última instancia judicial que corrige decisiones del Supremo que no comparte la mayoría progresista, como ocurrió con la condena por malversación al expresidente andaluz José Antonio Griñán y otros ex altos cargos de la Junta o ha pasado ahora con la amnistía a los líderes del procés.

Los tres jueces que firman el auto tiran de paralipsis y, tras decir que no se trata de abordar “en una resolución de esta naturaleza” los efectos que está generando en el Supremo esa “interpretación extensiva” del Constitucional, se detienen a denunciar esta situación. “La mutación del tribunal de garantías constitucionales en una última instancia con capacidad revisora de la interpretación de cualquier norma jurídica suscrita por el Tribunal Supremo está desdibujando el diseño que quisieron los constituyentes de 1978 al definir las relaciones entre los jueces independientes, inamovibles, responsables ante la ley (art. 117.1 de la CE) y quienes sin esas garantías y durante un período temporal cerrado de 9 años se ocupan de preservar ‘las garantías constitucionales”, afirman.

“Para la historia han quedado”, explica el Supremo, “resoluciones del Tribunal Constitucional en las que se afirmaba -por cierto, de forma unánime- que ‘el respeto’ que, de manera general, ha de observarse en relación con las decisiones de los órganos judiciales adoptadas en el ámbito de la interpretación y de la aplicación de la legalidad ordinaria, ‘debe ser, si cabe, aún más escrupuloso cuando la resolución que se enjuicia es... del Tribunal Supremo a quien está conferida la función de interpretar la ley ordinaria”, recalca la sala citando sentencias de 1996, 1998 y 2001. El tribunal asegura que la resolución del Constitucional que otorgó el amparo a la exconsejera catalana Dolores Bassa, que es la que ha asentado la jurisprudencia que ha derivado en la aplicación de la amnistía a todos los condenados por malversación, no es interpretada por ellos como “la manifestación de un conflicto institucional con el Tribunal Constitucional, sino como una ruptura de este órgano con su propia jurisprudencia histórica”.

Esa sentencia “se aparta” también, según el Supremo, de precedentes en los que el tribunal de garantías afirmaba que ‘la balanza de la Justicia constitucional no puede inclinarse en ningún sentido para optar entre dos soluciones igualmente razonables sin interferir en el núcleo de la potestad de juzgar, cuya independencia de criterio proclama la Constitución, ya que el amparo no está configurado como una última instancia ni tiene una función casacional". El Supremo acusa incluso al Constitucional de apartarse “de su propia ley reguladora”, que impone “un deber de contención argumental en su art. 54″. “En él se dispone que ‘cuando la Sala o, en su caso, la Sección conozca del recurso de amparo respecto de decisiones de jueces y tribunales, limitará su función a concretar si se han violado derechos o libertades del demandante y a preservar o restablecer estos derechos o libertades, y se abstendrá de cualquier otra consideración sobre la actuación de los órganos jurisdiccionales”, advierte la Sala Penal.

World.title: “Repetí curso, pero también me saqué la oposición en dos años y medio y fui la número uno”
World.content:
La jueza que pide que se enseñe empatía en el colegio | Pensemos el mañana (Episodio 6)

Dakota Sampedro fue una de las juezas más jóvenes de España y Ana Rosales, la alumna más destacada en su provincia de la PEvAU de 2024. Ambas charlan sobre cómo la vocación no la determina ni la excelencia académica ni los baches en los estudios, y abogan por la práctica del debate y el fomento de la empatía en el colegio para evitar conflictos futuros

El testimonio de Dakota Sampedro (Gijón, 30 años) demuestra que una mala temporada académica puede quedar enterrada en la excelencia de una carrera: “Repetí curso, pero también me saqué la oposición en dos años y medio y fui la número uno de mi promoción”, explica. El motivo de su transformación tras ese complicado tercer curso de la ESO fue los ánimos de su familia y su propia voluntad. Y, sobre todo, que encontró una motivación, un propósito: el Derecho. En 2022 consiguió entrar en la Escuela Judicial, en una prueba cuya ratio es de aproximadamente 20 aspirantes por plaza. Y desde 2025 ocupa la plaza número 1 de la Sección Civil y de Instrucción del Tribunal de Instancia de Torrox (Málaga).

“Las buenas notas te pueden dar muchas herramientas y ayudar a abrir muchas puertas, pero no te dan la respuesta definitiva a qué vas a ser en la vida”

Su caso sirve de inspiración para Ana Rosales (Alcalá la Real, Jaén, 20 años), una estudiante de ADE y Derecho en la Universidad de Granada. Ambas historias tienen puntos en común: las dos fueron estudiantes muy aplicadas. Rosales llegó a ser la mejor nota de la PEvAU en la provincia de Jaén en 2024. Cuenta que fueron sus profesores los que le insuflaron confianza: “Se me brindaron todas las oportunidades y herramientas posibles”.

“Gracias a mis profesores entendí que también había lugar para la gente que se esfuerza diariamente y que pretende alcanzar la excelencia académica”

Rosales y Sampedro comparten en Pensemos el mañana, un proyecto de Fundación Unicaja y EL PAÍS para responder a los desafíos que presenta la educación, una reflexión sobre qué hace el sistema con personas como ellas, que persiguen (sin desistir) el mejor desempeño académico. Rememoran a esos docentes que las espolearon, reconocen que un buen expediente no exime de las dudas vocacionales y recogen todo lo que descubrieron en las incontables horas de estudio. “Aprendí sobre todo a conocerme a mí misma”, desvela Sampedro. Como profesional y mediadora, afirma que algunos de los problemas que llegan al juzgado se podrían minimizar desde las escuelas. “Deberían enseñar a respetar los derechos de los demás y valores como la responsabilidad, que tú sepas que tus actos tienen consecuencias”, precisa.

Pensemos la educación del futuro ‘Pensemos el mañana’, un proyecto de Fundación Unicaja, busca fomentar el conocimiento, los valores de la educación, un aprendizaje sostenible y responsable y dar respuestas a los grandes desafíos de la educación del futuro. El proyecto pivota sobre seis ejes: 1 Aprendizaje y sentido vital 2 Bienestar y salud mental 3 Futuro y empleabilidad 4 Sostenibilidad y sentido colectivo 5 Tecnología y ética 6 Carácter y ciudadanía ¿Qué está ocurriendo en estos tiempos de cambios profundos y transversales? ¿Cuáles son los grandes retos para afrontar la transformación que viene? ¿Qué educación necesitamos? Diferentes personalidades de todos los ámbitos nos ayudarán a responder a estas y otras preguntas destinadas a impulsar cambios, dinamizar ideas y apoyar propuestas con impacto pedagógico y social. ‘Pensemos el mañana’ es un proyecto inspirador para las futuras generaciones llamadas a conquistar nuevas cotas del saber en un mundo complejo y cambiante.

World.title: Amsterdam hopes 20km/h cycle lane limit will change behaviour
World.content:
Amsterdam city council has introduced an experimental speed limit of 20km/h for cyclists to see if riders can be persuaded to slow down.

Tourists, commuters and shoppers have all complained in recent years of feeling unsafe on the capital’s congested bike paths, but the only speed restriction is a 30 km/h limit for motor vehicles.

A temporary speed limit has been set on a section of Amstelveenseweg, one of the main routes into the city from the south, for four weeks to gauge its effect on cyclists’ behaviour.

But instead of enforcing the limit through fines and cautions, the city council has put up boards showing people how many of their fellow bike users are staying below 20 km/h, in the hope they will nudge people into being more considerate.

Traffic alderman Elise Moeskops told AT5 the idea of the experiment is to see if the signs will encourage a shift in cycling culture.

“If you enforce everything in the city you end up with a very harsh police state, and we don’t have the staff for that,” she said.

Infrastructure problems

“Are people prepared to cycle more slowly if we remind them that that’s an option? The question is what the social norm is on the cycle lane, because we don’t really know.”

But Kees Bakker, spokesman for the cyclists’ union Fietsersbond, was sceptical of the idea. He said better infrastructure was the solution to crowded bike lanes.

“The cycle lane on that road is very narrow and poorly laid out,” he told Dutch News. “There’s a busy pavement alongside it, so pedestrians spill over to the cycle path.

“It doesn’t make much difference if the speed limit is 20 km/h or 50 km/h, because the path is too narrow and there’s no room to overtake.”

Bakker said speed limits were likely to be less effective in bike lanes because not all cyclists travel at the same speed and they need space to overtake.

“Cars mostly drive in file at 30 km/h, but the range of speeds is much wider for cyclists,” he said. “Some of them ride at 15 km/h, others do 25 or even 30. There needs to be room to accommodate everyone, including people who want to coast along side by side at 15 km/h.”

World.title: Dutch destinations: Go back in time in eastern Drenthe
World.content:
Eastern Drenthe is perhaps the most underrated part of the Netherlands. Its rolling scenery, its history and its villages – low thatched farmhouses, tiny brick churches and woodlands – make it a perfect place to spend a few sunny autumn days.

Assen is the provincial capital. It has the region’s main museum and boasts the second-biggest department store in the Netherlands. It is also home to the Dutch TT circuit, offering a wide variety of motorcycle races from April to October. But the real charm of the region is in the countryside.

A weekend is not enough to take in everything, so here is a taster of what eastern Drenthe has to offer.

What to do

Visit the hunebedden

Eastern Drenthe is all about hunebedden, the Neolithic burial chambers built by the Funnel Beaker people over 5,000 years ago. Drenthe is home to 52 of the 54 known hunebedden in the Netherlands, and many are concentrated around Borger, where the national hunebed centre is based.

The biggest hunebed, with the not-so-romantic name D27, is located in the woods next to the visitors’ centre. The grounds are also home to a bizarre collection of zwerfstenen, or boulders, which were brought down to the province from Scandinavia by glaciers. Many of the stones have labels showing exactly where in Sweden or Norway they came from.

In addition, the centre has a café and a sort of Neolithic playground – the Prehistoric Park – where children can check out recreations of ancient homes. During peak season volunteers in costume are on hand to explain about the lives of people who lived in the region and demonstrate ancient crafts. No dogs.

Walk along the Hondsrug

The Hondsrug (literally “dog’s back”) is listed as a Unesco Global Geopark because of its unique history, deriving from the last two ice ages. This 70-kilometre-long glacial ridge made of sand and clay is the only one of its kind in Europe. There are dozens of walking and cycle trails to explore, as well as small museums, such as the De Nabershof working farm near Emmen. You can find out more about the region’s geology at the visitors centre, next to the hunebed centre in Borger.

Stroll around Orvelte

About 20 minutes south of Assen is Orvelte, a Drenthe village untouched by time, which has become a sort of open-air museum. It’s car-free – you park on the outskirts – but there is a horse-drawn “bus” if you have little ones with you who don’t want to walk.

Stroll past the thatched farmhouses, stop off for what we were told is the best apple pie in Drenthe, and check out the little museums – which seem to be based largely on the locals’ hobbies, such as collecting model cars and rare sheep.

There is a good sprinkling of shops, some of which sell tourist tat, but some are upmarket outlets selling wonderful antique pottery and glass, as well as clothes and bric-a-brac. Plenty of options for lunch and morning coffee. If you are into Christmas themes, Orvelte will transform into a Christmas village from December 18 to 20.

Catch up on history at the Drents Museum in Assen

The Drents Museum in the provincial capital Assen hit the headlines in 2025 when criminals broke in overnight and stole a number of priceless gold relics, most of which have since been recovered. There is no Romanian gold on show any longer – the current special exhibition is about Angkor in Cambodia – but the museum is well worth a visit to find out more about the history of the region.

It is heavy on the infotainment, so there’s plenty to keep the kids occupied, but the museum nevertheless has something for everyone. Located in several buildings linked by tunnels and overground walkways, the museum has Neolithic finds, art (a couple of Van Goghs), recreated stijlkamers (period rooms), temporary exhibitions and a fine café for lunch.

Go on a tree walk

The Boomkroonpad – treetop path – takes you from the roots of an oak tree up into the treetops, where you can walk along a very solid metal structure and admire the forest from above. The path is also the starting point for five forest floor walks, ranging from three to 16.5 kilometres, and there are plenty of organised activities for families – deer and mushroom spotting, for example – all year round.

Where to eat

All the attractions we visited had cafés for lunch, mainly selling standard-fare sandwiches and broodjes kroket. Assen has a good selection of cafés and restaurants for dinner. We ate at our hotel, Rikus, which uses local produce and offers three-, four- and five-course menus. Be warned: the portions are big as well as being delicious.

Where to stay

Rikus, a small hotel in the village of Eext, about 20 minutes from Assen and Borger, has an eclectic interior and big bedrooms with views over the countryside. As a couple we paid €331 for bed, breakfast, a three-course dinner and drinks.

There is a hotel and a quaint-looking B&B in Orvelte, and Assen is home to Hotel de Jonge, with a large café terrace in the heart of the old city. Drenthe is popular with Dutch holidaymakers, so, as you would expect, there are plenty of campsites and holiday parks to choose from as well.

Anything else

Unless you are big on cycling or long walks, you really need a car to get around the region. The attractions can get very busy at weekends in the summer months, which may well dent their charm. The Dutch TT Grand Prix takes place on the last Sunday in June.

World.title: Primary school teachers reject four-day week amid staff shortage
World.content:
School leaders in the Netherlands are opting against the idea of a four-day week for primary schools amid a critical shortage of teachers.

A survey conducted by Nu.nl and the Academy & Association of School Leaders (AVS) found that of 308 heads of schools, only three (less than 1%) said they had chosen to reduce required attendance days for pupils as a solution to the crisis.

Primary schools are short of roughly 5,800 teachers nationwide, about 6.3% of all teachers, according to research institute Centerdata.

Despite an increase in teacher numbers since 2024, when the shortage stood at 8.1%, low salaries and long hours remain a problem for enticing people to join the profession. The previous generation of teachers is also retiring, worsening the gap.

Leanne der Steeg, a policy advisor at AVS, told Nu.nl that a four-day school week does not necessarily help the teachers and can harm education.

“A four-day school week also brings ‘hassle’ with it,” she said. “It is not just a matter of sending a class home. Thought must be given to the missed teaching time. Will it be made up at another time, will homework be assigned, and what about children of working parents? And if you free up a teacher for a day by opting for a four-day school week, it requires preparation before they can stand in front of another class.”

World.title: Rail fares to go up by 4.7% next year to help pay for new trains
World.content:
Dutch national train operator NS is set to raise fares by almost 5% on average in 2027, exceeding the rate of inflation for the third year in a row.

The increases are needed “to purchase new, comfortable trains, pay for rising costs and keep investing in good services,” Daan Schut, the management board member responsible for fares, said in a press statement on Tuesday.

NS is offsetting the increase by offering bigger discounts on off-peak fares for passengers who buy in advance. The maximum reduction on so-called PrijsTijd deals will go up from 60% to 80% next year.

The company said it also wanted to discuss reviving the discounted summer subscription rate, which allowed passengers to travel off-peak and at weekends for €49 a month in July and August, rather than the regular fee of €127.50.

The Railrunner fare for children, which allows under-12s to travel across the country all day for a flat rate, is being frozen at €2.50, and the KidsVrij subscription for families, which gives free travel up to the age of 11, will stay unchanged.

The minimum fare for short journeys is going up to €3.10, while the supplement for the high-speed line between Schiphol and Rotterdam is rising by 20 cents to €3.40.

Rail passengers’ organisation Rover criticised the above-inflation rises, pointing to the success of the summer discount as proof that people will travel by train if it is an affordable option.

“Now that NS is finally seeing its passenger numbers growing, passengers are being punished with big ticket increases. By constantly using the maximum room that NS has to raise ticket prices, it is holding back further growth,” a Rover spokesperson said.

Fares have gone up by around 6.5% for each of the last two years, partly to correct the 1.5% rise in 2023, when inflation was 10%. In 2024 prices were frozen thanks to a government cash injection of €120 million.

NS made a profit for the first time in years in 2025, recording a net gain of €380 million, though most of this came from a recalculation of its access charges during the coronavirus pandemic, when fewer trains ran. The charges are the costs the company pays to use the track network.

World.title: Millions to get compensation from takeaway apps over hidden fees
World.content:

Food delivery apps Thuisbezorgd and Uber Eats have been forced to stop hiding fees and advertising fake discounts after a complaint by consumer watchdog Consumentenbond.

Millions of customers will also receive a payout voucher in compensation ranging between €5 to €30, the watchdog said.

The companies were putting “small order fees” and other surcharges only at the end of orders, and were advertising misleading discounts for some takeaways.

The Consumentenbond accused Thuisbezorgd in July of hiding charges that often added €2 to €4 to an order. Fake discounts were also show; in one example, Indian snacks priced at €3.75 were later shown as “reduced” from €7.50 to €6.

Both companies told news agency ANP the changes followed “constructive” talks with the Consumentenbond. Uber Eats had already adjusted its charges in June.

World.title: Children of welfare households more likely to face unemployment
World.content:
Young adults who spent their teenage years in a household relying on benefits are far less likely to have a job by the age of 29, according to research by national statistics office CBS.

Some 69% of that group had a job at 29, compared with 89% of those whose families never claimed bijstand, the basic benefit for people with no other means of support.

The gap appears even after short periods on welfare. Of those whose household claimed for less than a year, 77% were working at 29 and 16% were living on benefits.

The same research shows education follows the same pattern. Around 20% of those who grew up partly on welfare had an hbo college or university degree by 29, against 50% of other young adults, and the number of years spent on welfare made little difference.

Those who do work earn less per hour, work fewer hours and are less likely to have a permanent contract: around 60% do, compared with 71% of employees who did not grow up on welfare.

The CBS followed 186,000 people who turned 18 in 2013 and lived in the Netherlands from age 12 to 18. One in 10 grew up at least partly in a household on welfare, and 3% for five years or more.

World.title: Albert Heijn owner files police report over cyberattack
World.content:
Ahold Delhaize, the parent company of Dutch supermarket chain Albert Heijn, filed a police report on Monday over the cyberattack that forced it to take systems offline more than a week ago.

The company said in a statement on Monday that its investigation had confirmed the suspicious activity in its IT systems was caused by “the malicious actions of others”. Until now it had described the problem only as a “cybersecurity incident”.

Police and the public prosecution service (OM) urged the company to file a report last week, because a criminal investigation cannot start without one.

It is not clear why Ahold Delhaize has now decided to do so, broadcaster NOS reported.

The company did notify the National Cyber Security Centre (NCSC), the justice ministry’s cybersecurity agency, within 24 hours of discovering the attack, as required under a new cybersecurity law that came into force on August 15.

Albert Heijn’s website and app are back online and home deliveries are expected to resume on Friday, October 23, the company said. The websites of drugstore chain Etos and drinks chain Gall & Gall, also owned by Ahold Delhaize, are available again.

Ahold Delhaize said it had so far found no evidence that sensitive data belonging to customers, staff or business partners had been taken. It declined to give further details while the investigation continues, saying they could compromise its security.

The Albert Heijn hack is one of the first major incidents since the new reporting law came into force. It covers some 8,000 organisations seen as vital to the country, from healthcare, drinking water and banks to the food sector, including supermarkets.

The problems began on Sunday, October 11, when Albert Heijn switched off part of its IT systems, halting home deliveries and work at its distribution centres and leaving empty shelves in some stores.

Security sources told NOS last week that servers in the US, Poland, Moldova and Turkey had been used in the attack. Sector insiders told the Financieele Dagblad that the outage was costing the company “tens of millions” of euros a day.

World.title: POW campaigners keep up fight after cabinet limits compensation
World.content:
Campaigners for the widows of former Japanese prisoners of war have said they will keep fighting for compensation after the Dutch government said only surviving partners would be entitled to receive their spouses’ unpaid wages.

Long-term care minister Mirjam Sterk announced last Friday that the partners of civil servants and servicemen who were held captive following the invasion of Indonesia in 1942 would receive 42 months’ back pay, covering the period until the liberation in May 1945.

But Sterk said only widows who are still alive when the compensation scheme is launched on February 1 next year, all of whom are well into their nineties or older, would receive the payouts because a more extensive ruling would be “too complicated”.

The government has also cut the total size of the fund from the €50 mln announced in its last spring budget statement to €11.5 mln, on the basis that only a few hundred widows of the 40,000 men who were captured by the Japanese still survive.

The decision follows decades of campaigning for victims of the camps to be given the same treatment as Dutch government employees who were forced to work in Germany during World War II.

Moluccans

They include Moluccans who later fought on the side of the Dutch during the Indonesian liberation war and were subsequently persecuted by the independent government, prompting them to flee to the Netherlands.

Earlier this year prime minister Rob Jetten apologised to the Moluccan community for the way they were treated when they arrived in the 1950s.

Peggy Stein, of campaign group Indisch Platform 2.0, called for the ruling to be backdated to include widows who were alive when parliament approved a motion by farmers’ party leader Caroline van der Plas on the issue last April.

“That was when these people heard they were going to get their wages, but some of them have died in the meantime,” she told Dutch News.

Stein added that the cabinet appeared to have pushed through the ruling without waiting for parliament to debate the extent of the compensation scheme first.

“We still had to talk to MPs and had asked for a committee debate, but never had a reply,” she said.

“This isn’t about care or morality, it’s purely and solely about the technical settling of a case for the lowest possible cost.”

No official records

Sterk said it was “practically impossible” to compensate relatives of former camp inmates who had died because the government had no central records, but Stein said her campaign group had compiled its own list of detainees and could provide documentation showing they worked for the colonial administration.

“I have a list, but they say the SVB [Dutch social security bank] is legally not allowed to use it,” she said. “But if they have €50 million to spend, why can’t they find other parties to distribute the money who are able to work with us?”

Stein said she was not calling for the regulation to be scrapped, but it should be backdated to 2025 or 2015, when the government first acknowledged that the POWs were in its service. Prior to that it had argued that the colonial government in Indonesia was a separate entity.

Stein said the campaigners would continue to press the cabinet to compensate all victims of the Japanese occupation, including those who were no longer alive. “We have made a promise to these elderly people, we have signed a petition, and we are going to keep fighting for it,” she said.

On Monday afternoon, following media reports of the arrest, a spokesman for the military police confirmed that they had detained a 31-year-old man of Polish and Ukrainian citizenship, who holds the rank of senior private reserve. The suspect, who had at the time been undertaking a course at the Military Medical Academy (WAM) in Łódź, is being held on suspicion of declaring readiness to act for the benefit of a foreign intelligence service against Poland. That crime is punishable by up to eight years in prison. W dniu 16 października 2026 r. żołnierze z Oddziału Żandarmerii Wojskowej w Łodzi, zgodnie z postanowieniem Prokuratora Działu do Spraw Wojskowych Prokuratury Rejonowej Łódź-Polesie w Łodzi, dokonali zatrzymania mężczyzny w wieku 31 lat, obywatelstwa polskiego i ukraińskiego, w… pic.twitter.com/MLpqzfT4iO — Żandarmeria Wojskowa (@Zandarmeria) October 19, 2026 The Polish authorities have not revealed which foreign intelligence service the suspect – who has been placed in detention for three months – is believed to be associated with. Speaking later to reporters, deputy defence minister Cezary Tomczyk said that the man had “clearly shown himself to be someone who is conducting reconnaissance of certain types of military installations belonging to the Polish armed forces”. He also revealed that the suspect had recently obtained Polish citizenship. While the authorities have not released further information, Rzeczpospolita, a leading newspaper, reported earlier on Monday that the suspect, whom it named as Vasiliy, had been found in possession of several different phones, documents, and a large amount of money and gold. Poland has recently seen a number of high-profile cases of individuals charged – and in some cases convicted – of spying on behalf of Russia and Belarus. Poland’s security services recently revealed that the number of espionage cases they launched last year was more than double the figure for 2024. Over those two years combined, there were more investigations than in the previous three decades. This month, a former Polish soldier was sentenced to five and a half years for spying on behalf of Russia. The tasks assigned to him included reconnaissance of Rzeszów-Jasionka airport as part of a possible plan to assassinate Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelensky while he travelled through Poland. In April, prosecutors charged a soldier from Poland’s Territorial Defence Force (WOT) with seeking to spy on behalf of Russia. The following month, three Polish citizens were charged with working on behalf of Russian intelligence to spread disinformation and conduct reconnaissance of NATO troops. In December last year, a Russian national was charged with running an espionage and sabotage network in Poland on behalf of Russia’s Federal Security Service (FSB). The agents whom he oversaw were mainly Ukrainians and Belarusians, as have been many others convicted of conducting Russian hybrid activities in Poland. Poland has detained and expelled 15 Russians and Belarusians who tried to take part in youth world karate championships that were taking place in the Polish city of Bielsko-Biała. “Eleven Belarusian citizens and four Russians entered the country on tourist visas, which was inconsistent with the declared purpose of their stay in Poland,” said border guard spokesman Szymon Mościcki. After being detained, they received orders to leave the country within eight days, which is “the shortest possible deadline”, he added, quoted by broadcaster TVP. Piętnastu obywateli Rosji i Białorusi zostało zatrzymanych przez Straż Graniczną. Przyjechali do Polski na wizach turystycznych, choć prawdopodobnie zamierzali wziąć udział w mistrzostwach świata w karate. Otrzymali decyzje nakazujące opuszczenie kraju.https://t.co/czcjQKZ2kw — tvp.info 🇵🇱 (@tvp_info) October 19, 2026 The announcement came one day after the karate world championships in the cadet, junior and U-21 categories had finished in Bielsko-Biała. In early October, Russia’s TASS news agency had reported that some of the country’s junior karatekas, as competitors are known, had planned to compete in the tournament. The World Karate Federation (WKF) allows Russian and Belarusian athletes to compete under a neutral banner. However, Poland has a strict policy of not allowing Russian and Belarusian athletes to compete in tournaments on its territory. This year, it banned them from taking part in a World Cup ski jumping event. It was also removed as host of two European junior weightlifting championships for banning Russian and Belarusian athletes. On 15 October, the day after the championships in Bielsko-Biała had started, TASS reported that none of the Russian athletes had been allowed to register by the Polish organisers. Paweł Połtorzecki, president of the Polish Karate Union (PUK), confirmed that, despite PUK warning them not to come, Russian and Belarusian athletes had sought to take part, prompting the organisers to ask the border guard to conduct an inspection. “The first sign was the appearance of a Russian at the refereeing course,” he revealed, quoted by TVP. “That’s when the first detention occurred.” Gazeta Wyborcza, a leading Polish daily, reports that the Russian karatekas had obtained tourist visas from other countries in the European Schengen area, of which Poland is part. Poland itself does not issue tourist visas to Russians. Poland has been removed as the host of two European junior weightlifting championships after refusing to allow Russian athletes to take part The European Weightlifting Federation says it "does not accept discrimination based on geopolitical circumstances" https://t.co/j7PfiTHZ1M — Notes from Poland 🇵🇱 (@notesfrompoland) January 9, 2026 Since Russia’s full-scale invasion of Ukraine in 2022, Poland has been one of Kyiv’s closest allies, providing military and humanitarian support while also pressing for tougher international sanctions against Moscow. Meanwhile, Poland has become the primary target in Europe for sabotage operations carried out by operatives working on behalf of Russia, including arson attacks and an attempt to derail a train. Russia has also repeatedly violated Polish airspace with drones, missiles and, most recently, a helicopter. In response to Russia’s aggressive actions, Poland has successively shut down all Russian consulates on its territory. Moscow responded by likewise closing all Polish consulates that it previously hosted. In January, Russia warned its citizens against travelling to Poland due to “Russophobia”. World.title: Poland breaks up international criminal group accused of laundering €77 million

Poland says it has broken up an international criminal group responsible for laundering an estimated 337 million zloty (€77 million) by using currency exchange offices to illegally process money obtained from internet scams. Nine suspects – eight Ukrainians and one Belarusian – have been detained in a series of raids, which also resulted in the seizure of gold and cash worth over 1 million zloty. Służby rozbiły międzynarodową grupę zajmującą się praniem pieniędzy z oszustw inwestycyjnych i kryptowalut. Zatrzymano 9 osób, a skala transakcji przekroczyła 337 mln zł. Zabezpieczono złoto i gotówkę wartą ponad 1 mln zł. @Straz_Graniczna @PolicjaCBZC @ABW_GOV_PL pic.twitter.com/g2NQoqaPvP — Marcin Kierwiński (@MKierwinski) October 19, 2026 The accused – four women and five men aged between 26 and 53 – were arrested in Łódź, Warsaw and Małopolska province, announced Krzysztof Kopania, spokesman for the Łódź regional prosecutor’s office, which is leading the investigation. The detainees are four female cashiers, three men running the exchange offices, and two couriers used to transport money. All have been charged with participating in an organised criminal group and money laundering. They could face up to 15 years in prison if convicted. Prosecutors say that the gang, which operated in the cities of Warsaw, Lublin, Wrocław, Katowice and Gdańsk, collected money that had been obtained through internet fraud and transported it to cryptocurrency exchanges. It was then processed without complying with anti-money laundering procedures. Proceeds were then transferred to bank accounts, sent abroad by car, or concealed in fictitious purchases of gold. Most money was ultimately invested in cryptocurrencies. “The scale of the operation was enormous,” said Kopania. “It is estimated that between February 2025 and July 2026, members of the group took steps to conceal the origins of approximately 337 million zloty.” The ringleader was a 34-year-old Ukrainian national who made the key decisions and oversaw the domestic and international channelling of funds obtained from illegal sources, according to the Internal Security Agency (ABW) and border guard, which were also involved in the operation. Seven of the accused have been placed in pre-trial detention for three (or in one case two) months, while two have been bailed and ordered not to leave Poland. World.title: Lithuania says Ukrainian drone that struck car entered its airspace from Poland
World.content: Keep our news free from ads and paywalls by making a donation to support our work! Notes from Poland is run by a small editorial team and is published by an independent, non-profit foundation that is funded through donations from our readers. We cannot do what we do without your support. This article has been updated to include a statement from Poland’s defence ministry issued on Monday afternoon. Lithuania says there is “no doubt” that a Ukrainian drone which exploded on its territory on Sunday, hitting a moving car, entered its airspace from Poland. However, Poland has so far said that there is no confirmation of an object crossing the border. Meanwhile, Ukraine has apologised for the incident, saying that Russian electronic warfare had diverted the drone’s path during an operation against military targets in Russia. Russia’s war of aggression against Ukraine is spilling over onto the Eastern flank of NATO and EU. This morning, NATO fighter jets stationed at Šiauliai Air Base scrambled once again after an unidentified object entered Lithuanian airspace. What appears to be a drone exploded… — Gitanas Nausėda (@GitanasNauseda) October 18, 2026 On Sunday morning, Lithuania confirmed that a drone had entered its airspace and exploded, causing damage to a moving vehicle. NATO jets were scrambled in response to the incursion but were not able to visually identify the object. President Gitanas Nausėda said that the incident was further evidence that “Russia’s war of aggression against Ukraine is spilling over onto the Eastern flank of NATO and [the] EU”. Meanwhile, Lithuanian defence minister Robertas Kaunas revealed that preliminary information indicated the drone had entered from Polish airspace. “I have already contacted the Polish defence minister and asked Poland to join the investigation so that we can look into this incident together,” said Kaunas, quoted by broadcaster LRT. However, a spokesman for Poland’s defence ministry, Janusz Sejmej, told the Polish Press Agency (PAP) on Sunday that “there is no confirmation [from our radar systems] of [an object] crossing the border from Poland to Lithuania”. Polsat, a leading Polish broadcaster, cited unnamed sources at Poland’s defence ministry saying that they believed the drone in fact took off from within Lithuanian territory, around 30 kilometres from the Polish border, and then flew deep into the country. In response, Deividas Matulionis, an advisor to the Lithuanian president, told the Baltic News Service (BNS) on Monday that “I can say very unequivocally we have credible evidence that the drone crossed the Polish border”. Later, the country’s prime minister, Mindaugas Sinkevičius, said that “there is no doubt that it entered…from the Polish side”. He also confirmed that the evidence indicates the drone “is of Ukrainian origin”. We regret the incident that occurred this morning in Lithuanian airspace, which may have resulted from Russian electronic warfare diverting drones during an operation against legitimate military targets in Russia. We apologise for any disruption, risks, and concern this may have… — Heorhii Tykhyi (@SpoxUkraineMFA) October 18, 2026 Those remarks followed a statement on Sunday afternoon from Heorhii Tykhyi, the spokesman for Ukraine’s foreign ministry, who appeared to confirm that the drone was Ukrainian. “We regret the incident that occurred this morning in Lithuanian airspace, which may have resulted from Russian electronic warfare diverting drones during an operation against legitimate military targets in Russia,” wrote Tykhyi. “We apologise for any disruption, risks, and concern this may have caused.” The spokesman said that Ukraine would “share all relevant information with our Lithuanian partners to establish the full circumstances of the incident”. However, he gave no further information on what type of drone was involved, where it was launched from, and what its target was. Lithuania borders Belarus, an ally of Russia, and the Russian exclave of Kaliningrad, as well as Poland and Latvia. In March and May this year, a number of Ukrainian drones aimed at targets in Russia entered the airspaces of NATO members Lithuania, Latvia, Estonia and Finland, likely due to Russian electronic jamming. On Monday afternoon, Poland’s defence ministry issued a statement “strongly refuting” media reports suggesting that sources within the ministry had identified the drone as having taken off within Lithuania itself. It added that the ministry, in cooperation with its Lithuanian partners, was still “conducting a detailed analysis” of what had taken place.
