World.title: Poland condemns attack by Israeli settlers on delegation that included Polish diplomats
World.content: Keep our news free from ads and paywalls by making a donation to support our work! Notes from Poland is run by a small editorial team and is published by an independent, non-profit foundation that is funded through donations from our readers. We cannot do what we do without your support. Poland has condemned an attack by masked Israeli settlers on a delegation of European diplomats – including Polish ones – that was visiting the West Bank. It called for a “decisive response from the Israeli authorities”, saying that the incident is “further evidence of the settler violence that the Palestinian population in the West Bank faces on a daily basis”. The attack has likewise been condemned by France and Belgium, whose nationals were also in the delegation, and the European Union, as well as by the Israeli foreign minister. Masked Israeli settlers attacked European diplomats, a French mayor and Palestinians in the occupied West Bank, prompting European condemnation. The violence comes amid unprecedented settler pogroms during the olive harvest. pic.twitter.com/wsP6edL62y — Al Jazeera English (@AJEnglish) October 18, 2026 On Saturday, the delegation – which included members from France, Belgium and Poland as well as representatives of the Catholic church – visited the mostly Christian Palestinian village of Taybeh near Ramallah in the Israeli-occupied West Bank. They had come to assess the situation following regular recent attacks by Israeli settlers on Palestinians trying to harvest olives on their own land. During the visit, the delegation came under attack, with parts of the incident caught on camera. France’s foreign minister, Jean-Noël Barrot, reported that Bernard Baudoux, mayor of Aulnoye-Aymeries in northern France, had been “violently assaulted” during the incident. He demanded that Israel arrest the perpetrators and “urgently put an end to these criminal acts of violence”. Late on Saturday afternoon, the spokesman for Poland’s foreign ministry, Maciej Wewiór, issued a statement confirming that the attack had taken place and that the delegation had included an unspecified number of Polish diplomats, who he said had not been harmed. “We express our deep outrage and strongly condemn this incident,” added Wewiór. “Poland consistently opposes violence by Israeli settlers in the occupied West Bank. Attacks on representatives of the diplomatic corps are absolutely unacceptable.” The spokesman said that Poland now “expects urgent and detailed explanations from the Israeli authorities” and for the perpetrators of the attack to be identified and held accountable. “We also expect effective measures to prevent similar incidents in the future.” ❗Potwierdzamy, że na Zachodnim Brzegu Jordanu doszło do ataku na konwój, w którym znajdowali się przedstawiciele korpusu dyplomatycznego, w tym polscy dyplomaci. Według wstępnych informacji za atak mogą odpowiadać izraelscy osadnicy. Polskim dyplomatom nic się nie stało. Z… — Rzecznik MSZ – Maciej Wewiór (@RzecznikMSZ) October 17, 2026 On Sunday, Poland’s foreign ministry issued a further statement in which it “condemned the attack by masked settlers…during a solidarity visit to a town known for its centuries-old Christian presence”. The incident “is further evidence of the settler violence that the Palestinian population in the West Bank faces on a daily basis”, they added, calling for a “decisive response from the Israeli authorities”. The attack was also “strongly condemned” on Sunday by the European Union’s diplomatic service, which said that it “expects full accountability as well as effective measures to prevent continued acts of violence and violent harassment against Palestinians”. Belgium’s foreign minister, Maxime Prevot, said that his country would continue to “press for EU sanctions against those responsible for this violence and those who support them”. 🇵🇸 I condemn in the strongest terms the attack by masked settlers in Taybeh, in the occupied West Bank, against Palestinians, our Consul General, French and Polish diplomats as well as catholic representatives. A French mayor was assaulted and a Belgian vehicle damaged. Our team… — Maxime PREVOT (@prevotmaxime) October 17, 2026 In the wake of the incident, Israeli Prime Minister Netanyahu had urged people to show “caution before drawing conclusions” over what had happened. He claimed that there is “a coordinated campaign to smear Israel and the Jewish residents” of the West Bank. However, the Israel Defence Forces (IDF) said that it “strongly condemns the severe act of violence that took place in the area of Taybeh, during which diplomatic representatives were attacked by Israeli rioters”. But it added that “the consulate’s visit was not coordinated with the IDF”, which is “important to prevent incidents of this kind”. Israel’s foreign minister, Gideon Sa’ar, also issued a condemnation of the attack and said that police had opened an investigation. The IDF strongly condemns the severe act of violence that took place in the area of Taybeh, during which diplomatic representatives were attacked by Israeli rioters. Police forces and forensic investigators from the Judea and Samaria District are entering the area accompanied by… — Israel Defense Forces (@IDF) October 17, 2026 The incident involving the diplomatic group came a day after around 80 Israeli settlers had attacked Palestinians harvesting olives, with Washington Post photojournalist Heidi Levine among those injured. Levine told the Committee to Protect Journalists, an American non-profit organisation, that she had been pushed to the ground by a group of masked settlers, who “were kicking me for I think at least 10 minutes”. That incident prompted criticism of Israel from the United States, whose ambassador, Mike Huckabee, called it a “despicable act of terror carried out by masked cowards”. Secretary of State Marco Rubio, meanwhile, said he was “disturbed” by the incident and confirmed that “we’ve asked the Israelis to crack down on that”. .@SecRubio on reporter Heidi Levine being attacked in the West Bank: "We're very disturbed by those images and what we're seeing….the President has been very clear, he's said this repeatedly, he does not want to see friction or crisis going on in the West Bank." pic.twitter.com/Xg10vteeXK — CSPAN (@cspan) October 18, 2026 In August this year, Poland summoned Israel’s ambassador to express its “great disappointment” that the IDF had discontinued an investigation into the strikes on an aid convoy in Gaza in 2024 that killed seven humanitarian workers, including a Pole, Damian Soból. In May, Poland issued a five-year entry ban on Israeli national security minister Itamar Ben-Gvir for his treatment of detained activists, including Polish citizens, from a flotilla seeking to reach Gaza. Last year, Israel criticised Poland’s prime minister, Donald Tusk, after he suggested that Israeli politicians are causing the starvation of mothers and children in Gaza. The Israeli foreign ministry called the remarks “unacceptable” and urged Tusk to “remember the lessons” of the Holocaust. World.title: Poland moves to allow more municipalities to charge tourist fee
World.content: Keep our news free from ads and paywalls by making a donation to support our work! Notes from Poland is run by a small editorial team and is published by an independent, non-profit foundation that is funded through donations from our readers. We cannot do what we do without your support. Many more municipalities in Poland will be allowed to charge a daily fee for tourists and other overnight visitors after a change to the law dropping environmental requirements for levying such charges. Kraków, which received 8.7 million overnight tourists last year, had in particular been pushing for the change. However, Poland as a whole has seen a recent boom in visitor numbers, recording the EU’s second-fastest growth in the number of nights in tourist accommodation last year. #Krakow #opłataturystyczna #ustawa 🚨🔥Z OSTATNIEJ CHWILI! 🔥🚨 📢 Prezydent RP podpisał nowelizację przepisów dotyczących podatków i opłat lokalnych, PIT oraz PCC. 🏨 Najważniejsze zmiany dla branży turystycznej dotyczą opłaty miejscowej i uzdrowiskowej. 🗓️ Od 2027 r. za jej… pic.twitter.com/9ATvENvNol — Kraków (@krakow_pl) October 15, 2026 Until now, a “visitor’s fee” could be levied by municipalities with beneficial climatic features, “scenic qualities” and the capacity to accommodate people visiting to benefit from these attributes, as well as localities in areas with the status of a “spa protection area”. In practice, this largely applied to seaside and mountain resorts. Kraków did charge a visitor’s fee between 2004 and 2015, but was subsequently unable to do so due to a toughening of environmental requirements. The city has long suffered from bad air pollution, though it has taken significant steps to tackle the issue. Now, under new legislation proposed by the government earlier this year and signed into law by President Karol Nawrocki this week, the requirement for beneficial climatic features has been scrapped, meaning many more places will be able to charge the visitor’s fee. From 1 January, municipalities with scenic qualities will be able to charge visitors up to 5 zloty (€1.14) for each night they stay in hotels, guesthouses and short-term rental accommodation for up to one month, a rise on the current maximum of 3.46 zloty. Additionally, whereas previously only people visiting for the purposes of tourism had to pay, the fee now applies to all visits, including for work or health purposes, reports broadcaster TVN. People with significant disabilities, children with certified disabilities and their carers will be exempt from the fee. In another change, fees will be collected directly by accommodation providers, who will be required to maintain detailed records, reports the Infor news service. Passing fees on in a timely manner will entitle providers to receive at least 10% of the money they collect. Poland saw the EU's second-fastest growth in tourism in 2025, behind only the Mediterranean island state of Malta https://t.co/WVkRbHtU7o — Notes from Poland 🇵🇱 (@notesfrompoland) January 19, 2026 In 2024, Kraków appealed to the government to be allowed to charge tourists a fee, noting that “overtourism leads to tensions and social discontent”, as the “local community suffers” and “residents increasingly feel like tourists in their own city”. With its UNESCO-listed Old Town, Wawel royal castle, and former Jewish district of Kazimierz, Kraków is regularly named as one of Europe’s best tourist destinations. Last year, a record 16.25 million people visited the city, of whom 8.7 million stayed overnight. While that is a boon to the local economy, it also often causes tensions with residents, who complain about noise and disruption. In 2024, the city created the new position of “night mayor”, whose role is to reconcile the needs of tourists, businesses and residents. Poland’s government has approved legislation that would allow local communities to ban short-term rentals of the type offered through services such as Airbnb. Such accommodation has boomed in recent years, often prompting a backlash from local residents https://t.co/8MRfRWTDxd — Notes from Poland 🇵🇱 (@notesfrompoland) September 3, 2026 Following this week’s change to the law, Kraków city hall confirmed that it would now again be able to collect a visitor’s fee “if the statutory conditions are satisfied and the municipal council adopts an appropriate resolution”. The city’s recently elected new mayor, Łukasz Gibała, who will be sworn in next week, said before Sunday’s election that he was in favour of a tourist tax of at least 20 zloty per night, four times the new maximum. “In western European cities there are rates of that size and higher,” Gibała said, quoted by financial news service Money.pl. “Maintaining the city in the face of the influx of tourists is costly. In Kraków, private business owners profit from tourism, whilst the city and its residents foot the bill.” Poland as a whole has also experienced a boom in tourism. Last year, the country recorded the European Union’s second-largest growth in the number of nights spent in tourist accommodation. Its increase of 7% was behind only the Mediterranean island state of Malta (9.9%). World.title: Poland drops proposal to criminalise providing help to illegal migrants following outcry
World.content: Keep our news free from ads and paywalls by making a donation to support our work! Notes from Poland is run by a small editorial team and is published by an independent, non-profit foundation that is funded through donations from our readers. We cannot do what we do without your support. Poland’s interior ministry has withdrawn a proposal to make it a criminal offence, punishable by up to three years in prison, to provide support to migrants who are in the country illegally. The idea had prompted criticism from human rights groups and even opposition from within the government. The interior ministry said the amendment had been intended to clamp down on migrant smuggling. But activists feared it would criminalise humanitarian aid, such as that provided to migrants who have irregularly crossed the border from Belarus. Za udzielenie bezinteresownej pomocy migrantom nie będzie groziła kara do trzech lat więzienia. Po burzy, którą wywołała publikacja „Rzeczpospolitej” i po sprzeciwie resortu rodziny, MSWiA wycofuje się z pomysłu „karania za podanie posiłku”.https://t.co/Q0N52IMRVn — Rzeczpospolita (@rzeczpospolita) October 15, 2026 Under current Polish law, anyone who facilitates the illegal stay of a person in Poland in exchange for financial or personal benefit can be jailed for up to five years. However, this week, the interior ministry proposed an amendment that would also have penalised anyone who knowingly “enabled or facilitated” the illegal stay of someone in Poland, even if not for financial or personal benefit. The offence would have been punishable by up to three years in prison. “Currently, this behaviour is not criminalised, creating a loophole for those who exploit such situations and, under the pretext of helping migrants, aid them in their illegal stay, thus serving as a springboard for further illegal migration,” wrote deputy interior minister Czesław Mroczek, quoted by the Rzeczpospolita daily. That immediately prompted concern that the law could be used against volunteers and residents of border areas who provide aid – such as food, water, medical treatment, clothing or shelter – to migrants who have crossed illegally from Belarus. Since 2021, tens of thousands of people, mainly from Asia and Africa, have tried to cross that border with the encouragement and support of the Belarusian authorities. They have sometimes used violence against Polish border officers. Poland and the EU accuse Belarus of “weaponising” migration as part of the “hybrid warfare” being waged by Russia and its allies against European countries. They have implemented tough border protection measures to prevent crossings and facilitate “pushbacks” of those who cross. However, many human rights and aid organisations argue that the migrants – over 100 of whom have died around the border since 2021 – are often victims of this process and need humanitarian support. Two dead bodies found in the river on Poland's border with Belarus likely belong to migrants from a group seen being pushed into the water by Belarusian officers as part of efforts to encourage irregular crossings into the EU, says a Polish minister https://t.co/xsnPd6FeO3 — Notes from Poland 🇵🇱 (@notesfrompoland) April 16, 2025 In response to the interior ministry’s proposal, 61 organisations, including Amnesty International, the Helsinki Foundation for Human Rights and the Auschwitz-Birkenau Foundation, signed a joint statement condemning the plans, which they said “violate international standards binding Poland”. The organisations warned that the proposed wording could expose medical staff treating migrants, lawyers providing legal assistance, facilities working with children, and organisations supporting victims of human trafficking to criminal liability. “This measure is not aimed at smugglers, but rather at activists or residents of border areas who provide humanitarian aid to foreign nationals who have crossed the border illegally and are present in Poland,” attorney Radosław Baszuk told the Rzeczpospolita daily. Baszuk previously represented five Polish activists who were prosecuted for providing food, clothing and shelter to a group of Middle Eastern migrants who had entered Poland from Belarus in 2022. A group of five activists have been found not guilty of enabling the illegal presence in Poland of Middle Eastern migrants whom they provided aid to after they had irregularly crossed the border from Belarus. Prosecutors had been seeking prison sentences https://t.co/RpfhVWL4hY — Notes from Poland 🇵🇱 (@notesfrompoland) September 8, 2025 They were acquitted last year, with the ruling made final in March this year after an appeal. But Baszuk told Rzeczpospolita that, under the interior ministry’s proposed amendment to the relevant law, his clients could been convicted. On Wednesday, Poland’s commissioner for human rights, Sylwia Gregorczyk-Abram, also wrote to the justice ministry to “express concern” that the proposed changes “could lead to criminal liability for charitable or humanitarian activities undertaken towards individuals whose residence status has not yet been regulated”. Even a member of the government, the minister for family, labour and social policy, Agnieszka Dziemianowicz-Bąk, expressed her “firm opposition” to the plans on social media. She is from The Left (Lewica), one of the junior partners in Poland’s ruling coalition. ‼️ Ciepły posiłek, nocleg, potrzebne leki – za to wolontariusz ma trafić do więzienia nawet na 3 lata? 😡 Nie ma zgody Lewicy na kryminalizowanie pomocy humanitarnej! Ministra Agnieszka Dziemianowicz-Bąk zwróciła się do ministra Waldemara Żurka ze stanowczym sprzeciwem wobec… pic.twitter.com/QskUfJmgsu — Lewica (@__Lewica) October 14, 2026 In response to the growing criticism, the interior ministry announced on Friday that it was withdrawing the proposal, saying it decided to do so “to eliminate any doubts and prevent the misinterpretation of regulations”. “From the beginning, the ministry’s sole objective has been to tighten the system and target the organisers of this practice [of migrant smuggling],” said the ministry, quoted by Rzeczpospolita. “Legal provisions must effectively protect the state’s borders against organised crime, while simultaneously fully safeguarding humanitarian values ​and life-saving activities.” The number of attempted illegal crossings by migrants from Belarus to Poland fell from 15,500 in the first half of 2025 to 235 this year – a drop of over 98% Poland also now claims a 100% success rate in apprehending migrants who manage to cross illegally https://t.co/RFZkd7CeIk — Notes from Poland 🇵🇱 (@notesfrompoland) July 20, 2026 Both the former Polish government and the current one, which took power in December 2023, have regularly faced criticism from human rights groups over their response to the migration crisis on the Belarus border. Earlier this year, the previous human rights commissioner, Marcin Wiącek, expressed concern over a ban on asylum claims introduced by the government in March 2025. He noted that the measures had been described as a temporary solution, but have remained in place ever since. The government, however, argues that its measures have been effective in preventing the illegal trafficking of migrants. Its data show that attempted border crossings from Belarus fell from around 15,500 in the first half of last year to less than 250 in the same period this year – a drop of over 98%. It also now claims to have a 100% success rate in apprehending migrants who manage to cross illegally. World.title: Heads of Polish and Ukrainian national remembrance institutes hold first meeting since 2018
World.content: Keep our news free from ads and paywalls by making a donation to support our work! Notes from Poland is run by a small editorial team and is published by an independent, non-profit foundation that is funded through donations from our readers. We cannot do what we do without your support. Senior delegations from Poland and Ukraine’s state institutes of national remembrance have held talks in the Ukrainian city of Lviv, marking the first time the heads of the two organisations have met in eight years. The meeting, at which the two sides discussed issues including exhumations of World War Two victims and possible joint research projects, comes as Poland and Ukraine seek reconciliation over historical issues that have regularly caused tensions between two otherwise close allies. 📢 14 października 2026 r. we Lwowie delegacja Instytutu Pamięci Narodowej spotkała się z przedstawicielami ukraińskiego Instytutu Pamięci Narodowej. Było to pierwsze bezpośrednie, robocze spotkanie szefów tych instytucji od 2018 r. ➡️ Stronie polskiej przewodniczył kierujący… pic.twitter.com/qHpZwLeCEa — Instytut Pamięci Narodowej (@ipngovpl) October 14, 2026 News of the meeting was announced on social media by Poland’s Institute of National Remembrance (IPN), which noted that it was “the first direct, working meeting between the heads of these institutions since 2018”. The IPN is currently headed by its deputy president, Karol Polejowski, because Poland’s parliament has been unable to agree on a permanent new president. The Ukrainian Institute of National Remembrance (UINR) is led by Oleksandr Alfyorov. “The first topic of discussion,” according to the IPN, was the planned reburial of 115 Polish soldiers recently exhumed in Lviv, where they died in 1939 defending the city (then part of Poland and known as Lwów) during the Nazi-German and Soviet invasions. Polish and Ukrainian researchers have exhumed the remains of 115 Polish soldiers who died in 1939 defending Lviv – now in Ukraine but then part of Poland and known as Lwów – during the invasions by Nazi Germany and the Soviet Union at the start of WWII https://t.co/yQNeq2D54E — Notes from Poland 🇵🇱 (@notesfrompoland) October 2, 2026 Their exhumation resulted from a diplomatic breakthrough last year between Warsaw and Kyiv that saw Ukraine lift a moratorium on exhumations that had been in place since 2017 in protest at the dismantling in Poland of a monument to the Ukrainian Insurgent Army (UPA). Ukraine has also allowed the exhumation on its territory of Polish victims of the Volhynia massacres, which were led by the UPA. Poland likewise recently granted permission for Ukraine to search for Ukrainian victims of a massacre led by the Polish Home Army in the village of Łasków (Laskiv in Ukrainian). At this week’s meeting, the UINR gave an update on its work in Łasków, where it has uncovered the remains of 30 people. The Ukrainian Institute of National Remembrance has found 30 human remains in a village in Poland where Polish partisans killed Ukrainian civilians in WW2 It thanked Poland for permission to search the site, calling it a step towards "true reconciliation" https://t.co/BeeEtl6gCa — Notes from Poland 🇵🇱 (@notesfrompoland) October 15, 2026 The IPN and UINR also discussed planned exhumation work in the now-depopulated village of Huta Pieniacka (Huta Peniatska in Ukrainian), where the local Polish population was massacred in 1944 by a Nazi SS regiment mainly made up of Ukrainians. There was also “willingness on both sides to restore cooperation in the field of historical scientific research”, said the IPN. “The possibility of undertaking joint educational initiatives was also discussed.” The two sides also agreed to hold another meeting in Warsaw, though no date has been set. This week’s meeting comes after a period of tension over historical issues between not only Poland and Ukraine more broadly, but also the two countries’ remembrance institutes. In February this year, the IPN criticised Alfyorov over an interview in which he initially called the Volhynia massacres “one of Poland’s state myths”, before later appearing to correct himself and saying it was “not a myth, but one of the key elements of the Polish grand narrative”. By contrast, “for most Ukrainians, this is just a local episode of history”, added Alfyorov. Referring to Poland’s recognition of the massacres as a genocide – a term Ukraine rejects – he asked if Polish massacres of around 28,000 Ukrainians during the war should also be called a genocide. In response, the IPN called Alfyorov’s remarks “outrageous” and declared that the Volhynia massacres were “not an ‘episode’, but rather one of the largest genocides against civilians in 20th-century Europe”. It also condemned Ukraine for honouring figures associated with the massacres. The UINR, for its part, criticised a law proposed by Poland’s president, Karol Nawrocki (a former head of the IPN), that would criminalise the promotion of ideologies associated with World War Two Ukrainian nationalist groups. Ukraine has criticised a law proposed by Poland's president that would criminalise promotion of historical Ukrainian nationalist ideologies, equating them with Nazism and communism It warns of "retaliatory measures" if the bill is passed https://t.co/TaX2Vj5z8v — Notes from Poland 🇵🇱 (@notesfrompoland) October 2, 2025 In another sign of reconciliation, in May the UINR and Poland’s Mieroszewski Centre held a historical congress in Warsaw, bringing together more than 100 historians “to discuss complex issues of the shared past and explore common approaches to their interpretation”, in the words of the Ukrainian foreign ministry. However, that same month, President Volodymyr Zelensky prompted a diplomatic crisis by approving the naming of a Ukrainian military unit after the “heroes of the UPA”. That prompted Nawrocki to strip Zelensky of Poland’s highest honour, the Order of the White Eagle. Since then, both sides have made efforts to reach a diplomatic solution, including a pledge by Zelensky to “grant a substantial number of permits for search and exhumation work”. World.title: Prague’s First Film Screening Took Place 130 Years Ago
World.content:
Prague’s first public film screening took place on October 18, 1896, at the Hotel U Černého koně on Na Příkopě Street.

Organized by the French branch of Thomas Edison’s company, the presentation introduced audiences to moving pictures, a technology that would soon transform entertainment across Bohemia.

The screening marked another milestone in a period of rapid technological change that had begun five years earlier.

In 1891, Prague hosted the Jubilee Provincial Exhibition, celebrating a century of industrial progress. The event helped reshape the city, leaving behind landmarks including the Industrial Palace, Petřín Lookout Tower and mirror maze.



The Hotel That Brought New Technology to Prague

The Hotel U Černého koně, or At the Black Horse, was among Prague’s most luxurious establishments in the late 19th century. Its owners, brothers Jindřich and Karel Cífka, were quick to recognize the commercial potential of new inventions.

Later in 1896, the hotel introduced another technological novelty, the X-ray machine. The device had been developed by German physicist Wilhelm Conrad Röntgen, who announced his discovery in December 1895.

Initially presented as an attraction, the machine soon acquired medical significance. In January 1897, physician Rudolf Jedlička used it to examine a patient suspected of having swallowed a foreign object. The image revealed a nail lodged in the man’s stomach.

Edison and the Lumière Brothers Compete for Audiences

The first film screening was organized by Adolf Oppenheimer, an optician and mechanic who operated a cinematograph supplied by Edison’s French company.

According to a contemporary invitation reproduced by Czech Radio, screenings took place daily, beginning at 4 p.m. and continuing hourly until 8 p.m. Additional shows were held on Sundays and public holidays. Admission cost 40 kreutzers, with discounts for schools.

Competition arrived almost immediately. Just five days after the Edison presentation, the Lumière brothers’ cinematograph was shown at the Hotel U Saského dvora on Hybernská Street.

Both companies promoted their technology as the genuine article. Their s emphasized the quality of their moving pictures and their international reputations, reflecting the intense competition surrounding the new medium.

Czech filmmakers soon began producing their own material. In June 1898, Národní listy reported on a cinematograph pavilion at the Prague Exhibition Grounds where two young architects presented original films, including scenes from everyday life in Prague.

Viktor Ponrepo Opens a Permanent Cinema

For several years, traveling cinematographs brought films to audiences around the country. A permanent venue eventually followed.

In September 1907, Dismas Šlambor, better known as Viktor Ponrepo, opened what is widely regarded as the first permanent cinema in the Czech lands. It was located in the U Modré štiky building on Karlova Street.

Originally a magician and illusionist, Ponrepo had become interested in image-recording technology after encountering Edison’s phonograph at the 1891 exhibition. He later toured the country with a traveling cinema before establishing his Prague venue.

Ponrepo became famous for greeting audiences with a bow before every screening. He eventually filmed the gesture and projected it before his shows, turning it into his personal signature.

By then, moving pictures had evolved from a technological curiosity into a new form of mass entertainment, with Prague among the cities embracing the change.

World.title: Meet Paulo Dias, the Expat Behind Prague’s Pintz Beer App
World.content:
Finding a good beer in Prague is rarely a difficult task. Finding the right pub, knowing what a pint costs and deciding where to go next is a different question.

For Paulo Dias, that challenge became the idea behind Pintz, a web app built to help people navigate Prague’s rich beer scene.

Originally from Portugal, Paulo has spent almost 15 years living abroad, moving between Slovakia and the UK before eventually taking a job in the Czech Republic.



He first arrived in the Czech Republic in 2021, spending several months in Opava before moving to Prague in February 2022. Even after the move, he was cautious about settling in. “When I moved to Prague, I wasn’t buying many things for my apartment, because if I moved again, I’d have to pack everything,” Paulo recalls.

That changed once his new job became more stable. By the end of the year, he was already thinking about staying.

I think the quality of life in Prague is quite amazing. It’s one of the best, if not the best, of the cities I know. I feel good here, I feel at home. That’s why I decided to stay.”

Prague’s pub culture

Prague’s pub culture became one of the ways Paulo built a social life after moving to the city. He started with local pubs in Žižkov.

“I started to make friends there, and then I thought it was a good opportunity for me to become more social.”

What struck him was how different the culture was from Portugal. He describes drinking there as more centered around wine, home gatherings, watching football with friends or celebrating birthdays, rather than regularly meeting at pubs during the week.

“I know people who meet every Monday. It’s impossible in Portugal, this mindset. People just stay at home or go for a coffee after dinner. There’s no culture like going to a pub.”

In Prague, meeting for a beer could instead become part of an ordinary weekday. That was something Paulo gradually came to appreciate about his new home.

“I don’t need to wait for the weekend to have my social life active.”

From sneaker prices to Pintz

The idea for Pintz grew out of a sneaker-price platform “The Real Sneaker Index” Paulo had been working on in his spare time. The two projects are quite different, but the first gave him a way of thinking about how prices could be collected and compared.

The connection to beer came almost as an afterthought. Paulo was already spending time in Prague’s pubs, and the idea eventually brought his side project closer to something he was experiencing himself.

“I was thinking, maybe I could apply the same idea to something more connected to everyday life. And then I thought, why not use it to track beer prices?”

What started as a price tracker gradually expanded into a way of exploring pubs. Users can now add information about individual places, from terraces and beer gardens to the beers they serve, while ratings give people a way to share their own experiences. “It’s not only about finding the cheapest beer. It started that way, but it’s really about quality.”

Pintz is now present in the US, Mexico, Atlantic Islands and across many countries in Europe.

Building it alone with AI

Paulo has been building Pintz alongside his Lead AI Platforms job, developing the platform himself with the help of AI. He works on it in the evenings, at weekends and whenever he can find the time.

“I’m not a coder, I’m not a developer, but I know what I want to do.”

AI has allowed him to take those ideas further without having to build every part of the platform from scratch himself. He sets up processes, monitors how they work and keeps adding and improving features as the project develops.

The speed at which he can turn an idea into something functional has been one of the biggest surprises for him.

“What impressed me the most is the capability of building anything with AI, especially digital products.”

What’s next for Pintz?

For now, his focus is on getting more people to use Pintz and bringing more pubs, breweries and beer brands onto the platform. He is also looking at sponsorships and other ways of turning the project into a sustainable business.

At the same time, he is conscious of how easily monetisation could get in the way of the experience he is trying to create. He does not want users to feel like they are constantly being sold something while using the app.

“I don’t want this to become an advertising app that people are annoyed to use.”

World.title: Prague Light Park at Žluté Lázně Takes Visitors Back to the 14th Century
World.content:
Prague’s Žluté lázně has opened a new edition of the Story of Lights, a seasonal light park inspired by the city’s medieval history.

Running from October 16, 2026, to January 31, 2027, the event features illuminated sculptures, interactive installations and, from November, evening boat trips on the Vltava River.



The park takes visitors back to 14th-century Prague during the reign of Charles IV, the Bohemian king and Holy Roman Emperor whose rule helped shape the city’s development.

Thousands of LED lights illuminate the grounds after dark, forming a route through displays inspired by the architecture, symbols and history of medieval Prague.

Among the installations are illuminated representations of Charles Bridge, Gothic towers, church arches, royal crowns and coronation regalia. The displays reinterpret historical motifs using modern lighting technology.

Some installations are interactive, with the organizers targeting families with children as well as adults looking for an evening activity outdoors.

The historical theme focuses on a period when Prague underwent major urban development.

Charles IV initiated the construction of Charles Bridge, founded the New Town in 1348 and helped establish Prague as an important political, cultural and religious centre in medieval Europe.

From November 6, visitors will also be able to combine their visit with an illuminated boat trip along the Vltava. The evening cruises are scheduled for Fridays, Saturdays, Sundays and public holidays.

World.title: Prague Expands Tram Network With Five Projects Underway
World.content:
Prague is expanding its tram network, with five projects now under construction across the capital.

Two new projects began in October 2026, extending the network from Malovanka to Strahov and from Libuš to Nové Dvory.

Work is also progressing on the tram line across Wenceslas Square, where the tracks have been connected between Vinohradská Street and the junction of Jindřišská and Vodičkova streets.



The projects aim to improve public transport connections to developing residential areas and strengthen links with other transport services, including the future Metro Line D.

New tram line to connect Malovanka with Strahov

Construction of the new tram line from Malovanka to Strahov began on October 5, following preparatory work. The tracks will run along Vaníčkova Street, starting at Bělohorská Street and continuing toward Strahov Stadium.

The Malovanka stop will also be modified and moved to a position before the intersection, allowing it to serve trams heading toward Strahov.

The existing Stadion Strahov stop, currently used for passengers to disembark, will be renamed Strahov.

Tram extension to Nové Dvory will complement Metro Line D

Construction of the second new line, extending the tram network from Modřany through Libuš to Nové Dvory, began on October 7, 2026.

The extension will introduce two stops, Přírodní and Nové Dvory. At Nové Dvory, the line will end in a loop using Durychova, Libušská and Chýnovská streets.

The new connection is being developed alongside plans for Metro Line D and the wider expansion of the surrounding residential area. It will provide a direct tram connection to central Prague, including the Palackého náměstí area, with a future connection toward Smíchov also planned.

The extension will change operations on tram line 17. Once the project is completed, the temporary dead-end terminus in Libuš will be removed, allowing single-ended trams to return to longer routes. A second tram line is also planned for the new tracks after Metro Line D opens.

Hodkovičky gains a new tram stop

The new Hodkovičky stop, located between Belárie and Černý kůň, is another addition to Prague’s tram infrastructure in the south of the city.

The stop is intended to improve access to public transport for residents of the growing residential developments nearby. Further housing construction is also expected in Nové Dvory, where the planned tram extension will provide additional transport capacity.

Tram tracks connected across Wenceslas Square

Work on restoring tram services across Wenceslas Square is also progressing. In early autumn, construction crews connected the tracks running from Vinohradská Street, past the National Museum, across the square and toward the junction of Jindřišská and Vodičkova streets.

The track infrastructure in this section is complete. Remaining work includes finishing the surrounding surfaces and installing overhead power lines.

Once these works are finished, the new line will restore tram services across Wenceslas Square, strengthening public transport connections in central Prague.

World.title: Prague Christmas Markets 2026 Start in November – Dates and Locations
World.content:
Prague’s Christmas markets will return in November 2026, with the first stalls opening at Náměstí Míru on November 20.

The main markets in Old Town Square and Wenceslas Square will follow on November 28, bringing traditional Czech food, handmade decorations and a program of seasonal performances to the city center.

Náměstí Republiky follows on November 25, and Tylovo náměstí opens on November 26.



The main markets at Old Town Square and Wenceslas Square begin on November 28 and continue until January 6, 2027. The other markets close on Christmas Eve, December 24.

Here are the opening dates and hours for the main locations.

– náměstí Míru — November 20 to December 24, 10 a.m. to 7 p.m.

– náměstí Republiky — November 25 to December 24, 10 a.m. to 8 p.m.

– Tylovo náměsti — November 26 to December 24, 10 a.m. to 7 p.m.

– Old Town Square — November 28 to January 6, 2027, 10 a.m. to 10 p.m.

– Wenceslas Square — November 28 to January 6, 2027, 10 a.m. to 10 p.m.

Smaller Christmas Markets Across Prague

Several markets open before the main city-center venues and offer alternatives for visitors who want to explore different neighborhoods.

Further options include the market at Anděl and Lesser Town Christmas on Kampa Island.

náměstí Jiřího z Poděbrad will host farmers’ markets during Advent, with a design market joining them every Sunday during the season. These events offer opportunities to browse locally made products and find gifts beyond the usual Christmas-market stalls.

World.title: Modeselektor to Open Spectaculare Festival at Prague’s ROXY
World.content:
Berlin electronic duo Modeselektor will open the 14th edition of Spectaculare on 3 March 2027, bringing their live show to ROXY alongside new music from their latest album, MDSLKTR

Gernot Bronsert and Sebastian Szary will perform a set combining techno, electro, hip-hop and bass music, accompanied by visual projections and lighting.

The concert comes shortly after the release of MDSLKTR, an album that revisits the sound and influences that have shaped the duo’s nearly three-decade career.



The record follows Classics Vol. 01, a project that revisited material from their early albums Hello Mom! and Happy Birthday! and drew on years of studio recordings and unfinished ideas.

With MDSLKTR, Modeselektor return to the sounds that first defined their music, drawing on Berlin rave culture, techno, electro, IDM and hip-hop while continuing to move between genres.

Since emerging from Berlin’s underground electronic scene, the duo have built an international following through their studio albums, live performances and collaborations with artists including Radiohead frontman Thom Yorke, Tommy Cash, Flohio and Blixa Bargeld.

They also formed Moderat with producer Apparat and run the independent record label Monkeytown Records.

View this post on Instagram A post shared by Festival Spectaculare (@spectaculare_music)

Berlin-based multi-instrumentalist Philipp Johann Thimm will open the evening. A longtime collaborator of Apparat, Thimm has worked across electronic and acoustic music as well as audiovisual projects. His work on Apparat’s album *LP5* contributed to a Grammy-nominated project, while his solo work explores the meeting point between electronic composition and live instrumentation.

World.title: Prague’s Día de Muertos Festival Returns to Holešovice on November 5th
World.content:
Prague’s Holešovice Market will host the fifth annual Día de Muertos festival on November 5, bringing Mexican food, live music, traditional decorations and family activities.

The event, organized in cooperation with Jarritos and Nuevo Progreso, will run from 11 a.m. to 10 p.m. Halls 13 and 11 will host a Mexican market and a carnival for children.

Visitors can arrive throughout the day, with the food stalls opening at lunchtime.



The selection will include Mexican and South American specialties, tortillas, grilled dishes and Jarritos soft drinks. A special beer brewed by Falcon brewery for the occasion will also be available.

The food zone will remain open until 10 p.m., giving visitors time to sample different dishes and explore the festival’s other attractions.

One of the main attractions will be a traditional ofrenda, or Day of the Dead altar, prepared by the Mexican Embassy. Decorated with photographs, flowers, candles and personal objects, the altar will introduce visitors to the traditions behind the holiday.

Día de Muertos is dedicated to remembering deceased family members and loved ones.

In Mexican tradition, the holiday celebrates their continuing place in family life and the belief that their spirits return to visit the living. Its customs differ from Halloween, combining remembrance with food, music, flowers and colorful decorations.

Hall 11 will become the PEDRO Kids’ Zone from 1 p.m. to 7 p.m., with a program designed for children and families.

View this post on Instagram A post shared by Holešovická tržnice (@holesovickatrznice)

Activities will include dance workshops, Mexican music, crafts, stories about the holiday and a game in which children throw balls at illuminated skulls. Visitors will also have the opportunity to meet a Xoloitzcuintle, the Mexican hairless dog traditionally associated with guiding souls to the afterlife.

Costumes are welcome, and the organizers have divided the program into six one-hour sessions beginning at 1 p.m., 2 p.m., 3 p.m., 4 p.m., 5 p.m. and 6 p.m.

Admission costs CZK 100 per person for adults and children aged three and older. Tickets are available through GoOut and at the venue, subject to availability. Each ticket covers one hour of activities, after which visitors can explore the rest of the festival.

The program will also feature mariachi musicians, stilt walkers, colorful masks and costumes, and a festival parade. DJs will provide music throughout the day, while a screening of the animated film Coco will offer another introduction to Mexican traditions surrounding death and remembrance.

World.title: Danish-Japanese Chain Sticks’n’Sushi to Open First Prague Restaurant
World.content:
Sticks’n’Sushi will open its first Czech restaurant in central Prague on Wednesday, November 4, introducing its combination of Japanese cuisine and Danish design to the local dining scene.



The restaurant will occupy a site on Jungmannovo náměstí in Prague 1. Ahead of the official opening, guests will be able to sample the menu at half price from November 1 to 3.

Those interested in attending the preview must register online. Registered guests will then receive a link to book a table for one of the available dates.

The menu combines sushi, sashimi and salads with kushiyaki, Japanese-style grilled skewers. The restaurant will also offer set menus intended for sharing, making them suitable for groups.

Among the dishes are Beef Tataki, served with miso aïoli, truffle ponzu and crispy Jerusalem artichoke, and the Temaki Setto, which allows diners to assemble their own hand rolls with ingredients including lobster, Wagyu tartare and avocado.

Another addition is the Ebi Sando, a sandwich featuring crispy shrimp, truffle and miso aïoli. The Sticks Setto features skewers of Japanese Wagyu beef, Iberian pork, shrimp and miso-marinated black cod, served on a hot stone at the table.

View this post on Instagram A post shared by Sticks’n’Sushi Czech Republic (@sticksnsushi_cz)

The drinks list includes sake, Japanese teas, cocktails and premium spirits. The restaurant will also serve a Japanese rice lager brewed for the chain by Danish brewery Mikkeller.

Zbyněk Pokorný, chief executive of Sushi Group s.r.o., which is bringing the concept to the Czech market, said the opening followed nearly two years of preparation.

“We believe that the combination of Japanese quality, Danish hospitality, and a strong focus on the overall guest experience is a perfect fit for Prague,” Pokorný said. He added that the company was looking forward to welcoming its first guests.

Reservations can be made through the company’s Czech website.

About Sticks’n’Sushi

Founded in Copenhagen in 1994, Sticks’n’Sushi was established by brothers Jens and Kim Rahbek, who have Danish and Japanese roots, and Thor Andersen. The first restaurant opened in a basement space in the Danish capital.

The business has since expanded into an international restaurant group, with locations in Denmark, Germany and the United Kingdom. Its interiors draw on Japanese and Danish influences, with individual restaurants featuring their own design elements within the brand’s overall concept.

World.title: Hungary to cut EUR 4 billion from government spendings next year – Here’s where the money will go instead
World.content:
Hungary’s government plans to cut state spending by HUF 1,465 billion (EUR 4 billion) in 2027 by eliminating wasteful expenditure, reforming public spending and reviewing contracts.

Huge cuts in spending from the government

Hungary’s Finance Minister András Kármán says the measures will help reduce the budget deficit while funding higher wages, pensions, family benefits and public services. Prime Minister Péter Magyar and Finance Minister András Kármán have outlined plans to reduce Hungary’s budget deficit from an expected 7.5% of GDP in 2026 to 4.9% next year.

The government says it has identified significant inefficiencies in the previous administration’s spending and intends to redirect public money towards social support and essential services. Kármán said the planned savings would amount to approximately 1.5% of GDP, while tax changes are expected to generate an additional HUF 665 billion (more than EUR 1.8 billion) in net revenue.

Where will the government save money?

The proposed spending cuts include HUF 246.1 billion (EUR 675 million) from unfavourable concession contracts, HUF 169.5 billion (EUR 465 million) from inefficient economic development subsidies and HUF 135 billion (more than EUR 370 million) linked to the expected abolition of an EU migration-related fine.

Other measures include reducing support for public foundations overseeing universities, cutting government communications and event spending, and reviewing prestige investments and state property expenditure.

The government also plans to reduce spending on public media, introduce more economical central procurement and review funding for politically connected foundations and organisations. Magyar said the government intended to terminate the existing motorway concession contract, although some ongoing projects would continue to generate costs in 2027.

Higher taxes for wealthy individuals and large companies

Hungary’s government expects tax measures to deliver HUF 929 billion (more than EUR 2.5 billion) in additional revenue, partly offset by HUF 264 billion (~EUR 724 million) in household tax reductions. A proposed wealth tax is expected to raise HUF 200 billion (~EUR 548 million) annually. Other revenue measures include higher taxes on large companies, tobacco products and environmentally damaging activities, alongside changes affecting retail, insurance and advertising businesses.

The government argues that these measures will make the tax system fairer and reduce opportunities for large companies to minimise their tax bills. However, Magyar acknowledged that businesses could pass some additional costs on to consumers, making enforcement and consumer protection important.

Families, pensioners and public services to receive more

Despite the planned savings, the government has announced substantial increases in social spending. Family allowance payments are set to double, while the minimum pension will rise fourfold to HUF 120,000 (~EUR 330) per month. A new pensioner SZÉP Card benefit is also planned.

The government intends to spend an additional HUF 510 billion (~EUR 1.4 billion) on healthcare and HUF 734 billion (~EUR 2 billion) more on social provision. A total of HUF 667 billion (~EUR 1.8 billion) is earmarked for sectoral wage increases in 2027, benefiting workers in areas including healthcare, education and social care. The personal income tax rate for minimum-wage earners is also set to fall to 9%.

Stay up-to-date: Government measures could give Hungary’s housing market the boost it needs

Deficit reduction remains a challenge

The government forecasts economic growth of 2.4% in 2027, rising to 3.1% by 2030. It also aims to reduce the budget deficit below 3% of GDP by 2030. However, the plans involve balancing significant new spending commitments against savings and higher tax revenues. The government’s projections will depend on whether the planned cuts materialise, economic growth accelerates and additional tax revenue meets expectations.

While the administration says its approach will restore stability and make public spending more efficient, the final budget legislation will provide further details on how the measures are implemented.

World.title: Dining Guide Top100: Hungary’s best pizzeria has been named – and it’s not in Budapest
World.content:
An iconic restaurant in Encs has retained its title as Hungary’s Best Pizza, while the Dining Guide’s 2026 top 10 includes five Budapest venues and five from elsewhere in the country.

Pizza has become much more than a quick weekday dinner. A well-made dough, patient fermentation and carefully selected ingredients can create an experience worth travelling across the country for. This year, the Dining Guide Top100 Restaurant Guide has highlighted ten pizzerias, with the capital and the countryside sharing the spotlight.

Alongside five Budapest venues, the list features restaurants in Encs, Miskolctapolca, Tata, Székesfehérvár and Nagyrákos. At the top is Anyukám Mondta in Encs, which has once again won the title of Hungary’s Best Pizza in 2026, following its success in 2025.

From classic Neapolitan pizzas to sourdough creations with beautifully puffed, bubbly crusts, there is something for every pizza lover. Here are the ten venues selected by the guide.

Never miss a headline: join Daily News Hungary’s official Telegram channel!

Hungary’s top 10 pizzerias in 2026

According to the Dining Guide Top100 Restaurant Guide, the country’s ten standout pizzerias are:

Anyukám Mondta, Encs Circo Pizza Avalon Ristorante, Miskolctapolca Belli di Mamma Fermento Pizzéria Pizza Manufaktúra Zsigmond Terasz & Pince, Tata IGEN, Budapest Ria Pékség és Pizzéria, Székesfehérvár Il Bandito Pizza Kertje, Nagyrákos

1. Anyukám Mondta, Encs

Anyukám Mondta

The passion and experience that brothers Szabolcs and Szilárd Dudás gained in Italy have helped shape one of Hungary’s most celebrated pizzas. Their light, airy dough, made with a high level of hydration, is based on a recipe that originated near Lake Garda.

Early in their careers, the brothers baked and served 300 pizzas every evening at a restaurant in Dró. Later, in Encs, their business evolved from Sarok Café into Pizza Sarok and eventually into the now-iconic Anyukám Mondta. Its pizzas have earned a reputation for their clean flavours and meticulous preparation.

A constant desire to improve, determination, curiosity and the warmth of a specially built oven are all part of the brothers’ approach. They have also built a close relationship with their customers along the way.

The brothers, who have received the Károly Gundel Lifetime Achievement Award, are affectionately known as the “Italians of Encs”. Their pizzas, along with the restaurant’s many other dishes, capture the relaxed spirit of the Mediterranean, combining good humour with consistently high quality.

If you missed it: Hungary’s biggest restaurant awards 2026 announced – here are the Dining Guide winners

2. Circo Pizza

Circo Pizza

Circo is a stylish yet relaxed dining spot where the distinctive dough of Neapolitan pizzas meets exciting toppings and inventive flavour combinations. Natural wines complete the atmosphere, making it a place to enjoy a drink alongside lunch or dinner – or simply to stop by for a pleasant glass of wine.

3. Avalon Ristorante, Miskolctapolca

Avalon Ristorante

Located in the heart of the Bükk Hills, Avalon Ristorante serves authentic, airy Neapolitan pizzas baked in one of the world’s most advanced Morello Forni ovens.

Fresh, local ingredients meet Mediterranean flair, creating a premium dining experience. The restaurant’s elegant yet welcoming, family-friendly atmosphere extends to its pizza offering, making it a destination for those seeking quality food in a distinctive setting.

4. Belli di Mamma

Belli di Mamma

Belli di Mamma gives the atmosphere of a traditional Neapolitan pizzeria a youthful, modern twist. Its long-fermented dough and authentic ingredients produce pizzas that are both refined and full of character, served with genuine hospitality.

5. Fermento Pizzéria

Fermento Pizzéria

Fermento is one of the freshest names on both the Víziváros and wider Budapest pizza scenes. Its team learnt the craft of dough-making from Italian masters, and the menu features Neapolitan classics, calzone, as well as vegan and gluten-free options.

A spirit of constant renewal and a genuine passion for Italian cuisine underpin the offering.

6. Pizza Manufaktúra

Pizza Manufaktúra

Pizza Manufaktúra is a long-standing favourite among Budapest’s pizza lovers. It serves around 20 varieties of pizza, made with airy dough and carefully chosen ingredients, without compromising on quality.

Its informal, playful atmosphere and personal service have helped turn it into a regular haunt for customers. Its pizzas also compete with those served at its sister venue on Víg Street in terms of the balance between crispness and an airy texture.

7. Zsigmond Terasz & Pince, Tata

Zsigmond Terasz

Near Tata Castle, Zsigmond Terasz & Pince pairs impressive views with Neapolitan-inspired pizzas. Its dishes combine local traditions with premium Hungarian and Italian ingredients, topped with carefully selected ingredients.

The terrace adds to the experience, making the venue appealing not only for its food but also for its setting.

8. IGEN, Budapest

IGEN

At IGEN, every bite celebrates the freedom and character of Neapolitan pizza. Expect airy yet flavourful dough, beautifully risen crusts and Mediterranean flavours.

The pizzeria founded by Nóri Vidó respects the strict standards of the Associazione Verace Pizza Napoletana (AVPN), while maintaining a relaxed, informal atmosphere. Here, pizza is both an everyday pleasure and something worth celebrating.

9. Ria Pékség és Pizzéria, Székesfehérvár

Ria Pékség és Pizzéria

Ria Pékség is a place to start the day with sourdough bread and handmade pastries, but its pizzas provide plenty of reasons to return, too.

The thin-crust pizzas are baked in a wood-fired oven, delivering simple yet striking flavours.

10. Il Bandito Pizza Kertje, Nagyrákos

Il Bandito Pizza Kertje

Il Bandito Pizza Kertje is the realisation of a teacher’s dream, brought to life during the summer holidays on the banks of the Zala in Nagyrákos.

In its shady garden, visitors can enjoy sourdough pizzas with beautifully bubbled crusts, including creative regional varieties topped with Hungarian-style ratatouille, túró-style curd cheese with pumpkin seed oil, or porcini mushrooms inspired by the Őrség region.

For hungry walkers exploring the surrounding countryside, it offers a distinctive combination of local flavours, relaxed outdoor dining and handcrafted pizza.

World.title: Shocking: Average net salary in Hungary’s richest settlement is more than 12 times the amount of the poorest
World.content:
The average monthly net salary in Hungary’s wealthiest settlement reached HUF 920,000 in 2025, compared with just HUF 75,000 in the poorest, which shows the country’s stark regional inequalities, according to a new analysis by GKI.

Where people live in Hungary can make a dramatic difference to their income. Data analysed by GKI Economic Research Co., based on 2025 personal income tax records from the National Tax and Customs Administration (NAV), reveal a striking divide between the country’s richest and poorest settlements.

Telki tops the rankings as Csenyéte struggles

Telki, a village in Pest County near Budapest, recorded the highest average monthly net salary at HUF 920,000 (more than EUR 2,500). This compares with just HUF 75,000 (EUR 205.80) in Csenyéte, in Borsod-Abaúj-Zemplén County. The difference means Telki’s average was approximately 12.3 times higher than Csenyéte’s.

Other affluent settlements included Nagykovácsi, with HUF 864,000 (EUR 2,370), Budajenő at HUF 848,000 (EUR 2,330) and Üröm at HUF 836,000 (EUR 2,295). Meanwhile, eight of the ten lowest-income settlements were located in Borsod-Abaúj-Zemplén County, in north-eastern Hungary.

GKI cautioned that these figures represent average salary calculated from tax records, rather than conventional average salaries. Employment rates, population composition and the proportion of residents earning taxable work income all influence the results.

Budapest earns almost 50% more than villages

Hungary’s average monthly net salary reached HUF 521,000 (~EUR 1,430) in 2025, an increase of 9.9% compared with the previous year. However, the figures varied considerably by settlement type. Budapest recorded HUF 666,000 (~EUR 1,830) per month, compared with HUF 550,000 (EUR 1,510) in county seats, HUF 502,000 (~EUR 1,380) in other towns and HUF 449,000 (EUR ~1,230) in villages.

Consequently, the capital’s average salary was approximately 48% higher than that of rural settlements. At county level, Pest led with HUF 577,000 (~EUR 1,580), followed by Győr-Moson-Sopron at HUF 553,000 (EUR ~1,520). Szabolcs-Szatmár-Bereg ranked last, with HUF 412,000 (EUR 1,130).

Never miss a headline: join Daily News Hungary’s official Telegram channel!

Are Hungary’s poorest regions catching up?

There is some encouraging news: GKI found that work incomes generally grew faster in percentage terms in less affluent areas during 2025. Researchers partly attributed this to increases in the minimum wage and guaranteed minimum wage.

Nevertheless, faster percentage growth has not necessarily narrowed the gap in cash terms. Average monthly net incomes increased by HUF 60,000 (EUR 165) in Budapest and HUF 54,000 (EUR 138) in Pest County, compared with HUF 38,000 (EUR 104) in Szabolcs-Szatmár-Bereg.

According to GKI, geographical location accounts for more than 80% of differences in work income between settlements. Although poorer regions are gradually catching up, the figures suggest that where people live remains a major factor in their economic prospects.

World.title: Government measures could give Hungary’s housing market the boost it needs
World.content:
The package of measures announced in the 2027 budget, including the Wekerle Plusz programme and the extension of the reduced 5% VAT rate on new homes, could give Hungary’s housing market fresh impetus, property portal ingatlan.com told the MTI on Tuesday.

Hungarian government announced huge reforms for 2027

In recent months, demand for homes has fallen significantly short of previous peaks. Changes to the system of housing support could therefore bring buyers who have so far been holding back into the market again, benefiting both newly built and existing properties.

László Balogh, chief economic expert at property advertising portal ingatlan.com, said in a statement that retaining the reduced 5% VAT rate on new homes was crucial for the new-build market and residential property development, and consequently for the housing stock as a whole. He added that this was in line with previous expectations.

How the new housing scheme could help people

The expert also welcomed the planned launch of the Wekerle Plusz programme, under which homebuyers will be able to apply for fixed-rate loans on preferential terms. The interest rate will be 3% for newly built homes and 5% for existing properties. This means that purchases of newly built homes, as well as their construction, will continue to be financeable through loans at an interest rate of 3%.

For existing homes, however, the interest rate on subsidised loans will rise to 5%. As an example, ingatlan.com noted that, for a typical HUF 35 million (EUR 96,400) Otthon Start loan taken out over 25 years, this would increase monthly repayments by HUF 35,000–40,000 (EUR 96.40–110). Nevertheless, the rate would still be more favourable than publicly advertised market mortgage offers, which start at 6.25%.

Another important change to housing policy is that subsidised loans could become more targeted. Applicants would need to be under 41 and own less than 50% of a property. First-time buyers would also be required to move into the property they purchase.

The Wekerle Sándor Housing and Student Accommodation Construction Programme could also help expand the supply of housing. An initial HUF 30 billion (more than EUR 82.5 million) would be allocated to building homes and creating student accommodation places.

Never miss a headline: join Daily News Hungary’s official Telegram channel!

Not just housing, but energy reforms as well

According to ingatlan.com, a new energy-efficiency renovation programme could encourage the modernisation of existing properties. Alongside a preferential loan of up to HUF 15 million (more than EUR 41,250), the scheme could provide a non-repayable grant of up to HUF 7.5 million (more than EUR 20,600). This could reduce the cost of maintaining homes and increase their market value.

One of the most significant changes could be the extension of energy-efficiency renovation support to people living in prefabricated apartment blocks.

István Kapitány, Minister for Economic Affairs and Energy, announced this on his Facebook page on Monday evening. Among other measures, he said that a multi-year home energy-efficiency renovation programme was being prepared, which could also create opportunities to improve the energy performance of flats in prefabricated blocks.

Stay up-to-date: What is Wekerle Plusz? Here’s the new housing programme the government offers instead of Orbán’s Home Start

More people could benefit from the programmes than before

In the statement, Balogh recalled that previous energy-saving programmes had been aimed at detached houses rather than flats in apartment blocks. More than one million people live in prefabricated flats, and these buildings are considered particularly energy-intensive. The programme could therefore trigger a new wave of home renovations in the coming years.

The Wekerle Plusz package will also see the return of a state-subsidised home savings scheme, which could help people planning to buy a property in the coming years save towards a deposit. The scheme could consequently provide additional support for future housing demand.

In its statement, ingatlan.com emphasised, however, that the precise impact of the housing policy measures announced on Monday could only be reliably forecast once the detailed terms and conditions of the programmes were known.

World.title: Hungary and Slovakia want EU to ease Russian energy ban rules
World.content:
Hungary and Slovakia are calling for greater flexibility and more EU funding as the bloc prepares to end Russian energy imports in 2027, warning that replacing existing supplies could prove costly for Central Europe.

Hungary and Slovakia are urging Brussels to ease the rules surrounding the phase-out of Russian gas and provide more funding to expand regional energy infrastructure, Euronews reports. They argue that their geographical position and dependence on existing supply routes make it harder and more expensive to diversify their energy sources.

Under the European Union’s plans, Russian energy imports to Central Europe are due to end in 2027, raising concerns in both countries about energy security, industrial competitiveness and the cost of replacing existing supplies.

Hungary and the EU are heading in the same direction on energy policy, but Hungary wants to move at a slower pace. Photo: depositphotos.com

Slovakia warns of energy supply challenges

Slovakia has historically served as an entry point for Russian oil and gas, but it now risks becoming a destination at the end of alternative supply routes, alongside Hungary, as the EU moves away from Russian energy.

Speaking at a press conference in Bratislava attended by European Commissioner for Energy Dan Jørgensen, Slovak Deputy Prime Minister Denisa Saková called for discussions with the European Commission on how the next EU funding period could address the region’s needs.

“We would like to discuss with the European Commission how the next EU funding period and the availability of EU funds can meet our needs, particularly regarding the expansion of oil and gas infrastructure in the Visegrád Four region,” Saková said.

Saková also stressed the importance of preparing new supply agreements ahead of the 2027 deadline, arguing that energy security requires clear rules for delivering oil and gas throughout the region.

If you missed it: Only one year left to use Russian gas: will the Hungarian economy truly grind to a halt without it?

V4 pushes for lower electricity bills

The latest appeal follows pressure from all four Visegrád countries at the European Council summit on 15–16 October. They called on EU leaders to reconsider measures intended to ease electricity costs across Central Europe. Their demands included greater flexibility in the ongoing review of the EU’s Emissions Trading System (ETS), the bloc’s carbon market, and postponing the introduction of its second phase, ETS2, until 2030.

The countries argue that high energy prices are making it harder for their industries to invest in electrification, the transition from fossil fuels to electricity-powered processes and technologies. The US-Israeli war against Iran has contributed to rising energy prices, adding to the pressure on households and businesses across Europe.

According to energy think tank Ember, wholesale electricity futures in Central Europe are now more than 60% above pre-crisis levels, leaving consumers in the region facing a particularly heavy financial burden.

Never miss a headline: join Daily News Hungary’s official Telegram channel!

Brussels acknowledges the problem but insists on limits

European Commissioner for Energy Dan Jørgensen acknowledged the “serious” situation facing Central European households but maintained that any response should consist of targeted and temporary measures.

He also warned against solutions that could undermine the EU’s broader objective of reducing its dependence on imported fossil fuels.

“We used to be dependent on Russia. We’re moving out of that. Now, that is good. But the current situation shows that we are now dependent on the global market, and events in the Middle East can affect citizens here in Bratislava,” Jørgensen said.

Hungary and Slovakia seek alternatives to Russian supplies

Budapest and Bratislava argue that meeting the EU’s energy diversification requirements will be particularly difficult without additional financial support. Both countries want investment in infrastructure that would allow them to receive oil and gas through alternative routes.

The Visegrád countries already have access to several non-Russian energy sources and supply routes. However, these alternatives can be more expensive, and the extent to which they are integrated into national energy systems varies across the region. Hungary and Slovakia therefore want Brussels to recognise these differences when deciding how to distribute EU funding.

Hungary has also challenged the EU’s plan to phase out Russian energy imports in court, with Slovakia supporting its legal action. Both countries argue that ending Russian supplies could put their industries at a competitive disadvantage compared with businesses elsewhere in the EU.

World.title: Billions, big promises and debt: opposition Fidesz and Mi Hazánk attack Tisza’s 2027 budget
World.content:
The debate on the 2027 budget should be conducted once the draft is known, Fidesz parliamentary group leader János Bóka said at Monday’s sitting of parliament, responding to the prime minister’s speech before the agenda. Our Homeland’s group leader, László Toroczkai, said the prime minister had not said in his speech what the budget would cost, while the Christian Democratic People’s Party (KDNP) group leader called next year’s budget hostile to the middle class.

Fidesz’s Bóka complained that Péter Magyar had spoken for more than two hours about a budget that has not yet been submitted. He added that the prime minister had not mentioned such key parameters as inflation, economic growth and the public debt figures on which next year’s budget was based.

The government, he insisted, was not keeping a single election campaign promise to each occupational group, and there would be no wage rises of the scale Tisza promised.

Read more about the 2027 budget:

Hungary’s 2027 budget: PM Magyar reveals major tax cuts, family allowance and pension rises

Péter Magyar announces huge housing and road spending reforms, food price cap removal

Meanwhile, Toroczkai said the prime minister had spoken about railway development, a rental housing construction programme and much else that would require the 6 trillion forints in European Union funding. He said that Tisza lawmakers and government members had earlier called that sum the cornerstone of the 2027 budget.

Bence Rétvári, the group leader of KDNP, called next year’s budget hostile to the middle class, employers and workers. The budget, he insisted, sought to smash the pillars of the earlier economic system that could have formed the basis of economic growth built on Hungarian businesses and Hungarian employers.

The government, he complained, had stripped the Fiscal Council of its veto right, although the council could genuinely have determined whether “the great pile of promises” would indebt Hungary.
