World.title: Study: Wetlands flora needs support to bounce back after restoration
World.content:
Restoring natural water levels alone may not be enough to rehabilitate severely degraded wetlands, according to a new study . Restoration efforts must also actively encourage vegetation recovery, writes Ilona Tamm, a junior research fellow at the University of Tartu.

Many wetlands around the world have been restored, but far less is known about whether these areas actually begin functioning as wetlands again. Monitoring often lasts only a short time and many projects lack sufficiently clear objectives against which to assess the success of restoration efforts.

When a peatland is drained, oxygen enters the peat, causing the organic matter stored there to decompose more rapidly and release carbon dioxide into the atmosphere. Raising the water level slows this process and helps prevent further peat loss, but a wet area is not necessarily a restored wetland. For that to happen, conditions must develop that allow vegetation characteristic of wetlands to grow again.

In our recently published study, my colleagues from the University of Tartu and the University of California, Berkeley, and I therefore examined two wetlands with long histories of drainage, tracking changes in water levels, vegetation and carbon dioxide and methane fluxes over four years following restoration. One of the wetlands, Ess-soo, is located on a former peat extraction site in southern Estonia, while the other, Hill Slough, lies in California's Sacramento–San Joaquin River Delta.

Both sites were restored in 2021 after decades of drainage and land use. Four years later, the results were surprisingly similar: restoring water levels had not led to significant vegetation growth.

Two very different wetlands, one similar concern

Vegetation generally struggles to recover at former peat extraction sites. Peat extraction removes much of the original vegetation and the seeds and other material needed for plants to spread. The remaining bare peat surface is acidic, nutrient-poor and dry. As a result, even a former peat extraction site that has been abandoned for decades can remain largely devoid of vegetation.

Ess-soo was originally a natural raised bog, but peat extraction in the second half of the 20th century fundamentally transformed the area. Restoration work began in 2021 at the 58-hectare former peat extraction site, which had been abandoned for nearly 30 years. The site was divided into several sections, with different restoration methods applied to each.

Our study focused on an 8.3-hectare section where drainage ditches were blocked and shallow pools were created to raise the water level and encourage the natural recovery of peatland vegetation. The aim was to keep the water level close to the ground surface and create conditions suitable for the return of vegetation characteristic of transitional mires.

Following restoration, a problem emerged at Ess-soo: conditions in different parts of the same site were either too dry or too wet. Lower-lying sections of the peatland remained permanently submerged, causing vegetation to decline, while water levels in higher areas fell too far below the surface.

During the dry summer of 2024, the water level remained too far below the surface across much of the study area for more than a month. Four years after restoration, vegetation still covered only about 30 percent of the drier ground. Sphagnum mosses, which are particularly important for the formation of new peat, were not found in the study area either before or after restoration.

At Hill Slough, the problem was different, but the outcome was similar. Located in a Mediterranean climate, the wetland underwent extensive diking and drainage beginning in the mid-19th century to make way for farming and livestock grazing. In 2021, the natural water regime was restored across the 100-hectare study area by opening the levees. The aim was to reintroduce tidal flows and improve habitats for wildlife characteristic of wetlands.

However, at Hill Slough, which had been cut off from its natural water regime for more than a century, the original wetland vegetation had undergone substantial changes. When the area was once again exposed to daily tidal fluctuations, leaving much of it frequently submerged, the vegetation that had been present before restoration rapidly declined.

Water levels fluctuated by more than a meter over the course of a day, while shifting soft sediments and unstable ground likely made it even harder for plants to establish themselves. As a result, Hill Slough became almost entirely a mudflat, with only a few plants managing to establish themselves along the higher edges of the site.

Lack of vegetation impacts climate benefits

Very slow vegetation growth means that wetland ecosystems recover only gradually, directly affecting the carbon cycle. Plants absorb carbon dioxide from the atmosphere through photosynthesis. When vegetation is sparse, carbon uptake also remains low.

At the same time, restoring water to a wetland has an important effect of its own. Under wet conditions, less oxygen can penetrate the peat, slowing its decomposition and potentially reducing carbon dioxide emissions. However, oxygen-poor conditions can also increase methane production. Therefore, assessing the climate impact of a restored wetland requires considering both carbon dioxide and methane.

Both study sites remained net sources of carbon throughout the monitoring period, meaning they released more greenhouse gases into the atmosphere than they absorbed. At Ess-soo, net carbon dioxide emissions during the drought year of 2024 were approximately 158 grams of carbon per square meter per year, compared with around 42 grams in the wetter year of 2025. Meanwhile, methane emissions increased from approximately six grams to nine grams. The lower carbon dioxide emissions were consistent with cooler, wetter conditions that may have slowed peat decomposition.

Emissions at Hill Slough were generally higher. Over the four-year period, net carbon dioxide emissions declined from approximately 334 grams to 270 grams of carbon per square meter per year. Methane emissions, meanwhile, increased after the first year and subsequently remained high, reaching approximately 22 grams.

The differences between the two sites are likely related to climate, vegetation and water regimes. For example, Estonia's cooler climate limits microbial activity and the decomposition of organic matter during winter. In other words, restoring water levels may have reduced some organic matter decomposition, but sparse vegetation meant that neither site had yet reached a point where carbon uptake by plants could offset emissions.

Slow recovery not inevitable

Such carbon fluxes are not unusual in restored wetlands with sparse vegetation. Carbon dioxide emissions at Hill Slough were similar to those measured at other restored wetlands in California's delta where vegetation had not returned. By contrast, strong carbon dioxide uptake has been recorded at restored wetlands with similar conditions but well-established vegetation.

Ess-soo's carbon balance was similar to that of partially vegetated former peat extraction sites undergoing restoration, while net carbon dioxide uptake has also been achieved at peatlands with more extensive vegetation. However, even well-established vegetation does not automatically mean that a wetland will become a net carbon sink every year.

The slow recovery of Ess-soo and Hill Slough does not mean that such outcomes should be accepted as inevitable. Vegetation in tidal wetlands typically becomes established within three to five years and, in the best cases, within just one year. There are also examples of former peat extraction sites, where recovery is generally slower, achieving full vegetation cover in approximately five years.

Rapid recovery often requires more than simply restoring water levels. Depending on the site, restoration efforts can include improving water management, preparing the soil, adjusting ground elevation and actively encouraging vegetation recovery, for example through planting or transplanting sphagnum mosses. No such active vegetation restoration measures were used in the sections of Ess-soo and Hill Slough examined in this study.

If monitoring shows that vegetation is not recovering or water levels are not behaving as planned, restoration measures should be adjusted rather than simply waiting. This requires setting clear, measurable objectives from the outset and monitoring results over an extended period. Sharing both successes and challenges is equally important, as comparisons between different sites can help improve the planning of future restoration projects.

This is precisely what the comparison between Ess-soo and Hill Slough demonstrates: similar obstacles can arise in very different wetlands. These findings do not diminish the need for wetland restoration. Rather, they show that successful restoration involves more than simply bringing back water — ecosystem recovery must be monitored and, when necessary, actively guided.

The study was published in the journal Restoration Ecology.

World.title: Ad agency Tank breaks apolitical streak to handle Reform Party's 2027 campaign
World.content:
According to agency founder and creative director Joel Volkov, the deciding factor was the Reform Party's values, which can stand up to far-right populist politics.

Kontuur Leo Burnett has previously handled most of the Reform Party's election campaigns, but the party decided to seek a new partner earlier this year.

Reform Party Secretary-General Kristo Enn Vaga told ERR that Tank was chosen for its fresh ideas and enthusiasm. Although the agency has no previous experience in political communications, Vaga believes it can bring new energy both to the party's campaign and to Estonia's broader political communications and public relations landscape.

Tank creative director Joel Volkov said the agency had ruled out working with other political parties but made an exception for the Reform Party.

"Tank has never produced political advertising in its 31 years of operation. When the Reform Party approached us in early spring 2026, we took some time to think before turning them down outright. This time, we decided to help," Volkov told ERR.

Volkov acknowledged that the Reform Party has struggled politically, with politicians making mistakes in difficult situations, going back on their word and communicating poorly. He said the party's declining approval ratings reflected those problems.

Nevertheless, Volkov believes the Reform Party retains considerable political value because of its liberal, pro-business worldview, which he considers essential to Estonia's future prosperity.

"We believe that these are precisely the kinds of values that can stand up to the rise of far-right populist politics without inciting hatred. Such politics are also spreading rapidly in Estonia, encouraged by foreign agents," Volkov said.

Joel Volkov. Source: Iris Tähema/ERR

According to Volkov, the Reform Party's main challenge is not name recognition, which remains high, but rebuilding public trust.

He argued that restoring trust requires politicians to acknowledge their weaknesses and mistakes rather than praise their own achievements. The process, he said, will take time, honesty and a willingness to demonstrate that the party understands voters' concerns.

Volkov described the Reform Party's new "pep talk" campaign as a creative response to that challenge, saying it could be one of Estonia's first election campaigns in which politicians focus on listening rather than dominating the conversation.

A clear enough campaign slogan?

Vaga said the party's campaign slogan, "A Clear Course for the Future," ("Kindel suund on tulevik") was developed in cooperation with Tank and carries a deeper political message.

He explained that certainty has traditionally been central to the Reform Party's messaging, particularly when it has held government responsibility. Given Estonia's challenging security environment, he said reassuring the public that the country is protected remains especially important.

The slogan's emphasis on the future is also intended to distinguish the Reform Party from political opponents that Vaga believes are focused on dismantling existing institutions and returning to the past.

Vaga said the Reform Party wants Estonia to continue developing as a country with expanding freedoms and a growing economy, arguing that building a more prosperous future for subsequent generations has been a central party objective for decades.

Prime Minister and Reform Party leader Kristen Michal made a similar argument on Vikerraadio Tuesday. He accused EKRE, the Center Party and Isamaa of wanting to move backward rather than forward in both their values and approach to technology.

Asked whether voters would understand the slogan's multiple meanings, Vaga acknowledged that not everyone would consider its deeper political message. However, he said the slogan would make sense to voters when presented alongside the Reform Party's name.

Kristo Enn Vaga. Source: Ken Mürk/ERR

Both Vaga and Michal also dismissed suggestions that the absence of Hanno Pevkur and Jürgen Ligi from campaign videos released over the weekend was deliberate.

Michal said the two politicians were likely traveling or otherwise unavailable when the videos were filmed. Vaga added that Pevkur had not yet confirmed whether he would run in the Riigikogu elections.

Election promises to be gradually unveiled starting in November

Looking ahead, Vaga said the Reform Party's campaign will include video and television ads, as well as outdoor advertising. The party will also begin announcing its election promises and revealing which electoral districts its candidates will contest.

While Vaga did not disclose any specific campaign promises, he said national defense and economic growth would remain key priorities. The party is also developing proposals on family policy, parental benefits, long-term energy planning and improving pensioners' living standards, including continued pension indexation.

According to Vaga, the Reform Party's election platform will be nearly 100 pages long, containing both specific proposals and broader commitments. The party plans to begin publishing it chapter by chapter in November.

Vaga also confirmed that the party will make changes to its lead candidates in several electoral districts, as some politicians who ran in the previous election will not be standing again.

He noted that Kaja Kallas, who headed the party's list in Harju and Rapla counties in the last election as Reform Party chair, now holds a senior position in Europe and is no longer active in domestic politics.

The late Siim Kallas will also be absent from the ballot.

Vaga said further details about the party's candidates and their electoral districts would be announced in November.

The Riigikogu elections are scheduled for March 2027.

World.title: Tallinn Old Town doubles as England for highly anticipated Indian film
World.content:
Tallinn Old Town recently transformed into early 20th-century England for the historical Indian film "The India House," bringing major Indian stars to the Estonian capital.

Directed by Ram Vamsi Krishna, the film follows Indian students in London who fought British colonial rule in the pre-independence era in the early 1900s.

The film takes its name from the North London student residence that became a key hub for Indian nationalist political activism between 1905 and 1910.

During filming around Tallinn's Old Town this fall, the picturesque Müürivahe tänav, for example, became Oxford Street, complete with British flags, while a major protest scene involving 150 actors was filmed by Cinema Sõprus.

Nafta Films founder and producer Esko Rips said that it was unusual for such a large crew to travel abroad for a shoot, with 47 Indian crew members in Estonia alongside Nafta Films' local team of around 70.

He said working across cultural and professional differences meant both teams had to adapt their communication and working styles. "We try to find common ground," Rips added.

'Tallinn feels like home'

Tollywood star Nikhil Siddhartha has more than 25 films to his name, including the 2022 Telugu blockbuster "Karthikeya 2," one of India's highest-grossing films.

Shooting for "The India House" marked Siddhartha's first-ever visit to Estonia, but he admitted it didn't feel that way.

"It just feels so welcoming," he said. "I don't feel like I've come to a different country; it feels like home."

Siddhartha also praised Tallinn's well-preserved Old Town and Estonia's collective efforts in supporting culture.

"Estonia is rich in culture," he said, "and I'm very happy to come visit it and shoot here."

Filming for Indian film "The India House" in front of Tallinn's Cinema Sõprus. October 2026. Source: press photo

Estonian slackliner Jaan Roose also joined the production as a stunt performer, handling falls, jumps and other action sequences. He said protective padding hidden beneath his costume helped cushion the impacts.

"I have to run on cobblestones, jump, fall and take a hit from a barrel," he said. "I'm doing anything that requires knowing how to fall."

The Indian production team considered filming in several European countries before choosing Estonia, Siddhartha said, thanking Rips personally for helping make the arrangements.

"The way they welcomed us, the way they described filming locations — we were blown away," the film star emphasized, adding that the film will also be shown in several Estonian movie theaters once released.

Film Estonia incentive's future uncertain

Rips said Estonia's 40 percent film production incentive helped secure the foreign film project. The "India House" team had visited other countries, including the U.K. itself, but filming there would have been more expensive.

After driving about 7,500 kilometers, scouting locations across Estonia a year ago, the filmmakers fell for Tallinn, choosing it over alternatives including Bulgaria and Lithuania.

The Estonian producer warned, however, that the Film Estonia incentive is poised to lose funding under the next government, set to be elected next March. Securing one production is only part of the challenge.

"I don't understand why our industry is being jerked around like this," Rips said. "Attracting a project here and working on it is one thing; attracting new projects is another, and we need them to keep the industry going."

World.title: Keidi Jaakson: How we talk about immigration matters
World.content:
In mid-October, Rainis Sinikas, head of the border and migration supervision department at the Police and Border Guard Board's (PPA) North Prefecture, told ERR that the situation with irregular migrants in Estonia is "difficult and could turn into a crisis situation," that administrative courts and local governments are overloaded and that the entire cooperation network is under great strain. A few days earlier, PPA chief Egert Belitšev warned that migration pressure could rise sharply as people try to leave Belarus ahead of winter, describing organized routes that cost each person up to €10,000. Interior Minister Igor Taro has called the situation "part of Russia's overall aggression tactics" and declared that Estonia must send a clear message that it cannot be used as a transit corridor. So far this year, the PPA has detained 542 people from 48 countries, both within Estonia and at its borders, and returned 120 of them to Latvia.

There are real operational and security challenges behind these numbers. According to Egert Belitšev, Russia and Belarus facilitate routes organized by criminal networks, with people paying thousands of euros to reach the EU. Processing people who arrive without documents, establishing their identities and routes and pursuing those responsible for facilitating irregular crossings is demanding work. ERR has reported that tighter border controls in Poland and Lithuania have redirected part of these flows towards Estonia. The pressure on local services is also documented: Rae Municipality, where the main detention center is located, is considering legal action against the state and the Social Insurance Board has acknowledged that it was unprepared for the increase. But public concern about immigration is not simply a reflection of how many people arrive across the border. It is also shaped by how much attention, and what kind of attention, the issue itself receives.

James Dennison and Andrew Geddes of the European University Institute's Migration Policy Center recently published "What Europeans Think About Immigration and Why It Matters," drawing on 25 years of survey data across Europe. Their research suggests that public attitudes towards immigration are more stable and more nuanced than commonly assumed and that, where they change, they tend to actually become more favorable over time. What changes more readily is what the researchers call salience: how much attention immigration receives as a political issue. This can be shaped by institutional communication, political rhetoric and media coverage. Speaking at the book's launch at the Center for European Policy Studies in Brussels, Dennison argued that people who consider immigration an important political issue are disproportionately likely to hold restrictive views. Raising the issue's profile can therefore benefit one part of the political spectrum. He also warned that political parties often confuse the growing prominence of immigration with a shift in what people actually believe about it, responding to heightened attention as though it necessarily reflected more restrictive public attitudes.

The language used to describe the current situation to the Estonian public should be proportionate to its scale. Repeated references to crisis and hybrid attacks can make the situation appear more acute and exceptional than the numbers alone suggest. Estonia has detained 542 people so far this year, while Latvia, which directly borders Belarus, recorded over 8,400 irregular crossing attempts by July 21. Across the EU, Frontex recorded approximately 74,000 irregular border-crossing detections in the first eight months of the year, down 35 percent compared with 2025. These figures measure different things and cannot be compared directly, but they provide context for assessing the language used. In an ERR report published on October 19, Taro himself said that Estonia had not yet exhausted its capacity to handle migrants and that the situation could only be described as a crisis once existing resources were no longer sufficient, with several hundred detention places across the country still vacant. By the interior minister's own measure, then, the situation has not reached the point of crisis, which makes the persistent language of potential crisis harder to account for.

Dennison and Geddes's research raises questions about how the current framing of immigration in Estonia may shape public perceptions. Detentions are routinely reported as separate events, often with considerable operational detail. PPA statements repeatedly warn that institutions are overloaded and that the situation could turn into a crisis. The interior minister has urged people to report suspicious individuals. Such communication may increase the prominence of immigration in public debate and encourage people to view it primarily through the lens of security, even if it does not change their underlying attitudes.

In the Spring 2024 Eurobarometer, 29 percent of Estonian respondents agreed that immigrants contribute positively to the country, tied with Cyprus for one of the lowest figure in the EU. The 2018 European Social Survey found that just over half of Estonians thought the state should allow few or no people of a different race or ethnic group to move to Estonia, though the same data shows that attitudes have been slowly becoming more favorable over time. Against this backdrop, repeatedly framing immigration as a potential crisis risks reinforcing the perception that it is primarily a threat.

The deliberate instrumentalization of migration by Russia and Belarus is a genuine security concern, yet recognizing that threat does not require treating everyone travelling along these routes as a threat in themselves. The largest groups among those detained this year come from Somalia, Sudan, Ethiopia, Eritrea and Bangladesh, several of which are affected by armed conflict or severe human rights abuses. EU law provides no visa for the purpose of seeking asylum, so in most cases protection can only be claimed once a person is already on European territory. Arrivals along these routes are unlikely to stop and Estonia needs the capacity to process them effectively.

And Estonia has demonstrated that it can mobilize considerable institutional capacity when the political and public context supports it. In 2022, more than 43,000 Ukrainian refugees arrived, amounting to over 3 percent of the population. The legal framework was different, the circumstances were different and the public solidarity was grounded in a shared sense of threat from Russia. But the experience shows what Estonia can organize when political priorities and public solidarity align. The question is whether the capacity can be rebuilt for people whose reasons for seeking protection may be less immediately legible to the Estonian public.

The debate also raises questions about who attracts suspicion and on what grounds. An operation in Nõmme on October 11 began when residents reported two dark-skinned men who appeared unfamiliar with the area. In August, ERR reported that police had already received unfounded reports about people based solely on their skin colour and PPA representative Indrek Aru acknowledged that in one case the person who had been reported "had all the necessary documents, was completely law-abiding and even spoke Estonian." In its account of the October incident, however, the PPA said that reports were generally prompted by behavior rather than race, while acknowledging that people from a different ethnic background stand out more in a suburb like Nõmme where residents tend to recognize one another. Sinikas also pointed to muddy clothing as one reason groups of migrants might attract attention in autumn.

The gender equality and equal treatment commissioner's 2024 report on racial discrimination documented experiences of racism among people of color in Estonia, including verbal abuse and physical threats, much of it unreported. The difficulty lies in how authorities distinguish legitimate reports based on specific behavior from suspicion based primarily on someone's appearance, particularly when the police themselves acknowledge that skin color can influence who attracts attention. That distinction deserves more public discussion than it currently receives.

World.title: Estonia could learn from Israel's crisis preparedness
World.content:
Estonia can learn from Israel's decades of experience with war, particularly when it comes to building shelters, warning the public about attacks and preparing people for crises, Israeli civil defense expert Yoram Laredo says.

Israelis have been hardened by various wars.

"Unfortunately, since the establishment of the state in 1948, there has been a war every 10 years. So, sadly, we have experienced different types of warfare," said Israeli civil defense expert Yoram Laredo on ERR's "Välisilm" foreign affairs program.

When it comes to shelters, for example, Israel is often held up as a model. However, the system in which everyone knows where to go has taken decades to develop. The turning point came with the 1991 Gulf War.

"That was a lesson we learned from the Gulf War. At the time, Iraq fired ballistic missiles at Israel for the first time. Following that tragic event, we introduced a rule requiring every newly constructed building and apartment to have a shelter. Today, 70 percent of Israeli citizens have a shelter in their homes. It takes time," Laredo said.

But what could be done more quickly, including in Estonia?

"My recommendation is to bring in engineers and inspect every underground parking garage. If they can be shown to withstand ballistic missile strikes, they can be designated as shelters for large numbers of people. These are things that can be done using existing resources," Laredo said.

The most important thing is to be prepared for a crisis.

"You need to prepare your citizens for what is coming and keep them informed. The information available must be shared because that is the first step toward resilience. People break down psychologically when something happens that they did not expect. If the government communicates with people and warns them that there will be power outages, communications disruptions and supply chain problems, and explains how these will be handled, citizens will be able to cope," Laredo said.

Estonia can also learn from Israel's approach to warning people about attacks.

"Israel has a highly sophisticated system that detects all objects flying toward the country, whether from nearby or far away, regardless of their shape or type. The most important element is the siren system. There are thousands of sirens on rooftops. In addition, mobile apps, the internet, radio and television all work in sync. Someone might be watching television, using their phone or standing outside — the system warns them that a missile is on its way. The best thing to do then is take shelter. After the first casualties, everyone knows what to do and people become very disciplined. Unfortunately, that is how it works," Laredo said.

However, when several generations have grown up without experiencing war, it is difficult to make people understand what they need to be prepared for.

"It is comparable to how we anticipate an earthquake in Israel. Our region experiences a devastating earthquake every 100 years. There has been no such earthquake in the history of modern Israel. The last one occurred 100 years ago, before the State of Israel was established. How do you convince the population that an earthquake could strike at any moment?" the expert said.

Israel learned a harsh lesson three years ago when one of the world's best intelligence services allowed the October 7 tragedy to happen because of overconfidence.

"You have to constantly reassess your strategic assumptions and paradigms. If you fail to do that and rely solely on technological superiority without questioning your interpretation of intelligence, things like this happen. That is Israel's most important lesson: Strategic assumptions and interpretations of intelligence must be constantly reassessed rather than rigidly adhered to," Laredo said.

Following October 7, the small state of Israel also had to evacuate large numbers of people.

"The State of Israel evacuated 125,000 people, including 60,000 from the north. Communities along the northern border were evacuated because, at the time, we did not know whether Hezbollah would open a second front there. Communities around Gaza were also evacuated. Those 125,000 people lived in hotels for almost two years. And that really costs a lot of money," Laredo said.

It is also essential to maintain a constant state of crisis preparedness.

"Preparing for a crisis is like a muscle that needs to be exercised constantly. If you do not exercise that muscle, you become exhausted and when a crisis strikes, you eventually break down psychologically. That is what we have learned. Unfortunately, we constantly face real incidents and wars, so we are practicing all the time," Laredo said.

World.title: Tallinn cancels Olympic swimming pool tender following ministry warning
World.content:
Tallinn City Council has canceled a tender to build an Olympic-standard swimming pool launched earlier this summer after the Ministry of Finance questioned the conditions. The project will now be delayed by at least a year.

The capital has floated plans to build a swimming pool next to the Tondiraba Ice Hall in Lasnamäe since 2019. The facility will include sports halls, a spa and an Olympic-standard swimming pool.

An international public procurement tender was launched in July to find a private company to build the center.

However, Mayor Peeter Raudsepp (Isamaaa) announced at a press conference on Tuesday that the tender would not go any further.

"Unfortunately, we have been forced to cancel the current swimming pool concession tender because the Ministry of Finance has warned the city that it is considering launching supervisory proceedings concerning the tender," he said. "This would mean endless disputes and potentially the invalidation of the tender."

Tallinn Mayor Peeter Raudsepp. Source: Siim Lõvi /ERR

According to the city council, the Ministry of Finance had raised questions over the tender conditions and its competitiveness.

Raudsepp said he disagreed with the assessment, but the city did not want to take risks that may jeopardize the construction of the swimming pool. The procurement model has now been changed to increase competition and ensure compliance with state aid rules in all circumstances, and preparations for a new tender are underway.

Tallinn's goal is still to build Estonia's first swimming center that meets international Olympic standards, serves elite athletes, recreational swimmers and children learning to swim, the mayor told the assembled media.

"We want to cooperate with the private sector because this will help reduce the building's maintenance costs in the long term and is a more economical decision in terms of taxpayers' money," Raudsepp said.

Year-long delay

City officials believe the new tender should give the developer greater freedom to operate.

The basic requirements will stay the same: a 50-meter competition pool with 10 lanes, a 25-meter training pool, teaching pools and a parking lot.

Prospective bidders will be able to design all other facilities according to their business plans.

Tiit Terik (Center). Source: Priit Mürk/ERR

"Several potential developers have expressed interest in the current tender, which shows that there is genuine market interest in the project. At the same time, the city cannot take the risk that a swimming pool project that has been in preparation for years will become bogged down in lengthy proceedings or court disputes. With the new tender, we can address the necessary issues from the outset and focus on building the swimming center," Deputy Mayor Tiit Terik (Center) said.

Tallinn is prepared to contribute up to €20 million for the project, which the city says is less than it would cost to build a swimming pool fully owned by Tallinn.

The project is now expected to be delayed by at least a year.

The Social Democratic Party, which is in opposition in Tallinn, has previously criticized the plan to build the swimming pool with the help of an investment grant, and sees a potential corruption risk.

Ministry made no demands

The Ministry of Finance on Tuesday afternoon said it is puzzled by Raudsepp's claims.

"We have not issued any order. We did not even get as far as initiating supervisory proceedings before they decided to cancel the tender themselves," said Elo Ellermaa, head of the ministry's communications department.

Former Mayor Jevgeni Ossinovski (SDE) told ERR on Tuesday that he had proposed the ministry launch supervisory proceedings to protect the public interest, citing the Porto Franco case.

"The European Commission would have demanded the repayment of illegal aid, the developer would have packed up and left, and we would have ended up with yet another project reeking of the Center Party, standing as an abandoned eyesore and blighting the cityscape for years," Ossinovski said.

Jevgeni Ossinovski. Source: Siim Lõvi /ERR

However, Ellermaa said the ministry has not made any decisions. It received a request to initiate supervisory proceedings, but before doing so, an assessment takes place.

"We were still only in the assessment phase, requesting additional information from the contracting authority, and no supervisory proceedings have been initiated or a position taken on the matter. At the request of the contracting authority, namely the Tallinn City Property Department, the deadline for providing explanations was also extended," Ellermaa explained.

"To our knowledge, however, the Tallinn City Property Department has decided to invalidate the tender on its own initiative," she said, adding that the organizers of the tender should be able to explain the reasons.

Ellermaa confirmed that if the public procurement procedure has been invalidated, the Ministry of Finance will not initiate supervisory proceedings.

This article was updated to add comments from the Ministry of Finance and Jevgeni Ossinovski.

World.title: Karl Lumiste: Reservists are both important and underpaid in Estonia
World.content:
Investments in ammunition and concrete are of no use without motivated fighters to back them up, writes reservist Karl Lumiste.

"The strength of Estonia's defense lies in reservists who have the support of society," former commander of the Estonian Defense Forces and Defense Minister Martin Herem said in a recent interview. Unfortunately, this is not reflected in actions, as reservists receive the smallest share of defense spending and are the last to see any of it.

Following an appeal by the chancellor of justice, former Defense Minister Hanno Pevkur increased reservist allowances in 2025 after they had remained unchanged for years. Nevertheless, only slightly more than half of the reservists who participated in a survey conducted during Exercise Hedgehog 2025 rated the allowances as very or somewhat good.

Since 2025, reservists attending training exercises have received daily allowances of €55 for enlisted personnel, €60 for noncommissioned officers and €75 for officers. During periods of heightened defense readiness, these amounts rise to €75, €80 and €100, respectively. Considering the median wage, these allowances are nowhere near adequate or respectful, particularly as lost wages are the biggest obstacle preventing reservists from attending training exercises.

The median wage has risen to €1,840 per month, meaning that the lowest allowance — the daily rate for enlisted personnel — falls well short of competitive compensation.

A week of reserve training clearly illustrates the difference. An enlisted reservist attending an exercise loses five working days' wages, amounting to €460 for someone earning the median wage (assuming a daily wage of €92 based on 20 working days per month). However, the reservist receives a state allowance of €55 per day for seven days, totaling €385 (as the exercise also includes the weekend). This leaves the reservist €75 worse off after just one week. Those earning above the median wage lose even more.

The allowance should not merely be enough to ensure that reservists break even when attending training. It should be substantially higher, so they are happy to attend and feel that their contribution is highly valued.

Such an investment would also create the best conditions for more reservists to willingly participate in training exercises, as they would no longer have to attend knowing they would lose income. The state must ensure that reservists receive decent compensation rather than relying on the goodwill of employers.

Raising allowances to a respectable level would be a small step for the state budget but a major step toward strengthening the will to defend the country. Money cannot buy the will to defend, but it can provide a tangible sign of respect, demonstrating just how important the contribution of the backbone of national defense really is.

Estonia's defense spending has increased to 5.4 percent of GDP or €2.4 billion for 2026. Given this, the state should not have to beg people for money through the Reservists' Fund to purchase equipment, recognize service members and support reservists.

Investments in ammunition and concrete are of no use without motivated fighters behind them who believe their country is worth defending. Unlike funding (phantom) foreign companies, investing in the people of Estonia keeps money circulating in our economy rather than allowing it to disappear abroad as dividends for defense industry investors.

The greatest asset to national security is a motivated fighter who wants to defend a country that values their contribution. The state exists for the people, not the people for the state. Following this principle will inevitably lead to success because investing in people creates the true foundation of trust between citizens and the state.

World.title: Aaviksoo, Lauristin, Raidla: A manifesto for modernizing the way Estonia is governed
World.content:
Estonia needs to modernize its system of government, strengthen political accountability and give citizens a greater role in decision-making to restore public trust and address future challenges, Jaak Aaviksoo, Marju Lauristin and Jüri Raidla write.

Estonia has made tremendous progress in the 35 years since it regained independence. Economic prosperity has increased, life expectancy has risen and Estonia has become a full-fledged member of the international community of democratically minded nations.

This successful development was driven by our desire for freedom and willingness to work toward a better future, as well as the democratic maturity needed to draft a balanced constitution and establish a system of government based on it that serves the interests of the country's citizens. The wise decisions made in those early years have sustained us for more than three decades.

Yet against this backdrop of progress, we sense that momentum is fading, dissatisfaction is replacing confidence in the future and mutual distrust is growing in society. Politics driven by a sense of mission and vision is in short supply. Most importantly, trust in government has declined. Government is perceived as self-serving and burdensome, leadership is lacking and the quality of governance leaves much to be desired at both the institutional and individual levels.

This is a question of power and alienation. More precisely, it concerns the relationship of trust between the people in whom supreme power is vested and those who exercise that power.

Power, which in the early years was exercised by involving broad interest groups and drawing on the expertise of people from different backgrounds, is becoming confined to political party bubbles and the career politics that perpetuates them. As a result, much of the nation's talent and expertise has been excluded from the exercise of power.

Bureaucratic layers and decision-making processes have proliferated, characterized by slow procedures, a lack of transparency and a disconnect from the problems people face in their daily lives. The role of the elected parliament has been reduced to that of a decorative appendage to the state bureaucracy, with no real ability to provide strategic direction to the government's activities.

At the same time, party-political considerations rather than the common national interest have come to dominate the actions of government ministers. The political elite has adopted a dismissive attitude toward civil society institutions.

Developments around the world demand that the Estonian state adopt a strategic vision for the future, demonstrate greater resolve and be prepared to make new efforts to preserve its free and democratic system of government while ensuring the continued viability of its economy, defense capabilities, the Estonian people and culture and social security.

Our society itself has also changed significantly.

On the one hand, over the past 35 years, we have become more knowledgeable and gained more experience in governing our own country than ever before.

On the other hand, a new generation of active citizens and leaders has come of age in a free and open society, working in business, culture and civil society. They have a broad international outlook and are adept at using new technologies, including the opportunities offered by artificial intelligence. This new generation of leaders is critical of political institutions and ways of thinking inherited from the last century, preferring data-driven, rapid decision-making and innovative forms of cooperation.

For the Estonian state to be capable not only of confronting threats but also of successfully pursuing new goals, both in international competition and in advancing the material, social and intellectual well-being of its citizens, the way the country is governed must also be capable of renewal and rest on trust and cooperation among all groups in society.

We believe that the way the country is governed needs to be modernized by making those in power more accessible to citizens, raising expectations and standards of accountability for the exercise of power, establishing a clearer division of political and administrative responsibility and making decision-making processes more data-driven, transparent and efficient.

We propose beginning this reform with three important steps.

First, make governance more open by ending political parties' monopoly over the formation and leadership of public institutions.

Given the limited membership of political parties, their poor ability to involve all significant groups in society, particularly the younger generation, and the experience of local elections, which shows that voters prefer electoral alliances to political parties, we propose expanding citizens' opportunities to participate in exercising state power. In addition to political parties, electoral alliances should be allowed to participate in Riigikogu elections on an equal footing with political parties.

Second, raise standards and strengthen accountability for the quality of governance. The Riigikogu's oversight of the executive branch should be strengthened. To improve ministers' ability to lead their respective policy areas, candidates for ministerial positions should undergo public hearings before the full Riigikogu, with the media present, including answering questions from members of parliament.

To clarify the division of political and administrative responsibility, ministers should be defined primarily as members of the Cabinet who lead their respective policy areas with the country's strategic development goals in mind and bear political responsibility for directing the activities of their ministries.

Ministers should report on the effectiveness of policies in their respective areas at least once a year at a public hearing of the relevant Riigikogu committee, with the media present. These hearings should also involve senior executives in the relevant field, experts and representatives of relevant civil society organizations. At the same time, the role and responsibility of ministry secretaries-general in overseeing and ensuring the functioning of their ministries and their areas of administration should be increased.

Third, establish an Estonian Future Convention as a new form of cooperation between the state and its citizens to broaden the democratic basis of state power and strengthen the country's strategic capabilities.

The Future Convention could function as an advisory body tasked with developing and evaluating potential strategic solutions to the key challenges facing Estonia's future, using a data-driven approach. This collaborative process would involve researchers from various fields, leading specialists, interest groups and representatives of all political parties as experts, while also allowing interested citizens to contribute ideas and proposals and express their views through an online citizens' assembly.

These changes could be implemented during 2027 and provide impetus for further steps toward modernizing Estonia's system of government.

World.title: Two oilfield operators in northern Iraq merge in $600 million deal
World.content:
Baghdad (IraqiNews.com) – Gulf Keystone Petroleum and ShaMaran Petroleum have reached a merger agreement, becoming one of the top private oil producers in Iraqi Kurdistan.

According to a statement from the corporation, the all-share acquisition is worth $601 million, Reuters reported.

As of October 19, shareholders of ShaMaran, who are listed on Euronext, will receive 0.075 shares of Gulf Keystone for each share of ShaMaran they own, reflecting a premium of 23 percent.

Each company’s stockholders will own roughly half of the merged business when the merger is complete.

According to the announcement, Gulf Keystone intends to cease its London listing and transfer its principal listing to Euronext Oslo Bors’ main list.

Following the completion of the deal, the listing of ShaMaran shares will end.

The proposed combination has received unanimous approval from the boards of Gulf Keystone and ShaMaran. December will see special meetings to complete approval.

With combined estimated reserves of 323 million barrels and daily production of 53,000 barrels of oil, the merged business is expected to profit from greater size and diversity.

As part of its ambitions to increase its oil production capacity, Iraq has given many contracts to businesses from the United States, China, France, and other countries.

As Baghdad looks to boost natural gas supply and oil output, British Petroleum (BP) and its US and Turkish partners took over operations at four oilfields in the northern Iraqi province of Kirkuk this week.

World.title: Iraq Stock Exchange records 2.5 billion IQD in weekly trading turnover
World.content:
Baghdad (IraqiNews.com) – The Iraq Stock Exchange (ISX) reported weekly trading turnover exceeding 2.5 billion Iraqi dinars ($1.68 million) for the previous trading week, according to an official market report published on Tuesday, October 20, 2026.

Across the five trading sessions, shares of 57 joint-stock companies were actively traded out of 103 listed entities. Equities of 36 firms saw zero transactions due to pricing bid-ask disparities between buy and sell orders, while 11 companies remained suspended from trading for failing to meet mandatory corporate financial disclosure and regulatory reporting deadlines.

Trading volume expanded by 6.8% compared to the prior week, reaching 1.852 billion traded shares. However, total trading value contracted by 67% to 2.560 billion dinars, executed across 3,676 transactions. The main price benchmark, the ISX60 index, closed at 943.57 points, shedding 1.54% from its previous session close.

Foreign investment activity posted net inflows into domestic equities. Non-Iraqi investors bought 158 million shares valued at 331 million dinars over 55 contracts, while foreign selling remained muted, tallying 5 million shares worth 10 million dinars across 38 transactions.

The exchange convenes trading across five weekly sessions from Sunday through Thursday, listing 103 joint-stock enterprises spanning banking, telecommunications, industry, agriculture, insurance, financial investment, tourism, and services.

World.title: US dollar edges down across Baghdad, Basra, and Erbil Exchanges
World.content:
Baghdad (IraqiNews.com) – The exchange rate of the U.S. dollar against the Iraqi dinar edged down across exchange shops in Baghdad, Basra, and Erbil on Tuesday, October 20, 2026, slightly paring back gains recorded earlier in the week.

In Baghdad, foreign exchange counters registered a dip of 500 dinars per $100 compared to Monday’s trading, setting the retail selling rate at 169,000 dinars against buying bids of 168,000 dinars.

In Erbil, the capital of the Kurdistan Region, trading displayed a similar softening, with selling desks quoting 168,200 dinars per $100 and buying transactions settling at 168,000 dinars.

In the southern commercial port hub of Basra, rates slipped by 250 dinars per $100 compared to yesterday’s levels. Exchange bureaus posted retail selling rates at 168,500 dinars against purchase bids of 168,000 dinars per $100.

Parallel market activity continues to reflect a sustained premium above the Central Bank of Iraq’s official statutory peg of 152,000 dinars per $100, driven by commercial merchant demand for physical liquidity outside the central electronic clearance platform.

World.title: Rubio lands in India for ‘trade diplomacy’
World.content:
Mumbai – US Secretary of State Marco Rubio arrived in India on Tuesday, his second official visit to the country this year, as he pursues an Asian tour blending diplomacy and trade.

Rubio visited Uzbekistan, where he called for stronger partnerships with Central Asian countries, before landing in Mumbai for talks with Foreign Minister Subrahmanyam Jaishankar and meetings with business leaders.

He visited New Delhi and Kolkata in May, when he also toured the Taj Mahal and met Prime Minister Narendra Modi.

Modi is not scheduled to meet Rubio this time.

The top US diplomat will visit Jamnagar, in the western state of Gujarat, a port and stronghold of billionaire Mukesh Ambani’s Reliance conglomerate and its flagship refinery, the world’s largest.

He is also due to lay a wreath in memory of the 2008 Mumbai attacks that killed 166 people.

Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelensky said on Tuesday he had also spoken to Rubio and raised issues with the US military satellite system that Ukraine uses, as well as missile delays.

Zelensky, expected in Oslo for talks with US envoys, said he told Rubio that “Starlink/Starshield needs to be restored” and that ballistic missile interceptors “are needed to protect lives”.

– ‘Energy supplies’ –

Rubio’s visit comes as India and the United States struggle to finalise a trade deal, a persistent source of friction between the two countries.

Speaking in Samarkand, Rubio said Washington and New Delhi were “very close” to an agreement.

However, a deal during his visit appears unlikely.

US President Donald Trump’s tariff war launched in April last year has added to friction over India’s imports of Russian oil and warming ties between Washington and Pakistan, India’s arch-rival.

Asked about temporary US sanctions waivers for Russian oil, of which India is a major importer, Rubio said Washington had to juggle multiple factors “including our bilateral relationships with other countries and what they realistically are capable of being able to do in terms of their own energy supplies”.

“You also can’t unravel the economy of other countries because of one central issue,” he said.

The two countries reached an interim trade agreement in February aimed at reducing US tariffs on Indian goods.

But days later, the US Supreme Court struck down Trump’s sweeping tariffs, fuelling uncertainty over when the agreement would take effect.

The two sides have been negotiating ever since.

Indian Finance Minister Nirmala Sitharaman said this month the talks had reached “a plateau, beyond which giving or taking might be very, very difficult”.

Jaishankar met with his United Arab Emirates counterpart in Mumbai earlier on Tuesday. The UAE is a key supplier of Indian energy, especially liquefied natural gas (LNG).

“The situation in the Gulf remains a matter of deep concern,” Jaishankar told UAE Foreign Minister Sheikh Abdullah bin Zayed Al Nahyan, in public comments broadcast before their meeting started.

He said India continues to support “free, safe and unimpeded flow of trade, energy and fertiliser”.

World.title: Iraq Green Observatory warns Baghdad Forests Project faces abandonment
World.content:
Baghdad (IraqiNews.com) – The Iraq Green Observatory issued a warning on Tuesday, October 20, 2026, over the risk of abandonment facing the “Baghdad Forests” environmental initiative at the Camp Rasheed site in southeastern Baghdad, expressing concern that the designated green zone could be repurposed into a commercial investment project.

In an official statement, the environmental monitor recalled widespread public and institutional optimism following the project’s launch with executive government endorsement, envisioning the forest belt as a vital green lung for an increasingly suffocated capital.

The observatory noted that Baghdad faces severe environmental degradation driven by emissions from industrial facilities, motor vehicle exhausts, and local diesel generators. It further cautioned that the uncoordinated expansion of commercial and residential developments has turned Baghdad into an urban “heat island” deficient in vegetation, placing it among the most pollution-burdened regional and global capitals.

The observatory emphasized that developing Camp Rasheed’s expansive footprint provides a strategic opportunity to rehabilitate an area long misused as an informal waste dumping ground. Realizing the forest project would substantially enhance air quality across neighboring residential quarters, most notably the Al-Za’faraniyah district, which suffers directly from heavy industrial emissions and recurring dust and sandstorms.

The watchdog voiced alarm over the complete absence of on-ground preliminary engineering or planting activities at the designated location. It warned against reallocating the vast state-owned land parcel for real estate or commercial ventures, insisting that the grounds remain ideally sized to establish an integrated ecological barrier capable of lowering atmospheric contaminants and mitigating urban heat across Baghdad.

World.title: Iraq’s Najlah Imad captures table tennis gold at Nagoya 2026 Asian Para Games
World.content:
Baghdad (IraqiNews.com) – Iraqi para-table tennis star Najlah Imad captured the gold medal on Tuesday, October 20, 2026, at the Nagoya 2026 Asian Para Games in Japan, defeating China’s Liu Xiaowu 3–1 in the women’s Class 6 singles final.

According to a formal statement issued by the Iraqi Paralympic Committee, Imad dominated the tournament bracket, dropping only a single set throughout her entire campaign in Nagoya—the sole concession occurring during the championship duel against her Chinese opponent.

The victory secures another continental accolade for Iraqi para-athletics and extends Imad’s record of international podium finishes.

Luay Al-Saray, President of the Iraqi Para Table Tennis Federation, commended the historic gold, attributing the success to deliberate institutional planning, rigorous preparatory training camps, and close alignment between the federation and the technical staff.

World.title: US bans use of China’s DeepSeek by govt agencies
World.content:
New York – The US government on Monday ordered its agencies to stop using artificial intelligence tools from Chinese startup DeepSeek, as the countries race for dominance in the fast-moving sector.

A notice from the Department of Homeland Security announced the ban on products developed by DeepSeek — and tools created using DeepSeek by third parties — saying they must be removed from IT devices.

The department can issue direction to civilian agencies, but not the military or intelligence services. Washington’s Department of Defense did not respond to an AFP request for comment.

“DeepSeek’s models present multiple threat vectors,” said a document attached to Monday’s notice.

Use of DeepSeek AI tools “may result in the transfer of sensitive data to (China) if used by US government employees or vendors,” the department warned.

Its servers are located in China, where the legal system permits the government “extensive authority” to access private company infrastructure, it said.

AFP has contacted DeepSeek for comment.

DeepSeek, one of China’s top AI labs, shook up the industry in January 2025 with a low-cost, high-performance chatbot, challenging assumptions of US dominance.

The firm released a long-awaited new model, V4, in April, and this month updated a faster, more lightweight version of V4.

The United States has accused DeepSeek and other top Chinese AI firms of systematically stealing the capabilities of cutting-edge models developed by American rivals.

Despite their fierce competition in the field, China and the United States in September agreed to set up a “communication channel” for AI incidents.

The topic is expected to arise again when the countries’ leaders meet next month at a summit in the Chinese city of Shenzhen.

World.title: Middle East fuel crunch drives solar push in tiny Fiji
World.content:
San Francisco – Power cables weave through palm trees high above Fiji’s Rukurukulevu Village, linking residents to the national grid and a select few to solar panels.

The settlement of about 400 people finally electrified its last building this year — a kindergarten, just metres from the sea.

But residents are struggling to keep the lights on as the Middle East war and other factors push up energy bills in this Pacific paradise.

It is challenging Fiji’s reliance on imported fossil fuels and driving a push towards renewables in the resource-scarce island nation.

“The prices of electricity here in Fiji (are) very high,” village spokesman Vereniki Nalio told AFP.

“Some houses, they got FJ$100 (US$44) and over. The church, community halls and church minister’s house, they’ve got about FJ$200, nearly FJ$300, for a month.”

Nalio said he paid about FJ$60 per month for electricity — “very, very high”.

Opposite his home stands another small house with one big difference: past the clothes hanging on the washing line lies a small array of solar panels.

Another home across the road boasts an even larger installation, showing how some in the village are seeking to move away from dependence on the grid.

Since the United States and Israel attacked Iran in February, fuel shipments from the Gulf have slowed.

Nalio said the subsequent global energy squeeze had led villagers to consider switching to renewables.

A basic solar power system costs around FJ$3,000, a higher up-front cost but an increasingly reasonable price to pay for theoretically unlimited, free electricity.

“They said we had no more fuel, no more petrol would come to Fiji. So at that time we think about solar,” Nalio said.

He added that the village hoped to install solar panels on communal buildings to reduce the shared cost of powering them.

Pointing to the sky, Nalio said Rukurukulevu should not have to import its energy.

“Solar is already here.”

– Rush for renewables –

Fiji hosted this month’s “pre-COP” United Nations climate summit, where Pacific Island nations pressed for faster access to climate financing for projects such as renewable energy.

The event was a precursor to next month’s main COP event in Turkey, where organisers will push for member states to commit to electrification — replacing technologies that burn fossil fuels directly, like diesel cars and gas heating, with electric alternatives.

Symbolising the challenges the Pacific faces, a major power outage on the second day of the event plunged the 4,000 attendees into darkness.

Government minister Ro Filipe Tuisawau blamed Fiji’s rising energy prices on overreliance on fossil fuels and El Nino.

The cyclical climate phenomenon is particularly strong this year and has brought weather patterns that are drying up Fiji’s hydroelectric dams.

They “will face a critical situation” if rainfall does not increase by mid-November, Tuisawau, whose remit covers public works, weather services and transport, told AFP.

“We would probably go into water rationing and power rationing in the next, maybe, four weeks if the situation doesn’t change,” he said.

“The hotels can enjoy (it) now, but we will cut off their water to the pool.”

Fiji spends as much as 12 percent of its GDP on importing fossil fuels — “a huge drain on our resources”, Tuisawau said.

The country is aiming for 90 percent renewable energy generation by 2035 and plans to spend FJ$2 billion on solar and hydropower development in the next decade.

That includes investing at least FJ$460 million in solar farms in the next four years, as well as FJ$650 million on two new dams and more than FJ$700 million to expand its main transmission lines.

For now, though, many islanders are still facing the sharp end of Fiji’s energy crisis, Tuisawau acknowledged.

“With the price, with geopolitical issues, and in addition El Nino right now, it’s a very difficult situation,” he said.

World.title: ‘Doing a real disservice’: Annamalai backs CJP leaders, questions their continued custody
World.content:
NEW DELHI: Former Tamil Nadu BJP president K Annamalai on Tuesday expressed Cockroach Janata Party and questioned Delhi Police's handling of the case against its leaders Saurav Das and Ashutosh Ranka.

While talking to reporters, Annamalai said that continued judicial custody of CJP leaders raises concerns about the rule of law.

"I'm a little bit concerned in our country. I have a feeling they (Delhi Police) have taken the law into their hands, and the judge gets recused... I may not agree with many of the CJP's modes of protest. I may not agree with some of the antics of CJP. That's a different argument. But I completely support CJP in terms of the questions they want to raise.

"It is for the government to answer. But to arrest them for a violation and again to drag them in terms of how they spend their time in jail, that is only going to make the leaders of CJP stronger. I'm afraid of saying that the Delhi police are doing a real disservice," he added.

He also said that Lok Sabha leader of opposition Rahul Gandhi has every right to question the SIR process, but institutional damage should not be caused.





"Rahul Gandhi has every right to question the SIR process, but institutional damage should not be caused," he further said.

Earlier on Monday, a Delhi court extended the CJP leaders' judicial custody by two days for allegedly entering Jantar Mantar, which is no longer a designated protest venue, and obstructing police personnel on duty.

Along with other CJP workers, they waved the national flag at the site and raised slogans against Chief Election Commissioner Gyanesh Kumar before being detained and placed under preventive custody.

According to their lawyer, their bail sureties were rejected due to a reported mismatch in documents. They will now be produced before the court on Wednesday.

Meanwhile, CJP founder Abhijeet Dipke questioned Prime Minister Narendra Modi's leadership and praised Das and Ranka for remaining defiant despite spending five days in judicial custody.

NEW DELHI: An Air India Express flight from Bhogapuram in Andhra Pradesh to Bengaluru suffered a bird strike but landed safely at Kempegowda International Airport, with all 148 passengers and crew members unharmed on Tuesday.The incident occurred on Monday, following which the aircraft was inspected by technical teams to assess any damage to its structure and engines. Such inspections are part of standard safety procedures after a bird strike to determine whether an aircraft can continue operating safely.An Air India Express spokesperson said the aircraft had been declared serviceable after the inspection and that there was no disruption to flight operations."Our Bhogapuram-Bengaluru flight reported a bird strike. While many such incidents cause little or no damage, they can require technical inspections and repairs before an aircraft is cleared for its next flight.
