World.title: Middle Corridor can expand Kazakhstan’s trade and industry - IFIMES
World.content:
BAKU, Azerbaijan, October 20. The Trans-Caspian International Transport Route (TITR, Middle Corridor) can help expand trade opportunities, improve regional connectivity, and attract logistics operators, according to an analysis by the International Institute for Middle East and Balkan Studies (IFIMES).

Kazakhstan's position between Europe and Asia has historically shaped its role in regional exchange. Its geographic advantage is gaining further importance as international logistics chains are reconfigured, e-commerce expands and businesses seek alternative routes for transporting goods, the analysis said.

IFIMES noted that Kazakhstan is developing transport infrastructure, rail and road corridors, logistics hubs and multimodal solutions. The Middle Corridor links China and Central Asia with the Caucasus and European markets via the Caspian and Black Seas.

"The development of such routes matters for more than transit revenues. It helps expand trade opportunities, improve connectivity between regions, attract logistics operators and create new avenues for industrial cooperation. The competitiveness of transport corridors, however, is determined by more than geography alone: it requires harmonised customs procedures, predictable delivery times, efficient port infrastructure and digital data exchange among all parties involved in freight transport," IFIMES said.

According to the analyses, cooperation with European partners offers Kazakhstan additional opportunities. The European market is of interest not only as an export destination but also as a source of technology, engineering solutions, investment expertise and modern standards for infrastructure management.

At the same time, Kazakhstan needs to develop its own logistics and production base so that it serves not only as a transit territory but also as a place where high-value-added goods and services are created.

"It is the combination of transport connectivity, industrial development and technological renewal that can turn geographic position into a lasting competitive advantage," the analysis states.

World.title: Sister of murdered UK MP Jo Cox wants Australia to tone down rhetoric
World.content:
The sister of murdered UK MP Jo Cox has called on Australia to see the attack that left Independent MP Helen Haines in a critical condition as a turning point.

Cox was murdered aged 41 in 2016, when she was shot and stabbed multiple times by a far-right extremist.

Since then former UK MP Ann Widdcombe was killed this year and sitting UK MP David Amess was killed in 2021.

Ms Haines was attacked outside her office in Wangaratta on Monday, when a car allegedly driven by 43-year-old Brendan Nugent struck her.

Independent Federal Member for Indi pictured in November 2024. (ABC News: Ian Cutmore)

Mr Nugent has now been charged with dangerous driving causing serious injury and intentionally causing serious injury.

He was also charged with the federal offence of causing harm to a Commonwealth public official — which carries a maximum penalty of 10 years' imprisonment.

In a statement, Victoria Police said officers would allege the incident was targeted.

Kim Leadbeater, who is now the MP of the constituency formerly held by her late sister, called on Australia to unite against these kind of attacks.

"Maybe for Australia this is your moment to think about what your politics looks like and how we can bring people together [and] find common ground," Ms Leadbeater told 7.30.

"That was something my sister was brilliant at and I would imagine it's something Helen [Haines] is good at.

"I am devastated for Helen and for her family, her friends, her colleagues, her staff, that I am probably one of the few people, I suppose, that can understand a little bit of what they're going through."

She echoed calls from politicians including Prime Minister Anthony Albanese for a calmer discourse.

Kim Leadbeater giving a speech to pay tribute to her sister Jo Cox in 2021. Cox was a Labour MP who was murdered in 2016. (UK Parliament: Jessica Taylor via Reuters)

"The really depressing thing for me is I've been giving a very similar interview for the last 10 years about how we need to look at our political culture in this country, and it would seem in other countries as well," Ms Leadbeater said.

"I find it really frustrating that we're having the same conversation and every time something so horrific happens."

She said while robust political debate is important, she believes more civilised comment is needed.

"Things don't happen in a vacuum and horrendous attacks and incidents like this don't happen in isolation," she said.

"They are part of a wider culture around politics and society [and] we all have a role to play in that."

Asked why her sister's death did not change the UK, Ms Leadbeater told 7.30 it was because once the shock wears off people go back to their daily lives.

"Something horrific happens and the focus is all on that horrific incident," Ms Leadbeater said.

"As a family, obviously, that day will be forever etched in our minds as something that we think about every single day, but most people then go back to their lives and remember something really bad happening, but they don't feel the pain every day in the same way that those who are directly affected."

Plibersek details horrid social media comment

Her calls for calm were echoed by both Social Services Minister Tanya Plibersek and Coalition MP Andrew Hastie.

Tanya Plibersek is disturbed by the escalation in threats against politicians.

Ms Plibersek shared a shocking story about the comments she faces regularly, including one made this afternoon on a social media post she shared to show support for Senator Jacqui Lambie, after she became a target of a One Nation cartoon.

"There's always been threats," Ms Plibersek told 7.30.

"Years ago, I had someone slip a note under my front door at home, no stamp on it or anything, they had obviously turned up in person saying they hope my children die of painful cancers.

"I couldn't even count the number of death threats, rape threats that I've had over the years, including ones that have ended up in court.

"The thing that's changed most is the industrial scale of that abuse now.

"Yesterday I posted something about Jacqui Lambie saying that I thought that the cartoon mocking her vaginal prolapse was an extremely poor taste.

"Twenty-four hours after I posted that, this afternoon, after this attack on Helen Haines, someone wrote under that post, defending Jacqui Lambie, 'she deserves to meet a LandCruiser'.

"I don't know what kind of person does that."

Mr Hastie said social media and the role it plays was also one of his key concerns.

"My concern is with the industrial scale of social media, potentially there are more people being reached with very emotive, negative messages, which could inspire action."

He said he had received an uptick in online abuse over the past six months and let his staff handle his social media as a result.

"We want people of talent coming into our parliament and that's why we've got to get this right. Otherwise our country is poorer because without the best people serving in our parliament, we won't get the best public policy outcomes for our nation."

Watch 7.30, Mondays to Thursdays 7:30pm on ABC iview and ABC TV

World.title: Banks, websites offline as Google Cloud services fail across Europe
World.content:
Google Cloud services have failed across Europe after a "power event" at a data centre based in London, according to the tech giant's website.

The issue has reportedly affected banks and other websites across the continent.

The Google Cloud website is not reporting serious issues in any other region, but said that services in parts of Europe could experience "elevated errors and intermittent network issues".

"Due to a power event we had suffered an outage within europe-west2-b zone," the Google Cloud website said.

Google said the incident began shortly after 6am UK time and that its engineering teams were investigating.

Customers of major UK banks were reporting issues accessing their accounts. (Reuters: Phil Noble)

Banking giant Revolut is among the institutions believed to have been affected by the outage.

"We are currently experiencing a service disruption affecting multiple services," the bank said in a statement on social media.

"We can confirm that all our customers’ money and data are safe."

Another major British bank, Halifax, wrote on X that customers were "having issues with our app and online".

Brand trial live stream affected

Court live streams, including that of the ongoing trial of comedian Russell Brand, were also reportedly down as a result.

"We’re aware of an issue affecting Cloud Video Platform (CVP), used for some remote hearings," the UK's Courts and Tribunals Service said on X.

British media outlets reported that other major companies, including Royal Mail, Microsoft and delivery company DPD were also experiencing issues.

World.title: Alberta voters reject move to separate from Canada
World.content:
Alberta residents voted to remain part of Canada in the province's first referendum on separation.

The result is a much-needed win for Prime Minister Mark Carney as he attempts to unify the country amid a trade war with the US.

CBC News, Canada's government-funded national broadcaster, called the result late Monday, local time, after 33 per cent of the vote had been counted.

At the time of the call, 76 per cent of tallied votes were in support of the "remain" side versus 23 per cent in favour of the province moving forward with a binding vote on separation. The referendum was non-binding.

A supporter of the Forever Canadian group, who wants Alberta to remain in Canada, waits for the results of the referendum. (Reuters: Todd Korol)

"Albertans made a clear choice," Mr Carney said in a statement.

"They chose unity, to build together, and to take care of each other."

"Canada is greater than the sum of its parts," he said.

Pollsters and analysts had repeatedly dismissed the possibility of a separatist victory, citing data that showed about one-third of residents in the western province supported a future referendum on leaving.

Alberta Premier Danielle Smith announced the referendum in May, saying it was "time to have a vote, understand the will of Albertans on this subject, and move on".

Late Monday, Ms Smith issued a statement on social media saying she was "very pleased" that early results show widespread support for remaining in Canada.

She said she would address Albertans on Tuesday to discuss the results and "where our province goes from here."

A small but vocal group of separatists has campaigned for months for an independent Alberta, arguing that the province's energy wealth is subsidising poorer parts of Canada and that Alberta would be far richer without Ottawa bureaucracy impeding its path.

A man votes during the Alberta Referendum in Calgary. (Reuters: Ahmed Zakot)

Last week, Mr Carney told a rally in Calgary that voting to leave Canada would be "a dangerous bluff that will lead to years of deep division," and appealed to Albertans to "vote like Canada depends on it".

Mr Carney, who grew up mostly in Alberta, acknowledged that Albertans have often felt slighted by Ottawa and said his government had approved a proposed new pipeline, adding that Alberta is critical to helping Canada reduce its dependence on the US.

Alberta's referendum follows two previous referendums on separation in the majority French-speaking province of Quebec.

Quebecers voted to stay in Canada in both instances.

First Nations groups have also objected to the idea of an independent Alberta, as their land treaties with Ottawa predate the province's creation within Canada.

CBC News reported strong turnout from First Nations.

One southern Alberta polling station in an area that is home to the Siksika Nation temporarily ran out of ballots, and then stayed open until after 10pm MT (15:00 AEST) to ensure everyone in line had the chance to vote.

Still, Monday's referendum is unlikely to end the separatist movement in Alberta.

Supporters of the Alberta Prosperity Project, a group that promotes independence from Canada. (Reuters: Jennifer Gauthier)

Before the referendum, some separatist leaders said they would continue to pursue another vote even if most Albertans voted to remain.

According to data released on October 16 by the pollster Angus Reid, 62 per cent of Albertans believe "there will never be an end to the separatist movement" in the province.

Alberta's referendum also included nine other non-binding questions on topics including immigration, access to provincial services — such as education, social care and healthcare — and voter identification requirements.

Results for those questions were still trickling in.

Reuters

World.title: Police lay three charges against Brendan Nugent over Haines attack
World.content:
Victoria Police have laid three charges against 43-year-old Brendan Nugent after he allegedly struck independent MP Helen Haines with his car on Monday.

Detectives tonight charged Mr Nugent with dangerous driving causing serious injury and intentionally causing serious injury.

Brendan Nugent was detained on Murphy Street after the incident. (Wangaratta Chronicle: Bailey Zimmermann)

He was also charged with the federal offence of causing harm to a Commonwealth public official — which carries a maximum penalty of 10 years' imprisonment.

He is due to appear in the Wangaratta Magistrates' Court tomorrow.

In a statement, Victoria Police said officers would allege the incident was targeted.

Helen Haines live updates: Get the latest about the attack on the Victorian MP in our blog.

The ABC has confirmed Ms Haines has lost one leg and doctors are fighting to save the other after she was pinned between two cars outside her electorate office in Victoria's north-east.

Ms Haines, 65, suffered critical lower-body injuries in the Wangaratta attack and was flown to The Alfred hospital in Melbourne.

Parliamentary colleagues and members of the community have expressed their shock and support for Ms Haines, who has been the member for Indi since 2019.

Helen Haines was critically injured when she was struck by a four-wheel-drive yesterday afternoon. (ABC News: Ian Cutmore)

Family of accused address 'devastating' incident

On Tuesday officers searched Mr Nugent's Tarrawingee home, roughly 15 kilometres east of the rural city of Wangaratta.

Family members of Mr Nugent also released a statement, saying "all of our love and all of our thoughts are with Helen and her family and friends".

In the statement, Mr Nugent's father Rod Nugent and Rod's partner Christine Cunningham said Ms Haines had been their friend for more than 20 years and Monday's events were "devastating and unfathomable".

"Helen Haines is a deeply respected, valued and much loved member of our local community," the statement said.

"We would like to sincerely thank members of the local community and police who came to Helen's aid yesterday after the shocking and horrific crime.

"We will be assisting Victoria Police in any way we can."

World.title: Australian military opens its ranks to PNG university students
World.content:
Papua New Guinean university students will be able to apply to join the Australian Defence Force from next month under a $65 million trial that could eventually see thousands of overseas recruits bolster Australia's military strength.

The announcement was made at a high-level meeting between Australian and PNG ministers in Port Moresby today, as the countries progressed a landmark military alliance that entered into force in July.

Australian and Papua New Guinean ministers have met in Port Moresby as the countries progress a landmark military alliance signed last year. (Supplied: Department of Foreign Affairs and Trade)

As well as enabling both nations to recruit each other's citizens into their militaries, the Pukpuk Treaty obliges the neighbours to defend each other in the event of a military attack.

The first cohort of successful applicants is expected to be sworn in by late 2027 under a pilot program aimed at recruiting 100 young Papua New Guineans over the next two years.

While they will initially enlist on temporary visas, PNG nationals will eventually have to obtain Australian citizenship to continue serving in the ADF.

The Pukpuk Treaty obliges Australia and Papua New Guinea to defend each other in the event of a military attack. (Supplied: Department of Defence)

Moira Digori, a fourth-year political science student at the University of Papua New Guinea, said she was keen to apply.

"I am patriotic and I think it would probably weigh on my conscience a little, serving in another country's military without serving in the PNGDF first," she told the ABC.

"But again, the opportunity to have a better life and potentially have citizenship in Australia is quite appealing to me, and I think it would be appealing to a lot of other students as well. So I think that would outweigh my patriotism."

Moira Digori said she wanted to apply. (Supplied: Moira Digori)

She expected a huge amount of interest when applications opened on November 16.

"The pull factor would be better financial stability and generally better living standards in Australia than there are currently in our country," she said.

Australian Deputy Prime Minister Richard Marles said the arrangement would benefit both nations.

Australian government ministers travelled to Port Moresby for meetings with PNG officials. (Supplied: Department of Foreign Affairs and Trade)

Recruitment shortfalls have been a major concern for the ADF, although recruitment numbers have improved in recent years.

"The pilot program will have smaller numbers to begin with, to ensure the right processes are in place ahead of further expansion to develop a program that is sustainable and provides enduring value for both Australia and PNG," Mr Marles said.

The trial will cost the Australian government $65 million, with the aim of eventually expanding recruitment on a much larger scale.

PNG and Australia's defence forces have been conducting exercises to increase their interoperability this year. (Supplied: Department of Defence)

Applications will initially be open to students and recent graduates from two major universities — the University of Papua New Guinea and Pacific Adventist University — in the cities of Port Moresby and Lae.

Australia, PNG sign new defence treaty Papua New Guinea and Australia formally sign a landmark new defence treaty, elevating the bilateral relationship between the two countries to an alliance and agreeing to "act to meet the common danger" if the other is faced with an armed attack.

To be eligible, they must be between 18 and 25 years old and cannot have previously served in PNG's military, police force or any PNG government security institutions.

They will also face the same security requirements and standards as Australian citizens who apply to join the ADF.

Currently, non-Australian citizens from Five Eyes nations who are permanent residents living in Australia are able to apply to join the ADF.

The arrangement was recently expanded to include PNG citizens who have Australian permanent residency, with 40 applications currently being processed.

World.title: Landholders and politicians push for tougher laws on renewable energy developments
World.content:
A coalition of rural community groups is demanding tougher laws governing renewable energy developments, including mandatory turbine setbacks, stricter decommissioning rules and stronger protections for neighbouring landholders.

Regional Voices Queensland (RVQ), a loose alliance of about 12 community action groups representing communities affected by renewable energy projects across the state, brought landholders, farming industry representatives and politicians together for its first major meeting today at the Franz family farm beside the Wambo Wind Farm at Diamondy, 280 kilometres north-west of Brisbane.

The meeting, co-organised by Member for Maranoa David Littleproud, focused on reforms to planning laws, with more than 70 participants travelling from communities including the Southern Downs and other parts of regional Queensland.

Regional Voices Queensland members are demanding tougher laws governing renewable energy developments. (ABC Southern Qld: Brandon Long)

RVQ chair and Property Rights Australia board member, Jim Willmott, described the alliance as a "supergroup" formed after community organisations dealing with individual projects identified common concerns.

"What we found is a lot of community groups were dealing with individual projects themselves, but they all had the same common issues," Mr Willmott said.

The group is calling for a minimum 3-kilometre setback from residences and up-front decommissioning bonds.

Queensland's wind farm code has not allowed developers to comply simply by meeting a specified separation distance since 2024.

Projects must meet all of the code's performance outcomes, including noise criteria at neighbouring dwellings.

David Littleproud says affected landholders wanted clarity around the issue. (ABC Southern Qld: Brandon Long)

Mr Littleproud said affected landholders were seeking practical safeguards rather than opposing renewable energy outright.

"They're not asking for anything irrational," he said.

"They're actually being quite considered and it's coming from a lived experience."

Farm co-owner Glenn Franz, who does not host the turbines, said the experience of living beside the wind farm had highlighted gaps in existing protections, particularly around visual amenity and the financial risks associated with dismantling turbines at the end of their operational lives.

"We've got 13 wind turbines surrounding us within a 3km zone," Mr Franz said.

"There's got to be safeguards for the future.

"It'd be nice to have the security up front, not as a pay-as-you-go-down-the-track sort of scheme."

Karl Stefanovic interviewed landholders at the meeting. (ABC Southern Qld: Brandon Long)

The Wambo Wind Farm, a joint venture between state-owned Stanwell and energy infrastructure group Cubico, received planning approval in 2020.

Mr Franz said while the project was well advanced, other communities were at the start of the process and could learn from the Diamondy community's experience.

Anna Lethbridge and Brendan Taylor from AgForce attended the meeting. (ABC Southern Qld: Brandon Long)

AgForce policy adviser Anna Lethbridge said safeguards needed to extend beyond project hosts to neighbouring producers, including protections against contamination and impacts on agricultural accreditation.

"From an AgForce perspective, we're not opposed to renewables," Ms Lethbridge said.

" If you are going to host a project, you need to be fully informed of all the risks so you can make an informed decision. "

Queensland regulates wind farm developments through its planning and environmental assessment framework, including State Code 23 and applicable approval conditions.

Since 2025, new wind farm applications must undergo impact assessment and provide financial security for decommissioning.

However, RVQ is concerned the wording is vague and could still leave landholders or taxpayers liable.

Developers must now also negotiate a community benefit agreement with the relevant council before lodging an application.

World.title: Gang arranged for 13yo to get semi-automatic rifle, police believe
World.content:
WA police are investigating whether a 13-year-old Victorian boy allegedly involved in a drive-by shooting in suburban Perth on the weekend was recruited by an underworld organisation which gave him a self-loading firearm.

The boy allegedly used a semi-automatic rifle to fire more than 20 shots into a Gosnells house, hitting a bedroom window and wall, around 12:40am on Saturday.

Seven people were inside the home at the time, including children. One man received minor injuries from shattered glass, but no one was seriously hurt.

However, they are not thought to be the intended targets.

Loading...

Detectives believe the boy was recruited by an underworld organisation and given a pick-up and drop off location for the gun, the ABC understands.

The instructions are understood to have been delivered electronically.

The semi-automatic firearm involved in the incident has not been found.

The ABC understands his family had only moved him to WA weeks ago.

Rare weapon

Two semi-automatic rifles were used in the devastating Port Arthur massacre in 1996 in which 35 people were killed.

The Category D weapons have been outlawed in Western Australia ever since, captured as part of the sweeping reforms following the mass shooting.

The shooting left multiple bullet holes in the Gosnells home. (ABC News)

Only police, the military and certain government agencies are legally able to use the long-arm weapons.

WA Firearm Traders Association president Bevan Steele said the weapon allegedly used by the 13-year-old boy was "a highly illicit firearm" that could only have been smuggled into the country illegally.

"We haven't seen these firearms in WA, in the legal environment, since 1996 … if you had one of these on your dealer's licence, it is gone, well and truly," Mr Steele said.

The upper floor of the Gosnells home was riddled with bullets. (ABC News)

In other states, Category D weapons are restricted to professional hunters, many of whom shoot out of aircraft.

Exactly how the lethal self-loading weapon allegedly got into the hands of a 13-year-old is not known.

"A 13-year-old boy having access to a weapon like that and carrying out that act, allegedly, is extremely concerning," Police Minister Reece Whitby said.

Police arrested the teenager on Monday and charged him with eight offences including unlawful use of a firearm, endangering life, possession of stolen property and no authority to drive.

He will reappear in Perth Children's Court next week.

World.title: Cumulative impacts of data centre gas plants overlooked, court hears
World.content:
A court has heard the "cumulative impacts" of a series of gas plants proposed to run data centres in the Southern Highlands are being ignored as a result of fragmented planning decisions.

Seven community members gave evidence at the site of the development in Moss Vale on Tuesday morning, kicking off a three-day hearing in the Land and Environment Court.

The court is considering developer Nakar Property's appeal of a refusal by Wingecarribee Shire Council for one of its projects on the site.

The application was for a 16-megawatt gas-fired power plant and battery storage system to power data centres.

Separately, the developer has secured approval for another gas-fired plant on the site, a 14MW facility, and is seeking state government approval for a third, 673MW plant.

More than 100 community members gathered on the site ahead of the Land and Environment Court hearing. (ABC Illawarra: Penny Burfitt)

A crowd of more than 100 community members, Land and Environment Court Commissioner Nicola Targett, and representatives for the council and the applicant gathered in an open field in Moss Vale for the first day of the hearing.

The first community member to address the court was Dane Shanahan, who introduced himself by his Gundungurra name, Mullyang.

The emerging knowledge-holder for the region's traditional landowners told the court his name meant "eagle" and, as he outlined his community's concerns about the project, two wedge-tailed eagles appeared in the sky above the open-air court.

After the proceedings, Mr Shanahan described the appearance of the birds as an "ancestral presence".

He was one of several speakers to urge the commissioner to consider the application for the 16MW facility in the broader context of the development.

"Each piece is being presented as small — each piece is being assessed on its own and no-one is looking at the whole," Mr Shanahan told the court.

The court is only assessing the appeal lodged by Nakar Property for the 16MW facility and battery, but Gabby Kent, who lives 1 kilometre from the proposed site, agreed with Mr Shanahan's argument.

"The planning processes may be separate, but the cumulative impacts to my family … and my community are not," she said.

Will McCarthy says the project needs to be looked at as a whole. (ABC Illawarra: Penny Burfitt)

Will McCarthy, whose home overlooks the development, echoed those sentiments.

"At some point the planning system needs to stand back at look at the development as a whole," he told the commissioner.

The court heard the applicant had submitted an amended plan for the development to speakers and parties ahead of the hearing.

That submission included changes such as painting exhaust stacks green to address visual amenity, and adding some onsite solar power generation.

Consultation challenged

Mr Shanahan told the court no Gundungurra people had been consulted as part of the development application's Aboriginal Heritage Assessment, despite the cultural significance of a waterway that would be cut off by the project.

"It is as significant to the Gundungurra as Genesis is to Christians," he said.

"The applicant has proposed to reshape an ancestral waterway without asking the people [whether] it will scar."

The power plant and battery would provide power to data centres on Cloud Carrier's Moss Vale site. (Supplied: Cloud Carrier)

Jacqueline Duc raised concerns about the health impacts of pollutants, telling the court carcinogens from gas power-plants had been linked to lung and childhood cancers.

She also raised concerns about the project being located within the Sydney water catchment, saying its tributaries eventually flowed into Warragamba Dam, which supplied 80 per cent of the city's drinking water.

The applicant's lawyer, James Smith, did not question any of the community speakers.

The court will hear from the applicant's attorney and the council's representative, Michael Staunton, in coming days.

World.title: Who is Brendan Nugent? What we know so far about the alleged attack on Helen Haines
World.content:
PoliticsFederalHaines attack Who is Brendan Nugent? What we know so far about the alleged attack on Helen Haines Natassia Chrysanthos Updated October 20, 2026 — 10:06pm ,first published October 19, 2026 — 11:13pm Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Gift icon Gift Gift icon 0 / 3 No gift articles left You've used all of your gift articles. 3 more will become available on the 1st of every month. Follow live updates on the Helen Haines attack Independent MP Helen Haines has lost one leg and remains in a critical condition after being struck by a four-wheel drive vehicle outside her electorate office in Wangaratta, north-east Victoria, on Monday afternoon. Prime Minister Anthony Albanese said it was an intentional attack that is being investigated by several agencies, including counter-terrorism teams. Tarrawingee man Brendan Nugent, 43, was charged with three offences on Tuesday night and will appear in court on Wednesday. Here’s what we know so far. Who is Helen Haines?



Helen Haines, 65, is the independent federal representative for Indi, a north-east Victorian electorate that stretches up to Wodonga near the NSW border. Before entering parliament, Haines had a decades-long career in healthcare. She worked as a nurse, midwife and health researcher, publishing dozens of academic articles. She grew up on a dairy farm in Eurack, in south-western Victoria, and has been married to her husband, Phil Haines, since 1986. The couple have raised three children and live on a beef farm outside Wangaratta. Independent MP Helen Haines is being treated in hospital after the attack. Alex Ellinghausen Haines’ political career began when she was elected as an independent in 2019. Her predecessor in the seat, Cathy McGowan, in many ways pioneered the community independent movement, when she won Indi from the Coalition with the backing of grassroots campaigners in 2013. It had been safely held by conservative parties for the previous 80 years. Haines seized on the same momentum and was endorsed by McGowan to run as the local MP. She was the first independent to succeed another independent in federal parliament, and has held Indi on an 8 per cent margin in the two elections since.



“When people can see another way, it’s empowering,” Haines told Good Weekend in 2023. “The fact that the nation has chosen a parliament that has the biggest crossbench in history since federation demonstrates the need for a diversity of views and greater collaboration.” Related Article Haines attack Independent MP Helen Haines in critical condition after ‘attack’ outside her office Haines’ recent election campaigns have been backed by the Climate 200 fundraising vehicle, although she keeps a distinct profile from the “teal independents” who have won city seats with a similar community campaigning model. Haines has advocated for climate change action and regional services, particularly healthcare. She has also been a strong advocate for integrity and transparency in politics, and was instrumental in campaigning for a national anti-corruption body. Haines is a widely respected member of parliament. Albanese described her as an incredibly hardworking MP on Monday night.



“She is fiercely intelligent, but most importantly, she’s just a thoroughly decent human being, full of integrity, respected right across the parliament, and from everyone who comes into contact with her,” he said. What happened at her Wangaratta office? Haines was returning to her electorate office in Wangaratta after attending a sod-turning event in the nearby town of Mansfield on Monday afternoon when she was struck by a white Toyota LandCruiser about 3.35pm. Police at the scene. ABC Witnesses said Haines was retrieving items from the boot of her car on Monday afternoon when a white Toyota LandCruiser conducted a U-turn to ram her against a vehicle before reversing and hitting her a second time.



Police said witnesses arrested the driver of the LandCruiser at the scene. In what the prime minister has labelled a heroic act, barbershop owner Ricky Jefferies intervened by wrestling the driver to the ground and waiting for authorities. “I don’t think I’m a hero. I was a person who had an opportunity to intervene in a safe-ish sort of way,” Jefferies said outside his shop on Tuesday morning. “I’m humbled, and I’m grateful and blessed to have been there to help.” Loading Who is the suspected attacker? Brendan Nugent, 43, was arrested by police at the scene of the crash and taken to Wangaratta police station. Police searched his property, which is a short drive from central Wangaratta, on Tuesday.



On Tuesday night, detectives charged Nugent with dangerous driving causing serious injury, intentionally causing serious injury and causing harm to a Commonwealth public official. Related Article Updated

Nugent commented on one of Haines’ posts in 2019, saying it would be good to see a politician like her “who takes climate change seriously”. He also claimed that Nugent had recently spent several weeks at a mental health facility in Wangaratta. Nugent’s most recent social media activity includes posts about Israel’s conduct in Gaza, British actor Russell Brand and child sex offender Jeffrey Epstein. Queensland government-owned energy company boss Michael O’Rourke has been quietly walked by the Stanwell board, five years since rising to the $1.1 million job in a company he worked in for decades. The corporation uploaded a statement to its website announcing the decision on Monday, citing the board’s view that it was the “right time for a leadership transition” as part of renewal in the sector. This leaves just one of Queensland’s five state-owned energy companies, CleanCo, yet to see a change of its chief executive in the two years since the self-proclaimed pro-coal Crisafulli LNP won government. Former Stanwell Corporation chief executive Michael O’Rourke, whose departure from the role was announced on Monday 19 October 2026. LinkedIn / Michael O’Rourke Stanwell board chair Justin Parer, a former Young LNP president shifted into the role from a port authority appointment last October, thanked O’Rourke for his leadership, with “full support and best wishes for the future”.



“Michael has played an important role in guiding Stanwell through a period of considerable change, strengthening the business and helping position it for the future,” Parer was quoted in the corporation’s statement. While uploaded on Monday, the statement or news does not appear to have been distributed on Stanwell’s email media list or posted on its social media accounts. Despite Treasurer David Janetzki being quoted also praising O’Rourke, neither he nor the government’s other shareholding minister (Finance Minister Ros Bates) had more widely shared the news. James Oliver, Stanwell’s chief operating officer, has been appointed to temporarily act in the role – with O’Rourke’s assistance – while a process to formally recruit a replacement is undertaken.





Amid the LNP’s unashamed pivot of energy focus from renewables back to fossil fuel power generation, governance of the sector has also been overhauled alongside the boards of other bodies. A Queensland Audit Office report earlier this year noted that “almost all board chairs and 76 per cent of board roles” had turned over since the election, warning about a loss of corporate knowledge. O’Rourke, Janetzki’s office, and Stanwell have been contacted for comment. Get alerts on significant breaking news as it happens.

Follow live updates on the Helen Haines attack Australian intelligence agencies will brief anxious federal politicians about a worsening security environment on Wednesday as independent MP Helen Haines remains in a critical condition after being struck by a four-wheel drive outside her regional Victorian office. The member for Indi, 65, lost one of her legs and surgeons were trying to save the other at Melbourne’s Alfred hospital on Tuesday. Victoria Police have charged Brendan Nugent, 43, over what they say was a targeted incident. He will appear in court on Wednesday. The town of Wangaratta came together on Tuesday, just hours after the horrific attack on Helen Haines. Jason South Haines’ parliamentary colleagues described the former nurse and midwife as “the best of us” as they grappled with the rare act of violence against a sitting MP, while the town of Wangaratta, in north-east Victoria, held a vigil and laid flowers outside her office.



The attack on Haines has alarmed state and federal MPs who have been subject to increasingly threatening behaviour in recent years. As One Nation leader Pauline Hanson blamed state premiers and the prime minister for enabling division and hatred, other MPs said it was time for reflection, not finger-pointing. The Home Affairs Department, ASIO and Australian Federal Police will address parliamentarians in several sessions on Wednesday, while Victoria is contemplating increased security at next month’s state election. “Everyone in public office carries a level of risk now – everyone,” Home Affairs Minister Tony Burke said on Tuesday. Federal police have received 1067 reports of harassing and threatening behaviour against high officeholders in 2025-26, up from 951 the financial year before. Former independent Indi MP Cathy McGowan, left, and a Haines supporter at a service in Wangaratta. Jason South But Haines seemed to MPs and her constituents an unlikely target, and politicians across the political divide on Tuesday described the non-partisan MP as a kind, decent, respectful and community-driven local member.



“When you go through the different scale of who we would have thought was the most at risk, no one would have thought Helen Haines,” Burke said. “Everybody looks at that and thinks, if it was Helen, it could have been me. Everyone is aware of that. But all our thoughts right now are with Helen.” Witnesses said Haines was retrieving items from the boot of her car on Monday afternoon when a white Toyota LandCruiser conducted a U-turn to ram her against a vehicle before reversing and hitting her a second time. In what Prime Minister Anthony Albanese has labelled a heroic act, barbershop owner Ricky Jefferies intervened by running to the driver’s side of the vehicle and wrestling him to the ground before waiting for authorities to arrive. Ricky Jefferies, the man who detained the alleged attacker, outside his barbershop. Jason South Victoria Police is leading the investigation, supported by the state’s counterterrorism team, the Australian Federal Police and ASIO. Police raided Nugent’s sprawling property near Wangaratta on Tuesday.



Detectives charged Nugent with dangerous driving causing serious injury, intentionally causing serious injury and causing harm to a Commonwealth public official. “He will be held overnight to appear at Wangaratta Magistrates’ Court tomorrow,” Victoria Police said in a statement. “Police will allege the incident was targeted.” Neighbours described Nugent as an unemployed man with few friends, and said they had become increasingly concerned about his erratic behaviour. He was involved in a road rage incident near Wangaratta last month in which he allegedly threatened a woman with a hammer, but no charges have been laid. The Tarrawingee man has a history of environmental activism but sources who knew him said he had changed dramatically since protesting logging in the local forest. Nugent’s social media history reveals he previously praised Haines and backed her independent campaign in the area. More recently, his posts focused on international issues, including criticising Israel’s conduct in Gaza. The property where Brendan Nugent lived. Jason South



His father, Rod Nugent, on Tuesday afternoon revealed Haines was a friend for more than 20 years. “What happened to her yesterday is devastating and unfathomable,” he said in a statement. “All of our love and all of our thoughts are with Helen and her family and friends. We will be assisting Victoria Police in any way we can.” ASIO director-general Mike Burgess said Monday’s incident had happened in an environment where increased levels of grievance, intolerance and polarisation had made violence seem permissible. “I have repeatedly put on the record my concern about the use of violent rhetoric in public discourse. Words matter,” Burgess said in a statement. “I genuinely believe the temperature of our security environment would be several degrees lower if we recommitted to conversing with civility, debating with respect and disagreeing with restraint.”



Prime Minister Anthony Albanese meets with law enforcement heads in Victoria. Paul Rovere Australian Federal Police Commissioner Krissy Barrett said 41 people had been charged with offences relating to threats against high office holders, including politicians, since special national security investigation teams were launched last October. Related Article Updated

Haines attack Suspect in Haines attack clashed with neighbours as his health unravelled Victorian Premier Ben Carroll said extra security measures could be imposed at voting booths at next month’s state election, while NSW Premier Chris Minns said he feared such incidents would deter other people from running for political office. Independent senator David Pocock described it as a “wake-up call”. “As a male parliamentarian, you get some threats. You get the angry phone calls, the awful emails, the anonymous comments,” he said.



“But I think we’ve got to look at what’s happening to female politicians, and just the ridiculous amount of threats and abuse that they have to cop, and as Australians, we need to stand up and say this is not OK.” Opposition Leader Angus Taylor said Coalition MPs had often discussed the increased threat of political violence as he stressed the importance of keeping an Australian culture of vigorous debate that never crossed the line into violence. “We need to do everything we can as elected representatives to prevent this ever happening again,” he said. Nationals leader Matt Canavan said Haines was a “lovely lady” who worked tirelessly for her community, while Greens leader David Shoebridge said the notion that Haines could be targeted for her work was “horrifying, senseless and shameful”. Hanson described Haines as a “beautiful lady” before blaming Albanese and state premiers for the deteriorating state of political debate. Liberal MP Andrew Hastie, whose own security has been recently upgraded, criticised that response.



“We all have a role to play and it can’t just be finger-pointing. I think it’s a bad move to point the finger on a day like this,” he said. Hanson also revealed she had ordered her cartoon creator to change a One Nation video that mocked Senator Jacqui Lambie’s struggles with vaginal prolapse. After Lambie condemned the cartoon on Monday, Hanson said she should “have a laugh” and “get over it”. But on Tuesday, she changed tone. “The video went up without my actually seeing it, and I was not aware of the content of the video,” Hanson said. “It wasn’t as tastefully done as it could have been, and I do apologise for that. I’ve already spoken to them about it and changing that.” With Nick Newling and Emily Kaine

World.title: New ACTU president warns AI is automating entire jobs
World.content:
BusinessWorkplaceAustralian Council of Trade Unions New ACTU president warns AI is automating entire jobs Millie Muroi October 20, 2026 — 10:00pm Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. The newly elected peak union body president has warned that AI is automating entire jobs, being used for surveillance and making management decisions, pledging to push for greater protections against job losses alongside higher wages and workplace flexibility. Emma Kingdon, 38, who is based in Melbourne and is one of the youngest people to be elected president of the Australian Council for Trade Unions (ACTU), will begin her term in December as part of a generational transition for the organisation. New ACTU president Emma Kingdon. Joe Armao In August, the council appointed Community and Public Sector Union (CPSU) head Melissa Donnelly as secretary, replacing Sally McManus, who left the role in July. Kingdon will take over from Michele O’Neil, who staggered her departure date from McManus by several months to assist with the leadership transition. Kingdon, who grew up in Perth’s outer suburban Rockingham, where she first worked in a fast-food KFC outlet and joined the retail workers’ union, said the cost of living remained the No.1 issue for working people.



“I come from a working-class family in Rockingham in WA and I get how hard it is to make ends meet, and that is what drives me every day to see workers get ahead,” she said. Related Article Opinion

AI Nightmare on Wall Street: The AI alarm bells are ringing louder Stephen Bartholomeusz Senior business columnist In an interview with this masthead, Kingdon said another major concern was the rapid introduction of AI into workplaces and industries. “It’s changing jobs by automating some tasks, and in some cases, it’s responsible for the automation of entire jobs,” she said. “There are issues around employers using it for surveillance, and AI making management decisions on things like rosters. “There are whole industries where AI tech bros are stealing creative work and journalists’ work, so there needs to be more protections for workers, and it’s an area that will continue to be a focus of the union movement.”



Kingdon took aim at employers – especially big businesses – saying they needed to do a “much better job” at consulting workers about changes including AI and job losses. “Today, NAB has announced that they’re going to be axing two and half thousand jobs,” she said, adding it was “outrageous” in a cost of living crisis. However, she said there was more that could be done “on all levels”, including by the government, which has created an “Office of AI” and was looking to develop mandatory requirements for large AI data centres. Kingdon has worked at the United Workers Union, Finance Sector Union, and with the council, including as its national campaigns director focused on driving union membership growth. The share of Australians holding union membership has fallen from 15 per cent a decade ago, but recovered from a record low to 13 per cent in 2024, driven largely by young workers who Kingdon said were “feeling like the system is rigged and stacked against them”.



Most recently, Kingdon has been an executive officer for the CFMEU administration after the scandal-plagued union was placed into administration in 2024. Related Article Australian Council of Trade Unions The 44-year-old working mother soon to lead the union movement “I went there and rolled up my sleeves: I don’t shy away from a challenge,” she said. “But it’s been in administration for two years and there’s still work to be done there.” Kingdon said she would be pushing for higher wage growth and supporting opportunities for workers to win back time. “Whether that’s through working from home, a four-day week or through additional annual leave, that’s obviously been a priority of working people,” she said. Kingdon, who is a mother of two, said she had “four great loves” in her life: family, the union movement, the Essendon Football Club and Star Wars.



O’Neil, who will finish her term at the start of December, said Kingdon was a “highly effective and formidable union campaigner” with experience representing workers across a diverse range of industries. Donnelly said Kingdon was a highly experienced campaigner who had taken on hard challenges and helped overturn bad workplace laws. “[Kingdon] dealt with some of the toughest corporate bosses in the major banks and has never left a negotiating table or a picket line without getting the best possible outcomes for her members,” she said. Richard Hale of Paddington thinks “Janice Creenaune’s daughter should end her Mothpocalypse Now party (C8) with the show MothBusters and let bogongs be bogongs.”

Haines attack Suspect in Haines attack clashed with neighbours as his health unravelled “He will be held overnight to appear at Wangaratta Magistrates’ Court [on Wednesday]. Police will allege the incident was targeted,” Victoria Police said in a statement. Earlier on Tuesday, Nugent’s father issued a statement saying Haines was deeply respected, valued and loved in the local community. “Helen has been our friend for more than 20 years and what happened to her yesterday is devastating and unfathomable,” Rod Nugent and his partner Christine Cunningham said.



Brendan Nugent has a history of environmental activism. His social media history reveals he once praised Haines and backed her independent campaign in Indi. Nugent commented on one of Haines’ posts in 2019, saying it would be good to see a politician like her “who takes climate change seriously”. A neighbour, who identified himself as Peter but requested his surname not be used, said he had made repeated calls to Triple Zero over the past year regarding Nugent’s allegedly concerning behaviour. He also claimed that Nugent had recently spent several weeks at a mental health facility in Wangaratta. Nugent’s most recent social media activity includes posts about Israel’s conduct in Gaza, British actor Russell Brand and child sex offender Jeffrey Epstein. The Nationals MP for the overlapping state seat of Ovens Valley, Tim McCurdy, said Nugent had previously been in contact with his electorate office. The property where Brendan Nugent lived. Jason South What is Haines’ condition?



Haines underwent surgery on Monday night at The Alfred hospital in Melbourne and remains in a critical condition. She has lost a leg as a result of her injuries, sources told this masthead, and surgeons are working to try save her other leg. “The patient remains in a critical condition, and we won’t be doing another clinical check until later this afternoon,” a statement from the hospital said. “We don’t comment or give out any other details to protect patient privacy.” Haines was initially taken to Northeast Health Wangaratta by ambulance before being airlifted to Melbourne, Victoria Police Acting Superintendent Ashley Mason said on Monday. Helen Haines arrives at The Alfred hospital in Melbourne on Monday night after being airlifted. Nine News What have the authorities said?



Krissy Barrett, commissioner of the Australian Federal Police, said the investigation into the alleged targeted attack was being led by the Victoria Police Security Investigation Unit. The investigation is being supported by the Victoria Joint Counter Terrorism Team, which includes Victoria Police, the AFP and spy agency ASIO. “At this stage it appears this is an isolated incident, and there are no known threats connected to this matter,” Barrett said. Related Article Analysis

Haines attack Helen Haines attack must be a turning point for Australia The AFP and ASIO have pointed to the increasing level of threatening behaviour being directed towards high office holders, including federal MPs. The AFP received 1067 reports of harassing or threatening behaviour against high office holders in 2025-26, which was up from 951 reports the year before. ASIO director-general Mike Burgess said Monday’s incident had happened in an environment where increased levels of grievance, intolerance and polarisation had made violence seem permissible.

Queensland government-owned energy company boss Michael O’Rourke has been quietly walked by the Stanwell board, five years since rising to the $1.1 million job in a company he worked in for decades. The corporation uploaded a statement to its website announcing the decision on Monday, citing the board’s view that it was the “right time for a leadership transition” as part of renewal in the sector. This leaves just one of Queensland’s five state-owned energy companies, CleanCo, yet to see a change of its chief executive in the two years since the self-proclaimed pro-coal Crisafulli LNP won government. Former Stanwell Corporation chief executive Michael O’Rourke, whose departure from the role was announced on Monday 19 October 2026. LinkedIn / Michael O’Rourke Stanwell board chair Justin Parer, a former Young LNP president shifted into the role from a port authority appointment last October, thanked O’Rourke for his leadership, with “full support and best wishes for the future”.



“Michael has played an important role in guiding Stanwell through a period of considerable change, strengthening the business and helping position it for the future,” Parer was quoted in the corporation’s statement. While uploaded on Monday, the statement or news does not appear to have been distributed on Stanwell’s email media list or posted on its social media accounts. Despite Treasurer David Janetzki being quoted also praising O’Rourke, neither he nor the government’s other shareholding minister (Finance Minister Ros Bates) had more widely shared the news. James Oliver, Stanwell’s chief operating officer, has been appointed to temporarily act in the role – with O’Rourke’s assistance – while a process to formally recruit a replacement is undertaken.





Amid the LNP’s unashamed pivot of energy focus from renewables back to fossil fuel power generation, governance of the sector has also been overhauled alongside the boards of other bodies. A Queensland Audit Office report earlier this year noted that “almost all board chairs and 76 per cent of board roles” had turned over since the election, warning about a loss of corporate knowledge. O’Rourke, Janetzki’s office, and Stanwell have been contacted for comment. Get alerts on significant breaking news as it happens.

World.title: Security briefing for anxious MPs as Helen Haines loses leg, remains in critical condition
World.content:
PoliticsFederalHaines attack Security briefing for anxious MPs as Helen Haines loses leg, remains in critical condition Natassia Chrysanthos Updated October 20, 2026 — 10:03pm ,first published 12:07pm Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Gift icon Gift Gift icon 0 / 3 No gift articles left You've used all of your gift articles. 3 more will become available on the 1st of every month. Follow live updates on the Helen Haines attack Australian intelligence agencies will brief anxious federal politicians about a worsening security environment on Wednesday as independent MP Helen Haines remains in a critical condition after being struck by a four-wheel drive outside her regional Victorian office. The member for Indi, 65, lost one of her legs and surgeons were trying to save the other at Melbourne’s Alfred hospital on Tuesday. Victoria Police have charged Brendan Nugent, 43, over what they say was a targeted incident. He will appear in court on Wednesday. The town of Wangaratta came together on Tuesday, just hours after the horrific attack on Helen Haines. Jason South Haines’ parliamentary colleagues described the former nurse and midwife as “the best of us” as they grappled with the rare act of violence against a sitting MP, while the town of Wangaratta, in north-east Victoria, held a vigil and laid flowers outside her office.



The attack on Haines has alarmed state and federal MPs who have been subject to increasingly threatening behaviour in recent years. As One Nation leader Pauline Hanson blamed state premiers and the prime minister for enabling division and hatred, other MPs said it was time for reflection, not finger-pointing. The Home Affairs Department, ASIO and Australian Federal Police will address parliamentarians in several sessions on Wednesday, while Victoria is contemplating increased security at next month’s state election. “Everyone in public office carries a level of risk now – everyone,” Home Affairs Minister Tony Burke said on Tuesday. Federal police have received 1067 reports of harassing and threatening behaviour against high officeholders in 2025-26, up from 951 the financial year before. Former independent Indi MP Cathy McGowan, left, and a Haines supporter at a service in Wangaratta. Jason South But Haines seemed to MPs and her constituents an unlikely target, and politicians across the political divide on Tuesday described the non-partisan MP as a kind, decent, respectful and community-driven local member.



“When you go through the different scale of who we would have thought was the most at risk, no one would have thought Helen Haines,” Burke said. “Everybody looks at that and thinks, if it was Helen, it could have been me. Everyone is aware of that. But all our thoughts right now are with Helen.” Witnesses said Haines was retrieving items from the boot of her car on Monday afternoon when a white Toyota LandCruiser conducted a U-turn to ram her against a vehicle before reversing and hitting her a second time. In what Prime Minister Anthony Albanese has labelled a heroic act, barbershop owner Ricky Jefferies intervened by running to the driver’s side of the vehicle and wrestling him to the ground before waiting for authorities to arrive. Ricky Jefferies, the man who detained the alleged attacker, outside his barbershop. Jason South Victoria Police is leading the investigation, supported by the state’s counterterrorism team, the Australian Federal Police and ASIO. Police raided Nugent’s sprawling property near Wangaratta on Tuesday.



Detectives charged Nugent with dangerous driving causing serious injury, intentionally causing serious injury and causing harm to a Commonwealth public official. “He will be held overnight to appear at Wangaratta Magistrates’ Court tomorrow,” Victoria Police said in a statement. “Police will allege the incident was targeted.” Neighbours described Nugent as an unemployed man with few friends, and said they had become increasingly concerned about his erratic behaviour. He was involved in a road rage incident near Wangaratta last month in which he allegedly threatened a woman with a hammer, but no charges have been laid. The Tarrawingee man has a history of environmental activism but sources who knew him said he had changed dramatically since protesting logging in the local forest. Nugent’s social media history reveals he previously praised Haines and backed her independent campaign in the area. More recently, his posts focused on international issues, including criticising Israel’s conduct in Gaza. The property where Brendan Nugent lived. Jason South



His father, Rod Nugent, on Tuesday afternoon revealed Haines was a friend for more than 20 years. “What happened to her yesterday is devastating and unfathomable,” he said in a statement. “All of our love and all of our thoughts are with Helen and her family and friends. We will be assisting Victoria Police in any way we can.” ASIO director-general Mike Burgess said Monday’s incident had happened in an environment where increased levels of grievance, intolerance and polarisation had made violence seem permissible. “I have repeatedly put on the record my concern about the use of violent rhetoric in public discourse. Words matter,” Burgess said in a statement. “I genuinely believe the temperature of our security environment would be several degrees lower if we recommitted to conversing with civility, debating with respect and disagreeing with restraint.”



Prime Minister Anthony Albanese meets with law enforcement heads in Victoria. Paul Rovere Australian Federal Police Commissioner Krissy Barrett said 41 people had been charged with offences relating to threats against high office holders, including politicians, since special national security investigation teams were launched last October. Related Article Updated

Haines attack Suspect in Haines attack clashed with neighbours as his health unravelled Victorian Premier Ben Carroll said extra security measures could be imposed at voting booths at next month’s state election, while NSW Premier Chris Minns said he feared such incidents would deter other people from running for political office. Independent senator David Pocock described it as a “wake-up call”. “As a male parliamentarian, you get some threats. You get the angry phone calls, the awful emails, the anonymous comments,” he said.



“But I think we’ve got to look at what’s happening to female politicians, and just the ridiculous amount of threats and abuse that they have to cop, and as Australians, we need to stand up and say this is not OK.” Opposition Leader Angus Taylor said Coalition MPs had often discussed the increased threat of political violence as he stressed the importance of keeping an Australian culture of vigorous debate that never crossed the line into violence. “We need to do everything we can as elected representatives to prevent this ever happening again,” he said. Nationals leader Matt Canavan said Haines was a “lovely lady” who worked tirelessly for her community, while Greens leader David Shoebridge said the notion that Haines could be targeted for her work was “horrifying, senseless and shameful”. Hanson described Haines as a “beautiful lady” before blaming Albanese and state premiers for the deteriorating state of political debate. Liberal MP Andrew Hastie, whose own security has been recently upgraded, criticised that response.



“We all have a role to play and it can’t just be finger-pointing. I think it’s a bad move to point the finger on a day like this,” he said. Hanson also revealed she had ordered her cartoon creator to change a One Nation video that mocked Senator Jacqui Lambie’s struggles with vaginal prolapse. After Lambie condemned the cartoon on Monday, Hanson said she should “have a laugh” and “get over it”. But on Tuesday, she changed tone. “The video went up without my actually seeing it, and I was not aware of the content of the video,” Hanson said. “It wasn’t as tastefully done as it could have been, and I do apologise for that. I’ve already spoken to them about it and changing that.” With Nick Newling and Emily Kaine

World.title: New ACTU president warns AI is automating entire jobs
World.content:
BusinessWorkplaceAustralian Council of Trade Unions New ACTU president warns AI is automating entire jobs Millie Muroi October 20, 2026 — 10:00pm Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Gift icon Gift Gift icon 0 / 3 No gift articles left You've used all of your gift articles. 3 more will become available on the 1st of every month. Close Share A A A

The newly elected peak union body president has warned that AI is automating entire jobs, being used for surveillance and making management decisions, pledging to push for greater protections against job losses alongside higher wages and workplace flexibility. Emma Kingdon, 38, who is based in Melbourne and is one of the youngest people to be elected president of the Australian Council for Trade Unions (ACTU), will begin her term in December as part of a generational transition for the organisation. New ACTU president Emma Kingdon. Joe Armao In August, the council appointed Community and Public Sector Union (CPSU) head Melissa Donnelly as secretary, replacing Sally McManus, who left the role in July. Kingdon will take over from Michele O’Neil, who staggered her departure date from McManus by several months to assist with the leadership transition. Kingdon, who grew up in Perth’s outer suburban Rockingham, where she first worked in a fast-food KFC outlet and joined the retail workers’ union, said the cost of living remained the No.1 issue for working people.



“I come from a working-class family in Rockingham in WA and I get how hard it is to make ends meet, and that is what drives me every day to see workers get ahead,” she said. Related Article Opinion

AI Nightmare on Wall Street: The AI alarm bells are ringing louder Stephen Bartholomeusz Senior business columnist In an interview with this masthead, Kingdon said another major concern was the rapid introduction of AI into workplaces and industries. “It’s changing jobs by automating some tasks, and in some cases, it’s responsible for the automation of entire jobs,” she said. “There are issues around employers using it for surveillance, and AI making management decisions on things like rosters. “There are whole industries where AI tech bros are stealing creative work and journalists’ work, so there needs to be more protections for workers, and it’s an area that will continue to be a focus of the union movement.”



Kingdon took aim at employers – especially big businesses – saying they needed to do a “much better job” at consulting workers about changes including AI and job losses. “Today, NAB has announced that they’re going to be axing two and half thousand jobs,” she said, adding it was “outrageous” in a cost of living crisis. However, she said there was more that could be done “on all levels”, including by the government, which has created an “Office of AI” and was looking to develop mandatory requirements for large AI data centres. Kingdon has worked at the United Workers Union, Finance Sector Union, and with the council, including as its national campaigns director focused on driving union membership growth. The share of Australians holding union membership has fallen from 15 per cent a decade ago, but recovered from a record low to 13 per cent in 2024, driven largely by young workers who Kingdon said were “feeling like the system is rigged and stacked against them”.



Most recently, Kingdon has been an executive officer for the CFMEU administration after the scandal-plagued union was placed into administration in 2024. Related Article Australian Council of Trade Unions The 44-year-old working mother soon to lead the union movement “I went there and rolled up my sleeves: I don’t shy away from a challenge,” she said. “But it’s been in administration for two years and there’s still work to be done there.” Kingdon said she would be pushing for higher wage growth and supporting opportunities for workers to win back time. “Whether that’s through working from home, a four-day week or through additional annual leave, that’s obviously been a priority of working people,” she said. Kingdon, who is a mother of two, said she had “four great loves” in her life: family, the union movement, the Essendon Football Club and Star Wars.



O’Neil, who will finish her term at the start of December, said Kingdon was a “highly effective and formidable union campaigner” with experience representing workers across a diverse range of industries. Donnelly said Kingdon was a highly experienced campaigner who had taken on hard challenges and helped overturn bad workplace laws. “[Kingdon] dealt with some of the toughest corporate bosses in the major banks and has never left a negotiating table or a picket line without getting the best possible outcomes for her members,” she said. World.title: Chrises clash on health, homelessness, cost of living in last leaders' debate
World.content:
The final leaders' debate for this election campaign is done and dusted, with the two Chrises clashing on health, homelessness, the economy and the cost of living.

At the outset, host Paddy Gower introduced 18-year-olds Finn and River, first time voters sitting in the audience.

He challenged National's Christopher Luxon and Labour's Chris Hipkins to win them over.

Throughout the hour they sold their plans to improve New Zealanders' lives, but they also spent a fair chunk of time having a whack at the other over their track records.

Here's how it all played out.

Health

Health was up first, with Hipkins saying the system was in crisis, and Luxon calling it challenging. (He said later it was a crisis, but he was focused on fixing the problem rather than debating terminology).

Hipkins said Luxon was "in denial" about the extent of the crisis: "If you won't listen to the doctors and the nurses who are telling you the health system is in crisis, then you are never going to be able to fix it."

He laid out Labour's plans to hire more hospital staff and offer people three free GP visits, while Luxon said his government was recruiting more staff, building another medical school and expanding pharmacists' remit.

Hipkins brought up the problems with staffing at Starship Hospital's cancer ward, saying nurses were "desperate" for more staff.

Luxon replied: "We should have a dispassionate, facts-based conversation about that," saying there were problems under Hipkins' leadership too.

The debate descended into an argument over the number of nurses that had been hired in the last three years - an argument that's been playing out for months between National and Labour.

Homelessness

The leaders were asked what they would do about rough sleeping.

Hipkins leapt at the chance to accuse Luxon of criminalising homelessness with the introduction of move-on orders.

Luxon said no one wanted to see people homeless, but his government's dealing with "intimidating, disturbing, disruptive behaviour" and giving police another set of tools.

Gower asked the pair whether a camp of 40 homeless people in Whangārei should be moved on.

Hipkins said no, and Luxon said the police should use their judgement on that.

The debate hosted by Paddy Gower (R). Supplied / Stuff

Social media

Would they stand up to big social media companies and the harm they cause?

Both Luxon and Hipkins said yes. Both their parties supported a social media ban for under-16s, and had committed to making it happen after the election.

Gower asked whether New Zealand should match Australia's plan to allow people to switch off the algorithm on their feed.

Hipkins said Labour would do that, while Luxon said he was open to it.

What about tax - is it morally acceptable for Facebook to pay 0.33 percent of its revenue in tax in New Zealand?

"I don't think that's acceptable, no," Hipkins said.

Luxon said there was a need to be pragmatic: "You're not going to solve that problem as New Zealand on its own, Paddy. You have to act in concert with like-minded friends around the world."

Economy and superannuation

Both National and Labour planned to return the government's books to surplus by 2028/29.

Luxon said Hipkins' promises were unfunded, and Hipkins said that was not true.

"All he's got is blame and excuses," Hipkins said.

What followed was minutes of Hipkins and Luxon talking over each other, bagging each other's record and crowing about their own.

Talk moved on to the "fiscal time bomb" of superannuation.

Hipkins said Labour would keep the age at 65: "It's not right to say that future generations of New Zealanders should pay for the retirement of today's retirees and then not get that themselves."

Luxon said he wants to raise the age slowly, gradually - but political consensus was needed.

"Yes, that instinctively is a position of the National Party. But I do want to work in a cross-party way with Chris to try and have a proper conversation about retirement."

Coalitions: who will work with who?

The polls have Opportunity holding the balance of power. Hipkins reiterated he'd work with them - although "it's unclear yet exactly what it is that they stand for", he said.

Luxon reiterated he would not. He refused to put his job on the line, though, and commit to resigning rather than governing with Opportunity.

"That's a ridiculous question," he said.

Gower brought up Green and Te Pāti Māori MPs' recent visit to a Mongrel Mob pad, and asked whether Hipkins would refuse to work with them.

Hipkins repeated they won't hold relevant portfolios (such as Corrections) and pointed to Luxon being happy to have a foreign minister "who makes racist comments about Indians".

Luxon replied: "You've got partners that want to be in coalition with the Mongrel Mob, my friend."

Hipkins said that was ridiculous.

The two leaders sold their plans to improve New Zealanders' lives - while also having a whack at the other over their track records. Supplied / Stuff

Cost of living

Luxon said his way of dealing with the cost of living was to grow the economy, because a bigger pie allowed more slices to be shared.

He added that, for some people, things were getting better.

Hipkins said that was completely untrue: "You are so out of touch ... you are not up to the job."

Luxon bit back saying Labour relied on bribes, handouts and unfunded promises.

Hipkins said a Labour government would bring down the cost of living, and laid out policies like free doctors' visits and public transport fare caps.

Education

Luxon said National was focused on the basics: attendance, reading, writing and maths.

"What we're doing is working," he said, adding that Erica Stanford would go down as one of the best education ministers.

Hipkins said Labour would start at improving early childhood education, increase attendance, and look to a future after school, promoting his plan to write off some student loan debt and get people into apprenticeships.

Luxon said Hipkins was "the most abysmal education minister".

"That's just petty and pathetic," Hipkins snapped back.

Luxon said Hipkins' record was "shameful" and he delivered no value, and did not move the system forward.

Hipkins said he started structured literacy and Luxon had continued it, and was claiming victory over it.

Quickfire consensus

Areas of agreement emerged in the quick fire round.

The pair had the same answers: is exploiting the MMP system to create an overhang cheating? Yes. Should child abusers receive a life sentence? They're open to looking at it. Should the government deploy noise cameras to snap boy racers? Yes. (This one is an ACT party policy). Should gambling ads around sport be banned? Yes. Should we have a referendum on a four-year term? Yes. Has the word Aotearoa become divisive? No.
