World.title: Search underway for man in kayak who went into the sea at Waihi Beach
World.content:
A search is underway for a man who went kayaking at Waihi Beach.

Police said the man went into the sea on Tuesday morning and had not been seen since.

A police spokesperson said a search and rescue operation was underway at the beach after the man was reported missing about 5.40pm.

The kayak was described to be blue with black and white mottled (camo) colour, and was a single seated sit-on-top vessel.

World.title: Ministry of Education pushes back on claims Gloriavale school shut down was rushed
World.content:
The Ministry of Education has pushed back on claims the process to shut down Gloriavale's school was rushed.

The ministry defended its decision to cancel the school's registration in the High Court at Wellington during the second and final day of a judicial review challenging the move.

The Secretary for Education Ellen Macgregor-Reid has twice tried to close the West Coast Christian community's school over student safety concerns.

On Tuesday, counsel for the ministry, Victoria Casey KC disputed Gloriavale's position that the Secretary had only one day to consider relevant information before making her decision.

Counsel for the ministry, Victoria Casey KC. (File photo) RNZ / Samuel Rillstone

"She had one working day and a weekend, and with respect the level of annotation throughout the entire report... doesn't support the submission that she didn't pay proper attention to it."

Casey said the entire process took five months which was neither truncated nor unfair - an argument that Gloriavale's lawyer, Richard Raymond KC, did not accept.

Raymond and Casey also tussled over whether Macgregor-Reid's second decision to cancel the 80-student school's registration was a continuation of a process initiated in 2025 or a fresh examination.

Macgregor-Reid first moved to shut down the school in December last year, but it remains open due to the legal challenge by the school's board.

She again confirmed the cancellation in September following a failed Education Review Office (ERO) report that found the school was not a physically and emotionally safe place for students.

Raymond argued the second review of the school had been a "fresh look" and the Secretary missed cruicial steps in the process, such as issuing a notice to comply.

Gloriavale's lawyer, Richard Raymond KC. RNZ / Samuel Rillstone

But Casey said such a notice issued in July 2025 remained relevant and argued the school was "absolutely on notice" about the Secretary's safety concerns pointing to December's cancellation bid and a letter to the board in April.

Casey also challenged the request by Gloriavale for the Court to correct the record in relation to information provided to RNZ under the Official Information Act.

The "disputed information" reported by RNZ in June, concerned a letter from ERO to Oranga Tamariki expressing wellbeing concerns, including that Gloriavale's school "knowingly employed staff with prior convictions unsuitable for work with children" and "in at least one instance, the school failed to act when behaviours placing students at risk were identified".

Gloriavale argued the information was false, however, Casey said the Ombudsman rather than the Court was the appropriate place to raise such issues.

Although the "disputed information" wasn't considered by the Secretary in her latest decision, Casey argued that the "substance of the concern was very real," citing a teacher's guilty plea to an historic assault and a recent complaint of an historic sexual assault committed by a staff member.

She said ERO had concluded there was a pattern of institutional failure to act on known risks to children.

Raymond asserted that the board had acted appropriately in response to the recently surfaced allegation.

Justice Karen Grau thanked the parties for the quality of their interesting but dense submissions, warning the public gallery packed with Gloriavale supporters that her decision would take time.

World.title: Police officer who stole police-issued firearm starred in police recruitment series
World.content:
A police officer who stole a police-issued firearm starred in a police recruitment series, and was awarded the Commissioner's Award for leadership in his recruit wing, it can now be revealed.

RNZ earlier revealed a police officer had been charged with stealing a police-issued firearm and being in unlawful possession of a police-issued firearm.

On Tuesday, the officer Steven John Karehana pleaded guilty to the charges. Following his guilty plea an interim suppression order was lifted. Karehana will be sentenced in December.

The summary of facts said Karehana graduated from Police College in October 2024, and was stationed in Whanganui.

Do you know more? Email sam.sherwood@rnz.co.nz

At the time of the offending he was assigned to a team that was based out of an agency site on Victoria Ave, Whanganui.

In March, 2026, police carried out an audit of police-owned firearms in the Central District policing area.

The audit confirmed a glock was missing, presumed stolen on or about 11 February, 2026. The glock is worth $1204.

The summary said the glock was one of several police firearms that were stored among four locked gun safes on the ground floor of the Whanganui Police Station.

Prior to the gun going missing, Karehana asked an associate if they would be able to get rid of a gun if he delivered one to them. The associate said they would.

About 7.15am on 11 February, Karehana entered the Whanaganui Police Station to begin his shift which started at 8am. He then took two glocks and two M4 rifles from the gun safe and put them into lockboxes in a police car.

He and his colleague for the day then went to the Victoria Ave site. Karehana returned to the police station alone about 1.40pm and accessed the gun safe which housed the glock.

"The defendant removed the glock and placed it into his backpack before leaving the building and driving home," the summary said.

"A short time after arriving at his home address in Martin, the defendant delivered the glock to the associate.

"This associate subsequently supplied the glock to another associate and obtained $10,000 cash for it."

Karehana did not know that his associate was going to on sell the weapon, the summary said. That evening Karehana was given $5000.

The glock was recovered by police in June.

When spoken to by police, Karehana denied the allegations.

The 42-year-old starred in the police recruitment video series, Ride Along.

His parts in the series appear to have since been removed from YouTube, and his name has been removed from a press release about the series.

In one episode seen by RNZ, Karehana spoke of his journey to joining the Police.

"I guess for me it was a long journey. Took me around about 20 years from my first application to being accepted into police college, and I've been out for about four months now.

"So I first applied in 2003, and I was denied because of what had happened in my youth, and I applied probably every five years after that until I got a job as a painter, and I stayed in that job for 16 years.

"It wasn't until I went and worked for my iwi, and through that journey, it reignited the love and passion for my community and my people."

A screen grab from Ride Along. NZ Police/Youtube

He said being an older recruit he brought "different life skills, life experiences to the police".

"My why for joining is to be a role model for our people.

"By showing them rather than just talking about it, it can go a long way into helping build those relationships once again."

Karehana's name has also been removed by Police from a press release put out in October 2024 celebrating Wing 378.

The original version, seen by RNZ, said he was awarded the Commissioner's Leadership Award.

"This is the beginning of our journey in the New Zealand Police, but for all of us graduating, there are many people who have sacrificed and worked hard to allow us to be here, and we are very grateful. We could not have done it without you.

"The call to service is one few answer, but it is a selfless sacrifice to put community above self and by graduating today we have all joined a proud and selfless organisation."

In a statement to RNZ, Central District Commander Dion Bennett acknowledged Karehana's guilty plea.

"While I am pleased that Mr Karehana has been prepared to accept responsibility for his actions, I know that I and all his former colleagues are bitterly disappointed that he let down the mana of our uniform but we will all work hard to repair the damage he's caused."

Bennett said as a consequence of Karehana's actions police had removed him from promotional materials in which he featured.

"He has demonstrated that he no longer holds the same values that previously led him to be selected for inclusion in Police promotions," he said.

World.title: Two girls injured after falling from Ferris wheel at Greymouth agricultural show
World.content:
Correction: An earlier version of this article stated three men were injured after falling from a ferris wheel at Rolling Meadows Festival. Two were injured.

Two teenage girls are recovering from injuries suffered in a fall from a Ferris wheel at an agricultural trade show in Greymouth over the weekend.

The girls fell several metres from the ride at AgFest West Coast and hit another girl on the ground on Saturday afternoon.

AgFest West Coast managing director Andy Thompson said it was unclear how far or why the girls fell, and WorkSafe had been notified.

"I didn't witness the incident myself, but it is fair to say more than two or three metres from what I can tell, and possibly more than that," he said.

Thompson said he had spoken to the mother of the girl who was hit on the ground, who said she was okay, but concerned for the teens.

"The other two girls, I have not had a direct report yet from the authorities on their wellbeing but I understand their injuries were minor - still that is just very, very lucky that they weren't injured any further," he said.

Thompson said everyone else was asked to get off the Ferris wheel. Operator Sturgeon Amusements shut down the ride and contacted the safety regulator.

He said police took photos and secured the scene.

The event ran from Friday to Saturday and was only 30 minutes from closing when the girls fell, Thompson said.

"We'd had an incredibly successful day with over 10,000 people attending so it was a real shame that in the final few minutes an incident occurred. All the protocols and procedures we had in place, with the on-ground medical staff, police and communications with St John meant it was handled quickly and professionally."

Sturgeon Amusements has been contacted for comment.

A WorkSafe spokesperson confirmed the regulator had been notified and inspectors were making enquiries to understand the circumstances of the fall.

"An inspector has issued a prohibition notice while our enquiries are ongoing. This notice prevents use of the Ferris wheel while a competent person is engaged to assess the Ferris wheel and provide a report to the owner, Sturgeon Amusements Ltd, and WorkSafe," the spokesperson said.

Two men were injured after falling from a Ferris wheel operated by Event Hire at Rolling Meadows Festival in Christchurch on New Year's Day.

World.title: Scott Watson's appeal being heard in Supreme Court
World.content:
Scott Watson's defence lawyers argue police pressured and "primed" a key witness to identify Watson as the man he saw boarding a yacht with Ben Smart and Olivia Hope in the early hours of New Years' Day.

The argument came as Watson's appeal of his double-murder conviction is being heard in the Supreme Court.

Watson was sentenced to life imprisonment for murdering Ben Smart and Olivia Hope in the Marlborough Sounds and has now been behind bars for 27 years.

The Blenheim friends, aged 21 and 17, were last seen stepping off a water taxi onto a stranger's yacht in Endeavour Inlet the early hours of 1 January, 1998, after a New Year's Eve party at Furneaux Lodge.

Their bodies have never been found.

Watson was found guilty of the murders in 1999 after an 11-week jury trial involving about 500 witnesses.

He appealed his convictions after the trial but the application was dismissed. He made another two applications that were unsuccessful before a 2017 bid for a royal pardon was granted, with the case heard by the Court of Appeal in 2024.

Watson's Supreme Court appeal focuses on one key point - the photo identification process used in the original trial.

Ben Smart and Olivia Hope. NZ Police

Water taxi driver Guy Wallace identified Watson by photo montage on 20 April 1998 as the mystery man with Smart and Hope boarding a yacht - the last place they were ever seen.

Defence lawyer Nick Chisnell KC said that photo montage evidence was "inadmissible" and "tainted", but had been a "crucial part" of the Crown's case.

Chisnell said by the time Wallace was shown the montage, it was about three and a half months after Watson was identified as the suspect, and Hope and Smart disappeared.

"We say that it was profoundly contaminated by outside influences earlier in the investigation," Chisnell said.

He said police had had already shown Wallace a photo of Watson in early January 1998, but Wallace had told police he didn't recognise the man.

Chisnell argued police pressured Wallace in the days after this, saying Watson had been identified by others as the "lone" man, the "sleazy" man, the "mystery man", which suggested he was the key suspect.

"Media saturation" also identified Watson as a suspect and his boat Blade as featuring heavily in the investigation, Chisnell said.

"Then we say the final nail in the unfairness coffin, is the fact that the police created an unfair and improper montage that predisposed Mr Wallace and others to select Mr Watson."

Chisnell referred to expert evidence raised the Court of Appeal which criticised the photo identification process as a "show up" - by police showing a single photo of Watson, and their naming of him to Wallace, they "directly communicated" to an eye-witness who the central suspect was.

"...In my submission, police primed Mr Wallace to identify Mr Watson, and that tainted the identification procedure in that point onwards."

Chisnell KC said a detective applied "moral pressure" to Wallace in a video interview, suggesting he wasn't telling the truth about who he saw, and that he needed to for Smart and Hope's families.

Chisnell also criticised the photograph of Watson police used in Montage B, with his eyes only half open.

He said police could have used other photographs with Watson's eyes fully open, taken from a front on perspective, similar to photos of other people they provided.

He said that Wallace said at time of the trial that he was drawn to this characteristic of the eyes in the photo montage, in the context of a trial about a party and intoxication.

Watson's second lawyer Kerry Cook KC said if this appeal is successful, there shouldn't be a retrial, due to the effect of the passage of time and the media involvement, including news coverage, and books.

"That's very difficult to unwind."

Wallace - a key eyewitness - had died, Cook KC said.

"This case is singular in the way in which the media and the nation has been captured by it, and that has implications."

World.title: Live: South Africa skipper reaches ton after Boland snares his fifth
World.content:
Bavuma defends, Harmer thinks about a single, Bavuma sends him back in the nick of time.

SWING AND A MISS! That's a bit more expansive from Bavuma. A bit of an attempted slog down the ground.

Maybe Bavuma is going to look to up the tempo here. He lofts over cover but without perfect timing, so only for two.

FOUR RUNS! Nothing expansive about that, just a gorgeous drive back down the ground for four. Looks so easy for him today.

World.title: Tedesco parachutes in as Kangaroos captain in first Test since 2023
World.content:
James Tedesco will be elevated straight to the captaincy when he runs out for his first game for the Kangaroos in three years.

Tedesco has been named at fullback for Australia's men's Rugby League World Cup clash with Fiji in Brisbane on Sunday.

It marks the 33-year-old's first cap in green and gold since the 2023 Pacific Championship final, when he led the Kangaroos to a shock 30-0 loss to New Zealand.

Since his last Test appearance, Tedesco has won back his NSW jersey, claimed last year's Dally M Medal and was the Clive Churchill medallist as Roosters captain earlier this month.

On Sunday night at Lang Park, Tedesco will return to the team after coach Kevin Walters made the decision to rotate through his squad to try to find his best line-up.

Rugby League World Cup quick hits From Kalyn Ponga's magnificent Test debut to a mighty Tongan victory years in the making here are the quick hits from week one of the Rugby League World Cup.

Walters named four debutants in the 23-strong squad, with halfback Sam Walker, centre Bradman Best, hooker Blayke Brailey and back rower David Fifita all set to start.

Walker's debut will double as a play-off with halves partner Tom Dearden as both bye to replace the injured Mitchell Moses in the seven jersey for the rest of the campaign.

The bench and extended squad are filled out by starters from the Kangaroos' 24-22 win over the Kiwis in their tournament opener, including regular captain Isaah Yeo and fullback Reece Walsh, who staked his claim in a barnstorming return from injury with a long-range solo try and a try-saver on opposite number Kalyn Ponga.

If Tedesco aims up, it could leave Walters with a major selection call to make at the pointy end of the tournament.

"Those big moments; he hadn't played in six, seven weeks but he turned up in big moments and nailed them," Tedesco, the oldest member of the squad at 33, said of Walsh.

"He was great all week, asking for advice, but it's not a competition. I've got an opportunity and all I can do is make the most of it and do my role.

"Walshy does things on the field so it's about knowing my game and being an experienced leader.

"Walshy, he was soaking up anything I had to say last week and I enjoy that role."

The Jillaroos have also named two debutants for their Women's Rugby League World Cup clash with England on Saturday night.

Sydney Roosters premiership winner Sariah Paki will become a dual international, while Maroons forward Makenzie Weale has been named to make her debut from the bench in Perth.

Their first caps come after five-eighth Jocelyn Kelleher entered the international arena with a bang in round one, claiming player of the match honours against Samoa.

World.title: Aussie Opal's block fires Dream to WNBA finals win
World.content:
Australian rookie Izzy Borlase has helped the Atlanta Dream to their historic first WNBA finals victory, shining in a series-levelling 79–65 triumph over Golden State.

Dream superstar Angel Reese was a dominant figure in game two at San Francisco's Chase Center on Monday (Tuesday AEDT), posting a monster double-double with 30 points and 16 rebounds.

The Dream's win was their first in a title-deciding best-of-seven series, after being swept in their three previous appearances and losing game one against the Valkyries this year.

Coach Karl Smesko's team will enjoy home-court advantage in the next two games as they chase their first WNBA championship.

Borlase could play a key role after being entrusted with almost 17 minutes on court in game two, finishing with two points, one assist, one steal and one block.

The 22-year-old missed all four field-goal attempts in the first half, but sank a pair of free throws and made a huge play to help Atlanta to a 39–37 lead at the main break.

Borlase's block on Veronica Burton late in the second period led to an Allisha Gray (18 points) triple and forced the Valkyries to call a time-out.

It drew huge praise from Reese, who made a beeline for her teammate and celebrated with a chest bump and double-fist to the chest.

Atlanta seized control in a dominant third quarter and took a 60–46 lead after Jordin Canada (13 points) banked a long-range three on the buzzer.

Overrun after leading late in game one, the Dream held firm this time to record their breakthrough finals victory.

Reese became the third player in WNBA history to have at least 30 points and 15 rebounds in a finals game.

Another Australian Opals star, Miela Sowah, sat on the bench for the Valkyries and will remain there throughout the finals due to her restricted status as a development player.

The ABC of SPORT Sports content to make you think... or allow you not to. A newsletter delivered each Saturday.

World.title: Diamonds boosted by imminent return of vice-captain
World.content:
Diamonds vice-captain Kate Moloney is on track to return from injury and give Australia a much-needed boost for the Constellation Cup.

Moloney was forced to watch the netball world's number-one side suffer a shock 56–50 loss to the Silver Ferns from the sidelines after a finger laceration in the lead-up to the Auckland series opener.

The Diamonds were already without defender Jo Weston (managed), and the experienced duo were sorely missed against the Commonwealth Games champions.

Diamonds centurions forced to the bench in Constellation Cup loss It was defender Courtney Bruce's 100th milestone game to start the Constellation Cup but the brand new centurion and her captain Liz Watson were both sent to the bench in Australia's 56-50 loss to New Zealand in Auckland.

New Zealand stormed to a 15-goal lead in the first of four matches, forcing Diamonds coach Stacey Marinkovich to bench captain and midcourter Liz Watson alongside goalkeeper Courtney Bruce in her 100th game.

Jamie-Lee Price took over centre duties against New Zealand's Adelaide Lightning star Kate Heffernan, while Jessie Grenvold was tasked with containing Silver Ferns goalscoring superstar Grace Nweke on debut.

Australia cut the deficit to just six goals in the fourth quarter, but the damage had been done.

Georgie Horjus was the only Diamond who remained on the court for four quarters, finishing with a game-high 19 gains and 38 feeds as wing attack.

With the Diamonds set to name their squad this evening, Marinkovich said Melbourne Vixens captain Moloney's return was imminent.

"We'll definitely see her back in the series," Marinkovich said.

"It was a bit of a nasty laceration to her finger, so we had to wait till it pretty much stuck back together.

"It's just one of those innocuous things that happen at training, but she's been able to do all the running and the movement, and yeah, look forward to having her back."

But the midcourt will not be the only area of focus for tomorrow night's game in Christchurch.

Looking to end their five-year drought on Kiwi soil, the Diamonds will need to find a way past the towering defensive duo of Kelly Jackson and Karin Burger.

With goalkeeper Jackson standing at 192cm and goal defence Burger at 184cm, Australia's attacking roster of Kiera Austin, Cara Koenen, Sophie Dwyer and Sophie Garbin struggled to fire.

Marinkovich is urging her Diamonds to start with "immediacy" on the court.

"We were slightly off our pace [in game one], and our numbers would show that we weren't as aggressive as what we needed to be on the ball," she said.

ABC Sport will have live blog coverage of Game II between the Diamonds and Silver Ferns on Wednesday, October 21.

AAP

World.title: Jockeys cleared over Ohope Wins's fatal Caulfield Cup fall
World.content:
A Racing Victoria investigation into the fall at the Caulfield Cup that resulted in the euthanasia of Ohope Wins has finished, clearing all jockeys involved of any wrongdoing.

Ohope Wins, ridden by Jye McNeil, and Half Yours, ridden by Mark Zahra, both went down in the final straight at the 150th running of the famous 2,400-metre race.

Zahra and Half Yours fell first after getting tangled in the pack chasing eventual winner Kingswood, with Ohope Wins going over the top of the fallen gelding.

Loading...

Last year's Melbourne Cup winner Half Yours suffered superficial cuts and scrapes, but Ohope Wins was assessed on track as having a "serious racing injury" and was put down by on-course veterinarians.

Both jockeys were thrown from their mounts and taken to hospital, delaying the conclusion of the inquiry into the incident, which once again prompted calls for the racing industry to be made more accountable for racehorse deaths.

After hearing evidence from McNeil, Zahra and three other jockeys in the race, Racing Victoria stewards said they "could not attribute the incident to the careless actions of any one particular rider".

The hearing at Racing Victoria headquarters found contact between Kings Valley and Green Spaces with about 300m to go resulted in the latter becoming unbalanced.

Half Yours ran the rest of the course without a rider. (Getty Images: Robert Cianflone)

Green Spaces, ridden by Rachel King, then turned inward and made more contact with apprentice rider Jabez Johnstone's Kings Valley, who also turned inward, resulting in Half Yours being squeezed for room between Kings Valley and Zahrann.

"A short distance later, Half Yours subsequently fell," the stewards' report read.

"Ohope Wins that was trailing was subsequently brought down when unable to avoid the fallen Half Yours."

The incident has been referred to Racing Victoria's Veterinary Services Department, as is standard practice.

Trainer Tony McEvoy said Half Yours was recovering well from injuries and would be rested, while Zahra was meeting with doctors today about a timeline for his return to riding.

McNeil was cleared of any injury and is expected to ride at the Geelong Cup tomorrow.

World.title: Collingwood AFLW captain to leave at end of season
World.content:
Collingwood captain Ruby Schleicher will leave the struggling AFLW club to return to her native Western Australia.

Schleicher informed the Magpies of her decision on Tuesday after suffering a season-ending shoulder injury in their round 9 loss to St Kilda.

The 28-year-old inaugural Collingwood player is expected to land at West Coast, with the Eagles reportedly offering a four-year contract.

Do you have a story idea about women in sport? Email us abcsport5050@your.abc.net.au

A two-time All-Australian, Schleicher's departure is a massive blow to perennial competition strugglers Collingwood, who have only won one game after 10 rounds this season.

"This has been a really tough decision for me to make but one that is ultimately the best for where I am in my life and career," Schleicher said in a club statement.

"Collingwood has been my home for my entire adult life … I'll always consider myself a Collingwood person.

"I'm excited for my next chapter, but also for the club's next chapter."

Collingwood chief executive Craig Kelly expressed the club's disappointment in Schleicher's decision.

Schleicher reportedly turned down a one-year deal to remain at the Magpies after strong interest from the Eagles.

Joining the Magpies ahead of the inaugural AFLW season in 2017, the defender-turned-midfielder has played 82 games for the club and took over as captain from Bri Davey in 2025.

Schleicher was moved to the forward line this season under coach Sam Wright and kicked 10 goals before fracturing her shoulder against the Saints.

"While we are disappointed to see Ruby depart our Club, we respect her decision to return home," Kelly said in a statement.

"We thank Ruby for everything she has given to Collingwood and wish her all the very best for the next chapter."

Like Schleicher, Davey is among several senior leaders set to come off contract at the end of this campaign, while vice-captain Jordy Allen's contract runs until the end of the 2027 season.

AAP

World.title: NFL QB in hospital at 4am before London game due to blood clots
World.content:
Philadelphia Eagles quarterback Jalen Hurts has blood clots in both lungs, according to his team and his agent, with media reports saying the former Super Bowl MVP is expected to miss the rest of the 2026 season.

Hurts was clinically stable but his treatment would involve blood thinners, which would rule him out of contact activities, the Eagles and agent Nicole Lynn said in a statement.

The 28-year-old was initially diagnosed with a left calf superficial vein thrombosis after an ultrasound in London before Philadelphia's 19-17 loss to the Jacksonville Jaguars at the Tottenham Hotspur Stadium, which Hurts played in.

The current diagnosis is a deep vein thrombosis and bilateral pulmonary emboli. A bilateral pulmonary embolism is where a blood clot travels from a deep vein in the body, often the leg, and blocks an artery in both lungs.

"Jalen's prognosis is very good, and we expect a full recovery," the statement said.

"We anticipate that he will have the opportunity to resume contact football activities when off the blood thinners."

It said no long-term effects were expected.

According to an ESPN report, Hurts was in the hospital in London until 4am on the day of the game and did not sleep the night before the contest as a health precaution.

Speaking at a press conference on Monday, local time, Eagles head coach Nick Sirianni said the team cared about its players and he trusted the medical staff.

"I'm a football coach. I lean on our medical experts in every situation. I have full trust and full faith in them," Sirianni said.

"We get medical information from our guys, and we always put the players' health first and foremost in every situation. And, you know, that's where we were there."

The Eagles said in a statement on Thursday that their medical staff and doctors in London reviewed the ultrasound results and concluded that "activity and mobility were important" and that Hurts could safely play in the game against the Jaguars, adding that he "played without limitation".

Hurts guided the Eagles to the Super Bowl title in February 2025, throwing for two touchdowns and running in another against the Kansas City Chiefs to earn the game's Most Valuable Player trophy.

Reuters

World.title: Quick hits: Renshaw floored by miracle grab as Bavuma's six stops traffic
World.content:
Matt Renshaw has been shocked by his own miracle grab, while Temba Bavuma's soaring six has stopped the Gqeberha traffic on a day when a soggy outfield threatened to ruin it all.

Here are the quick hits from day two of the second Test between Australia and South Africa.

1. A soggy outfield almost ruins it all

Things did not look good as the scheduled start of play approached on day two. Dark skies and pouring rain meant a delay was inevitable.

But within two hours, the rain had ceased, and another hour after that, the sun was beating down in Gqeberha.

The St George's ground staff had a lot on their plate on day two. (Getty Images: Richard Huggard/Gallo Images)

The St George's outfield, however, just wasn't playing ball. Three surface inspections came and went, with the umpires and ground staff determining the soggy turf too treacherous for play on each occasion.

The two areas of particular concern, both deep in the outfield, were simply refusing to drain.

It was Test cricket at its exasperating, excruciating worst, and the threat of an entirely lost day loomed on the horizon.

But five hours after the scheduled start of play, and more than three since the last downfall, the officials finally determined the field fit for purpose.

By the time the Australian bowlers were going through their warm-ups, it was a glorious day in the Eastern Cape.

2. Hazlewood the latest to succumb to sickness

But when the Australians finally got on the field for a 30-over evening session, they were without one of their most dangerous weapons.

Josh Hazlewood was battling sickness and nowhere to be seen at St George's Park, leaving just the — admittedly serviceable — trio of Pat Cummins, Mitch Starc and Scott Boland for the South African batters to contend with.

A day earlier umpire Chris Gaffaney was forced to withdraw from the Test with a bout of food poisoning, the saga no doubt leaving those in attendance wondering if there might be a dish to avoid at the St George's canteen.

Hazlewood is expected to return on day three.

3. Carey poised for 200

Scott Boland picked up from where he left off as play finally got underway. (Getty Images: Richard Huggard/Gallo Images)

It was typically outstanding stuff from Boland as day two belatedly began.

The Victorian had Temba Bavuma swinging and missing dramatically with the first ball of the afternoon. He only had to wait until his second set of the day to claim his third wicket of the match, luring Marques Ackerman into a drive and nicking off the debutant for six.

Meanwhile, behind the stumps, Alex Carey was nearing a major milestone.

And when Mitchell Starc had Matthew Breetzke edging through to the Australian wicketkeeper only moments later, Carey was one take away from becoming the fifth Australian gloveman to take 200 catches in Test cricket after Adam Gilchrist, Ian Healy, Rod Marsh and Brad Haddin.

Carey will hope to join that group on day three.

4. Bavuma interrupts traffic with massive six

It was an absolutely massive six, and it came from absolutely nowhere.

Bavuma had been so composed and diligent in steadying ship after the losses of Ackerman and Breetzke, and looked set to defend his way to stumps.

But the South Africa captain absolutely exploded in hooking Cummins over the backward square leg boundary.

Temba Bavuma's six interrupted the Gqeberha traffic. (Fox Cricket)

The ball sailed over the rope, out of the stadium and then rolled onto the road, where a security guard was forced to weave through the Gqeberha traffic to collect it.

5. Renshaw stunned by own miracle grab

With only a matter of minutes remaining in the day's play, Australia was pushing for the one final wicket that would put them well on top in the game.

Shadows were lengthening, light was fading quickly, and Marnus Labuschagne had just put down a relatively simple catch at leg slip.

Visibility clearly wasn't great but, somehow, Matt Renshaw produced something remarkable.

Renshaw took a remarkable catch late on day two. (Fox Cricket)

It was definitely Carey's catch, but the Australian wicketkeeper was rooted to the spot as Ryan Rickleton edged towards the men behind the wicket.

The ball looked destined to fly between the keeper and slip, but there he was, Renshaw, diving at full stretch and managing to get his right hand between ball and turf.

Matt Renshaw was blown away by his stunning catch. (Fox Cricket)

The Queenslander looked absolutely stunned to have taken the catch that had South Africa rocking at 5-97 at stumps.

Tech.title: Adobe Lightroom mobile can now open closed eyes in photos with a simple tap
Tech.content:
is a senior reporter who’s been covering and reviewing the latest gadgets and tech since 2006, but has loved all things electronic since he was a kid.

Adobe announced yesterday that the mobile version of Lightroom, available for iOS, iPadOS, and Android, can now open closed eyes in photos using generative AI with just a single tap. When the app detects a person, or a group of people, have their eyes closed in a photo it will automatically present users with a new Open Eyes Quick Action that appears as an icon over the image providing easy access to the new feature.

Being able to easily save an otherwise great photo by opening a subject’s eyes has been a feature in Adobe’s Photoshop Elements for nearly a decade, but as DPReview points out, Elements sources the replacement from another photo of the subject with mixed results depending on variations between the two images. Open Eyes in Lightroom mobile instead relies on generative AI so the replacement eyes match the lighting and pose, and the app will use other images of the same person in your Lightroom library as reference so the open eyes will accurately match the color, size, and shape of their own.

You can perform a similar fix in other Adobe apps like Photoshop using its own generative AI tools, but it’s not a one-tap fix, and it’s not free. Those using the free version of the Lightroom mobile app can try the Open Eyes feature twice before they’re given a prompt to subscribe to an Adobe Creative Cloud plan that includes more credits for its various AI-powered tools, according to DPReview.

Tech.title: Wii Sports is back on the Switch 2, and it rules
Tech.content:
Wii Sports holds an important place in Nintendo’s history. It’s the best-selling piece of software the company has ever made, one that permeated culture in surprising ways, and its success helped rejuvenate Nintendo after a period of steady decline. It also kicked off one of the company’s most important and unassuming franchises. While subsequent sports titles from Nintendo never sold quite as well as the original Wii Sports, they’ve become a fixture for each new console, much like a new Mario Kart or Pokémon. And now the Switch 2 has its own version, Nintendo Switch Sports Resort, and it’s the best so far.

You’d be forgiven for not realizing that Nintendo Switch Sports Resort is launching this week. The game is coming out during a particularly hectic time for new video game releases, and it’s sandwiched between two flashier Switch 2 titles in Fire Emblem: Fortune’s Weave and the upcoming remake of The Legend of Zelda: Ocarina of Time. Amid all of that, it’s easy to forget a game about thumb wrestling and bowling. But Sports Resort is also a refined and expansive version of the concept, and one that will likely become a constant over the Switch 2’s life.

The core of the game is the same as always: giving you a bunch of athletic activities — they’re not exactly all “sports” — that require some form of motion controls to play. That means swinging a Joy-Con controller to simulate using a tennis racket or tossing a bowling ball. There are 12 sports in all, and they vary quite a bit. The aforementioned returning favorites tennis and bowling are joined by things like skateboarding, thumb wrestling, and flying a plane.

Image: Nintendo

What makes the game work is its simplicity. Almost each activity is incredibly easy to pick up; I don’t know much about golf, but it only took me a minute or so to get down the fundamentals of swinging a club using a Joy-Con. This means that Sports Resort excels as an arcade-style experience, the kind of game you pull out when friends are over and you want to have some fun. Thumb wrestling is ideal for this. It’s so simple — you move your hand back and forth and use a single button to try and “pin” your opponent — yet gets extremely intense and fun in the competitive two-player mode. And unlike IRL thumb wrestling, no one can actually cheat.

There are some exceptions to the general simplicity. I still find basketball to be a little too complex, and I just can’t seem to figure out a successful strategy in table tennis. But there are enough games in Sports Resort that you’re almost certain to find a handful of favorites you’ll stick with, so having a few duds isn’t the end of the world. There’s also a decent amount of depth, both in terms of the skill ceiling for games — I have spent hours trying to perfect the spin on my bowling release — but also the various modes for each sport. Bowling, for instance, includes the returning option to play with 100 pins at once, which is chaotic as it sounds.

But the biggest addition to Sports Resort is that it now takes place in an open world. That may sound strange for a collection of arcade games, but it also allows it to introduce three new activities that are centered on exploring the beautiful island setting. There’s prop plane (where you hold the Joy-Con like a paper airplane to fly), power cruising (where you hold two Joy-Con horizontally, like the handlebars of a Jet Ski), and skateboarding (where you use the Joy-Con’s mouse controls to simulate controlling a tiny skateboard). There are competitive ways to play these games, like a skateboard race, but I’ve spent most of my time with a sightseeing mode where the goal is to find as many landmarks and secrets across the resort as you can within a five-minute time limit. It’s sort of like a more fleshed-out version of the free roam mode in Mario Kart World. The island is surprisingly detailed and interesting to explore, with lots of caves and hidden paths, and the three modes of transportation let you check it out via land, water, and air.

Image: Nintendo

These exploration-focused modes add a nice new dimension to the experience, fitting snugly within the more traditional sports while offering a very different vibe. I’ve become particularly drawn to skateboarding — there’s something very satisfying about pulling back on the Joy-Con to simulate pushing a board — especially since you can collect items that let you purchase new clothes and other accessories to customize your character.

One of the biggest keys to Nintendo’s success during the Switch era has been consistency. Even in the midst of a tumultuous period for the broader games industry, the company has managed to put out a steady stream of games, many of which have had a surprisingly long life. Nintendo’s biggest hits aren’t always what you expect. The first Nintendo Switch Sports has sold more than 18 million copies, topping beloved games like Super Mario Bros. Wonder and Splatoon 3.

A little over a year into its existence, that style of perennial seller is exactly what the Switch 2 needs, the kind of game that people pick up alongside Mario Kart when they buy a new console. Wii Sports showed just how transformative a game like that can be, and Nintendo Switch Sports Resort is quietly keeping that spirit alive.

Nintendo Switch Sports Resort launches on the Switch 2 on October 22nd.

Tech.title: Final Fantasy dips back into the SNES golden era with Resonance
Tech.content:
Final Fantasy is a lot different than it used to be. While many of the early Final Fantasy titles look and play similarly to each other, the series has since grown to encompass blockbuster games like Final Fantasy XVI and the gargantuan Final Fantasy VII Remake trilogy, which don’t play much like the classics. But there’s still an audience for retro RPGs and old-school Final Fantasy games, especially thanks to the HD-2D style that mixes gorgeous pixel art with detailed 3D graphics to great effect. Square Enix has made a bunch of HD-2D games already, like the remakes of early Dragon Quest titles, but this week, it’s launching the first HD-2D Final Fantasy game: Final Fantasy Resonance.

Resonance, thanks to the HD-2D art, kind of looks like what the classic Final Fantasy games feel like in my memory, but I was surprised at how old-school Resonance feels to actually play, too — which, for the most part, is a good thing. In Resonance, I’ve spent a lot of time wandering around a big world map to get from place to place, tackling random battles along the way and investigating little sparkles to pick up items. The towns have a familiar feel, with the classic inn, item shop, and weapons shop setup. Similarly, battles are traditional turn-based fights, so I’ve found myself spending a lot of time in various battle menus to plan out my attacks. Enemies even flash right before they attack, just like in older RPGs.

Image: Square Enix

At times, Resonance can almost feel rudimentary; I’ve recently been working my way through Final Fantasy VII Remake again ahead of Revelation, and Remake’s action-heavy fights feel much more contemporary. But there’s something soothing about Resonance’s familiar patterns. I really like just grinding through some random baddies to level up.

The story is pretty standard fare, at least during the 10 hours I’ve played. You play as Rain, a plucky blonde hero who is morally pure and fights for those less fortunate than him. After a great magical crystal is destroyed, you and your best bud Lasswell head out on an adventure to stop the destruction of other crystals. So far, Resonance’s story hasn’t done a lot to innovate on a familiar formula — I’ve already come across two people who have amnesia, a JRPG staple — but it all moves along breezily enough that it’s not a huge deal.

Resonance isn’t all old-school, though, as there are a lot of modern touches. In fights, enemies have health bars and stagger bars, forcing you to be strategic instead of just mashing basic attacks; it’s usually smarter to whittle down a stagger bar by exploiting weaknesses through magic and skills. You can speed up fights and even skip long attack animations (of which there are many). On the world map, you can fast travel to any location you’ve already visited, which is especially useful during the multipart side quests. In dungeons, you can teleport from a save near a boss fight back to the entrance if you need to resupply before a big battle.

Image: Square Enix

Resonance also lets you bring in characters from other Final Fantasy games to aid you in battle. (It’s a holdover from Resonance’s roots as a mobile title; the game is an “adaptation” of the first story arc of Final Fantasy Brave Exvius, which was shut down in 2024.) As you move through Resonance, you’ll recruit “Visions” of characters like Final Fantasy VI’s Terra Branford or Final Fantasy VII’s Cloud Strife, and each of the game’s characters can “equip” one Vision to give them new moves in battle. Over time, while using a Vision with a Resonance character, you unlock more moves and abilities that you can use even when you don’t have that Vision equipped. It’s a clever system that offers a lot of possibilities for interesting builds, making the hunt for more Visions feel like more than just a way to get a hit of nostalgia.

But I’m already getting sucked into Resonance like I used to with classic Final Fantasy titles. At one point, as I was nodding my head to heart-pumping music during an intense boss fight on a moving train, I realized I was completely absorbed by the game in a way that only a Final Fantasy can pull off. The game’s old-school structure with modern improvements lets Square Enix have it both ways, as the old-school approach sits comfortably alongside a big-budget game like Final Fantasy XVI. The series has come a long way since the games that Resonance uses as inspiration, but it pulls in enough from newer titles that playing it feels like enjoying the best of both worlds.

Final Fantasy Resonance launches on October 22nd on Nintendo Switch, Nintendo Switch 2, PC, PS5, and Xbox Series X / S.

Tech.title: Antigravity just halved the price of its drone — by swapping its headset for wristwatch control
Tech.content:
is a senior editor and founding member of The Verge who covers gadgets, games, and toys. He spent 15 years editing the likes of CNET, Gizmodo, and Engadget.

Posts from this author will be added to your daily email digest and your homepage feed.

DJI ban: how the world’s biggest dronemaker is getting shoved out of the US

Last year’s Antigravity A1 is the best beginner drone I’ve ever tried. I put a friend who’d never flown into its virtual cockpit and didn’t worry one bit. The A1’s also nice for people who’d prefer to think about flying rather than filming, because you can reframe its 360-degree footage after.

But until today, that meant wearing the company’s FPV goggles and spending upwards of $1,599 on the complete set. Now, Antigravity is halving the price of entry to $799 in the US with a new “Follow Me” kit that replaces the original headset and motion controller with a wristwatch and ring instead.

The idea is that Antigravity can be your robot cameraman, automatically flying, following, and filming you with a minimum of gear.

I took the new kit for several test drives this fall, and I’m cautiously impressed.

Instead of powering on a headset and finding a safe place to sit while you block out the world, you can now pull a drone and a watch out of your bag, power them both on, hold a button to launch the drone from your hand, then walk or ride while the Antigravity A1 automatically films and follows you, dodging obstacles along the way.

You can even wave your arm like a magic wand to nudge the drone left, right, down, up, towards, or away while it’s filming. You get a swipeable preview of what the drone sees on the watch’s touchscreen, and can select various quickshots there or summon a couple of sliders (forward/backward, ascend/descend) to manually fly the A1 out of a jam. The ring doesn’t do anything you can’t already do with the watch; it’s just an extra button so you can launch and reposition it one-handed.

The ring is just a button, and technically the watch is a modular screen you could attach to other mounts too — there’s a quick release button to detach it from the watchband frame. Photo by Sean Hollister / The Verge

As I discovered after three crashes, the A1 is not yet intelligent enough to dodge everything or stay with me through thick and thin. I took it all around my neighborhood on a kick scooter, and you might want to be careful around power lines, thin branches, or the vertical guy wires holding utility poles in place.

There’s also a lot of rough edges I hope Antigravity will fix, like the sluggish experience swiping around the touchscreen, or how it won’t land on my hand without switching back to manual mode, or how I can’t get it to automatically start tracking and filming me — I always have to find myself on the watch screen, tap on myself, then tap another button to begin. I also ran into an issue where it wouldn’t follow me once I crested a high hill, because it thought it was flying at too high an altitude.

Most of all, I hope Antigravity will figure out how to keep the drone from drifting out into the street or over a neighbor’s fence when I tell it to follow right behind. It’s far smaller than me, so anywhere I go, I feel like it should fit!

But as you’ll hopefully see in a video I publish later today, it’s not bad at following me through a dense suburban environment! None of my crashes so far have crippled the drone, and I like how the watch automatically plays the last seconds of footage before a crash. It made it very easy to find the drone after.

Antigravity’s price chart is so comprehensive, I decided to share it in its entirety. Image: Antigravity

Antigravity’s new full-coverage propeller guards can also help in case of impact; I saw the drone bounce right off one obstacle and keep flying. They’re included in the $799 set, though existing Antigravity A1 owners can buy the accessories too: it’s $340 for the watch and ring, and $40 for the guards, with a 20 percent discount for those who can prove they already own the aircraft.

Antigravity’s A1 is kind of like the folding Skydio I wish that company had made before it left consumers behind to serve industry instead. The self-flying Skydio 2 similarly had a few crashes in my tests and wouldn’t always stay in its lane. But I’ve long wanted a folding version I could easily stick in a bag, and the Antigravity A1 seems like the next best thing.

You can remove the propeller guards fairly easily; there’s room in the kit’s bag for all four of them plus the folded drone, whose cameras are now protected by a new quick-release cover. Photo by Sean Hollister / The Verge

Tech.title: Spotify’s new podcast memberships let you pay for extra perks
Tech.content:
Posts from this author will be added to your daily email digest and your homepage feed.

Spotify is enabling podcast creators to earn more money through the platform by providing their fans with a way to pay to access exclusive content. First announced in May, the new Memberships subscription feature is starting to roll out in 34 regions today, allowing podcasters to offer perks including additional content, early access, bonus episodes, and reduced ads behind a paywall.

Users can find Memberships on a podcast’s Spotify page, with the ability to subscribe, pay, and access the exclusive benefits “in just a few taps,” according to Spotify. Podcast creators can set their pricing options and bundle benefits across multiple subscription tiers, and keep 90 percent of membership revenue. Spotify is providing podcasters with tools to analyze and build their Memberships audience, including targeted promotions and free trial offers, alongside community engagement features like member badges, welcome clips, and more.

That makes this more like a Patreon-style membership system in which fans can choose to give additional support to their favorite creators, and is distinct from the podcast subscription feature that Spotify introduced in 2021. Podcasters can utilize Memberships alongside other Spotify revenue streams, including ads and the Spotify Partner Program.

To qualify for Memberships, shows must be hosted on Spotify for Creators or Megaphone, and have at least 100 consumption hours, 100 listeners or viewers, and three published episodes. Spotify is also making it easy for podcasters who manage their subscriptions on other services to try Memberships, allowing them to bring their paywalled content to Spotify via its Open Access feature.

Tech.title: Some Google Home Speakers caught downloading hundreds of gigs of data
Tech.content:
Some Google Home Speaker owners are currently experiencing an issue in which hundreds of gigabytes of data are being continuously downloaded to their device in the background. The bug, reported by 9to5Google and several Reddit users over the last week, may be caused by the speakers failing to correctly download and install a firmware update, with one Redditor finding that his device was consuming more than 200GB per day.

Thankfully, Google is aware of the issue. In a statement to 9to5Google, the company said that “a fix is already rolling out that should address this for users.” Most of the reports are tied specifically to the new Google Home Speaker model, but it isn’t clear how widespread the issue is. We’ve reached out to Google to request more information about the cause and confirm impacted devices.

My colleague Tom Warren confirmed that his own speaker is unaffected, and 9to5Google reports another Home Speaker in a different household downloaded just 2GB in the past month, compared to to 132GB used by an impacted device over the same period. A big concern for anyone with a limited data plan here is that the bug could quickly eat through the allotted limit, and they wouldn’t know unless they regularly check to see how much data their devices are using.

Tech.title: Baseus’ new security camera has a spotlight that tracks and follows moving targets
Tech.content:
is a senior reporter who’s been covering and reviewing the latest gadgets and tech since 2006, but has loved all things electronic since he was a kid.

Baseus announced a new addition to its lineup of AI-assisted security cameras that’s more proactive about discouraging unwanted visitors instead of just recording and alerting you to their presence. The Baseus Security PrimeSentinel U2 Pro Outdoor 3K Dual Camera introduces a motorized spotlight that shines directly on a moving target, even as they’re running across your property, so they know they’ve been detected. The targeted light also improves the quality of video captured in the dark to increase the chances of a subject being identified, and it can assist your family with after-hours activities like taking the dog out.

The Baseus U2 Pro is now available through Amazon in the US for $269.99, while European availability starts on October 15th at €269.99. Alongside the spotlight feature, the U2 Pro pairs a 3K fixed camera designed to constantly monitor a specific area of your property with a second 3K camera that can zoom, tilt, and pan 360 degrees to monitor everywhere else. Full-color night vision capabilities make it easier to identify people, animals, or even the color of a suspicious vehicle.

An included solar panel can be mounted atop the camera or installed a short distance away to ensure it gets adequate sun exposure. Image: Baseus

Using “AI-powered analysis,” the U2 Pro will provide alerts when motion is detected with summaries and descriptions of what was seen that differentiate between people, pets, vehicles, and activities like delivered packages. It’s also smart enough to ignore movements that aren’t relevant, such as tree branches blowing in the wind, or activities that regularly occur so as not to overwhelm you with notifications. Footage is captured only when motion is detected and is stored locally on a 512GB encrypted memory card. It can be accessed remotely through Baseus’ mobile app, while live views from the cameras can also be monitored on Amazon Alexa or Google Home smart devices.

Baseus claims the U2 Pro can be installed in about two minutes using mounts that connect to walls or ceilings. The camera connects wirelessly to your home network and features a rechargeable battery good for up to 150 days of use, although that will potentially be reduced depending on how much activity there is on your property. An included 3W solar panel can be mounted atop the cameras or a short distance away to ensure it can see the sun. Just 40 minutes of sun exposure generates enough power for a full day’s use.

Tech.title: Elon Musk’s proposed SpaceX stock giveaway would go into ‘Trump Accounts’

Tech.title: US orders federal agencies to remove China’s DeepSeek AI from their systems
Tech.content:
The U.S. has ordered federal civilian agencies to stop purchasing services and products developed by Chinese AI startup DeepSeek and remove them from government IT systems over national security concerns tied to the Chinese AI startup’s operations in China, according to the Department of Homeland Security. The order goes beyond banning DeepSeek’s own product, but also covers third-party products and services built using DeepSeek technology, though agencies can request exceptions.

The DHS raised concerns about DeepSeek’s handling of user data, warning that sensitive information from US government users could potentially be accessible to Chinese authorities under Chinese law, the order said.

The move comes amid intensifying tech competition in AI between the US and China. The Chinese AI model challenges its U.S. rivals, including OpenAI and Meta, with low-cost open-weight models.

China pushed back against the U.S.’s move. Foreign Ministry spokesperson Mao Ning said Tuesday that Beijing opposes “overstretching the concept of national security and politicizing technology and trade issues,” according to an official briefing. “We will resolutely safeguard the legitimate rights and interests of Chinese enterprises,” the spokesperson added.

The U.S. has already taken steps to limit DeepSeek’s use in government. A law passed in December 2025 targeted its use in intelligence’s national security systems. The latest order extends the restrictions to federal civilian agencies, covering both new purchases and existing IT systems.

Meanwhile, China is reportedly considering export restrictions on 23 AI-related technologies, including chip designs and certain advanced AI models, to address security and misuse risks, Bloomberg reported last week.

The Chinese AI lab has faced scrutiny from governments and regulators across the globe since its R1 reasoning model shook the AI industry in January 2025, triggering a sharp sell-off in Nvidia shares.

The U.S. accused DeepSeek and five other Chinese AI companies, including Alibaba and Moonshot AI, of using large-scale model distillation to extract information from American AI systems, according to a September report.

In addition, OpenAI and Anthropic have separately raised concerns about DeepSeek’s alleged use of model distillation, a technique that uses outputs from one AI model to train another. Earlier this year, OpenAI told U.S. lawmakers it had observed suspected attempts by DeepSeek to distill its models, while Anthropic said it had identified unauthorized attempts by DeepSeek and other Chinese AI labs to collect outputs from Claude.

Tech.title: Eka is worth $1.45B thanks to a physical AI model that has experts raving
Tech.content:
Robots still aren’t that good at picking things up, despite billions of dollars of investment and endless videos fed into deep learning models.

That may be about to change, thanks to a manipulation architecture built by Eka Robotics, which encompasses a force-sensitive gripper and a new kind of deep-learning model. Founded by MIT professor Pulkit Agrawal and former Google DeepMind researcher Tuomas Haarnoja, the startup just closed an $150 million Series A round that values it at $1.45 billion post-money, led by venture funds a16z and F-Prime.

“They are already exceeding superhuman performance for certain tasks, and so we think over the next few months there will be superhuman performance in many dexterous manipulation tasks,” Raghu Raguram, the a16z general partner who co-led the fundraising round, told TechCrunch.

In an era of never-ending robotic demonstrations, Eka’s capabilities are shocking veteran robot builders.

Kris Hauser, a professor at the University of Illinois Urbana-Champaign, said it had a “wow factor” compared to other robot demos he saw recently. The Eka robot “was able to adapt to a large number of different objects without retraining,” Hauser said, adding that it also had an aspect of “humanness, creepy humanness that it would try over and over again if it failed the first time.”

Another roboticist, who asked for anonymity because of their work at a frontier lab, told TechCrunch that seeing Eka’s robot in action was an emotional experience, comparable to when robots first achieved reliable legged locomotion five to ten years ago. Take a look for yourself:

Loading the player…

What’s notable here? How smoothly and rapidly the robot moves. It can pick up about 1,500 objects that weigh up to 1 kg in an hour, compared to about 600 for a human; Eka says it reliably picks up objects more than 95% of the time. And the robot arm is strong enough to hurt itself as it moves that quickly. That indicates, per the frontier lab observer, that “they have a lot of trust in their algorithm not breaking the robot. I wonder how many robots they broke along the way?”

When the frontier lab roboticist met Eka’s robot, they handed it a raspberry, the lab’s apparent favorite test item. “The experience of a big, heavy robot rushing towards my arm and then slowing down just in time and very gently touching me is a feeling that I am, as we speak, carrying this feeling in my body,” they told TechCrunch.

How not to squish the raspberry

These capabilities are a consequence of how the foundational model was built. Rather than a vision-language-action model — which is trained to understand the relationship between language, visual inputs, and actions — the schema here is a vision-force-action model, which focuses on the relationship between language, force inputs, and actions. Critics of the current direction of generative AI robotics models, like Rodney Brooks, say that they will fail without an attempt to represent force and touch; Eka’s results suggest such critics have a point.

“Vision is not the primary way in which you close this last millimeter problem,” Eka co-founder Agrawal told TechCrunch. “Vision tells you roughly where the object is, what the pose is, but the actual grabbing, the actual searching is happening through forces.”

Eka had to design a unique robotic hand that was more flexible than traditional grippers, and included more force sensors; it reacts to contact, which is why it doesn’t crush the raspberry. The founders are cagey about how they achieved that for obvious competitive reasons, but it comes down to using a physics simulator to model the multiple forces the robot will encounter as it attempts to grasp something, and using that to create a reinforcement learning environment that can be run at scale. They say they can generate thousands of hours of robot experience in minutes.

“Rather than being limited to the data that you’re collecting from, say, human demonstrations, Eka is pushing through reinforcement learning this approach where the robot can surpass any kind of demonstrations that are given to it,” Hauser said. “What’s really exciting is that they’re able to not be limited to the data that is presented to them for training.”

Agrawal and Haarnoja, who first met in graduate school at the University of California, Berkeley, are leading researchers in the field of reinforcement learning for robotics control. Eka’s key bet was that this technique could be done at scale through simulation, rather than relying on videos collected by gigworkers or robot operators performing tasks over many hours. Simulation was key to achieving their robot’s reliable manipulation, a feat that in the past that has proven more difficult for tasks that require interacting with objects, rather than avoiding them.

“What EKA is bridging is the generality-performance gap, which plagues a lot of modern robotics,” Agrawal argues.

Making a general-purpose robot useful

Right now, the most generalizable physical AI models—the ones that can attempt lots of different tasks—aren’t particularly good at them. But AI models trained to be highly capable at a single task may not close the business case for a company: The promise of generative AI is that robots can quickly learn multiple tasks, even novel ones.

The current approaches are good at producing robots that are more generally intelligent than before — Astra, ChatGPT’s latest LLM, can operate a robot in an unfamiliar setting and perform tasks with it, but slowly and at a high cost. The promise of a model like Eka’s is that it handles the physicality while a more general model makes decisions about how to solve a problem. Astra, for example, might know that plates get stacked in a cupboard when they come out of the dishwasher, but Eka’s model is capable of picking up a dish without breaking it.

“Most of the field has been focusing on the planning,” Eka co-founder Haarnoja says, “so they approach from the top: high-level intelligence, pushing that down towards the physical. Whereas we think about it from the bottom up.”

Eka still needs to prove itself in the field, though. The company is working in secretive pilots with a number of industrial customers doing pick-and-place and wire manipulation, but the leap from lab to line is almost as big as the gap between sim and real.

“What’s going to be a big challenge is when they work with integrators on real assembly lines, and it needs to run without breaking for an entire year,” Hauser said. The other open question is “‘how generalizable these techniques can be to different tasks?’ What I’ve seen is pick and place, but many industry tasks that are value added involve more than just pick-and-place.”

Agrawal is also focused on deployability; right now, he says Eka’s gripper hardware — which costs less than $1,000 — is rated for 5 million duty cycles, but the ultimate goal is to hit the 20 million cycle bar set by standard industrial arms.

“What we are building is that engineering of how to design entire workflows, but we are starting off being very pragmatic, and saying here are two verticals in pick, arrange, place, and wire handling, let’s make them be home runs,” Agrawal said. “Once we have made home runs on them, the sky is the limit in how much we can do with the approach we are developing.”

Tech.title: Inspired Capital closes $450M fourth fund as New York pushes back on Silicon Valley’s gravitational pull
Tech.content:
Inspired Capital, the early-stage firm founded in 2019 by Alexa von Tobel and Penny Pritzker, has closed its fourth fund with $450 million in commitments. The new capital will bring the firm’s assets under management to nearly $1.4 billion, von Tobel tells TechCrunch.

The raise comes as venture dollars are piling up on the West Coast. Between 2020 and the end of 2025, the Bay Area had raised $352 billion for VC funds — roughly 46% of all U.S. venture capital, according to PitchBook. Last year, that percentage shot up even higher, with Bay Area firms locking down 55% of the total new commitments to U.S. venture funds.

New York-based Inspired’s new fund is a reminder that capital is accruing elsewhere, too. In fact, Inspired is growing: it closed a $330 million third fund in early 2024, following a $281 million second fund and its $200 million debut fund.

Despite having money to invest, von Tobel says the firm is sticking to its formula. Inspired backs roughly 10 companies a year, which can be anywhere between “napkin” stage and Series A, writing checks between $1 million and $15 million. Pritzker, the former U.S. Commerce Secretary, remains an active co-founder in the firm.

With six years of investing experience under her belt, von Tobel is now willing to talk about results, too. She says that 12 companies across the firm’s first two funds have become unicorns, representing about 15% of the portfolio. “Ten of them have passed $100 million in revenue, four have crossed $400 million and one has crossed $500 million,” she says.

Perhaps more relevant to the firm’s limited partners, Inspired counts more than 10 exits, including MosaicML (acquired for $1.3 billion in June by Databricks), DeepTune (which Mercor acquired in July for an undisclosed amount), and Saturn (snapped up last year by Snap).

Another portfolio company, TeamShares, a fintech startup that buys up other businesses, went public in June through a special purpose acquisition vehicle. Von Tobel claimed the firm’s second fund ranks in the top 5% of its cohort by all metrics, though she declined to share cash-on-cash returns, citing the relative newness of the firm.

To be clear, Inspired is not squarely focused on New York. Its portfolio is split roughly 45% East Coast, 45% West Coast and 10% elsewhere. That balance reflects the way that startups grow, she says. “A company that’s getting quite big in Silicon Valley often wants and needs a second talent footprint, and New York becomes really important,” she says.

Of course, for others, New York is the only choice. On that front, von Tobel says she has been pitched by at least 10 founders in recent weeks who selected New York specifically to avoid hiring job-hopping employees who have little allegiance to any one company, as is often the case in San Francisco.

Von Tobel definitely doesn’t dismiss the Valley. She says that someone from her team is on the ground in the Bay Area every week, and that she’s in the area routinely, too. “We have to pay extreme attention to both [coasts],” she says.

As for strategy, she describes a firm that picks themes early and avoids the herd as much as possible. While many companies chase AI applications, for example, Inspired has backed physical AI and quantum computing startups, she says. Inspired came upon the creator-commerce platform ShopMy by following that thesis.

Where Inspired isn’t so different is in its penchant for backing serial entrepreneurs. Von Tobel says roughly a third of the firm’s portfolio is by repeat founders.

Asked about her stance on secondaries, she says Inspired will sell “a few chips” once companies reach multi-billion-dollar valuations, but it tends to keep more than 90% of its ownership, mostly using secondaries to add to positions in breakaway portfolio companies. That said, Inspired will lead later primary rounds if it misses an early one, and it has written checks for companies that are already valued above $100 million, according to von Tobel.

Von Tobel, who launched her online financial learning platform LearnVest on the TechCrunch 50 stage in 2009 and sold the company six years later to Northwestern Mutual for a reported $375 million, insists that Inspired’s strongest edge is patience and its ability to combine the best of both coasts.

“We bring West Coast ambition with East Coast financial discipline,” she says.

Tech.title: Spotify launches paid podcast memberships with perks beyond bonus content
Tech.content:
Spotify on Tuesday launched paid memberships, a new way for podcasters to make money from their biggest fans beyond paywalled bonus episodes. Creators can decide which perks to offer listeners, which could be bonus audio or video, fewer ads, early access to shows, or some combination of these.

The streaming service first previewed the idea at its Investor Day in May, where it also introduced AI capabilities that let listeners ask questions about what they’re listening to or watching and debuted new tools for managing creator sponsorships.

Image Credits:Spotify

As the company explained at the time, memberships would help to “create a natural path to go deeper, unlocking new and exclusive experiences for fans and new revenue opportunities for creators.”

The feature is now rolling out to 34 markets globally, including the U.S.

The launch is the latest example of Spotify’s effort to make its platform more attractive to podcast creators, particularly as it moves further into the video space to compete with YouTube. Though podcasters have long been able to monetize through ads, the new memberships could entice more fans to support creators by offering more than just an occasional bonus episode.

Creators keep 90% of the membership revenue and can package their benefits across multiple tiers and pricing options to appeal to fans at different levels of commitment. To qualify, podcasters must host their shows on Spotify for Creators or Megaphone, have at least 100 consumption hours, 100 listeners or viewers, and at least three published episodes.

Image Credits:Spotify

Fans will see memberships promoted on the show’s Spotify page, where they can subscribe, pay, and immediately access the exclusive content. (The company tells us that memberships will be purchased on the web, not through in-app purchases).

A handful of shows will offer memberships at launch, including “The Adam Friedland Show,” “Making Sense with Sam Harris,” “Shawn Ryan Show,” “The Sculpt Society,” “Two Hot Takes,” as well as YMH Studios, which is bringing memberships to 12 shows across its network.

Memberships join other Spotify monetization tools, including advertising and the Spotify Partner Program, as well as features that help creators grow their audience, like promotions, free trials, and analytics. Soon, Spotify says creators will be able to offer fans membership badges and welcome clips, too.

Tech.title: Oura adds new fitness metrics to show how workouts impact your body
Tech.content:
As competition in the smart ring market escalates, Oura is introducing two new features to give people more insight into their workouts and how they impact their bodies. The company announced on Tuesday it’s rolling out Cardio Effort and VO₂ max metrics to expand workout tracking beyond exercise duration and heart rate zones.

While Oura has largely dominated the smart ring market for years, rivals like RingConn and Ultrahuman are emerging to dethrone it, putting pressure on the company to keep innovating. By launching more advanced workout metrics, Oura is looking to differentiate itself from competitors.

With Cardio Effort, users will be able to see how much a workout taxes their cardiovascular system. This measurement is aggregated over the week relative to each user’s individual baseline to provide more insights. Oura explained that this metric shifts users’ focus from “How many minutes did I move?” to “Am I maintaining my fitness, building it, or overdoing it?”

Since Cardio Effort accounts for both intensity and duration, a shorter, more intense workout can yield a similar score to a longer, less intense one, the company says.

Image Credits:Oura /

Oura notes that the metric has two components: Workout Cardio Effort and Weekly Cardio Effort. The first metric evaluates the impact of an individual workout, while the latter aggregates effort into a weekly total, categorized as “Light,” “Fair,” “Maintaining,” “Building,” or “Reaching.”

Oura measures elevated heart rate relative to each member’s long-term resting heart rate, avoiding the variability associated with maximum-heart-rate estimates. Weekly effort levels are then determined using personalized ranges based on recent activity patterns.

Cardio Effort is rolling out to Oura Ring Gen3 and later models.

As for VO₂ max, the metric shows how workouts contribute to long-term fitness. It measures how effectively the heart, lungs, and muscles work together to deliver and use oxygen during exercise. Previously, measuring VO₂ max typically required a lab test or a six-minute walking test. Oura can now estimate it passively using GPS-enabled workouts.

Image Credits:Oura /

After completing five qualifying activities, users receive an initial VO2 Max estimate. Within the My Health Heart Hub, they can view their current VO2 Max estimate in ml/kg/min, their fitness category (Low, Fair, High, or Peak), how their estimate has changed over time, and when it was last updated. Users also receive insights highlighting meaningful changes in their VO2 Max or indicating when their estimate remains consistent.

VO₂ Max is launching in Oura Labs, the company’s hub for experimental features, for members with Gen3 and newer Oura Ring devices.

Oura says these two new features are designed to work together to show users how hard they’re working and how that effort is adding up over time.

Tech.title: Yelp can now call on your behalf to check wait times at a restaurant
Tech.content:
Over the last few weeks, personal assistants like Instinct, Fo, and Muse have enabled users to call businesses for customer support and appointment booking. Following this trend, Yelp is adding the ability for its app users to get a voice agent to call a restaurant to check wait times.

The new feature, Check for Me, will show up on restaurant pages in the app, where users can enter their party size and phone number. The AI agent then calls on behalf of the user to check wait times and texts them the results to decide if they want to go to that particular restaurant.

Last year, Yelp debuted its voice solution for restaurants and service providers. With this new feature, the discovery platform is fulfilling the consumer side of the equation, though there is a possibility that a user’s agent will talk to the restaurant’s agent, and agent-to-agent communication might break down the conversation.

Image Credits: Yelp Image Credits:Yelp

The company is also updating its Yelp AI assistant that helps users discover restaurants and services. With the new OpenTable integration, users can easily book a restaurant without leaving the app.

Yelp is adding better personalization to its assistant by having it remember preferences that you might have mentioned in previous chats. Plus, you can access your chat history from the past 30 days in the app, with full history available soon.

Users can ask the chatbot to set custom reminders, such as sending suggestions for weekend activities every Friday. The company is also letting users build their own lists, starting with two “Been Here” and “Want to

Go” lists. You can filter your lists by location, category, and cuisine, reorder, add notes to items, and share them with others.

Next month, the company will start showing weekly personalized recommendations based on your saved items and rankings. Yelp is also working on converting collections to lists and giving the lists tab a new look, rolling out later in the year, along with a maps view.

Image Credits: Yelp Image Credits:Yelp
